Russo-Ukrainian war, day 1679: Russia raises its war budget by 27% to a record as it looks to grow its war in 2027
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
21:51:11 UTC
06:51:11 KST

Exclusives
Military
Russia drained the Kakhovka Reservoir. Now it hides in the dry bed to creep toward Zaporizhzhia. A frontline commander expects small Russian groups to slip into the city by winter. A leading analyst calls that far too categorical—and says the front is moving the other way.
Vivaldi counteroffensive advanced after Ukraine took Russia’s drones out of the fight, ISW assesses. Armored vehicles reached heavy Russian fortifications in the Lyman sector without coming under drone attack, which the analysts read as a sign of Ukrainian drone overmatch.
Russia’s mass drone attacks on Ukraine have a goal—likely Ukraine’s capitulation by spring 2027, ISW says. Until his new theory of victory has played out, Putin is unlikely to soften his demands or enter serious ceasefire talks, according to ISW.
Russia’s pipeline into Kupiansk is now its escape route—with kidnapped civilians as human shields, Ukraine says. Ukrainian drones filmed the column on 27 September. Khartia warned Russia could pass the footage off as an "evacuation" or "rescue" of civilians.
Ukraine makes local gains on Pokrovsk front despite sustained Russian attacks. The marines cleared 5 square kilometers and captured two Russian soldiers.
A Ukrainian Hornet drone hit a Russian radar 120 km behind the front. It was likely a $100 million Nebo-M. The strike is part of a push to cut Russian logistics and strip Russian forces of radar and electronic warfare systems, a brigade officer says.
Ukraine hits railways of Bryansk, Russia’s launchpad for strikes on Kyiv: downed bridge and 28 derailed cars, region’s governor says. Ukraine's drones reportedly hit the region's railways.
Intelligence and technology
Mavic vs Slavic: Ukrainian developers adapt reconnaissance drones to the modern battlefield. “The drone was developed as a Ukrainian alternative to Chinese commercial quadcopters,” Vyriy Industries said.
A Ukrainian firm now rents out drone jammers by the day—but the deposit is the device’s full price. The daily fee comes off a deposit worth the whole device—rent long enough and the jammer becomes yours.
Ukraine just caught a Geran-5 at 425 km/h—the jet drone that has often outrun Ukrainian interceptor drones since January. Ukrainian crews now stop just over half of Russia's jet-powered drones, against more than 90% of the older Shaheds, even as Moscow builds them by the thousand.
Russia is stepping up fake Ukrainian government pages as bait for recruiting agents, Ukraine’s security service says. Russian intelligence uses the counterfeits to spread disinformation and to harvest data on the Ukrainians who subscribe.
Russia is launching a faster Geran-5 at Ukraine that satellite jamming may no longer knock off course, a monitoring channel says. The drone can steer by images of the terrain below, and its extra speed makes it harder for interceptors to catch, though Ukrainian officials have not confirmed the system.
International
Russia ordered arson attack on Estonian military robot-maker supplying Ukraine, Estonia confirms. Estonia says its intelligence service established that Russia’s special services ordered the August fire at Milrem Robotics, as Russian sabotage operations spreads across Europe.
Belgium rushes three F-16s to Ukraine as Russia expands its drone and missile assault. Zelenskyy says the aircraft will arrive by the end of 2026, strengthening Ukraine’s ability to intercept Russian air targets and conduct combat missions.
Russian jet-powered drone hits near Yahodyn, just 1.5 km from Poland, as Warsaw changes air defense rules. Poland plans to allow decisions to engage aerial targets based on radar data.
Lithuania gets its US tank battalion back while the Pentagon weighs pulling up to 40,000 troops from Europe. The Lithuanian leader calls the decision an encouragement and says fewer American soldiers will remain on the continent overall.
Humanitarian and social impact
Russian troops enter homes and threaten starving Oleshky residents for food and alcohol, officials say. Residents who escaped the occupied Kherson Oblast city describe threats and abuse by Russian troops amid severe shortages of food, water, and medicine.
Russian mercenaries blew off African prisoners’ legs to practice battlefield medicine, Wagner fighter says. A Russian mercenary captured by Ukraine describes alleged Wagner training sessions where prisoners were deliberately maimed and killed so recruits could practice battlefield medicine and killing techniques.
Russia hits a Kharkiv high-rise overnight, injuring 43 people, then kills four in daylight strikes on central Kyiv and Dnipro. A pre-dawn strike on Ukraine's second city gave way to drone attacks on a business center and then a national science institution during working hours.
Political and legal developments
Russia raises its war budget by 27% and expands the army again – both to new records – even as its budget deficit widens and oil revenues fall. Moscow plans to spend a record 17.1 trillion rubles on defense in 2027 as it raises taxes and borrowing to cover a widening deficit.
The Kremlin calls mobilization talk “nonsense”—Zelenskyy says it has already begun, with North Korean reinforcements. The claim comes from Ukraine's military intelligence, which has tracked Russian preparations for a larger call-up for months.
War is costing Ukraine $155 billion per year. With Western aid running late, Kyiv is freezing everything but army, pensions, and public wages. Kyiv froze parks, fountains, and road repairs to pay its army and pensioners first.
After Russia hits Kyiv’s Academy of Sciences with jet-powered drone, the Kremlin says Ukraine must “pay a price”. Peskov calls Russia's intensified strikes part of that price.

‘as a spectator, you also have a responsibility’ fabio cherstich on the boundaries of art and theater
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
21:47:42 UTC
06:47:42 KST

‘as a spectator, you also have a responsibility’ fabio cherstich on the boundaries of art and theater
the italian director's unique approach to performance has taken him to new york archives, miu miu performances in shanghai, and even the countryside home of the late painter, lucia di luciano.
Cherstich, a theater director among other things
Fabio Cherstich is a theater director. Not the theaters of days of yore, but the type of theater where a face may flash onto a screen that backgrounds the stage, glowering down on its audience. The kinds of productions that slink into the piazzas of Rome, carrying actors, pomp, and circumstance by means of long-haul semi-trucks. Or a spectacle that forms around vintage cars racing from Venice, Italy, through the Dolomites, for Louis Vuitton’s Classic Run. Chatting with designboom in his home-studio in Milan, Cherstich speaks about art on and off the stage, his collection of Alessi moka pots, and how difficult it has been for him to condense all this into a website.
on the woes of making a website
As the list of his projects, which seem to leap and saunter between the worlds of painting, film, and the performing arts, grows, the container that is ‘theater director’ starts to bulge at the seams. Perhaps it’s best remarked on by the man himself on his website, a work in progress, blank page with just a sans serif font that starts with ‘a note instead of a website.’ At the end of the list of all the things he has done – opera, theater, contemporary art, film, books – he adds, ‘and other territories that are not always easy to name.’
In his kitchen on a Sunday morning, in an apartment that looks out onto a historic Milanese palazzo fitted with a church’s bell tower that chimes on the hour, he expands more on his difficulty in creating this website, a journey that extends well beyond HTML and CSS. ‘But the problem for me is how I define myself,’ he says of trying to form his experience into a zippy portfolio. ‘This was a very important topic with my psychotherapist for two years. I have to say, ‘I am a director,’ but it’s not true. I work as a director, but this is the definition of my job, it’s not the definition of myself.’
design, a coffee maker, and aldo rossi
He pontificates on this while making coffee in La cupola, a moka pot designed by Aldo Rossi for Alessi. ‘Since I was very young, I liked stories. I always ask myself, how could I tell an audience this story? Maybe the most important thing that I learned from theater is always speaking about an audience. Storytelling, for me, has been crucial.’
Behind a conical silver pot for olive oil bordering his stove, two more coffee makers by Rossi perch nearby. He mentions La cupola was a gift from a friend. It soon becomes clear that most of the things in his home studio are materializations of his life, his friendships, or his career. And often, the boundaries between even these three are understood to be quite porous. ‘You see? Design! Alessi is always with us,’ he says as he puts a second pot on the stove. For the first one, he had forgotten to add water, but was delightfully unbothered by the mistake. In his kitchen, there is a large work next to the window made by friends who had staged a performance in that very home.
things you can Learn from design, art, and beyond
As the conversation moves into his living room, a lamp made by Formafantasma frames a monumental, pink, upside-down triangle, a work by Jade Guanaro Kuriki-Olivo, also known as Puppies Puppies. ‘I learned something about theater through the point of view of Simone Farresin from Formafantasma, who comes from the world of design. This is why I love doing collaborations, especially with people who didn’t study theater.’ Cherstich had worked with the Milan-based design studio back in 2024 on Staging Modernity, a scenography in Teatro Lirico Giorgio Gaber on the occasion of Cassina’s 60th anniversary of industrially production of pieces by Le Corbusier, Charlotte Perriand, and Pierre Jeanneret. In that 2025 show during Milan Design Week, visitors could walk among the seats, amble onto the stage, and peer over the mezzanine – the scene blurred the line between spectator and the show itself.
This fluidity, between viewer, performer, and stage, is a hallmark of Cherstich’s work. In 2016, Operacamion, which was conceived for Teatro dell’opera di Roma, brought operas into the streets of the city, performed in an open container on a truck bed. ‘I am particularly proud that it has become a Harvard case study in culture and has even been cited recently by New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani as an example of how opera can reach new audiences and move beyond traditional theatre spaces,’ he says of the work that is still continuing today, nearly 10 years later, although under different direction.
‘as a spectator, you also have a responsibility’
Although theater is something of an ancient craft, Cherstich touches on how it may be even more imperative today to practice it. ‘I do think that today working in the fields of theater and performance is quite necessary because things are happening live between real bodies. Everything is becoming more and more digital, flat, transformable,’ he says of the current media ecosystem. ‘So you need to assume responsibility, both if you are on stage and in the audience. On stage, you have a responsibility because what you are telling to people comes from a very vulnerable but also powerful place. But as a spectator, you also have a responsibility. You are in front of real bodies. You need to own your point of view. You need to invest time. And I do think that today, this dynamic is quite incredible because it’s the opposite of what is happening outside the theater.’
in 2019, Cherstich directed the opera Turandot with graphics created by the art collective, AES+F
his projects and their ever expanding boundaries
He takes these lessons beyond the stage. Currently, Cherstich is the curator of The Estate of Larry Stanton, in line with his interest in the queer scene of New York in the 80s and 90s, which he explores in his performance, A Visual Diary. He’s gone on to create art books and even films on the likes of artist Lucia di Luciano and Annina Nosei, Basquiat’s first gallerist, both of whom were close friends of his. Thinking back on Cherstich’s website woes, it’s perhaps not because the artist struggles to define himself, but more because he pointedly defies the confines of the medium, the temporality, and the contexts presented in each of the projects he pursues.
project info:
name: Fabio Cherstich | @fabio_cherstich
This interview is part of designboom’s SPECTATOR AND SPECTACLE chapter, asking how wonder gets built, presented in partnership with SolidNature, and how it might return some mystery to a world that has measured most of it away. Discover more stories that turn onlookers into participants, alter perception and disrupt the everyday here.

Fatma Zehra Solmaz
30 September 2026•Update: 30 September 2026
Turkish sides Anadolu Efes and Fenerbahce Tarfin secured victories in the second week of the EuroLeague on Tuesday, with Anadolu Efes beating Real Madrid 94-84 and Fenerbahce cruising past Bayern Munich 100-76.
Anadolu Efes secured its first win of the season in the competition, while Real Madrid suffered its second defeat.
Real Madrid led 29-27 after a closely contested opening quarter in which both teams shot at a high percentage.
Anadolu Efes took control late in the second quarter, scoring several consecutive 3-pointers in the final 3 minutes and 40 seconds to build a double-digit lead. The hosts went into halftime ahead 53-41.
Real Madrid cut the deficit to seven points in a fast-paced third quarter, but Anadolu Efes entered the final period with a 72-65 advantage.
The Spanish side reduced the gap to four points at 82-78 with three minutes remaining after finding success from inside the paint.
Anadolu Efes, however, made no mistakes in the closing minutes and pulled away to seal the 94-84 victory.
Fenerbahce Tarfin meanwhile maintained its perfect start to the EuroLeague season with a 100-76 win over Bayern Munich at home.
The Istanbul club improved to 2-0, while Bayern Munich suffered its first defeat.
Fenerbahce took control early, leading 16-9 after the opening five minutes before extending its advantage to 18 points at 31-13 late in the first quarter.
Despite a basket by Oscar da Silva with two seconds remaining, Fenerbahce finished the opening period 31-15 ahead.
The hosts continued their effective play in the second quarter and went into halftime with a 50-31 lead.
Fenerbahce maintained its tempo after the break, staying effective at both ends of the court and extending its advantage to 27 points at 70-43.
The Turkish side entered the final quarter with a 75-51 lead and did not allow Bayern Munich to close the gap, securing a 100-76 victory.
Before the game, former Fenerbahce and Turkish national team goalkeeper Sukru Ersoy, who died Tuesday, was commemorated.

Six Flags Closes Its X2 Roller Coaster After Brain-Injury Lawsuits
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
21:39:01 UTC
06:39:01 KST

The Six Flags theme park company announced on Tuesday that it would permanently close the X2 roller coaster at its Magic Mountain park in Valencia, Calif., following allegations of serious brain injuries linked to the ride.
The closure has renewed questions about how the intense forces generated by extreme roller coasters can affect the brain. Experts told TIME that abrupt acceleration, twisting, and changes in direction can stretch brain tissue and blood vessels, potentially increasing the risk of concussions and bleeding.
Three lawsuits filed in late September allege that riders suffered brain injuries after riding X2, and attorneys told CNN that more than 100 people have contacted them with similar allegations. The suits came in the wake of a CNN investigation published in August about the ride's long history of incidents, including at least two deaths.
"After almost 20 years, we have decided to permanently retire X2," wrote Magic Mountain president Brian Oerding in a blog post. "While X2 consistently passed a multitude of safety tests, we have decided to close the ride because we believe it’s the right thing to do. Ride safety is a cornerstone of our business, and when we see guest confidence affected, we take it seriously."
X2 was a two-minute thrill ride that reached a top speed of 76 miles per hour and opened in 2002, according to a Six Flags webpage about X2, which is no longer online. In July 2026, two women—six days apart—were hospitalized after riding X2, CNN reported. Both suffered from a subdural hematoma, or bleeding on the brain.
The first woman, who was 40, had emergency surgery and was unconscious for two weeks. Upon awakening, she had to relearn how to walk and talk. She is “very lucky to be alive,” one of her surgeons told CNN in August. The second woman, 26, underwent similar surgery and is still in a coma, the news outlet reports. On July 12, Six Flags closed X2 indefinitely—a closure made permanent at the end of September.
Billed by Six Flags as a “fifth-dimension wing roller coaster,” X2 ran along 3,610 feet of track. Its seats did not sit directly on the track. Rather they were mounted on wings on either side of the track—essentially suspending riders in space—and rotated 360 degrees. “Your body will be flipping around the entire time,” the now-removed Six Flags website says. “Quite simply, you will be spun into another dimension.” (Earlier this month, in response to a request from TIME for more details about the ride, a spokesperson for Six Flags said only that “the ride remains closed at this time.”)
The troubled history of roller coasters
“You are supposed to have a good time,” says Brian Avery, a faculty member at the University of Florida who teaches legal and risk management in the attractions, sport, and entertainment industries. (He does not have ties to Six Flags.) “You are supposed to walk away with enjoyment and a great experience. You aren’t supposed to leave in an ambulance or potentially dead. This is a serious problem that the industry needs to contend with.”
X2 is not the only American roller coaster that has caused concern—and alleged injury. In 1895, developers opened what was named the Flip Flap Railway—a short, single stretch of wooden track notable for a tight, tear-shaped loop in the middle—at Captain Paul Boyton’s Sea Lion Park in New York. Given the narrowness of the loop, the ride has historically been said to have produced a crushing amount of G-forces—or the pressure a rider feels relative to Earth's gravity.
Designers of early roller coasters like this “didn't know from a ride’s dynamics perspective and the tolerances on a person's body,” says Avery, “and unfortunately, a lot of people were injured as a result.” By 1902, the ride had closed.
Wooden roller coasters don’t have anywhere near the flexibility of steel roller coasters. First introduced in 1959, and throughout the second half of the 20th century, a “roller coaster arms race” took off, Avery says, with designers building tracks “taller, faster, more extreme.”
X2 was part of this boom, going into operation in 2002 and undergoing an upgrade in 2008, during which the rotating seats were introduced. Brain-injury allegations linked to the roller coaster date back to at least 2009 when, according to the CNN investigation, a 62-year-old man alleged he suffered a brain bleed as a result of the ride, recovering after surgery. The next year, a 28-year-old woman died on X2 when a congenital vascular abnormality in her brain ruptured after the ride, medical experts suspected.
What roller coasters can do to the brain
The shearing, tearing, and torquing forces at work on extreme roller coasters affect the brain, experts say.
“Brain tissue has very low rigidity (similar to jello), so it is prone to shearing and twisting during head motion,” wrote Lyndia Wu, an associate professor in the department of mechanical engineering at the University of British Columbia who studies the mechanics of brain injuries, in an email to TIME. “The tissue shearing and twisting can be amplified when the head rapidly accelerates or decelerates, such as when it moves in one direction and then abruptly whips in another during a roller-coaster turn, or when it strikes a headrest or another object. Blood vessels can also be experiencing stretching and twisting, posing risks of rupture and bleeding.”
The high levels of acceleration the coasters generate are a complicating factor. The head, which moves and swivels throughout a ride, may take more of a pounding than, say, the relatively stationary torso. G-force calculations, Wu says, only apply to “whole body accelerations that can be measured [or] estimated at the seat level when the roller coaster is designed. The head can be experiencing different acceleration profiles during a ride, which bring about additional brain injury risk considerations.”
While these forces can be damaging when an adult is in the coaster seat, they can do even more harm when the rider is a child. “Roller coasters are inherently higher risk in children than adults,” says Dr. Michael McDowell, associate professor of neurosurgery at Penn State Hershey Medical Center and Penn State Children's Hospital, and a co-author of a 2025 paper in the American Journal of Emergency Medicine on roller coaster injuries in minors. “Children are simply physically smaller on average and the forces they are subjected to are higher relative to their body mass. [In addition], the head is disproportionately larger in a child than an adult. The head and neck are functionally a bowling ball on a toothpick. A high energy turn on a roller coaster can snap the head in a direction which stretches the neck beyond the normal limits.”
Dr. James Mooney, assistant clinical professor of neurosurgery at Virginia Commonwealth University and another author of the 2025 paper, adds that “concussions have been documented in children after roller coaster rides, including in our study.”
Even if it were possible to model and correct for all of these factors perfectly when a roller coaster is being designed, not every set of metrics applies to every rider equally. “It could be just how you sit in a seat, how you're striking your head on the back of the seat,” says Avery. “It could be the height that you are in relation to a piece of the seat.”
The question of how to make roller coasters safer
What this means for the safety of roller coasters is uncertain. Wu suggests that research being conducted on brain injury in sports such as football may offer some “transferrable considerations” that can help in making roller coaster rides safer. “More research needs to be done to investigate possible head accelerations during rides beyond the seat acceleration levels, and the effect of factors such as neck strength [and] control to stabilize the head during rides, as well as possible impact of the head with the headrest.”
At the very least, operators of other roller coasters around the world can—and should—see the X2 as a cautionary tale. Even before Six Flags shuttered the ride, Avery thinks the damage had already been done. “I would have a complete review before this thing is reopened to see if they can isolate the cause,” he said at the time. “If they can, and it can be corrected, fine, correct it and move forward. [But] usually, when you've gotten to a point where a ride has made this much noise…the ride could be tainted in the sense that the public perception of it is deemed, ‘Hey, this is not for me.’”

US supreme court allows Trump officials to resume deportations to third countries
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
21:38:19 UTC
06:38:19 KST

The Trump administration can resume quickly deporting immigrants to a “third countries”, or countries other than those immigrants’ homeland, without giving them any opportunity to contest their removals, the supreme court ruled on Tuesday.
The six-justice conservative majority of the high court temporarily lifted a lower-court decision that required the administration to provide immigrants sufficient notice and the opportunity to claim fear of torture or persecution in the countries where they are being sent. The Trump administration had claimed this stipulation had prevented it from “efficiently removing aliens” from the US.
As is typical in emergency orders, the justices did not explain why it granted the administration’s request.
The three liberal justices of the court, Sonia Sotomayor, Elena Kagan and Ketanji Brown Jackson, dissented from the order.
Tuesday’s ruling will take effect while the supreme court considers the larger question in the case. Justices said they would hear oral arguments in December.
It is the second time the supreme court has sided with the Trump administration over “third-country” deportations.
Todd Blanche, the attorney general, called the administration’s policies “entirely lawful and a critical tool for immigration enforcement” in a social media post following the supreme court’s order.
“Unlike the lower court, SCOTUS waited to hear from both sides before making the decision,” Blanche wrote.
The supreme court’s intervention comes days after the administration filed an emergency request to the justices, hoping to continue deporting immigrants to third countries – including those that the US state department considers dangerous.
The Trump administration has entered into a series of agreements with other countries that have allowed it to deport more than 25,000 immigrants to at least 29 countries, according to Third Country Deportation Watch, a project run by Refugees International and Human Rights First.
Countries that have received US deportees include the Central African Republic, which is grappling with unrest and terrorism due to political and militia instability, and South Sudan, where a humanitarian crisis has been unfolding because of political and economic collapse.
On Monday, two dozen UN human rights experts warned that the deportation of thousands of migrants from the US to third countries has set off a “cascade of human rights violations” that could have “deadly” consequences.
Many third-country deportees have faced dire conditions and violence after they ended up in countries without any legal status. Earlier this month, two men that the Trump administration expelled to Equatorial Guinea were bound, fitted with bags over their heads, beaten and pushed down a flight of stairs, all in plain view of other US deportees, according to witnesses and human rights lawyers. Detainees said the men were facing retaliation for speaking to journalists and human rights experts about the poor conditions they faced.
“This cruel and inhumane policy is a black eye on Lady Liberty,” said Adelita Grijalva, a Democratic representative from Arizona. “We are a nation that promises to welcome the ‘poor’ and ‘huddled masses’ yearning for freedom. Instead, we are sending vulnerable people into harm’s way – and, in some cases, potentially to their deaths.”
One of the men who was beaten in Equatorial Guinea was her constituent, Ahmed Soliman – a gay man from Egypt who had fled discrimination in his home country and spent most of his life in Phoenix.
Lawyers for the immigrants have challenged the “third country” deportation policy, arguing that they had not been given “notice and a meaningful opportunity to present fear-based claims”.
Lawyers for the administration have said there’s no need for individual fear-based claims because countries willing to accept immigrants have already agreed not to persecute or torture anyone. Solicitor general D John Sauer, the government’s attorney, wrote to the supreme court that the lower-court orders “created substantial logistical problems with ongoing removal operations – including the cancellation of flights – and led to added expense, potential diplomatic issues, and the inability to remove dangerous criminals”.
Prior to the supreme court’s order on Tuesday, two lower courts had separately sided with the immigrants.

Ceuta mass migrant crossing handling 'responsibility of all EU,' Spanish king says
MADRID, Sept 29 - European countries should have shown more solidarity and offered more support to Spain after the mass arrival in Ceuta of tens of thousands of migrants, Spanish King Felipe VI said on Tuesday during a gala dinner to mark a visit by French President Emmanuel Macron.
In an unusually outspoken address reflecting the depth of the crisis facing Spain following the Ceuta border rush that took place two months ago on Wednesday, the king said what happened in the enclave on the North African coast was "unacceptable" and generated an enormous security, public order and humanitarian challenge.
"It's a situation that ought to have as a consequence a reinforcement of collaboration between member states in resources and cooperation," he said. "The European countries that suffer the most pressure from being on the external borders of the European Union cannot alone bear a responsibility that also belongs to everyone."
The king spoke during a dinner at the Royal Palace in Madrid also attended by Spain's Socialist prime minister, Pedro Sanchez, a rare European proponent of the benefits of migration who launched a mass regularisation of irregular migrants that concluded in the summer. Sanchez, however, has proposed possible changes to asylum rules to return arrivals more quickly, which NGOs and lawyers say would violate human rights conventions.
Asked in a news conference about the plans, territorial policy minister Angel Victor Torres said the government was "analysing the possibility" of a legislative amendment but that it was "not easy" due to questions of international law.
Following the mass crossing of 72,000 migrants into Ceuta on July 30, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen commended Spain's swift action in returning most arrivals to Morocco. Other leaders were less understanding, however, with Italy suspending the European Union's border-free Schengen arrangements with Spain for one month.
European Migration Commissioner Magnus Brunner unveiled a plan on Tuesday to strengthen EU border controls in the wake of Ceuta.
The plan, which requires the approval of member states, would strengthen the mandate of Frontex, the EU border protection agency, and give it a standing corps ready for immediate deployment. REUTERS

America’s foreign policy of coercion must end
Trump’s routine use of threats and ultimatums in place of diplomacy may yield immediate gains, but it inflicts lasting damage to America’s global standing
3-MIN READ3-MIN

Zhou Xiaoming is a senior fellow at the Centre for China and Globalisation in Beijing and a former deputy representative of China’s Permanent Mission to the United Nations Office in Geneva. 
If you want to understand how Washington exercises power in the world, watch what it does when its closest allies try to deepen ties with each other.
When EU chief Ursula von der Leyen proposed making Canada the European Union’s first-ever “associate member”, US President Donald Trump’s response was swift and blunt: “If they do that, if I think it’s at all a hostile act, I will put very serious tariffs or stop trading with Europe, on many things.” He called the idea “laughable” and Canada – America’s neighbour and closest ally – a “terrible trade partner”.

The examples are too many to list.

Costa Rica's Grynspan narrowly ahead in race to be next UN chief, sources say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
21:27:48 UTC

Costa Rica's Grynspan narrowly ahead in race to be next UN chief, sources say
UNITED NATIONS, Sept 29 - An informal poll by the United Nations Security Council on Tuesday placed former Costa Rican Vice President Rebeca Grynspan as the frontrunner in the race to become the 10th UN secretary-general, sources close to the process said.
The fourth secret poll by the 15-member Security Council followed the gathering of world leaders at the General Assembly in New York last week.
The first and third polls, held in July and September, also showed Grynspan narrowly ahead while an August poll placed Guyana's UN ambassador Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett in the top spot.
After former Chilean President Michelle Bachelet dropped out of the race this month, seven candidates are vying to succeed Antonio Guterres. The former Portuguese prime minister steps down at the end of this year after two five-year terms. More candidates could still enter the race.
Whoever wins will have to tackle multiple crises, including several wars, cutbacks in American contributions to the UN, and the UN's declining political relevance.
Ultimately, the five Security Council veto powers — the United States, China, Russia, France and Britain — need to agree on a candidate. When Guterres was chosen in 2016, it took six straw polls for the Security Council to reach agreement.
The Security Council will eventually formally recommend a candidate to the 193-member General Assembly for election. The assembly has long been expected to approve the council's choice.
In the more than 80-year history of the UN, there has never been a female secretary-general.
In the straw polls, which are expected to continue for several more rounds, Security Council members are asked on secret ballots if they "encourage," "discourage" or have "no opinion" on candidates.
Grynspan received 10 encourage votes, three discourage and two no opinion. Rodrigues-Birkett received eight encourage votes, six discourage and one no opinion, sources close to the process said.
Argentina's Rafael Grossi, the high-profile director general of the UN nuclear watchdog, also received eight encourage and seven discourage votes. REUTERS

Morocco's King Mohammed VI names Fatima Ezzahra El Mansouri as prime minister
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
21:25:35 UTC
06:25:35 KST

Moroccan King Mohammed VI has appointed Fatima Ezzahra El Mansouri as prime minister, making her the first woman to hold the post in the nation's history.
The appointment follows the September 23 parliamentary elections, in which Mansouri's Authenticity and Modernity Party (PAM) secured first place with 97 seats, the Ministry of the Royal Household, Protocol and Chancellery announced in an official statement.
Under Morocco's constitution, the monarch appoints the prime minister from the political party that secures the most seats in the 395-seat House of Representatives, the lower chamber of parliament, with cabinet ministers subsequently appointed on the prime minister's proposal.
The palace statement confirmed that King Mohammed received Mansouri, the coordinator of the PAM's collective leadership, at the Royal Palace in Rabat, formally tasking her with forming the new government.
Coalition consultations
Speaking after the audience, Mansouri described the monarch's decision as a "historic moment" for the nation.
"This is the first time that a woman has been appointed to head a government, which is a source of pride for me and for all the women of the country," she said.
Mansouri confirmed she will immediately commence consultations within her party and across other political factions to assemble a governing coalition.
"We are fully aware of the importance of this stage and of the high expectations of citizens, particularly young people," she stated, adding that "we will draw up a programme offering realistic and concrete solutions."
In the legislative elections, the National Rally of Independents (RNI) finished second with 66 seats, followed closely by the Istiqlal Party with 65 seats and the Justice and Development Party (PJD) with 54 seats.
Mansouri rose to political prominence after the party's founding in 2008 and made history in 2009 when she became Marrakech's first female mayor.

Donald Trump has agreed to stop fighting in court the disbursement of E Jean Carroll’s $5m verdict in her 2023 sexual abuse and defamation civil trial against him, a procedural development as these funds were already distributed to her.
While the decision does not change anything about Carroll’s receipt of the payout, its revelation effectively means that Trump will no longer oppose the monetary outcome he had long fought.
This decision was revealed Tuesday by the United States court of appeals for the second circuit.
Trump’s second circuit fight had already been made moot by a supreme court decision not to reconsider his opposition, so this morning’s filing marked a formality.
“The parties stipulate to dismiss this appeal with prejudice … and [Trump] withdraws his motion for a stay pending appeal,” the Second Circuit said in a mandate. “The stipulation is SO ORDERED. The stay motion … is deemed WITHDRAWN.”
“He’d previously given up in district court, now he’s given up in circuit court,” said Neama Rahmani, founder of West Coast Trial Lawyers and a former federal prosecutor, of the money-related order. “It’s a final nail in the coffin. There’s absolutely no way Trump can go after Carroll for this five million plus dollars.”
Trump in July unsuccessfully asked the second circuit to postpone disbursement of this money while he appealed a lower court’s decision mandating its distribution. The money was held in a court-administered fund pending Trump’s appeal of the 2023 verdict.
Manhattan federal court judge Lewis Kaplan on 8 July ordered disbursement of this money after the US supreme court’s 29 June decision not to review Trump’s appeal. Less than an hour after this decision, Trump asked the second circuit to grant him a stay so he could fight Kaplan’s mandate.
The second circuit rejected this request. The court-held funds, which totalled $5.8m due to accrued interest, were released on 9 July, court records dated 14 July indicate.
The supreme court in August rejected for the second time Trump’s efforts to overturn this jury verdict, denying his request for a rehearing. Trump is asking the US supreme court to throw out a second, much larger payment of $83m awarded against him for defaming Carroll in her January 2024 civil trial.
Asked for comment, a spokesperson for Trump’s legal team said: “The American People stand with President Trump as they demand an immediate end to all of the Witch Hunts, including the Democrat-funded travesty of the Carroll Hoaxes.
“President Trump will keep winning against Liberal Lawfare, as he continues to focus on his mission to Make America Great Again,” the statement added.

Blue-and-white National Team needs accountability, not more excuses, after last loss - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
21:22:00 UTC
06:22:00 KST

Israel’s 3-0 defeat to Ireland this week was not simply another disappointing result. It was a performance that raised serious questions about the direction of the national team, the preparation of the players and, ultimately, the responsibility of head coach Ran Ben Shimon and the Israel Football Association.
Ben Shimon should have resigned immediately following the defeat. If he was unwilling to step down, IFA chairman Shino Zuaretz should have made the decision for him.
That may sound harsh, but there comes a point when accountability has to mean something.
Ben Shimon failed to prepare his team, both mentally and physically, for a match of enormous significance. He knew what was at stake, not only from a sporting perspective but also given the political climate surrounding the game and the country itself.
Let no one tell you that sports and politics don’t mix. They always do.
The head coach had a responsibility to ensure that his players were fully prepared for the challenge ahead. Instead, Israel looked completely unprepared and delivered a performance that was nothing short of disgraceful.
Ben Shimon himself acknowledged as much.
“We started the game embarrassingly. It was an embarrassment,” he said. “We will need to really take a good, hard look at what went wrong, and although we prepared really well for this match, I have to take the blame for that. We deserve all of the criticism that we will be levied upon us over the next few days. I have to apologize to everyone for this.”
Why was did the team looked so unprepared when the match begun?
Those are powerful words from the coach, but they also raise an obvious question: If Israel was supposedly prepared so well, how could the team look so completely unprepared when the match began?
Captain Eli Dasa, one of the most experienced players in the squad, offered an equally damning assessment.
“There is no good way to explain it. We failed and failed miserably today,” Dasa said. “There’s no need to hide behind anything. It’s an enormous disappointment and I have no other way to describe it. I’ve made 80 appearances for the national team and this is undoubtedly the most painful game.”
Dasa went further, accepting full responsibility on behalf of the players while making clear that he did not believe the coaching staff was at fault for the lack of effort.
“The coaching staff did a fantastic job preparing us and gave us a very good game plan, but we didn’t come out and perform,” he said. “The responsibility lies 100% with the players.”
Manor Solomon was equally blunt.
“I agree that it’s a disgrace. We have no words. We’re all heartbroken,” Solomon said. “We need to look at ourselves, each and every one of us, in the mirror, because we simply didn’t show up today.”
There is certainly plenty of responsibility for the players to accept. International footballers cannot simply blame a coach every time things go wrong. They have to execute, compete and take responsibility on the field.
Responsibility doesn't end there
But the responsibility does not end there.
The coaching staff must also answer for a team that has repeatedly struggled to create consistent scoring opportunities and has been unable to eliminate the fundamental mistakes that have plagued Israel.
After 180 minutes of Nations League action, the blue-and-white have scored just one goal. Where are the goals supposed to come from? Where is the creativity? Where is the organization? Where is the plan when things go wrong?
And why was Dor Peretz, arguably Israel’s best player and leading scorer, left on the bench before being introduced at halftime?
Those are legitimate questions for the coaching staff, not merely the players.
Ben Shimon spoke confidently about finishing first or second in the group. After losing the opening two matches, however, Israel now faces the very real possibility of finishing last.
The issue is not simply that Israel lost. Teams lose.
The issue is how Israel has lost, and the fact that many of the same problems continue to appear without any meaningful evidence that they are being corrected.
Years ago, when Andi Herzog was Israel’s head coach, he delivered an infamous postgame assessment following another disappointing European qualifying campaign.
“We always say that this is good, but we always concede three goals,” Herzog said. “We are not professional enough.”
He continued: “We are always talking about qualification and then we make mistakes. That’s not possible. We always talk about something we dream about, but we have to do the decisive things on the field.”
Herzog’s words remain painfully relevant today.
Years later, Israel is still making the same mistakes, struggling with the fundamentals of the game and failing to translate its ambitions into results.
The players must take responsibility, but so must the head coach and his staff. Nothing will change until everyone involved is held accountable.
Unfortunately, accountability has become a familiar problem in Israeli football. When things go wrong, responsibility is too often shifted elsewhere rather than accepted by those in charge. The national team cannot afford to continue operating that way.
If Ben Shimon does not resign, the IFA must make the decision for him.
He should not be on the sidelines for Thursday’s match against Kosovo or the subsequent meeting with Ireland in Serbia. After two consecutive defeats and such a disastrous performance, the federation must seriously reconsider its direction.
There are plenty of potential replacements, both Israeli and foreign. Barak Itzhaki, who led Beitar Jerusalem over the past couple of years, is among the domestic candidates who could be considered. There are also numerous other coaches who could take over and attempt to turn things around.
The IFA cannot afford to sit back and hope the situation somehow improves.
Ben Shimon failed to deliver during World Cup qualifying, and Israel has now opened its Nations League campaign with two defeats. The results and performances demand a serious response.
With Euro 2028 qualifying set to begin in March 2027, the IFA still has time to make a change and give the national team a fresh start. A new coach would have an opportunity to address the team’s shortcomings, correct its persistent mistakes and build a squad capable of competing at the international level.
Ben Shimon’s record as Israel’s head coach stands at eight wins, 11 losses and three draws, a 36.4% winning percentage. For a national team with aspirations of reaching a major tournament, those numbers raise serious questions about the current direction of the program.
The IFA desperately wants Israel to qualify for a major tournament for the first time since the 1970 World Cup.
But simply talking about that ambition will not make it happen.
At some point, ambition has to be matched by action.
The national team belongs to the people of Israel. The supporters deserve a team that competes with pride, commitment and determination, regardless of the circumstances. They deserve players who fight for the shirt and a coaching staff that prepares them to meet the challenges ahead.
Losing is part of sports. Sometimes even the best teams come up short.
But failing to show up, failing to compete and repeating the same mistakes without learning from them is something entirely different.
The question facing the IFA is no longer simply how Israel can recover from one disappointing defeat.
It is whether those in charge are willing to accept responsibility and make the difficult decisions necessary to ensure that this kind of performance does not become the norm.
The time for excuses is over.
The time for accountability is now.

Trump says Iran 'will give up,' compares its nuclear ambitions with North Korea

US President Donald Trump said Tuesday that Iran would eventually give up, although he stopped short of predicting when, during remarks at a White House event attended by leading technology executives.
Asked whether Iran was about to concede, Trump replied: "Well, they're doing very poorly. I don't know if they're going to give up yet, but they'll give up, but they're doing very poorly."
He also claimed that more oil had moved through the Strait of Hormuz over the preceding two days than at any previous point in history, including before the war.
Trump made the remarks following a luncheon for tech leaders and artificial intelligence (AI) moguls held in the White House's East Room.
The US president did not provide figures to substantiate the claim. He reiterated that preventing Iran from acquiring a nuclear weapon remained the central objective of the military campaign.
"Iran will not have a nuclear," he said, ending the sentence without completing the phrase.
The remarks came during an event largely devoted to artificial intelligence, which Trump wants to rename "superintelligence," or SI.
Trump: Kim Jong Un 'happens to be a friend of mine'
Trump returned to the nuclear issue when a reporter asked why North Korea had been allowed to develop nuclear weapons while the United States was determined to prevent Iran from obtaining them.
"Ah, that's interesting. You know why? Because you had a different president, and they could have stopped him," Trump replied, blaming his predecessors for failing to halt Pyongyang's nuclear program.
He then spoke about his personal relationship with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un.
"He happens to be a friend of mine, Kim Jong Un. He's a friend of mine. He likes Trump. Doesn't like a lot of other people," Trump said.
"I'm about the only person in the entire world that he likes, and I like him. I get in a lot of heat when I say that."
Trump acknowledged that North Korea possesses a substantial nuclear capability.
"He does have a nuclear capacity, a large nuclear, pretty large nuclear. Not like us, but he has a nuclear capacity," he said.
He again contrasted the situation with his approach to Iran, saying previous presidents "didn't do what I did."
Trump criticizes UK over RAF Fairford suspects
The president also addressed an investigation near RAF Fairford, a British airbase used by US forces, including for operations involving Iran.
Trump said American authorities had been involved in the investigation and criticized the decision to release five arrested men on bail.
"How do you give bail to a terrorist?" he asked, referring to the suspects.
"They put them out on bail. I assume they have them watched closely. But these were serious people, seriously bad people, and they should not have done that."
British counterterrorism police said Tuesday that no improvised explosive devices had been found during the investigation, although petrol had been recovered from vehicles. The five men remain under investigation following their release on bail. Police have said the decision was made as part of their investigative strategy.
Authorities are examining several possible explanations for the incident, including whether individuals may have been acting on behalf of a foreign state. An Iranian connection has not been established, and Iran has denied involvement.
Xi meeting and the race for AI
Trump said his recent meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping had been discussed with the technology executives gathered at the White House.
"We had a great meeting with President Xi. A lot of respect for President Xi," he said.
The discussion then turned to competition between the United States and China over AI infrastructure.
Trump argued that American companies must be able to build data centers domestically rather than move projects overseas.
"If we're not smart, they'll end up building data centers in other countries, and those other countries will make a fortune, and we won't," he said.
He suggested that China would welcome American investment that failed to materialize in the United States.
"Elon and I sat with President Xi the other day, and he will take every data center that we don't want," Trump said, referring to Elon Musk.
Trump also praised the American technology industry's position in the global AI race.
"Our companies are dominating the world," he said. "They're dominating China. They're dominating everyone. We want to keep it that way."
The White House said following Xi's recent visit that the two countries had agreed to use the term "superintelligence" and establish a dialogue on the technology's risks and benefits.
Musk predicts 'an age of abundance'
Musk was asked what superintelligence could mean for workers concerned that their jobs may disappear.
"I think by far the most likely outcome is an age of abundance, where we don't have just universal basic income. We have universal high income," he said.
Musk argued that advances in robotics and superintelligence could eventually make medical care far more widely available.
Pressed on what people would do without jobs, he said: "Well, jobs are going to change. Jobs have always changed."
He compared the potential transition to the disappearance of jobs once devoted to performing calculations by hand, work that is now done by computers.
Not every executive offered an unqualifiedly optimistic view.
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei emphasized that AI presents significant risks alongside its benefits.
"I think the technology has very real risks, and you know, the mechanism by which we address those risks is still under discussion," he said.
Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg described an agreement among industry leaders on internal controls, outside audits and independent reviews by company boards. He characterized the commitments as an initial step rather than a complete solution.
Trump, meanwhile, expressed confidence that the companies had strong incentives to ensure their products were safe.
"If something goes wrong, their companies are at stake," he said. "They're not going to let that happen."
The exchanges illustrated how an event intended to promote America's technological ambitions became a forum for questions extending from AI safety and competition with China to the Iran war and security concerns in Britain.

US Supreme Court allows Trump administration to resume deportations to third countries
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
21:17:23 UTC
06:17:23 KST

The US Supreme Court has let President Donald Trump's administration resume deporting migrants to countries other than their own.
The court granted the Justice Department's emergency request to put on hold Boston-based US District Judge Brian Murphy's ruling that the Department of Homeland Security's policy to remove migrants to third countries is unlawful.
The court also agreed to hear arguments in the dispute in December, with a formal ruling on policy to follow.
Murphy's ruling came in a class-action lawsuit filed by immigrant rights groups on behalf of migrants seeking to prevent the US government from sending them to third countries without notice and a chance to assert the harms they could face.
More than 25,000 migrants have been deported to 29 countries under the policy implemented last year, according to a tally by human rights groups, with the vast majority going to Mexico.
The administration has carried out third-country deportations to South Sudan as well as Uganda, Equatorial Guinea, Liberia, the Central African Republic, and other nations.
The Supreme Court previously sided with the administration in the legal challenge, suspending a preliminary order that Murphy issued earlier in the case halting the removals.
Swiftly removed
The policy provided that migrants could be swiftly removed without notice to third countries that have provided credible diplomatic assurance that they will not persecute or torture the individuals.
For countries that have not provided such assurance, deportees would be notified of their destination, and US authorities would assess the likelihood of persecution or torture only if the individual raises such fear on their own.
In February, Murphy ruled that the policy violates immigration law procedures and due process protections under the US Constitution's Fifth Amendment.
Due process generally requires the government to provide notice and an opportunity for a hearing before taking certain adverse actions.
In its emergency filing to the Supreme Court, the Justice Department said third-country deportations are "an essential tool to remove certain aliens, including some of the worst criminal aliens."
More than a dozen UN rights experts have written to the US government urging a halt to policies that they said on Monday were putting migrants at heightened risk of abuse, including torture and persecution, by deporting them to third countries.

AI risks ‘spiraling out of control’ – Nobel-winning group chief
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
21:12:48 UTC
06:12:48 KST

AI risks ‘spiraling out of control’ – Nobel-winning group chief
Artificial intelligence could develop beyond human control unless governments and private companies work together to establish safeguards, the head of the Nobel Peace Prize-winning Pugwash Conferences on Science and World Affairs, Karen Hallberg, has told RT.
Speaking at the Valdai Discussion Club outside of Moscow on Tuesday, Hallberg compared AI with nuclear technology, saying both can bring major benefits while also posing serious dangers.
“AI is also a dual-use technology because AI has brought a lot of benefit for humanity,” she said, citing the technology’s use in medicine and everyday life.
However, she warned that AI capable of recursively improving itself could develop in unpredictable ways. “We have to really listen to the experts of these big corporations when they say that this is already happening – spiraling out of control,” Hallberg said.
Governments must work directly with companies developing AI to establish common rules, she added, noting that unlike during the early nuclear era, much of the technology is being developed by private corporations.
“The human being has to have total control,” Hallberg said, calling for safeguards to be built into AI algorithms.
Warnings over the potential consequences of increasingly powerful AI have also come from the companies developing it. US firm Anthropic, which is expected to go public as early as mid-October, has warned prospective investors that advanced AI could pose “catastrophic or existential risks to humanity.” According to Reuters, around 80 pages of its 261-page IPO prospectus are devoted to risk factors.
Pugwash brings together scientists and public figures seeking to reduce threats from armed conflict and weapons of mass destruction. The organization was jointly awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 1995 with its co-founder Joseph Rotblat.

Weapons makers and SpaceX in government's key investment fund portfolio

analysis
Weapons makers, SpaceX and semiconductors feature in Australia's Future Fund portfolio
How much has Australia's Future Fund profited from investing in weapons manufacturers in the last six months?
How many SpaceX shares has it bought? How many Tesla shares has it sold?
Australia's sovereign wealth fund published its latest six-monthly investment report on Monday. It published it quietly, without a press release or public announcement.
The Future Fund is two decades old and it has grown its initial $60 billion investment, from 2006, into $290 billion (and it manages an additional $66 billion across six smaller funds).
This latest report shows what stocks the fund bought and sold between December 31 and June 30, and what returns its stock holdings generated in the first half of this year.
Semiconductors and microchips
The Future Fund has profited immensely from its investments in the global semiconductor and chip industry.
But an interesting thing here is that it hasn't gone on a spending spree.
In fact, it has been selling down its stake slightly in a number of companies. But the share price of some of the companies has risen so much in the past six months that the value of the fund's holdings in the companies has soared.
For example, the value of its holdings in SK Hynix (a South Korean semiconductor company) surged by 199 per cent in the last six months, from $280.2m to $837.3m, even though the Future Fund sold 74,000 shares in the company.
The value of its holdings in Micron Technology (a US semiconductor company) exploded by 304 per cent, from $470.5m to $1.9 billion, as the fund bought an extra 42,000 shares in the company.
The table below shows its holdings in nine specific companies in the industry.
The value of its holdings in those nine companies has increased from $4.8 billion to $8.3 billion (+73 per cent) in the last six months alone:
The 'Magnificent 7'
The so-called "Magnificent 7" stocks include Tesla, NVIDIA, Alphabet (Google), Microsoft, Meta Platforms, Apple and Amazon.
The value of the Future Fund's share holdings in those seven companies fell by $1.4 billion in the first six months of this year.
It was worth $11.1 billion at the start of the year, but by the end of June it was worth $9.7 billion.
That decline in value reflects both falling share prices and the Future Fund's share sales. The fund sold shares in every one of those companies, except for Microsoft.
The value of its Telsa holdings declined by 28 per cent (from $519.1m to $374.8m), and the value of its Meta holdings fell by 26 per cent (from $1.2b to $923.7m).
The value of its holdings in Microsoft fell 24 per cent, even though it bought 48,000 more Microsoft shares:
Fund buys SpaceX and Palantir, sells some Tesla shares
The Future Fund bought into SpaceX this year, Elon Musk's aerospace company.
SpaceX went public on the NASDAQ on June 12 and by the end of the month the Future Fund owned 40,185 shares, valued at $9.9 million.
Norway's sovereign wealth fund also bought into SpaceX.
While the Future Fund bought some SpaceX shares, it sold some of its Telsa shares (it sold 152,363 of them, leaving it with 617,352).
SpaceX's initial public offering (IPO) was extremely controversial. NASDAQ's rules were changed to force passive funds to buy SpaceX shares within weeks. And the voting rights of SpaceX shareholders were severely restricted.
The Future Fund's investment managers also considered Palantir Technologies to be a good investment.
In December, the fund held 620,169 Palantir shares worth $165.3 million, and in June it held 680,569 shares (60,400 more shares) worth $114.6 million ($50.7m less in value, despite owning more shares).
Earlier this month, Coles Supermarkets announced it was cutting ties with Palantir after its three-year contract ends in 2027. The move followed a pressure campaign from the activist group GetUp! and growing concerns about Palantir's surveillance technology.
In February, Will Hetherton, the Future Fund's chief corporate affairs officer, defended the fund's investments in Palantir.
During a Senate estimates hearing, Greens senator Barbara Pocock asked Mr Hetherton if the Future Fund had done any due diligence on Palantir's human rights record before investing over $100 million in the company, given its role in the immigration crackdowns in the US and the growing use of its surveillance and AI-powered military software globally.
Loading...
"The investment that the board has in Palantir … is held through two index-focused investment managers," Hetherton said in February.
"The board sets the overall strategy in terms of the risk exposures that we seek, but the actual selection of stocks and the application of strategies — and in this case they're effectively passive index-tracking strategies — is a matter for the managers. So we're not involved in selecting individual stocks.
"I would observe that Palantir is a very widely held stock by investors globally," he said.
Defence, aerospace, and weapons
The Future Fund also continued to make money from its investments in "defence companies" — that includes global weapons manufacturers and aerospace companies.
It bought more defence giant Thales shares in the first half of this year, and the overall value of its Thales holdings jumped by 64 per cent ($13.4m to $22.1m).
It bought another 8,000 shares in the Israeli company Elbit Systems, with the value of its holdings in the defence technology and electronics company jumping by another 128 per cent (from $8.6m to $19.7m).
Two years ago, the Future Fund only held $1.3m worth of Elbit Systems shares.
The table below shows the change in value in the Future Fund's holdings in some well-known defence and aerospace companies and weapons manufacturers:
Norway's sovereign wealth fund — the world's largest — has been prohibited from investing in a number of companies that the Future Fund invests in.
Norges Bank Investment Management (NBIM) manages Norway's fund and its exclusions list includes Airbus SE, BAE Systems, Boeing, Caterpillar, Elbit Systems, General Dynamics, and others — all of which the Future Fund invests in.
In comparison, the Future Fund's exclusions list is dominated by companies involved in the tobacco industry.

Former RBA boss says government spending has driven inflation
Former Reserve Bank governor Philip Lowe says a lack of productivity growth is driving Australia's high inflation.

But Treasurer Jim Chalmers has denied that government spending is a part of the problem.
Speaking to the Institute of Public Affairs podcast The Prosperity Question, Lowe begged to differ.
"Government spending contributes to inflation because inflation comes when demand is greater than supply," Lowe says.
"Supply is driven in broad terms by population growth and productivity, productivity has been zero, so the supply side of the economy has been growing very weakly. That means, unfortunately, demand has to grow weakly," he said.
Lowe says Australia needs to become a better place for firms to invest, expand and hire people, in order to get productivity increasing again.
"We need to make the economy more dynamic, more efficient, more productive," he said.
"Our political class, for whatever reason, has stopped doing that."

"I would never downplay them. But I will also tell your viewers at home, I would prefer to be Australia than any other country in the world."
Nationals senator Bridget McKenzie, who has appeared on the panel with O'Neil, wouldn't say where the opposition would cut.

Syria arrests Hezbollah cell accused of deploying missile launchers near Israel border

Syrian internal security forces announced Tuesday evening that they had arrested a cell affiliated with Hezbollah that tried to deploy missile launchers in the southwest of the country, near the border with Israel.
Syrian reports said the cell was thwarted as part of a proactive security operation carried out by internal security forces together with the General Intelligence Directorate, targeting hostile activity in the Yarmouk Basin area of Daraa. According to the reports, the arrested cell consisted of three Hezbollah operatives. Their identities were not disclosed, with only their initials released.
The operation followed close surveillance of the cell’s attempt to deploy missile launchers that were “intended to be used to carry out attacks aimed at undermining security and public order.” Syrian reports said the launchers were dismantled and the investigation of the detainees is continuing ahead of their transfer to the relevant judicial authorities for prosecution.
Since coming to power, the government of Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa has been acting against the activities of Lebanon’s Hezbollah, which was aligned with the regime of former President Bashar Assad. As part of those efforts, Syrian officials have reported in recent years the capture of individuals affiliated with the terror group and weapons that were being transported to it. Hezbollah, for its part, routinely denies in statements that it operates in neighboring countries.
In July, Syria’s pro-government Alikhbaria channel cited a source in the Interior Ministry in Damascus as saying that “special units thwarted an attempt to smuggle a shipment of advanced weapons and missiles across the border with Iraq.” According to the source, “initial investigations confirm that the seized shipment was intended to pass through Syrian territory to Hezbollah.”
About two weeks ago, Syria announced that it had arrested a Hezbollah terror cell in the western Damascus province that had planned to carry out operations inside Syria aimed at threatening the country’s security and stability. Rocket launchers, 19 Grad rockets, anti-tank missiles, personal weapons and additional ammunition were seized from the cell.
In February, after months of reports in Syria of attacks targeting Damascus, including with rockets, the Syrian Interior Ministry announced that a terror cell involved in the attacks had been captured along with weapons. According to the ministry, initial interrogations of the detainees revealed that they were linked to “foreign entities” and that the rockets used in the attacks, as well as drones, had come from Lebanon’s Hezbollah. Syrian authorities also claimed that the detainees admitted they had planned to carry out additional drone attacks before they were arrested.
In both cases, Hezbollah denied any connection to the incidents, saying: “We have no presence or activity on Syrian territory. We are interested in preserving its stability and the security of its citizens.”

Breadcrumb
Syria says arrested Hezbollah-affiliated cell planning attacks
Syrian authorities said on Tuesday that they had arrested a Hezbollah-affiliated cell in the country's south near the Israeli-occupied Golan Heights, accusing it of planning attacks on unspecified targets.
The new authorities in Damascus, who ousted longtime ruler Bashar al-Assad in 2024, are hostile to the Lebanese militant group, which is a sworn enemy of Israel and fought on Assad's side during the Syrian civil war.
Tuesday's announcement came hours after Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said there were "indications" that Israel's enemies could try to attack ahead of elections scheduled for late October.
Syrian intelligence services and security forces "thwarted a sabotage plot in the Yarmuk basin in Daraa (province) and arrested a Hezbollah-affiliated cell composed of three individuals", Syrian state television reported, quoting a statement from the internal security forces.
The Yarmuk basin area, where state media has previously reported Israeli incursions and shelling, borders the Israeli-annexed Syrian Golan Heights, as well as Jordan.
"The operation followed careful monitoring of an attempt by the cell to prepare rocket launch platforms with the aim of carrying out attacks to destabilise security and stability," the statement said.
It did not specify the target of the alleged planned attacks and said investigations were ongoing.
Syrian authorities have previously said they dismantled several Hezbollah-linked cells preparing attacks in Syria, accusations the group has denied.
Authorities have also previously announced several seizures of weapons they said were bound for Hezbollah, which lost a key supply route from its backer Iran when Assad was toppled.
In recent weeks, Netanyahu and Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz have issued repeated warnings to Iran and Hezbollah promising retaliation in case of any attack.
Hezbollah drew Lebanon into the Middle East war in March with rocket fire at Israel, which responded with airstrikes and a ground invasion.
The latest war and a previous round of hostilities with Israel in 2023-2024 have weakened the militant group.
Israel has carried out hundreds of strikes in Syria since Assad's ouster and sent troops into a UN-patrolled buffer zone that had separated Israeli and Syrian forces in the Golan since 1974.
It has also carried out repeated incursions deeper into Syrian territory and has vowed to keep troops in a so-called "security zone" in southern Syria, where it seeks a broader demilitarised area.
Israel captured most of the Golan Heights from Syria in the 1967 Arab-Israeli War and later annexed the areas under its control, a move only recognised by the United States and Colombia.

Under the deal, her monthly payments would be capped at about $570 for the next eight years, taking up roughly 30 percent of her pension.

Sandu to be Moldova’s first president to face impeachment proceedings — ex-president
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
21:02:00 UTC
06:02:00 KST

CHISINAU, September 29. /TASS/. Impeachment proceedings against President Maia Sandu, the first ever in Moldova’s history, is a signal that she will be held accountable after resignation, leader of Moldova’s largest opposition Party of Socialists and the country’s former President Igor Dodon said.
"Impeachment proceedings against a president have never been initiated before in our country, and the fact that all opposition parties in parliament have rallied to impeach Maia Sandu sends a strong signal that, following her resignation, she will be held accountable for the violations of the law she committed," he told TASS.
He recalled that Moldova’s Constitutional Court had previously established a mechanism for removing the country’s president from office, which stipulates that such a motion may be proposed by at least one-third of parliament members (at least 34 out of 101 votes).
"The grounds cited were violations of the constitution and the country’s laws by the head of state. The document, which was supported by 46 lawmakers representing all opposition parliamentary parties, cites the usurpation of power, violations of the principle of separation of powers, the undermining of sovereignty, participation in election campaigns, violations of fundamental human rights, and other crimes. In particular, the document cites Sandu’s repeated statements that she supports the dissolution of the Moldovan state and its unification with Romania, excluding the territory of unrecognized Transnistria, which is unacceptable for the guarantor of statehood. Evidence is also presented of illicit enrichment and corruption on the part of the head of state’s associates and relatives," Dodon stated.
Under the country’s constitution, a proposal to remove the president from office may be put forward by at least one-third of lawmakers, while two-thirds, or 67 votes, are required to remove the president from office. If parliament supports the move, a nationwide referendum on the president’s resignation is to be held within 30 days. The president is considered to have been ultimately removed from office if a majority of participants in the referendum vote in favor of this, provided that this majority is not smaller than the number of those who voted for the president during the election.
Bearing in mind the fact that the ruling party controls the majority of seats in parliament, the idea of impeachment looks practically unimplementable, but, according to observers, it will undoubtedly have serious consequences for Sandu and her party in the future.
