====================================================================================================

The True Story of the Extreme Makeover Reality Show in The Swan: Behind the Mirror
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
20:50:34 UTC
05:50:34 KST

“There is the everyday nastiness baked into reality shows that manipulate cast members into bad-mouthing and backstabbing each other, and then there is The Swan.” That’s how TIME introduced an indelible early aughts series in its list of the 50 most influential reality TV seasons ever, and there’s no mistaking it: The Fox show was as much of a sensation as it was a locus of controversy.
The Swan was premised on the kind of concept you’d expect from a Black Mirror episode: Women undergo extreme physical transformation to shed their identities as “ugly ducklings” and become beautiful swans, at least in accordance with conventional beauty standards. The first season, which premiered in 2004, averaged more than 9 million viewers an episode. Media critic Jennifer L. Pozner called it “the most sadistic reality series” in her book Reality Bites Back. The show received countless extremely negative reviews received during its run, too. Gone Girl author Gillian Flynn, then a critic for Entertainment Weekly, called it “a misogynistic mix of TV’s twin vices: commercialism and conformity.” All of this was perhaps a harbinger for it cancellation, after just two seasons.
More than two decades later, a new documentary from Erin Lee Carr (Britney vs Spears, Murdaugh: Death in the Family),The Swan: Behind the Mirror, is shining a new light on not just the reality series but its aftermath. As the doc arrives on Hulu and Disney+, Carr and two participants from both The Swan and Behind the Mirror, Season 1’s Kristy Garza and Season 2’s Kari Bravata, spoke to TIME about the most notorious reality show ever made.
How the Swans opened up
Before The Swan could take flight, it needed to cast a crew of willing participants. So the producers behind the show launched an advertising campaign that emphasized the idea of transformation. Prospective contestants would be treated to a cornucopia of all the plastic surgery they could imagine, as well as therapy, life coaching, and personal training.
‘It really seemed like a golden ticket,” Garza says of her initial reaction to a seemingly bountiful offer.
The Swan held open casting calls all over the country. The show cited figures as high as 200,000 to 250,000 applicants, though Carr says she’s never been able to verify that statistic. “That seems extremely high, given that it was an unknown show,” she says. “One of the tactics used with the swans was, ‘We picked you out of 200,000 people.’ In my opinion, that has a compliance effect. You got chosen above everybody else. You can't say no.” Carr estimates the figure might have been closer to 75,000.
Convincing some of these women to open up, years later, for Behind the Mirror, proved more difficult. The Swan’s effects on contestants’ self-esteem still lingers, and it was frightening for both Garza and Bravata to speak about their experiences, having been manipulated for the sake of television in the past. But both credit Carr for creating a safe space.
“I knew from the very first conversation that Erin was genuine. She cares about women's stories. She cares about empowering women,” says Garza. “The questions that she asked right off the bat, you could tell she wasn't setting us up for something else,” Bravata adds.
“I remember sitting in the chair, and she said, ‘Kristy, take a breath. This is about you. This is for you.’ And in that moment, I felt this weight lifted, and my bleeding heart poured all over the floor,” says Garza.
That comfort was created in the details. Carr had each swan choose a song they loved to be their “walk-on” song, to lighten the mood before filming, and a “walk-off” song to celebrate the completion of their interviews.
It was equally important for Carr to highlight the experiences of the women who were on the show over everything else. “Revisiting docs are often about the producers, and not about the people that actually lived through the experience,” says Carr. “While it was instrumental to talk to the producers, these women went through an experience that somebody called the most sadistic reality show of all time. That's what I wanted to understand.”
The dark side of The Swan
Carr recorded accounts from 12 different swans, as well as several producers and one of the show’s plastic surgeons, Dr. Randal Haworth. Carr credits one of the participating swans, Kelly Alemi, with providing essential research materials. Carr recalls that she brought with her to set the “Swan Binder,” which the contestants received at the beginning of filming and detailed what they would experience, as well as Alemi’s personal calendar from the reality show. “It was this calendar with German Shepherds on it,” recalls Carr. “And she had written ‘pain’ day after day on the calendar. I saw that and thought, ‘That really epitomizes part of this experience.’”
Garza remembers her situation before the show well: “I was getting ready to end my five-year military enlistment, and I wasn't really sure what I wanted to do.” The ad she found promised things like a life coach, career counselling, fitness training, and a full plastic-surgery makeover. “So I went to a live audition. You go into this first little room, and there's a panel of people sitting at a little fold-out table and they were like, 'Tell us what you don't like about yourself.’ I was ready, willing, and able to do what I needed to be chosen.”
The first season threw the contestants one surprise after another. The first was that when the swans arrived to stay in the apartments they’d be living in for the next three months, all the mirrors and reflective surfaces had been removed. For three months, they wouldn’t be able to look at themselves.
The show put the swans through extreme regimens over those months: head-to-toe surgeries that required long, arduous recoveries, combined with constant exercise and strict dieting (including limiting intake to 1,200 calories a day). “All of it was on a schedule and very specific,” explains Carr. “You had times where you were on and going to the doctor, and you had handlers that were going to move you from one location to another that had to be careful about you looking in any mirrors. Other times you had these huge swaths of downtime. There were no phones. They told me that they watched the Food Network all the time because they were not eating a lot of food. They really were, in a word that we understand now—quarantined from others.”
It was in that downtime when the swans really got to know each other. They became one another’s support systems and began to form a genuine sisterhood. They commiserated over promises the show made and then underdelivered on. “I only got three therapy sessions,” remembers Garza, “but all they wanted to talk about was my relationship. I was like, ‘Am I here for me, or am I here for my relationship?’" The so-called life coaching, Garza says, was little more than someone berating them and telling them how fat they still were. And as they began to lean on each other more and more, it turned out the producers had a huge twist up their sleeves: The swans weren’t just undergoing big physical changes—they were going to compete with one another in a pageant. 
The women learned this just before the dramatic moment on screen when they finally saw their transformed selves for the first time. “We were each other’s cheerleaders. They said we’re going to be pitted against each other, and only one of you moves on,” remembers Garza. “I was absolutely shocked. You gave me all of this to build me up, and then you immediately took it away. It was very debilitating from a mental-health standpoint.”
When Garza went head to head with another contestant, she lost. "In my mind, I'm like, I just had a $250,000 makeover, and I'm still not good enough for your fly-by-night pageant. It was drilled into us the whole time that we had to get to the pageant." Then they brought her in for the pageant as a wild card. "They told me again that I was not chosen, and it was devastating.” Garza shares perhaps the worst indictment a contestant could offer: “I left there with less self-esteem than I went in with.”
A twist that might have broken a family
For Bravata, who participated in Season 2, the audition process was different. Casting for the second season began while the first season was airing, and it was actually her sister Gina who began the application process. Gina had seen in an ad on Craigslist that the production was looking for sisters, so she reached out. When she received an enthusiastic response, the sisters officially applied together. But only Kari would get on the show.
“When they told me I was going to be a swan, I immediately shut down. I thought, ‘Why would you tell me this if my sister’s not here?’ recalls Bravata. “That was the first time I thought, something’s not right. This isn’t what I signed up for. They don’t have good intentions.” The producers then told Bravata that she would have to tell Gina, on camera, that she hadn't made it. “I genuinely feel like that was one of the worst days of my life. It’s a hard memory for me,” says Bravata.
But that wasn’t the end of the sisters’ story on the show. It turned out Bravata wasn’t going to be the only sister competing on The Swan. Gina was going with her. But Gina’s participation was to be kept a secret—one the entire season hinged on. “The second I drive away, they turn the camera on Gina and tell her, ‘You’re going to be there, and your sister doesn’t know.’ And then they threaten her for the next three months of the show that she’ll be liable for $5 million if she breaks the secret. She has to make sure I don’t find out,” Bravata says.
Bravata sees all this as further proof that The Swan was designed to tear women apart instead of delivering them the promised better life. “The twist was trying to break a family. They wanted competition,” Bravata says. “There is nothing in our DNA that would even allow us to compete with each other like that. I’m not sure what they thought they were doing, but what they did is they made us hate them,” she says.
An unexpected upside
The most remarkable thing about The Swan: Behind the Mirror is that this isn’t the tragic story you’d anticipate. Though the reality show was predicated on the entertainment value of tearing women apart, Behind the Mirror shows an aftermath in which the opposite outcome somehow came to fruition. Through the stories of these resilient women, Carr crafts a larger narrative of sisterhood.
“When we were in production and we were shooting it in L.A., I recognized the laughter and the sweetness from these women,” says Carr. “I thought to myself, ‘Is there a real way for this film to have a happy ending?’ She found it by way of DeLisa Stiles, the winner of Season 2, whose walk-off song was ‘F-ckin’ Perfect’ by Pink. "As soon as I heard that—and by the way, I did not have the rights to the song—it came to me: I want everybody to lip sync that song. It was literally when this woman played this song, and it crystallized in my head. It's one of my favorite things I've ever done and will do.”
But before that moment comes a deeply touching reunion between the swans. Though they talk constantly through group chats and Facebook groups, they live scattered across the United States and don’t often get to see each other in person. But Carr’s film granted them the opportunity to come together and reconnect over their shared experiences. Their simple joy in being with one another is a surprising moment of warmth in the film. The ladies cheer to “tits, teeth, and trauma,” and “to being enough.” 
This collective scene was essential, for Carr, to show audiences how an unexpected positive came from such a harrowing experience. Pulling it off was no small feat. “Most networks will say, ‘You get three characters. We cannot follow 12 different people,’” says Carr. “So I said, ‘Hey, if we’re doing this, I need to follow everybody. We all need to be interviewed, and then I need for them to come together and do a reunion.’ That is extremely expensive. I was not sure if it was going to be a yes, but that was my dream. And when your dream is realized as a documentarian or filmmaker of any kind, you feel extremely special.”  
Bravata is excited for people to see that the show’s participants are far from wounded animals. “I think it's human nature for people to assume the worst for us now. They want to see how crazy our lives have become, and I just think they're gonna really enjoy that we're thriving, that we are friends, and that we're doing great.”
There was one question I still had to ask the swans: Would Bravata and Garza, despite everything, do it all again?
“I would do it again 1,000 times,” says Bravata. "I would like to think I’d do it on my own terms. I’d do it without allowing anyone to make me feel less than what we all deserve to feel. The plastic surgery and friendships and this bond we all have—I would do it again.”
Garza agrees. “For me, the good outweighs the bad. I felt shame for the past two decades. I loved the plastic surgery and the way it made me look. I feel everything happens for a reason, and sometimes the most traumatic, terrible things in your life are actually the most beautiful things. You have to decide whether you’re a victim of life circumstances, or if you’re going to use that to empower yourself. I love who I am now.”
By and large, the swans didn’t regret the plastic surgery. Many of them were happy with the results, and all of them went on the show because they wanted the operations. The documentary does detail that some of the work they had done hasn’t been as successful as it was originally envisioned to be, and the dentist who performed the dental surgeries ultimately had her license suspended. Still, the biggest problem for the swans was in how they were treated, and how they were presented on screen. “It made us look really weak, and made us look like broken women,” Garza reflects. “I used to joke that I’d rather tell people I had an STI than admit I was on The Swan because of the way it was edited.”
“We didn’t hate ourselves. We didn’t go there because we thought we were ugly,” says Bravata. “We went there and were told we were ugly. If I could share one thing, it’s that we’re amazing women. We are stronger than anyone could ever imagine because that was not for the faint of heart. We are on the other side, we survived, and that should be celebrated.”
Adds Garza: “In the original fairy tale of the Ugly Duckling, it turned out that it was a swan the whole time. It was just in the wrong nest.”

US sanctions 10 entities for allegedly supporting Iran’s military
Individuals and firms in China, Pakistan, Turkiye, Iran and Saudi Arabia have been sanctioned as part of broad-reaching economic pressure campaign.
United States President Donald Trump’s administration has added a group of 10 individuals and companies to its list of global entities being sanctioned over alleged ties to the Iranian military.
In a statement on Tuesday, the US Treasury accused representatives and technology firms based in China, Pakistan, Turkiye and Saudi Arabia of procuring weapons and parts for Iran’s military. Three of the sanctioned entities were located in Iran.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Iraq seeks US exemption from ban on Iranian flights
- list 2 of 3Flights between Iran and Iraq’s Najaf resumes amid US aviation sanctions
- list 3 of 3Iranians stock up on food and medicine as fears of new US fighting grow
“Today’s action further degrades the Iranian regime’s ability to reconstitute its weapons programs and increases the costs for those who choose to aid Tehran’s military procurement efforts,” the US Treasury said.
The sanctions were undertaken as part of Operation Economic Outcast, a Treasury Department effort to further restrict Iran’s access to global markets.
Iran has been locked in a war with the US and Israel since February 28, after the two allies launched a series of deadly attacks targeting Tehran’s leadership and military.
But critics have argued that the war has no clear end in sight, despite claims of victory on both sides.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced Operation Economic Outcast in August, aimed at pressuring Tehran into agreeing to a deal to end the war.
Trump claimed the operation would usher in “economic warfare and isolation on an unprecedented scale”, and he warned that any country that participates in trade with Iran would face “tremendous” consequences.
As part of the campaign’s initial volley of sanctions, China-based firms and business leaders were targeted.
But China remains one of Iran’s largest trading partners, and the Trump administration has faced scrutiny over how forcefully it would confront Beijing over its participation in Iran’s economy.
At the time, Bessent defended the administration’s decision to delay certain sanctions by saying, “We’re giving everyone the opportunity to remedy bad behaviour. Why would I want to blow up the global financial system?”
Trump recently hosted Chinese President Xi Jinping for his first state visit to the White House in more than a decade, after which Trump touted progress in the trade talks between the two countries.
Despite the warming ties, several Chinese firms were among those sanctioned in Tuesday’s announcement.
They included the Hong Kong-based company EC Mojo Technology Co Ltd, as well as one of its representatives, Li Fen.
EC Mojo had “provided electronic components” to the Iranian military, while Li “attempted to evade sanctions and export controls”, Treasury claimed.
Another designated firm was Saudi-based Cavalier Dynamics for Technologies Company. As part of its announcement, the US Treasury said it would take action “in coordination with Saudi government partners”.
All those included in Tuesday’s sanctions were allegedly involved in procuring “weapons and weapons components for Iran’s Ministry of Defense and Armed Forces Logistics (MODAFL), the entity responsible for weapons research, production and acquisition for Iran’s armed forces”.
Operation Economic Outcast has also sanctioned Iranian economic sectors not directly tied to its military.
Recent sanctions on the civilian airline sector have left some passengers stranded, after some Iranian airlines and international carriers suddenly cancelled flights to and from Iran.
But experts have questioned how effective the heightened sanctions campaign may ultimately be. Iran has faced heavy US sanctions for years, though on Tuesday its currency fell to a record low, amid war-related pressures.

U.S. President Donald Trump said Tuesday he is considering establishing a 10-member committee to oversee the artificial intelligence sector following talks with leading technology executives at the White House.
Trump also said the tech executives signed an agreement that is "morally binding," without providing details.
Pressure is mounting on the Trump administration to address risks posed by AI, after OpenAI and Anthropic reported their AI agents had gone rogue and hacked into other companies' systems. The intrusions prompted researchers to warn that some AI developers believe the technology could kill humans within a decade, fueling calls for action from both Democratic and Republican lawmakers.
Trump also said tech companies will work to make communities "happy" about the construction of data centers, as the industry faces growing local opposition to the facilities' expansion.
Data centers, which provide the computing power used to develop and run AI systems, are a central component of the AI boom. Their expansion has drawn opposition in communities nationwide over concerns about electricity demand, utility costs and other local impacts, prompting companies to offer incentives aimed at easing those concerns.
Data centers are "going to do things for the community that will be really financially beneficial," Trump told reporters.
Executives in Tuesday's White House meeting included Anthropic's Dario Amodei, Meta's Mark Zuckerberg, Google's Sundar Pichai, Nvidia's Jensen Huang and Palantir's Alex Karp. From the Trump administration, tech adviser Michael Kratsios and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick attended, as did U.S. House Speaker Mike Johnson.
Trump met with the executives the same day his aides announced a new AI tool that they say will make it easier for the public to use government services. Silicon Valley executives attended the launch event on Tuesday, including Meta's Dina Powell McCormick and Sequoia partner Shaun Maguire. Airbnb co-founder Joe Gebbia led the design of the new tool. Silicon Valley companies Google, SpaceX, Meta and 8VC were listed in the launch event's program as sponsors.
Trump said at the launch event that he does not want to work with Chinese President Xi Jinping on governing AI technology, adding that doing so would make it harder for U.S. companies to build better AI products than their Chinese counterparts. Trump also said that he discussed AI with Xi when he visited the U.S. last week, adding that the US already works with Xi's government "in so many ways."
"We're leading now over China and everyone else, and I want to keep it that way," Trump said at the event.
Bipartisan legislative efforts in the Senate centered around AI regulation have stalled. U.S. Senator Ted Cruz of Texas, one of the Republicans involved in the discussions, said on Tuesday that he hopes to "move forward with it" after the November midterm elections.

The unexpected El Niño threat lurking behind heat and drought
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
20:39:15 UTC
05:39:15 KST

In Brief
- Severe frosts caused by El Niño have destroyed crops in Papua New Guinea.
- Australian crops could face the same issue.
In the highlands of Papua New Guinea, crops have been killed by drought and frost.
Severe frosts have destroyed food crops such as taro, sweet potato, bananas and sugarcane, leaving some local communities scrambling for food.
El Niño is producing similar conditions as previous frosts including those of 1972, 1997–98 and 2015–16 – that left thousands of Papua New Guineans without food and water.
This may seem like a faraway, albeit worrying, problem for those in Australia. After all, we typically talk about climate change through the lens of heat and drought.
But for Australian farmers, frost risk is a growing concern. This is particularly true as the strengthening El Niño — a naturally occurring weather phenomenon that drives variations in temperature and winds across the Pacific — threatens to bring increasingly fierce and frequent frosts to farming regions.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
How frost forms
Radiation frost, commonly known as frost, typically forms after a cold, clear and windless night.
Clear skies, rather than cloudy ones, allow more heat to be released into the atmosphere. This causes the temperature of the soil and air to drop. Dry conditions can speed up the cooling process because parched soils store less daytime heat. While moist soil can retain more warmth and buffer the effects of subzero temperatures, it can’t completely protect crops or plants from severe frosts.
Cold air is generally heavier than warmer air, meaning dense cold air flows into valleys and other low-lying areas. These are known as frost hollows. Calm conditions stop this cold air moving or mixing with warmer winds.
Chilly temperatures can indicate when frost may strike. Depending on where you are, if the minimum forecast temperature is 3°C or below, you could be in for a frost. This is because the ground can drop below 0°C even when the official air temperature is higher.
All about timing
Frost can be devastating for crops.
Severe frosts can cause the water in and around plant cells to freeze and rupture. This irreversibly damages or even kills the plant.
In cereal crops, such as wheat, barley and oats, the biggest risk is reproductive damage. During the process of flowering, crops produce delicate reproductive structures that together form the grains we eat and feed to livestock.
If frost hits during flowering, the freezing temperatures can kill these parts of the plant, potentially wiping out an entire crop in one night. This can leave farmers without enough grain to sell and then cover the cost of growing that crop.
The extent of damage depends on various factors, including the timing, length and severity of a frost. However, growers can reduce their frost risk by selecting crop varieties that flower outside the main frost window. Researchers are also working to identify genes that could make future varieties less susceptible to frost. However, none of these traits make a crop immune to freezing temperatures.
Australian growers on alert
For Australian farmers, severe frosts are a growing concern.
The Birchip Cropping Group, Australia’s biggest farmer-led agricultural research organisation, reported in August that northwest Victorian crops were on track for an impressive harvest after an unusually wet start to winter.
However, growers immediately turned their attention to potential risks — particularly damaging frost. Their worries were well-founded, with Australia’s Bureau of Meteorology issuing multiple frost warnings across the country. Some farmers in the southern Mallee have reported minor crop damage and at Wickepin North in Western Australia. But thankfully this year, most Australian growers appear to have dodged the frost bullet.
What we can do
For Australian farmers, staying informed is key. To protect their crops and businesses from the effects of frost, grain growers can identify potential frost hollows, choose crop varieties that flower at different times, and keep an eye on short-term weather warnings. They should also check their paddocks after a night of cold, clear weather.
Governments in Australia and across the Pacific can support farmers by funding local weather stations. They should also continue to invest in crop research to identify varieties that are more resistant to frost, as well as drought and extreme heat.
Papua New Guinea’s mountain communities are struggling to salvage what’s left of their crops. Australian farmers can avoid the worst effects of frost, but only if the government continues to fund the forecasting services and research they urgently need.

how LAS art foundation transforms quantum computing and clubs into art
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
20:35:24 UTC
05:35:24 KST

how LAS art foundation transforms quantum computing and clubs into art
from berghain to venice, the organization takes immersive exhibitions beyond traditional museums, using unconventional spaces to reach new audiences.
LAS Art Foundation in Berlin and beyond
LAS Art Foundation, formerly Light Art Space, is the Berlin-based organization that looks to create works of art that are born from the bleeding edge. Some of its most famous shows, born from a synergy between art and technology, have occupied Berlin’s Halle am Berghain and Kraftwerk. These club and event venues are fitting environments for the typical LAS show, where monumental use of sound, lights, and moving digital images transforms the spaces into a pulsating, immersive experience that couldn’t be contained in the traditional white cube. In conversation with designboom, LAS CEO and co-founder Bettina Kames talks about their first exhibition with artist Refik Anadol, their mission for new media, and their approach to AI and quantum computing.
a technology forward approach to art
Although LAS is often associated with the German scene, it’s fundamentally a nomadic organization. It has been able to fill infamous Berlin clubs with sprawling works by artists like Ian Cheng, Laure Prouvost, and Jakob Kudsk Steensen. Now, they’ve gone on to occupy spaces in Venice, the home of the contemporary art biennale, with exhibitions like Josèfa Ntjam’s swell of spæc(i)es and Natasha Tontey: The Phantom Combatants, alongside hosting an online residency that is supporting the works of Xin Liu & Eunjo Lee. But no matter the URL or IRL, a LAS show is easy to recognize for its forward-thinking approach to applied technologies. Reflecting on this identity, Kames looks back to its founding days in 2016, when she and co-founder Jan Fischer were asking themselves, ‘why another art foundation?’
‘it really needs to be an art foundation about the future,’ says Kames, recounting the conversations and ideas shared between her, Fischer, and the people around them. ‘That’s why LAS is at the intersection of art, the latest technologies, the latest breakthroughs in science.’ One such example of this is Laure Prouvost’s 2025 exhibition, WE FELT A STAR DYING, which uses a multisensory experience to untangle the complexities of quantum computing. In their online explanation of the exhibition, LAS even includes a short pop-up window that explains what a quantum computer is for those who come from a non-technical background.
The intersection between art and technology
‘Often when we talk about the present, but also the future, it’s related to massive changes, rapid developments and technology,’ remarks Kames on this didactic approach to exhibition making. ‘It’s linked to something like AI. For example, we did this exhibition about quantum computing [Laure Prouvost’s] and often these are topics that are quite complex and sometimes hard to understand, sometimes even frightening. So we said it’s important to build bridges into society, to take society along. And art can be this kind of door opener’
forms of accessibility in art
Kames goes on to talk about the different modalities they’ve used to make the exhibitions more accessible, which have included guided tours and inviting high school students to get involved. Seeing as their events are often very bright and involve sound elements, they’ll also have lower-impact versions of the show, where the lights and sounds are more muted, to accommodate these needs. And perhaps the most particular of these moves toward accessibility is its choice of venue. ‘It’s very important that we always activate different spaces like Berghain or like Kraftwerk. And it’s often spaces that don’t have the same barrier like a museum space. It’s easier to come to Berghain. It’s easier to come to Kraftwerk if you’re not part of the art scene or cultural scene,’ says Kames on how these spaces don’t have the same perhaps intimidating presence that traditional art spaces might have. Additionally, being in these new contexts encourages both artist and audience to consider what the boundaries of ‘art’ can be.
Engaging the senses beyond the screen
One of the first things audiences gather from an LAS show like Anadol’s or Cheng’s is that it’s incredibly engaging, looking more like a nightclub than anything seen at a typical museum. But Kames points out that the lights and sound don’t detract from the theory and artistic rigor. ‘It’s really an exhibition by the leading artists of our times on the highest curatorial level. And with all your senses doesn’t always mean a flashy LED screen. It could be a smell or these beautiful sculptures. It can mean many things even though obviously some of our content is digital.’
Evaluating and re-evaluating the cutting edge
Although their programs reach into different mediums, LAS is, at its core, a space for technological collaboration. On this, Kames remarks, ‘one of the reasons to launch the quantum sensing program,’ with Prouvost’s exhibition, ‘was really to embrace a new ecosystem, a new territory of technologies related to quantum computing, and experiment with them and to develop new artistic media with them. So Laure’s exhibition, for example, which was a collaboration with Google AI quantum and their lead scientist, we developed our own quantum AI diffusion model, because there wasn’t one in the world for moving image.’
She goes on to address some of the controversy that arises in regard to the use of AI in the art space, saying, ‘what we’re trying to achieve with LAS is a neutral platform to have discourse, for experimentation, for debate. That applies to AI, same applies for quantum technologies, same applies for whatever. We see this polarization in the world and I think it’s important to create spaces that are not feeding into that and do quite the opposite.’ Kames refers back to Refik Anadol’s exhibition in 2019, Latent Being, reflecting ‘back then, like we did that first exhibition on machine learning already arguing [a technology that’s] at the center of what we’re facing now. And we debated then, ‘what is our position on that? What is important for LAS? or what is maybe also missing that we can contribute?’
project info:
organization: LAS Art Foundation, formerly Light Art Space | @las_artfoundation
CEO & co-founder: Bettina Kames

France intends to borrow record €340 billion as Covid-era debt comes due
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

France intends to borrow record €340 billion as Covid-era debt comes due
The French government will sell a record amount of bonds to investors next year as it faces a surge in Covid-era debt due for redemption and needing to be refinanced, the public debt management office said on Tuesday amid mounting concern about France's surging public deficit and borrowing rates.
France indicated Tuesday it plans to borrow a record amount on the bond market next year, even as worries about the government's spending has seen borrowing rates hit levels unseen since the global financial crisis.
The AFT agency that manages the government's borrowing on debt markets said it plans to borrow 340 billion euros ($385 billion) in 2027, some 28 billion euros more than this year, to help finance government spending and repay debt coming due.
AFT, in its announcement two days ahead of the presentation of the government's 2027 budget, said it plans to issue a mixture of medium- and long-term bonds to raise the funds.
The French government is forecasting an interest rate of 4.3 percent for its 10-year bonds in 2027.
On Tuesday, French 10-year bonds were trading on the secondary market at 4.8 percent.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
In recent weeks the yields on French government debt have hit levels last seen during the global financial crisis.
Investors have become increasingly concerned about the size of France's debt, but also the latest data which has shown the government has been unable to reduce deficit spending.
France's public deficit – the annual shortfall of revenue to spending – came in at 5.1 percent of GDP last year and instead of reducing that level as originally planned the government now forecasts it will hit 5.4 percent this year.
Under EU rules, the public deficit is meant to be no more than three percent of GDP.
The higher interest rates on its debt means that the French government has to pay investors more to borrow, leaving it with less funds for current spending.
France's prime minister Sébastien Lecornu vowed earlier this month to cut the deficit next year without resorting to austerity, but with presidential elections just months away the government will be hard pressed to cut spending.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP, Reuters)

Türkiye’s Vatican envoy stresses human dignity, dialogue as foundations for peace
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
20:25:33 UTC
05:25:33 KST

Türkiye’s Ambassador to the Vatican Fahrettin Altun said on Tuesday that religion and diplomacy can play a key role in promoting peace by encouraging dialogue, human dignity and coexistence among people of different backgrounds.
“Can humanity learn to live together, in peace, while remaining different?” Altun asked in a speech at an event organized by the Carita Politica organization, arguing that the question was particularly relevant amid wars, displacement, inequality and a crisis of confidence in international institutions.
Altun said the world was experiencing not only political and geopolitical crises but also “an anthropological and moral crisis,” arguing that modern consumer culture increasingly defines people through what they possess, consume and desire.
He said religious traditions offer an alternative understanding of humanity by emphasizing responsibility, sacrifice, meaning and the ability to transcend the boundaries of the self.
“Religious traditions also represent a profound moral challenge to the reductionist conception of the human being in our age,” he said.
Referring to the Quran, Altun highlighted the principle that human dignity belongs to all people, regardless of political identity, nationality or ethnicity.
He also cited the Quranic concept of lita'arafu, meaning “so that you may know one another,” saying differences should be understood as an invitation to encounter rather than a source of conflict.
“When we encounter difference, we essentially have two choices,” he said. “We can perceive the other as a threat. Or we can attempt to know the other.”
“The first produces fear. The second makes dialogue possible,” he added.
Altun said diplomacy should go beyond the management of relations between states, describing it as “the art of recognizing the existence of the other.”
He stressed that dialogue does not require people to abandon their religious or cultural identities.
“A Muslim can remain a Muslim. A Christian can remain a Christian. A believer and a non-believer can remain faithful to their respective convictions,” he said. “And still they can meet around the dignity of the human person.”
“Unity does not require uniformity,” he added, calling for “commonality without uniformity,” “difference without hostility” and “identity without exclusion.”
Altun said international politics cannot rely solely on calculations of power and interests, and that sustainable peace requires a sense of justice.
“When international relations are reduced entirely to calculations of power, sooner or later the interests of the powerful commence to override the requirements of justice,” he said.
He said religious traditions could remind policymakers of the human consequences behind political decisions, including those concerning war, sanctions and migration.
On artificial intelligence, Altun said technological advances also raise fundamental questions about humanity, such as: “What does it mean to be human?”
“Technology cannot answer these questions for us. Markets cannot answer them. Power cannot answer them,” he said, arguing that they require philosophy, ethics and religion.
Altun said peace should not be understood solely as the absence of conflict or the signing of agreements.
“Peace starts precisely there,” he said, referring to the moment when one person can recognize another as “a fellow human being” across borders, religions, civilizations and political disagreements.
Archbishop Paul Richard Gallagher, the Holy See’s secretary for relations with states and international organizations, said the Vatican considers freedom of religion and worship the first of fundamental rights.
Gallagher said the Vatican and religious communities can contribute to peace and diplomacy, describing the Vatican as “probably the oldest institution of operational diplomacy.”
Referring to crises in the multilateral system, Gallagher said: “We are witnessing the self-determination of the multilateral system turning into crises that no one can now end.”

‘Reformed hacker’ busted over links to group behind FBI breach
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
20:17:52 UTC
05:17:52 KST

‘Reformed hacker’ busted over links to group behind FBI breach
FBI Director Kash Patel and Dutch police have announced the arrest of a high-profile hacker suspected of being a leader of ShinyHunters, a cybercrime group that recently claimed to have stolen data on “almost all” FBI agents.
Dutch authorities first disclosed the arrest on Monday, before officials in both countries confirmed it on Tuesday. Patel described ShinyHunters as a “global cybercrime and threat actor group linked to cyberattacks in the United States, the Netherlands, and around the world.”
Dutch police said the suspect was arrested on September 15 on suspicion of cybercrime offenses and attempting to instigate at least two murders abroad. US and Dutch officials said further arrests in the case could follow.
Neither agency identified the suspect. However, Benjamin Korper, head of Amsterdam-based cybersecurity firm Neo Security, said the person arrested was the company’s offensive security lead, Pepijn van der Stap.
Korper said Van der Stap had been carefully vetted after his release from prison in December 2025 and before joining the company, adding that he was shocked by the arrest.
The supposedly reformed 24-year-old hacker gained international notoriety back in 2023 when he was convicted of data theft and extortion. He subsequently publicly disavowed cybercrime. Van der Stap has claimed his cybercriminal background ultimately gave him knowledge useful “for building and protecting, not breaking.”
The ShinyHunters group, however, has denied any connection to Van der Stap. “That individual has no association with us. Frankly, we are laughing,” the group told Cybernews in a statement, mocking Dutch police as “unskilled and incompetent.”
“Dutch police are chasing attention and public favor after the massive embarrassment as a result of the Odido hack. They want to seem like they are ahead of the FBI in investigating ShinyHunters,” the group added, referring to a major breach and subsequent extortion attempt suffered by the Netherlands’ largest mobile operator this February.
Media reports on the affair suggested Van der Stap might have been a victim of an elaborate ruse, presumably set up by a ShinyHunters spinoff faction, known as the Scattered Lapsus$ Hunters. According to Brian Krebs, an American investigative journalist focused on for-profit cybercriminals, Van der Stap has been engaged in a bitter dispute with the leader of the spinoff, known only as ‘Rey,’ over control of the ShinyHunters branding.
Sources told Krebs that the faction may have deliberately used Van der Stap’s former alias ‘Umbreon’ – a popular Pokemon character – to implicate him. Namely, the Umbreon imagery was used by the group during a recent attack on a rival ransomware gang and the targeted attack on the FBI, with both incidents occurring after Van der Stap’s arrest and now suspected of being a part of the ruse.
Previously, the group said that the alleged FBI breach, during which personal data of “almost all” agents was stolen, was “not financially motivated.” Instead, ShinyHunters demanded the agency pull a cybersecurity advisory, claiming it contains false allegations about the group. The group originally set up a one-week deadline for the FBI to heed the demand but ultimately dropped it and said it was never a “threat” and “nothing” would happen should the agency refuse to accept their demands.

UAE vice president visits Saudi Arabia in first visit since rift
Sept 29 - UAE Vice President Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahyan visited Saudi Arabia on Tuesday and met with the Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and the kingdom's defence minister, the first visit by a senior UAE official to the kingdom since a deep rift emerged between the two Gulf powers last year.
The visit, following an invitation by Saudi Defence Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman, occurred as Riyadh faces increasing pressure from the Iran-backed Houthis, who have for weeks fired salvos of missiles and drones at the kingdom.
Saudi Arabia has been trying to rally international support to confront the Houthis, but it was not immediately clear if that request extended to the UAE.
The United Arab Emirates was once Saudi Arabia’s main regional partner in the war against the Houthis.
Sheikh Mansour and Prince Khalid discussed topics of mutual interest and ways to enhance cooperation and coordination between the two countries, according to a post by the Saudi defence ministry on X.
Sheikh Mansour, in a separate meeting with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman on Tuesday, reviewed the "fraternal relations" between the two countries and developments in the region, the Saudi state news agency reported.
The UAE and Saudi Arabia's years-long disagreements over everything from geopolitics to oil policy came out into the open in December when an advance by a UAE-backed southern Yemeni separatist group brought it close to Saudi borders.
Saudi Arabia condemned the UAE’s involvement and carried out an airstrike on a UAE-linked weapons shipment at the port of Mukalla in Yemen.
The UAE then announced it had withdrawn all its forces from Yemen but tensions have remained.
Yemen has been caught in a 12-year-long civil war since the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa, prompting a Saudi-led military intervention. REUTERS

EU top diplomat says bloc wants to 'upgrade' Syria partnership
EU foreign affairs chief Kaja Kallas said on Tuesday in Damascus that the European Union wanted to "upgrade" its partnership with Syria and help boost its recovery but called for further domestic reform.
"The European Union is using its political and economic tools to help Syria on the path of inclusive and peaceful transition," Kallas told a press conference with Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani.
After the new authorities toppled longtime ruler Bashar al-Assad in December 2024, the EU lifted its economic sanctions on Syria and in May this year restored an EU-Syria cooperation agreement.
"Now we aim to mobilise even more investment and upgrade our partnership. But that's also very much dependent on Syria's side," Kallas said, while also calling for institutional and security improvements.
"Aid alone cannot build Syria. Foreign and domestic investment needs trust, and trust needs security, clear rules, rule of law, functioning institutions" and the equal participation of women in society, as well as reconciliation and transitional justice, she said.
"We are ready to help to build the institutions," she said.
The 27-nation bloc has launched a new chapter with Syria since Assad's fall, with EU chief Ursula von der Leyen telling President Ahmed al-Sharaa in January that Europe would "do everything it can" to support Syria's recovery.
The country is trying to rebuild, reboot its economy and attract investment after more than 13 years of conflict that killed more than half a million people and ravaged the country's infrastructure and industry.
Kallas noted that the EU "is already providing 620 million euros for recovery, humanitarian needs and strengthening institutions".
The war also sent millions of Syrians fleeing abroad, and Syrians have made up the lion's share of asylum-seekers in the bloc over a decade, with a push for large numbers to eventually return home.
Shaibani said that he and Kallas had "discussed several tracks, beginning with achieving a new partnership agreement" to replace the one dating to the 1970s, indicating that steps to advance the issue would continue into next year.
He noted that Syria had been "active in combatting cross-border crime, combatting illegal migration, drugs and human trafficking".
"We discussed ways to support the capacities of the Syrian coast guard, in the belief that the security of the Mediterranean also begins with our shores," he said.
"Syria's security is an integral part of Europe's own security," he added.

TV Networks Resume White House Pool Coverage, But Questions Remain Over CNN’s Access
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
20:11:10 UTC
05:11:10 KST

Major TV networks are resuming their pool coverage of President Donald Trump this week after uniting to suspend it following Trump’s move to ban multiple media outlets from the White House. But with uncertainty lingering over CNN’s access, two people familiar with the situation tell TIME that coverage will be decided on a day-by-day basis moving forward.
The five networks that currently make up the White House TV pool—CNN, ABC, CBS, Fox, and NBC—suspended their pool coverage of the President last week in a display of solidarity against the White House’s decision to bar CNN, along with POLITICO and MS NOW, from the grounds.
“The public has a vital interest in receiving accurate, independent information about its government,” the networks said in a joint statement on Sept. 21, when CNN—whose journalists had their press credentials revoked by White House officials days earlier—was scheduled for pool duty. “No administration should restrict a news organization because it objects to its reporting.”
After the Trump Administration began granting journalists from CNN, POLITICO, and MS NOW access to the White House grounds again following a judge’s order on Thursday, the network pool decided to make a good faith effort to resume normal operations on Friday, according to a person familiar with the situation. CBS resumed its normal, rotational pool duty, and CNN was granted access to complete a pool assignment at an event at the National Archives, the person familiar with the situation says.
But, according to that individual, later on Friday, the White House contacted the pool and wanted to know if it would replace CNN for its scheduled pool duties on Saturday. The person says that the White House told the pool that it was going to make a day-by-day decision on the situation. The White House ended up blocking CNN from traveling with the President on Air Force One on Saturday.
CNN declined to comment.
The pool decided not to replace CNN with another TV network for its pool duties on Saturday, according to the person familiar with the situation. The networks individually decided whether to cover any events that were open press that day.
The person familiar with the situation says that the TV networks are continuing pool coverage this week, but the situation is fluid. Going forward, if the White House won’t grant CNN access when it’s CNN’s turn on pool duty, the TV pool will decide whether to replace CNN that day or not, depending on if the news that day merits it. The person says that there will likely be a high bar to meet to justify replacing CNN with another network on pool duty, if something is very newsworthy that day.
What is the White House press pool—and why does it matter?
The White House press pool comprises journalists from multiple news organizations who accompany the sitting President to events. Space at these gatherings is often limited, so the pool system enables news organizations to collaborate and share resources. The five networks in the TV pool are tasked with recording video footage of the President at pool-designated events on a rotating basis.
It is rare for a sitting Commander-in-Chief to travel or hold events without the TV pool in attendance. The White House Correspondents’ Association, which acts as a “go-between” for journalists and the White House and helps ensure that journalists have access, has called pool duty “an essential element of the work of White House correspondents because one never knows when the world will need good information about precisely where the president of the United States is and what he is doing at any moment.”
“The press is acting as a representative of the public in these spaces and they need access to these spaces because they can get information that they can’t get over the phone or watching a video feed or being outside of the grounds of the White House,” says Erin Carroll, a professor at Georgetown Law. “You can see things, you can ask questions, you can have conversations when you’re in these spaces that are not possible if you’re not allowed into them.”
Trump previously told reporters that there weren’t any specific stories that spurred him to bar CNN, POLITICO, and MS NOW from the White House, but that “it’s really just cumulative stories over the last few years, you get sick of it,” adding that “they purposely write negative news.”
Carroll pushes back on Trump’s complaint.
“The press’s key role under the Constitution is to act as a watchdog,” she says. “In acting as an independent watchdog, it may be that those stories or things that journalists print feel ‘negative’ or ‘critical.’ That is the press’s constitutional role, and so that is what the press is doing in these situations. For Trump to complain that stories are overly negative is unfair because, in one sense, that’s the press’s job—they’re there to check the three branches of government.”
Where do Trump’s efforts to ban CNN, POLITICO, and MS NOW stand?
On Sept. 18, Trump announced that he was banning CNN, POLITICO, and MS NOW from the White House grounds. The following day, journalists from those three organizations were not allowed into the White House and officials revoked their press credentials.
On Sept. 21, CNN, POLITICO, and MS NOW sued the Trump Administration, saying in a joint statement that they were doing so “to protect our First Amendment rights and defend the principle that the government does not decide what the press reports or publishes.” Trump said later that morning that “the White House is not instituting an assault on the Free Press, something which I cherish,” but that “it is instituting an assault on the FAKE News.”
On Thursday, a federal judge issued a temporary restraining order against the White House’s decision to bar the three news outlets from the grounds, saying that the ban “likely violated” the “constitutional due process rights” of CNN, POLITICO, and MS NOW. The judge ordered that the Trump Administration grant access to journalists from the three news outlets, effective immediately “until further order of the court or the expiration of this temporary restraining order.”
Following the order, journalists from the affected news outlets have once again been permitted to access the White House grounds.
The judge’s temporary order will expire on Oct. 8, but the three news outlets on Monday requested that the court extend their journalists’ access to the White House and ensure that the Trump Administration grants the three news outlets “the same access to the White House and the President that they had before September 18, 2026, including the restoration of all hard passes revoked on or about that date.”
Theodore J. Boutrous Jr., a lawyer representing CNN, MS NOW, and POLITICO, argued in a statement shared with news outlets following the latest court filing that the White House’s effort to block his clients was “a blatant violation of the First Amendment and due process.”
“The President and his administration have continued to make clear that this ban has only one purpose: to punish reporting he doesn’t like. That’s retaliation and viewpoint discrimination, pure and simple,” Boutrous argued in the statement. “With the district court’s temporary restraining order expiring next week, it is critical to ensure that the White House continues to be prevented from implementing this unconstitutional ban on the free press.”
What does that mean for CNN’s access to perform its White House pool duties?
Whether or not CNN will be allowed access to resume its pool duties going forward is unclear.
Although CNN was blocked from traveling with the President on Saturday, the network is currently scheduled to be on pool duty this coming Thursday. But it remains unclear if CNN will actually be called to perform its pool duty that day; Trump is scheduled to travel this coming Wednesday, when CBS is scheduled for pool duty. According to the person familiar with the situation, CBS will stay on pool duty until Trump returns to D.C., which, at the moment, is scheduled to be this coming Friday.
The person familiar with the situation tells TIME that it is unclear what will happen with CNN’s next shift on pool duty next week.
In a statement to TIME, a White House official called Trump “the most accessible President in history,” adding that he is “holding open press events, regular gaggles and interviews, taking questions nearly every day, and speaking directly to the American people through social media.”
“But if a reporter walks into an interview with their headline and narrative already decided, why do they need to be in the room? They can write their garbage from anywhere,” the official said. “Even after outlets were given access to the White House, they declined to cover various events proving this isn’t about access. It’s performative and dishonest.”
The statement did not address TIME’s question about the current status of CNN’s participation in the press pool.
Carroll says that the federal judge’s order from last week is limited to ordering the Trump Administration to give back CNN, POLITICO, and MS NOW their press credentials to the White House grounds; the temporary restraining order doesn’t say anything about the press pool.
In a separate case, The Associated Press filed a lawsuit against Trump Administration officials in 2025, after the organization’s journalists were banned from the White House press pool following the news outlet’s decision to continue using the original name for the Gulf of Mexico in its coverage, instead of “Gulf of America,” per an Executive Order issued by Trump.
A federal judge in that case ruled that The Associated Press had to be allowed back into the press pool, but a federal appeals court later issued a temporary ruling that paused that decision, with one of the judges writing that the White House “retains discretion to determine, including on the basis of viewpoint, which journalists will be admitted” to what the judge called “private workspaces” of the President, such as Air Force One and the Oval Office. That case is still ongoing.
It’s unclear what will happen going forward in terms of whether CNN will be granted access to resume its pool duties, Carroll says.
CarRoll says it was “very heartening” to have seen the TV network pool band together in protest of the White House blocking CNN’s access, adding that “the more that press entities can stand together” in these situations, “the better off the free press generally is and democratic institutions are.”

Israel on alert after Netanyahu attack warning, but IDF reports no specific threat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
20:10:31 UTC
05:10:31 KST

Despite Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s statement that “there are signs that our enemies will try to attack us ahead of the election,” Israel’s defense establishment has not identified an imminent threat. Security officials have long been preparing for scenarios involving escalation and possible Iranian retaliation, which would not necessarily take the form of missile launches. At the same time, Tehran is troubled by the economic pressure it faces and could attack Israel ahead of the U.S. midterm elections in November in an attempt to draw President Donald Trump into negotiations from a position of strength.
According to these assessments, if the Iranians do launch an attack, they could do so shortly before or after Israel’s election. With Tehran seeking to retaliate against Jerusalem, Israel must remain vigilant on all fronts, but there is currently no specific warning or concrete threat.
In an unusual move, a meeting that had been scheduled to take place at the Prime Minister’s Office was moved to another location. Similar steps were taken in the days leading up to and during the war with Iran. However, this was a routine situation assessment attended by members of the inner security Cabinet and senior defense officials, covering several fronts, rather than an emergency meeting. Netanyahu and his military secretary’s security briefing with opposition leader Yair Lapid, meanwhile, was held Tuesday evening at the Prime Minister’s Office.
After the meeting, which lasted about half an hour, Lapid said: “Security threats must be handled professionally and responsibly. Israel’s security and IDF bases are not backdrops for campaign videos. Without going into details, the IDF, Shin Bet and police are prepared for the election, and there is no reason to send the public into a panic. The IDF chief of staff has raised 10 red flags over a shortage of combat troops and attrition in the IDF. If Netanyahu is so concerned about the security situation, he should enlist the 15,000 Haredi men the IDF is lacking.”
Earlier, Lapid and former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett said they had consulted ahead of Lapid’s security briefing with Netanyahu. “Bennett and Lapid stressed the need to discuss the serious and immediate security threat posed by a shortage of 20,000 soldiers and the severe consequences for the reserve forces of the government’s refusal to draft all sectors of Israeli society,” a statement on their behalf said. “They also discussed ways to ensure the integrity of the electoral process and keep political considerations out of security missions.”
No change in the situation assessment
Against the backdrop of the warnings and political statements, Israel’s defense establishment remains on high alert, both defensively and offensively, because of the holiday period and the tense period ahead of the election. However, security officials stress tht there has been no change in the situation assessment in recent days and that, as of Tuesday evening, Israel has no specific, concrete intelligence indicating that hostile actors intend to launch a particular attack.
The defense establishment has been careful to avoid being drawn into the political arena and the exchanges between the parties and has therefore refrained from officially responding to Netanyahu’s statement. In addition, various security officials are exercising caution and prefer not to make statements that could be interpreted as a confrontation with the political leadership.
The IDF stresses that Netanyahu’s statement does not reflect a change in its assessment and that it is not aware of any special preparations or heightened alert beyond what is routinely in place during holidays. Since the ceasefire with Iran, the Israeli Air Force and Military Intelligence Directorate have compiled an updated target bank. At the same time, Israel has maintained closer, more direct coordination than ever with the U.S. military as part of preparations for various defensive and offensive scenarios. The IDF has also recently made operational changes and conducted a series of exercises along Israel’s various borders to ensure an appropriate response in the event of a ground attack.
Despite the general state of vigilance, IDF forces have been scaled back in various sectors. This has included a reduction in forces along the Lebanese border, while the main focus of operations is currently in Judea and Samaria, also known as the West Bank. At bases where the situation assessment permitted it, service members were released for the holiday.
The Home Front Command, meanwhile, has made no changes to instructions for the public and has issued no notice of any development requiring special preparations. The prime minister’s statement did raise public concerns about an imminent attack, but the defense establishment views the situation in considerably less alarming terms. Officials say situation assessments are conducted continuously and evolve daily, with regular intelligence updates on threats across all fronts.

The consignment comprised 15,000 red, pink, white, and orange Lilium blooms cultivated at an altitude of 10,600ft at the world’s highest flower field at Choglamsar, Leh.
SRINAGAR: The first consignment of Ladakh-grown Lilium flowers was dispatched to major flower markets in India on Tuesday, in what the Union Territory administration called a major step towards boosting new economic opportunities and entrepreneurship in the cold desert.The consignment comprised 15,000 red, pink, white, and orange Lilium blooms cultivated at an altitude of 10,600ft at the world’s highest flower field at Choglamsar, Leh. These “A-grade” Liliums have four to five buds on each stem and fetch a premium price of around Rs 150-200 in retail markets. The flowers, with a shelf life of five to seven days, will be sold in various domestic markets, primarily Delhi, Mumbai, and Chandigarh.Ladakh lieutenant governor Vinai Kumar Saxena, who flagged off the consignment at Leh airport, said: “This first-of-its-kind high-altitude commercial floriculture project in Ladakh represents a major agricultural and visual shift for the region, which has, since ages, been identified by its rugged mountains and barren valleys. Millions of Liliums have added a vibrant contrast to this dull landscape.”
Saxena said the “historic” initiative had emerged as a powerful economic tool for creating alternative sustainable livelihoods in Ladakh.
Fifteen women cut, sort and package the flowers at these fields for a daily wage of Rs 900 each. A young, qualified botanist markets the produce to flower markets across the nation. The employees are all locals.The UT administration has directed deputy commissioners of Kargil, Drass, Sham, Changthang and Zanskar districts to replicate the high-altitude floriculture model by identifying at least 20 acres of land in each district.The flower field in Leh, which houses more than 25 lakh blooms, was developed and readied within just two months. It was opened to the public on Sept 17 this year and has since received an overwhelming response from visitors.

Can’t deny employee security clearance based on kin’s antecedents: J&amp;K high court

The committee said CID’s denial of security clearance was not based on any adverse material concerning his conduct, integrity, character or antecedents but stemmed exclusively from 'the alleged antecedents of his brother and the perceived possibility of a security risk arising therefrom'
SRINAGAR: A Jammu and Kashmir high court (HC) panel Tuesday rejected a CID report against an HC staffer, observing that an employee cannot be denied security clearance solely because of his brother’s alleged antecedents.HC engaged Pampore resident Firdous Ahmad Sheikh as a daily-rated worker on April 1, 2010, and posted him at its Srinagar wing. On July 4, 2024, HC regularised his services as an orderly under the Regularization of Services of Daily Wagers in the High Court of Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh Regulations, 2022.Like other appointments, Firdous’s regularisation was subject to CID verification, as is required for govt employment in J&K. On Jan 1, 2026, CID denied him security clearance, citing the “heightened adversity of his brother, Abdul Qayoom Sheikh”.The matter was placed before the Chief Justice, who referred it to the Committee for Appointment and Promotion of Officials, Officers of the High Court Staff, for consideration.
The committee verified Firdous’s testimonials and found them genuine. It said CID’s denial of security clearance was not based on any adverse material concerning his conduct, integrity, character or antecedents but stemmed exclusively from “the alleged antecedents of his brother and the perceived possibility of a security risk arising therefrom”.
The panel said Firdous had served the HC since 2010, and nothing adverse had been reported about his conduct, integrity or performance. “On the contrary, the record reflects that his work and conduct have remained satisfactory and that no vigilance enquiry or complaint is pending against him,” it said.Quoting J&K HC’s Feb 11, 2025 judgment in the Mohd Amir Malik v. Union of India and others case—which held that a person cannot be deprived of his legal or service rights solely on account of the conduct or antecedents of his relatives—the panel noted that liability cannot be fastened upon an individual merely on account of the alleged acts or antecedents of a close relative in the absence of any cogent material establishing the individual’s own involvement, association, complicity or misconduct.

Jordan Bardella, Le Pen’s intended prime minister, faces antisemitism allegations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
20:02:56 UTC
05:02:56 KST

French far-right leader Marine Le Pen, her National Rally party and its allies rallied Tuesday behind her partner in next year’s presidential race, Jordan Bardella, following media reports alleging that he made antisemitic remarks when he was a young party member.
Bardella, 31, is a rising star of France’s hard right. Le Pen has said that if she wins the presidential election in May next year — an election in which polls predict a historic victory for her — she will appoint him prime minister.
But investigative website Mediapart published a report Monday citing allegedly antisemitic statements written by Bardella in the summer of 2013, when he was 17. Among other things, he allegedly wrote that “the banks are all owned by Jews,” “the Jew must dominate other peoples, crush them and rob them” and “a Zionist is necessarily Jewish, inherently and profoundly.”
According to Mediapart, the statements came from Bardella’s private correspondence, though it did not say whether the messages were sent by email or through another medium. The website said it had independently authenticated the correspondence but did not explain how it obtained it.
According to Mediapart, Bardella wrote the remarks about a year and a half after joining the National Front, the far-right party founded by Marine Le Pen’s father, nationalist and Holocaust denier Jean-Marie Le Pen. Marine Le Pen later took control of the party and, following further antisemitic remarks by her father, led efforts to expel him. She then embarked on an extensive campaign to distance the party from his legacy and rehabilitate its image, an effort that became known as the “de-demonization” strategy.
Through those efforts, Marine Le Pen has turned the National Rally into France’s largest political force. Her party now has the largest bloc in the National Assembly, with 119 lawmakers. A poll published Monday indicated that she would comfortably defeat all her rivals in the presidential election next April and May. In the first round, the poll showed her finishing first with about 36% of the vote, followed by far-left candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon with about 18%. In a second-round runoff, the poll showed Le Pen defeating Mélenchon 69%-31%.
If center-right candidate and former Prime Minister Édouard Philippe, currently polling in third place in the first round, were to overtake Mélenchon and advance to the runoff, the poll showed Le Pen defeating him 57%-43%.
Le Pen, it should be recalled, learned only recently that she would be able to run for president after an appeals court reduced her sentence in a corruption case in which she was convicted, including shortening a five-year ban on holding public office. While Le Pen awaited the ruling on her appeal, Bardella, her protégé, waited in the wings. Had the original ban remained in place, he would have replaced her as the party’s presidential candidate. Since she was cleared to run, Le Pen’s campaign has proceeded without significant setbacks, and the Mediapart report marks its first major obstacle.
Le Pen: 'I have complete confidence'; Bardella: 'This is all-out war'
Allegations of antisemitism are particularly sensitive for Le Pen and the National Rally because, to reach the Élysée Palace, she must overcome the obstacles that blocked her path in her three previous presidential campaigns, including perceptions that her party has antisemitic roots.
In recent years, the National Rally has courted Jewish voters, portraying itself as a bulwark against Islamist extremism in France and emphasizing Le Pen’s sustained efforts to distance herself from her father’s legacy and combat antisemitism. Bardella himself, who serves as president of the National Rally, last year became the first leader of the far-right party to be invited by the Israeli government to visit Israel for a conference on combating antisemitism organized by Diaspora Affairs Minister Amichai Chikli.
Yonathan Arfi, president of onseil Représentatif des Institutions (CRIF), the umbrella organization representing French Jewish institutions, said that if the statements attributed to Bardella prove authentic, they would amount to a “stinging repudiation” of the party’s effort to rehabilitate its image.
“How is it possible that a political figure who made such repugnant antisemitic remarks could subsequently rise to such senior positions of responsibility within a party that claims it has changed and that it fights hatred of Jews?” Arfi wrote on X.
Bardella has strongly denied writing the statements attributed to him and said he has begun pursuing a defamation lawsuit against Mediapart. He described the allegations as a “dirty tricks operation” and said: “These remarks are completely absurd. They are not mine.”
Senior National Rally figures presented a united front Tuesday and rallied to Bardella’s defense. At a meeting of the party’s parliamentary group, Le Pen, Bardella and their ally Éric Ciotti sat side by side and described the Mediapart allegations as the opening salvo in an effort to damage the National Rally and Le Pen ahead of the presidential election.
“This is the beginning of an all-out war, of attempts to destabilize the presidential campaign, attempts that, I tell you, will be directed against us one after another,” Bardella said.
Le Pen expressed “complete confidence” in Bardella, who enjoys considerable popularity among young voters and has a massive following on social media. Addressing those she said were plotting campaigns to undermine her party, she said, “We will not let them do it.”
“Know that we will take heavy blows, that the system will do everything and our opponents will do whatever it takes — including the dirtiest tricks imaginable — to try to stop this momentum,” Le Pen said, promising that the National Rally would establish “who is behind this manipulation.”
Left condemns remarks: 'No cosmetic makeover will change the far right'
Mediapart, which specializes in investigative journalism, has become a leading French news outlet since its launch in 2008 and boasts more than a quarter of a million subscribers. The investigative website has exposed a series of major political scandals in recent years, including allegations that Libya financed former President Nicolas Sarkozy’s election campaign and former Budget Minister Jérôme Cahuzac’s undeclared Swiss bank account.
The investigation into Bardella has also reverberated across France over the past 24 hours, prompting a series of condemnations, including from presidential candidates.
“The far right will always remain the far right. No PR firm and no cosmetic facelift will ever change that,” said Raphaël Glucksmann, a candidate in the social democratic primary. Marine Tondelier, leader of the Greens, known as The Ecologists, demanded that Bardella immediately resign from all his positions.
Radical-left leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon, a staunchly anti-Israel candidate who has himself faced accusations of antisemitism, including over his refusal to describe Hamas as a terrorist organization or its actions on October 7 as a “massacre,” also “unequivocally” condemned the statements attributed to Bardella.
He said they were “steeped in conspiracy theories and absurd antisemitism of the most ludicrous kind, if he was indeed the one who made them.”

Merve Aydogan

OpenAI executives brushed aside internal and external warnings about security weaknesses months before its artificial intelligence models escaped testing environments and attacked outside organizations, The New York Times reported Tuesday.
Two employees told the newspaper they emailed senior leaders with concerns that new models were not adequately monitored or secured during testing. Executives reportedly replied that testing had to move quickly to meet release deadlines, and no extra safeguards were added, according to the workers, who spoke anonymously.
The models later broke out of their testing environments and targeted AI firm Hugging Face and other organizations.
In about a dozen incidents, OpenAI's systems tried to breach organizations, including US government agency websites, concealed mistakes, fabricated data and moved files onto the open internet without instruction, according to the outlet.

Hacktron said its July report was first dismissed, while the Objective-See Foundation said its September bug report stalled until it was escalated informally. OpenAI paid them $6,500 and $500, respectively.
Objective-See's Patrick Wardle described the response as "not the mature security program you'd expect."
OpenAI spokesman Drew Pusateri said the company takes security concerns seriously and acted immediately on researchers' findings.
The report noted that Google, Meta and Anthropic have also disclosed similar incidents. OpenAI has paused training of its most advanced models and said Monday it would not release GPT-6.1 Astra because of security concerns raised by its researchers, according to the Times.
