‘The Problem Is Infinitesimal’: What the Trump Administration's Intensifying Hunt for Non-Citizen Voters Is Showing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
20:01:56 UTC
05:01:56 KST

With the midterms approaching, the Trump Administration has ramped up its investigations into non-citizen voting around the U.S. But far from substantiating the President’s claims of widespread fraud, the results the effort is producing appear to underscore how vanishingly rare non-citizens registering or casting ballots is.
In recent months, the Administration has doubled down on its push to access and review state voter rolls with the stated goal of cracking down on fraud and threatened to withhold funding or prosecute election officials if they don’t purge any improperly registered non-citizens.
In the lead-up to the November elections, the Administration has also reportedly diverted a number of federal personnel to an effort to scour voter rolls for non-citizens—an initiative a federal whistleblower has alleged may have involved methods that violate state laws.
A Department of Homeland Security (DHS) official tells TIME that the department’s principal investigative arm, Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), “is actively rooting out and investigating election fraud wherever it can be found.”
“We have repeatedly demonstrated that aliens can and do vote in our elections. Under President Trump, HSI is committed to restoring integrity to our election systems and ensuring that American citizens and only American citizens are electing American leaders,” the official says, citing four past instances of non-citizen voting they say the government has identified. “Our message to aliens who vote in American elections is clear. We will find you, arrest you, and you will face the consequences — including criminal charges and deportation.”
Yet while Trump and DHS have claimed that hundreds of thousands of non-citizens are illegally registered to vote in states around the U.S., the number of people the Administration has so far charged in its efforts to crack down on such fraud are much smaller. Federal officials revealed in an update last week that DHS has pursued 1,600 voter fraud cases since January 2025, of which 160 have led to arrests.
That arrest figure, which represents roughly 0.00009% of the roughly 174 million registered voters in the U.S., broadly aligns what previous research and state investigations have shown: that instances of non-citizen registration and voting are exceedingly rare.
In Nevada, meanwhile, state election officials said last week that after reviewing suspected non-citizens that DHS flagged on the state’s voter rolls, they had determined that every one of the voters was a U.S. citizen.
“There's no reason to think that there is widespread non-citizen voting,” Stephen Richer, an elections expert at the public policy think tank the CATO Institute, tells TIME. “And the federal law enforcement's announcements to date affirm that this is a minuscule issue.”
How the Administration is attempting to find and prosecute non-citizen voters
Trump, who has for years promoted false claims that non-citizen voting is a pernicious problem in U.S. elections, has made rooting out alleged voter fraud a focus of his second term.
Two months after Trump returned to office last year, he signed an Executive Order directing DHS to compare state voter rolls against federal databases to “identify unqualified voters” and the Department of Justice (DOJ) to prioritize prosecuting non-citizen voting in conjunction with states.
To that end, the Trump Administration has demanded that states turn over their voter rolls and sued dozens for not complying, arguing that the federal government requires the rolls to verify their accuracy.
Over the summer, the Administration also threatened to withhold federal homeland security funding from states if they did not adopt a series of changes to their elections, including phasing out specific electronic voting systems and running voter rolls through a DHS database.
The Justice Department later in the summer sent letters to election officials in all 50 states warning them that they could face criminal charges if they knowingly allowed non-citizens to stay on voter rolls.
Those moves have faced challenges in court. Of the more than 30 lawsuits the Administration has filed in an effort to gain access to state voter rolls, 25 have been dismissed. Several of the other cases are still pending, while the DOJ has appealed many of the decisions against it. A judge on Monday meanwhile blocked the Administration from withholding counterterrorism funding from states that don’t meet its demands regarding their election practices.
Trump has also aggressively—and unsuccessfully—pushed for Congress to pass the sweeping SAVE America Act, which would require voters to submit proof of citizenship documents to participate in elections, along with imposing other voter ID restrictions.
And the Administration has additionally pressed for federal agencies and states to use its revamped version of a DHS database called Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements, or SAVE, to verify voters’ eligibility. The database, which has compiled records from multiple agencies in order to enable officials to check individuals’ immigration status, has drawn controversy, with critics contending that it violates voters’ rights to privacy and that its findings are at times inaccurate. But in a win for Trump, the Supreme Court last week permitted the Administration’s overhauled version of the database to be used in verifying the eligibility of voters ahead of the midterms.
With the elections nearing, the Administration has also reportedly launched an initiative aimed at identifying non-citizens on state voter rolls and surged hundreds of federal agents to assist in the endeavor.
Earlier this month, Democratic Sens. Alex Padilla of California and Minority Leader Chuck Schumer of New York made public a whistleblower report that described the effort, called the “Unlawful Voter Initiative,” from the inside and alleged that federal personnel involved in the initiative may have employed illegal methods. The whistleblower alleged that DHS agents were being directed to use data acquired from a department database to effectively pose as voters or people acting at voters’ behest to access information on voter registration websites.
"The Whistleblower has reason to believe that, with the knowledge and at the direction of leadership at headquarters, the Unlawful Voter Initiative has potentially already committed thousands of violations of state law in an effort to improperly access individuals' voter records,” the report reads.
The Trump Administration has defended its methods in statements to media outlets in response to the allegations.
Justin Levitt, who served as the White House's first senior policy advisor for democracy and voting rights under President Joe Biden, tells TIME that “what the Administration is trying is unprecedented” because states have the authority under the Constitution to run their own elections without federal interference.
“The president just doesn't have a lot of authority flat out to intervene in the election system,” Levitt says.
States push back on the Trump Administration’s claims
In addition to fighting the Administration’s demands to access their voter rolls in court, states have also pushed back on claims federal officials have made about non-citizens registering and voting in their elections.
In a July address to the nation, Trump made sweeping claims that 278,000 non-citizens were on voting rolls in the four Democratic-led states of California, New Jersey, Pennsylvania, and Nevada. DHS then released what it characterized as a specific breakdown of the numbers of suspected non-citizen voters in those states the following day, without providing evidence to support the figures.
All four of the states pushed back against those claims. And in Nevada, state election officials dug into DHS’s figures and found them to be unfounded.
The department, which earlier informed Nevada that there could be as many as 15,903 non-citizen voters on their rolls, in August identified 185 people as non-citizens who had improperly voted in a list sent to the Secretary of State’s office. But when state election officials subsequently reviewed the 185 records, they determined that all of them were for U.S. citizens.
“What state and local officials are finding is that DHS's information is effectively hot garbage,” Levitt says. “DHS has stepped out into the world with some pretty implausible claims that have, on further examination, evaporated.”
Nevada Secretary of State Francisco Aguilar tells TIME that the Administration’s accusations about non-citizens on Nevada’s voter rolls have been “shockingly unprofessional because of the fact that they truly don't have a system or a process to professionally determine eligibility of voters at the state level.” Describing classifying citizens as non-citizens as “detrimental,” he contends that the Administration doesn’t take doing so seriously enough.
“If you're going to try to take somebody's fundamental right away, you better have the ability and the facts and the information to accurately make the accusation,” he says.
Aguilar adds that Latino citizens in particular have expressed fear over the possibility of encountering federal agents or being classified as non-citizens at the polls in November.
“This is a direct attempt to dissuade and to interfere in elections and to prevent Latinos from voting,” Aguilar says.
What data shows about non-citizen voting
Nation-wide studies and state audits have consistently demonstrated that non-citizen registration and voting are extremely rare.
A 2017 Brennan Center survey that spanned 42 jurisdictions in 12 states found just 30 incidents of suspected non-citizen voting in the 2016 presidential election, a rate of roughly 1 suspected case per 783,000 votes. Of the jurisdictions included in the survey, 40 of them reported zero known incidents of non-citizen voting in 2016.
The regular audits that states conduct of their voter rolls in an effort to root out any instances of election fraud have similarly turned up very few instances of non-citizens being registered or casting ballots. A 2025 Michigan Department of State audit, for instance, found only 15 credible cases of individuals who appeared to be non-citizens having cast ballots in the 2024 election out of more than 5.7 million total votes. In October 2024, Georgia officials reported that a similar audit had “conclusively” identified 20 non-citizens on the state’s voter rolls out of 8.2 million registered voters, with nine having voted in previous elections.
Levitt says that there is simply no incentive for non-citizens, who can face hefty fines and deportation, to vote.
“You've heard of the perfect crime. Non-citizen voting is basically the least perfect crime. There is always, literally always, a paper trail connecting the person to the deed,” he says. “It just doesn't make any sense for anybody to do … It's exceedingly, exceedingly, exceedingly rare.”
And the rare instances when non-citizens do vote have no bearing on the outcomes of elections, Richer emphasizes.
“The electoral impact on this is negligible, beyond negligible,” Richer says. “You have to have a realistic sense of just how big the problem is, and by all indicators to date, the problem is infinitesimal.”

====================================================================================================

Maternal psychopathic traits predict teens’ callous-unemotional traits a year later
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
20:00:06 UTC
05:00:06 KST

Teenagers with serious conduct problems tended to show more callousness and less empathy a year later when their mothers reported the emotional features of psychopathy in themselves, such as not feeling bad about hurting others. This link held even after accounting for how callous the teens were at the start, and it was tied to this emotional dimension rather than to mothers’ manipulative, impulsive, or rule-breaking tendencies. The findings, published in Frontiers in Child and Adolescent Psychiatry, point to caregiver personality as a possible marker of family risk, though the study cannot say whether genes, parenting, or both are responsible.
Conduct disorder is a mental health diagnosis given to children and teenagers who show a repeated pattern of breaking rules and violating the rights of others through behaviors such as fighting, stealing, lying, or destroying property. Within this group is a smaller set of young people who also display what psychologists call callous-unemotional traits. These include a lack of empathy, little guilt after doing something wrong, and shallow or muted emotional expression.
These traits tend to mark the most persistent cases. Young people with high levels of callous-unemotional traits are more likely to use aggression deliberately to get what they want, respond less to punishment, and face a higher risk of developing psychopathy as adults. Major diagnostic manuals now let clinicians add a label called “with limited prosocial emotions” to a conduct disorder diagnosis to flag these youth, and recent research suggests roughly one in five young people with conduct disorder qualify for it.
Where these traits come from does not fit neatly into nature versus nurture. Callous-unemotional traits are moderately to highly heritable, meaning a sizable share of the differences between young people can be traced to genetic differences. In a 2016 adoption study of 561 families, biological mothers’ history of severe antisocial behavior predicted callous-unemotional behaviors in their toddlers, even though the children were raised by adoptive parents and had little or no contact with their birth mothers. Adoptive mothers who often praised and rewarded their children, however, appeared to offer some protection against these behaviors.
Parenting itself also seems to play a part. A 2018 study of identical twins found that the twin who received harsher parenting tended to show more callous-unemotional traits and more aggression than the other twin. Because identical twins share the same genes, those differences within each pair point to an environmental influence. Taken together, this work suggests that a parent’s traits could relate to a child’s callousness through inherited tendencies, through the home environment, or through both at once.
The new study focuses on one parental characteristic in particular: psychopathic traits. Psychopathy is a personality pattern that researchers often divide into four facets. The interpersonal facet involves manipulation and deceit; the affective facet involves shallow emotions and a lack of empathy and guilt; the lifestyle facet involves impulsivity and thrill-seeking; and the antisocial facet involves rule-breaking behavior. The affective facet closely resembles the defining features of callous-unemotional traits in young people.
Earlier studies have linked parents’ psychopathic traits to callous-unemotional traits in their children, but most focused on younger children, relied on a single overall psychopathy score, and seldom accounted for how callous the child already was. Nicholas D. Thomson and Jessica J. James of Virginia Commonwealth University wanted to know whether mothers’ psychopathic traits predicted teens’ callous-unemotional traits a year later, beyond the teens’ starting levels, and whether any single facet stood out. They expected the affective facet to show the strongest link.
The researchers recruited 99 teenagers and their mothers through a large healthcare system in Virginia, for a total of 198 participants. All of the teens, who were between 13 and 17 years old with an average age of about 15 and a half, had already been diagnosed with conduct disorder by a licensed mental health professional. About 68 percent were boys. Sixty percent identified as Black or African American, 36 percent as white, and 4 percent as American Indian or Alaska Native.
The mothers, most of whom were the teens’ biological mothers, ranged in age from 29 to 68. Three fathers had also taken part, but the researchers excluded them because there were too few to analyze as a separate group. The data came from a larger project, funded by the National Institute of Mental Health, examining how fear responses relate to the development of callous-unemotional traits.
At the start of the study and again 12 months later, the teens completed a 24-item questionnaire measuring callous-unemotional traits. Mothers completed a 28-item questionnaire measuring their own psychopathic traits, with seven items for each facet. Sample items included having pretended to be someone else to get something (interpersonal), not feeling bad about hurting people (affective), doing something dangerous just for the thrill of it (lifestyle), and tricking someone into giving them money (antisocial).
The researchers used statistical models that accounted for the teens’ starting callous-unemotional scores, as well as the teens’ age, sex, and race and their mothers’ age. This approach asks whether mothers’ traits help predict where a teen ends up a year later beyond what could be predicted from where the teen started.
Callous-unemotional traits showed moderate stability over the year. Teens who scored higher at the start tended to score higher at follow-up, though the relationship was far from perfect, leaving room for change. Boys also tended to score somewhat higher than girls at follow-up.
The teens’ starting scores and demographic factors together explained about 21 percent of the variation in callous-unemotional traits a year later. Adding mothers’ overall psychopathy scores raised this to about 26 percent, with higher maternal scores linked to higher teen scores at follow-up.
When the researchers split psychopathy into its four facets, the model explained about 31 percent of the variation. Only the affective facet was linked to teens’ later callous-unemotional traits. The interpersonal, lifestyle, and antisocial facets were not statistically significant predictors once all four were considered together.
To give a sense of scale, with the other factors held constant, a mother scoring about four points higher on the affective items, which was roughly the typical spread among mothers in the sample, was associated with her teen scoring nearly four points higher at follow-up. The average teen score at follow-up was about 30.
The researchers also checked whether the pattern differed for boys and girls. Adding this set of comparisons as a group did not significantly improve the model’s predictions, which calls for caution. One specific comparison did stand out, however: the link between mothers’ affective traits and teens’ later callous-unemotional traits appeared among girls but not among boys. Girls made up only about a third of the sample, so this result will need confirmation in larger studies.
The findings are in line with research covered by PsyPost in 2022, which found that parents with more psychopathic traits tended to have adolescents with more callous-unemotional traits, partly through harsher and less warm parenting. That earlier study drew on a community sample of twins, whereas the new study followed teens already diagnosed with conduct disorder over the course of a year.
Thomson and James suggest that the emotional side of a mother’s personality, rather than manipulation, impulsivity, or rule-breaking, may be most relevant to whether callous traits persist or grow during adolescence. People high in affective psychopathic traits tend to show less empathy, take others’ perspectives less often, and have trouble identifying and describing emotions. Developmental theories propose that these are the same skills parents draw on to help children build empathy and a conscience, although the study did not measure parenting directly.
The authors also note that the sex difference might reflect something specific to mother-daughter relationships rather than girls being more sensitive to family influences in general. Because treatments that involve caregivers tend to work better for disruptive behavior problems than those focused on the child alone, the researchers suggest that assessing caregivers’ emotional traits could help clinicians understand a family’s risk, though they stop short of recommending specific interventions.
As with all research, there are some caveats to consider. The study shows an association over time, not a cause. Because most participating mothers were biological mothers, the link could reflect shared genes, the way mothers with these traits interact with their children, or a mix of both, and the design cannot tell these apart.
The mothers in the study were not diagnosed with psychopathy. The questionnaire measures traits along a continuum, and the analysis compared mothers who scored somewhat higher or lower on it. Both mothers and teens also reported on themselves, so their answers may have been shaped by how willing or able they were to describe their own emotions honestly.
The sample was relatively small, came from a single healthcare system, and included only teens already diagnosed with conduct disorder, so the results may not apply to teens in the general population. The study also did not measure whether the teens had experienced childhood maltreatment, which may contribute to callous-unemotional traits. The authors call for future studies that combine genetic information with direct observations of how parents and teens interact, and that include fathers, to clarify how caregiver personality and caregiving together shape these traits over time.
The study, “Maternal psychopathic traits prospectively predict youth callous-unemotional traits,” was authored by Nicholas D. Thomson and Jessica J. James.

Argentina's Kirchner challenges fraud conviction at UN, seeking political return

Fernández was sentenced in 2025 to six years in prison and a permanent ban from public office following a fraud conviction, a ruling her defense team argues violated her fundamental rights during legal proceedings.
• Her lawyer, Rafael Valim, said the team is seeking a committee hearing in October, which could require Argentine courts to review the ruling before year's end.
• A recent opinion poll by Zuban Cordoba showed Fernández with a 42% approval rating, surpassing President Javier Milei's 36.1%.
• Fernández remains one of Argentina's most divisive political figures but polls as high as Milei in voting-intention surveys, giving her potential prospects in Argentina's October 2027 presidential election if the ban is lifted.
• She governed Argentina from 2007 to 2015 and served as vice president from 2019 to 2023.
• "We are working so the case is examined in October, at the committee's next session," Valim, a Brazilian lawyer who played a role in leftist Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva's defense, told Reuters.
• The move invites comparisons with Brazil's Lula who challenged his corruption conviction before the UN Human Rights Committee and was later imprisoned and barred from the 2018 election. Brazil's Supreme Court annulled his convictions in 2021, restoring his political rights and paving the way for his return to the presidency the following year.

The festivities took place mainly in the front area of the compound, whereas in past years, they were held in the back area. Notably, many areas that were previously open to the public were cordoned off.

Emphazis on culture, sport at Herzog's sukkah

Admittedly, there was much competition for the public in Jerusalem, with many varied attractions available for the holiday.
Although people still showed up, the early birds who arrived at 9:30 a.m. didn’t get to see much, as organizers were still setting up. Once everything was in place, President Isaac Herzog and his wife Michal toured the exhibits, posed for photos, and chatted with exhibitors.
The Herzogs were particularly interested in the wheelchair-bound athletes who were playing basketball, as well as in the display of special wheelchairs designed to suit the individual needs of people unable to walk or stand.
The Herzogs stood in the sukkah at various times, spending up to an hour shaking hands with visitors, posing for selfies, and holding toddlers. In fact, the event was largely geared towards children. Event held for children to meet President Herzog

What attracted them most was a drum ensemble inside the building and a storytelling section outside, where they sat on colored bolster cushions and listened to a man onstage read stories to them.
Meanwhile, film buffs were interested in scenes taken from Israeli movies and recreated on small stages. One such film was Zot hi Ha’aretz (“This is the Land”), made in 1935 and dealing with early settlement in Israel.
Scenes from the iconic Eskimo Lemon and Kazablan films were also included, though the man featured in the scene from Kazablan bore no resemblance to the young Yehoram Gaon, who was its star on both stage and screen.
Herzog said that he was excited to welcome the diversity of the Israeli public to the spirit and symbols of Israel’s wonderful culture and sport.
“I want the children of Israel to experience our culture and to be strengthened by it,” he said.
Relating to the upcoming Knesset elections, Herzog said that Sukkot provided an opportunity for all Israelis to come together and talk, and that, afterward, “we will all go together to vote in the democratic elections.”
The festival also featured symbols of Israeli patriotism, with blue and white blimps bearing the menorah and Star of David.

WeWork's Adam Neumann says switching off for 25 hours every week for Shabbat helped him be better

04:50:42 KST

WeWork co-founder Adam Neumann said observing Shabbat had helped him understand himself better and strengthen his relationships, and persuaded host Steven Bartlett to try a day without screens during an interview on The Diary of a CEO podcast released Monday.
Asked about the most effective practice he had adopted to get to know himself better, Neumann pointed to the Jewish day of rest.
“About 10 years ago, I started keeping Shabbat, which, for those who don’t know, means that on Friday, we disconnect from technology for 25 hours,” he said. “And I just spend my time with my family, my friends, and taking part in something greater than myself.”
Shabbat begins before sunset on Friday and ends after nightfall on Saturday. Traditionally observant Jews refrain from work and the use of electronic devices during that period.
“That disconnection actually makes a lot more connection than anybody understands,” Neumann said.
A day without a phone
Neumann urged listeners to try spending 24 hours away from their phones, saying the first few hours could reveal how deeply ingrained the habit of checking them had become.
“The first two hours, the number of times your hand’s going to go to your pocket, thinking your phone is there, will show you how addicted you are, because it’s an actual addiction,” he said.
He suggested planning the time in advance, including dinner with friends and activities outdoors. By the end of the day, he said, the experience could leave people feeling better and thinking more clearly about their priorities.
“Some of the best ideas you’ve had in some time are going to come to you, including who you should be surrounded with, what business you should focus on, what is your next move.”
Bartlett agrees to try it
Neumann then pressed Bartlett to put the advice into practice. The host acknowledged that his fiancée had repeatedly asked him to disconnect and admitted that the prospect made him uncomfortable.
Bartlett eventually agreed to try a day without screens and report back. As they discussed the terms, Neumann clarified that the challenge focused on technology and allowed activities such as driving and brainstorming on paper.
“I'm not asking you to keep Shabbat,” he told Bartlett.
Earlier in the interview, Neumann credited his wife, Rebekah, with introducing him to spiritual practice shortly after they began dating. He said she had challenged his focus on material success and encouraged him to seek fulfillment. For him, that exploration began with Kabbalah, the Jewish mystical tradition.
The discussion formed part of a wider interview about Neumann’s career, his experience at WeWork and his subsequent residential real estate venture, Flow. Describing his weekly time with his wife and six children, he said:
“That 24 hours where it’s us together has been phenomenal,” he said.

Migrant shipwreck off Tunisia leaves at least two dead, six reported missing
German charity group Sea-Watch said on Tuesday it had rescued 28 migrants and recovered two bodies, including that of a child, following a shipwreck off the coast of Tunisia.
The group's ship Aurora found five survivors and the dead bodies in a deflated rubber dinghy in the early hours of Tuesday, the charity said.
It rescued another 23 survivors, including a toddler, from an offshore oil and gas platform where they had taken refuge after the shipwreck.
Those rescued reported that at least six people, including three children, were missing, Sea-Watch said on social media, adding the Aurora was now heading to the Italian island of Lampedusa.
"Governments celebrate falling arrival numbers as a success. We see what that ‘success’ means: at least two dead and six missing, including three children," said Sea-Watch spokesperson Julia Winkler, calling for a state-run European search-and-rescue programme.
Over 22,000 sea migrants have arrived in Italy so far in 2026, interior ministry data showed, compared to more than 50,000 reported in the same period of 2025.
In the same period, more than 1,970 people have died or gone missing in the Mediterranean in a bid to reach Europe, Sea-Watch said.

Developing nations push for stronger voice in shaping AI rules at UN
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
19:25:38 UTC
04:25:38 KST

Developing nations are demanding a greater role in shaping AI rules, warning that the technology could deepen global inequalities if its development and regulation remain concentrated in wealthy countries.
The debate at last week's UN Security Council session in New York brought together leaders from Africa, Asia and Latin America, as concerns grow over AI safety and its potential risks.
“Developing countries cannot be reduced to the role of mere users of technologies designed elsewhere,” said Foreign Minister Therese Kayikwamba Wagner of the Democratic Republic of Congo.
“We must ensure that technological transformations of the 21st century do not reproduce the economic imbalances of previous decades,” she added.
The session featured OpenAI chief Sam Altman and Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, who urged governments to work together to manage the technology.
‘A question of governance’
Bangladesh Foreign Minister Khalilur Rahman said 128 delegations had addressed AI at this year's UN debate, compared with five addresses four years ago.
“Many framed AI as a question of governance: Who designs it, who benefits? Who bears the risks, and who is accountable when harm occurs?” he said.
The World Bank has said AI could help developing countries gain a century's worth of development in a decade if they close gaps in power, connectivity and skills. The IMF said AI could boost Sub-Saharan Africa's economy by about 4 percent over the next decade under the right conditions.
UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres compared AI risks with the climate crisis, saying developing nations should have an equal voice in addressing both.
“Artificial intelligence moved at a speed that has blindsided even those who created it,” Guterres said, calling for coordinated global action.
US President Donald Trump, however, has dismissed AI risks as vastly overblown, comparing them with what he called exaggerated warnings about climate change.
Belize Prime Minister John Briceno said AI could widen access to knowledge and improve public services if well governed, but warned that poor governance could deepen inequality, displace workers and leave developing countries dependent on rules designed elsewhere.

The Greens are about to pick a new leader. Who are the contenders?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
19:22:38 UTC
04:22:38 KST

The Greens are about to pick a new leader. Who are the contenders?
In short:
Sarah Hanson-Young and Mehreen Faruqi are among the top contenders for the Greens leadership after the shock resignation of Larissa Waters.
David Shoebridge and Steph Hodgins-May are also in the mix and are expected to run on a joint ticket.
What's next?
The Greens are expected to select a new leader today or tomorrow.
The Greens will meet this morning to settle on a new leader following the sudden resignation of Larissa Waters, who took on the job only a little over a year ago.
Senator Waters said she was stepping back due to difficulties managing a chronic kidney disease, leaving the party again in search of a leader after losing Adam Bandt in a shock election upset in 2025.
The party has been recalibrating since that election left just one Greens MP in the lower house.
Senator Waters, well-regarded and well-liked within the party and across the parliament, was chosen to reunite the party after its election drubbing.
Greens sources say whoever is chosen next will face more pressure to "take the leadership and run with it", with a central question being how directly the party takes on a surging One Nation.
While senators Sarah Hanson-Young, Mehreen Faruqi and David Shoebridge are considered the most likely contenders, in a small party room of just 11, the Greens can also turn out unexpected results.
The small party room means personal relationships can also heavily influence the outcome, often more-so than questions of policy or strategy — though differences of opinion do sometimes emerge.
A recent example is the split on the Senate floor earlier this month when senators Nick McKim, Vanessa Bleyer, and Jordon Steele-John voted against the party over a carbon credits scheme.
While there are processes for a leadership vote if the issue cannot be resolved, the Greens generally prefer to resolve the leadership by consensus in a fluid process that can also involve picks for deputy leadership, though a leadership change does not require a spill of the deputy role, currently held by Senator Faruqi.
Greens senators and the party's lone federal MP Elizabeth Watson-Brown will come together in Sydney over two days for a pre-arranged meeting, with hopes the leadership can be resolved quickly.
The victor will lead a party which has 10 seats in the Senate, where it wields some influence as a voting bloc, as well as Ms Watson-Brown's lower house seat.
Former leader Bob Brown told ABC Afternoon Briefing that he felt "very confident" in whoever is elected, given the calibre of candidates.
"What I can say is it now has a depth of talent for leadership. There are three or four people in there who would make excellent leaders," Mr Brown said.
He said whoever was chosen would be able to "take on" One Nation's Pauline Hanson in a debate on a matter of topics and "wipe the floor with her".
With the party hoping it can find a way to replicate the successes of UK and US counterparts, former MP Max Chandler-Mather said that would require opening the leadership vote to all Greens members.
"People often ask how to recreate the political success and energy of UK Greens leader, Zack Polanski or New York Mayor, Zohran Mamdani," Mr Chandler-Mather wrote in an open letter to the party room.
"The recipe for their success doesn't just lie in their policies, rhetoric or even organising strategy. It lies in the process by which they won their elections.
"In both instances they were elected by direct member elections."
Who are the potential contenders?
So who are the likely contenders for the leadership?
Senator Hanson-Young, from South Australia, and Senator Faruqi, from NSW, both confirmed they would stand for the leadership on Tuesday afternoon.
The pair both threw their hats in the ring last year.
Tasmanian senator Nick McKim will run as Senator Faruqi's deputy.
The ABC has confirmed Senator Shoebridge, from NSW, will run on a joint ticket with first-term Victorian senator Steph Hodgins-May as his deputy.
Mehreen Faruqi
Senator Faruqi, 63, is the current deputy leader of the Greens — a post she has held since 2022.
In 2018, she became the first Muslim senator in the federal parliament.
Senator Faruqi grew up in Lahore, Pakistan, and is a former engineer and academic.
The senator has previously been considered as a stronger voice of protest for the party, who might take a more hardline stance in negotiations with government.
She has been a vocal critic of the war in Gaza, leading a walkout of Greens colleagues from the Senate in a protest for Palestinians in 2023, and last year holding up a sign at the governor-general's address which read: "Gaza is starving. Words won't feed them. Sanction Israel."
She also yelled out to the prime minister as he left the chamber, calling on him to sanction Israel.
Those actions were deemed "utterly disrespectful" and Senator Faruqi was subsequently banned from taking part in overseas parliamentary delegations.
In 2024, she won a racial discrimination case after One Nation senator Pauline Hanson told her to "piss off back to Pakistan", which Senator Hanson has said she will appeal.
Senator McKim, 61, is currently the Senate whip and will be running as her deputy on a joint ticket.
The former environmental activist, hiking guide, and an advertising executive was co-deputy leader of the Greens alongside Senator Waters between 2020 and 2022.
Announcing their candidacy, the pair said the Greens need to grow to "meet the moment".
"Our politics is unapologetically bold, and we want to lead with hope over hate and people over profit."
Sarah Hanson-Young
Senator Hanson-Young, 44, is the current manager of business in the Senate and the longest-standing federal Green in the mix.
She was elected to the Senate in 2007 at 25 years old — the youngest person elected to parliament at the time.
The South Australian senator has been a successful negotiator for the party in discussions with government, particularly in last year's environmental reform negotiations — and is seen as a more pragmatic option for the party.
Prior to becoming a senator, she worked briefly as a bank teller and then as a campaign manager for Amnesty International for four years.
She made headlines in 2009 after her infant daughter was ejected from the Senate chamber, which prompted the party to call for a change to "archaic" rules.
Announcing her candidacy, Senator Hanson-Young said the party was at a "defining moment".
"People deserve better than the failed policies and weak excuses from the Labor and Liberal parties and the hate peddling from Pauline Hanson's One Nation,"
"I will fight with everything I've got."
Shoebridge and Hodgins-May team up
In a late entry to the race, senators Shoebridge and Hodgins-May signalled their leadership ambitions on Wednesday morning.
"Labor has proven they can't stop One Nation because they made the conditions of them to thrive in. Only the Greens can," they said in a social media statement.
They said they answer to the rise of the right-wing party was "giving people hope" and economic and environmental security.
"We do not seek to reform Labor, but to replace them."
Senator Shoebridge, 55, has built a reputation as a sharp politician and an effective operator in Senate estimates.
The NSW senator is a former barrister and was previously a member of the NSW parliament.
While being in parliament for just two years, Steph Hodgins-May has quickly built a profile since entering parliament following former senator Janet Rice's retirement.
Senator Hodgins-May, a former environmental lawyer, has strong credentials on a core issue to the party, and spearheaded the Greens campaign for a tax on gas exports.
With greens parties globally seeking to replicate the success of now-New York mayor Zohran Mamdani's progressive campaign, the young senator has been considered someone who could recapture attention for the party, which has been unable to capitalise on frustration with the major parties since the 2025 election.
Editor's note (30/09/2026): An earlier version of this story said that Senator Faruqi was the first Muslim woman elected to federal parliament. Anne Aly was the first Muslim woman elected to parliament. Senator Faruqi became the first Muslim senator in 2018.

Lavrov destroys BBC’s ‘hybrid war’ play (VIDEO)
Unknown

2026-09-29
19:18:18 UTC

Lavrov destroys BBC’s ‘hybrid war’ play (VIDEO)
Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov has treated an accusation from a BBC correspondent with the contempt expected of a veteran diplomat.
The British state broadcaster’s Steve Rosenberg asked Lavrov if he would admit “that Russia is waging a covert hybrid war against European countries?”
“Are you referring to when we destroy the drones and missiles that Britain and continental Europe supply to Ukraine, which are then fired at us?” the Russian foreign minister retorted. “Is that what you mean by hybrid war?”
Rosenberg then dropped his line of questioning and switched to criticizing Russia for its use of “brute force” in Ukraine.
BBC’s Rosenberg: Do you admit that Russia is waging a covert hybrid war against European countries?
Lavrov: Are you referring to when we destroy the drones and missiles that Britain and continental Europe supply to Ukraine, which are then fired at us? Is that what you mean by… pic.twitter.com/XkLe49xcNX
“If you are referring to the destruction of infrastructure used by the [Ukrainian] Nazi regime – with Western support – to wage war against the Russian Federation, then we are resorting to hard power to neutralize this direct threat to us,” Lavrov replied.
Rosenberg’s question to Russia’s top diplomat followed several days of high-pitch war hysteria in the UK press, including a significantly over-reported ‘security incident’ near an RAF base.
European politicians regularly describe drone sightings, fires and accidents at weapons factories, and even natural disasters as examples of a Russian “hybrid war” against the West. The term “hybrid war” is typically used in reporting cases where no hard evidence exists, as was the case when a small quadcopter drone was discovered next to a Ukrainian transport plane at Leipzig Airport in Germany last month.
In the latest such incident, Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna blamed Russia on Tuesday for a fire at a drone factory in Tallinn last month. Although the Kremlin has denied any role in the blaze, the UK, France, Latvia, Lithuania, and Sweden all backed Tsahkna’s story and pledged on Tuesday to increase military aid to Kiev.
Amid an upsurge in supposed “hybrid war” incidents, Western military leaders have escalated their war rhetoric, with members of the UK’s Labour and Conservative parties both claiming last week that a military clash with Russia is inevitable, and Spanish media claiming that Italy, France, and Spain are all at risk of a Russian drone attack from the Mediterranean Sea. The latter claim, though widely echoed across the international press, was summarily debunked by senior French and Italian officials.
“We have no intention to fight with Europe…that is utter nonsense,” Lavrov told journalists at the UN General Assembly on Saturday. “But Europe is preparing for war with us, and each day they reaffirm the fact. This could become a self-fulfilling prophecy because they are investing vast amounts of money into weapons production.”

Trump administration ad sparks protests from artists and complaints to regulators - media
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29

Trump administration ad sparks protests from artists and complaints to regulators - media
Kyiv • UNN
Musician JMSN demands that the use of the song in Trump’s videos without permission be stopped. Public Citizen called the video campaign advertising.
Television spots funded by taxpayers and featuring U.S. President Donald Trump came under renewed criticism on Tuesday: the performer of a song used in one of the videos is demanding that the White House stop using his music, while a government watchdog organization has asked federal regulators to take the spots off the air, UNN reports, citing Reuters.
These developments intensified criticism of three nationally broadcast advertisements touting America's "golden age" five weeks before the midterm elections; ethics experts and lawmakers from both parties are questioning the appropriateness of using public funds to promote Trump politically.
Lawyers for Christian Berishaj, known by his stage name JMSN, sent the White House a formal demand to stop using the material, saying that his song "Love Me" had been used without permission. Meanwhile, the organization Public Citizen filed complaints with regulators, arguing that the spots are campaign advertisements that should not be produced or distributed at taxpayers' expense.
Democratic Senators Patty Murray and Chris Murphy on Tuesday asked Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin to provide explanations regarding the spots, saying that the administration had redirected $20 million from the department's budget to the advertising campaign.
"The administration's justification for using American taxpayers' money to broadcast these spots is as absurd as it is offensive," they said in their letter to Mullin.
The White House did not immediately respond on Tuesday to Reuters' questions about the cost of the spots or criticism that they are effectively political advertisements paid for by taxpayers. The administration had previously defended the videos, calling them "public service announcements" intended to promote patriotism rather than campaign advocacy.
The spots conclude with the message: "Paid for by the U.S. government."
In addition
In one of the advertisements, Trump declares that "America will never become a communist country," while a choir repeats the words "love me." Another combines images of Mount Rushmore with footage of Trump praising "America's golden age." The third describes a "decisive battle" against the "deep state" and closely resembles one of Trump's 2024 campaign advertisements.
In an Instagram post, Berishaj said that he "would never have given permission for my music to be used for any political purposes or campaigns."
Public Citizen asked broadcasters to stop airing the spots and also called on the federal government to investigate whether executive branch officials had engaged in improper partisan political activity.
"These spots are part of campaign advocacy; they should be created and distributed as part of a campaign and without the use of taxpayers' money," the organization said.
Critics argue that the videos may violate longstanding restrictions on government propaganda and political activity.

US Supreme Court lifts limits on third-country deportations
- The US Supreme Court lifted restrictions on deporting immigrants to third countries, agreeing to review the issue fully in December.
- The Trump administration argues third-country deportations are vital as some home countries refuse to accept deportees.
- Opponents warn such deportations risk abuse and indefinite detention, while US policy forbids sending people to countries where they face danger or torture.
AI generated
WASHINGTON - The US Supreme Court on Sept 29 lifted restrictions on the deportations of immigrants to countries that are not their own, while agreeing to hear the issue on its merits in December.
The conservative-dominated high court granted an emergency request by the Trump administration to suspend a lower court ruling that restricted, but did not outright ban, so-called “third-country removals.”
The lower court had said that people targeted with deportation must be given effective notice ahead of time about where they are being sent to allow them to raise concerns about potential persecution.
The three liberal justices on the nine-member panel said they would not have granted the Trump administration’s request.
US President Donald Trump campaigned on promises to expel millions of undocumented migrants from the United States and has taken a number of actions aimed at speeding up deportations since returning to the White House in 2025.
The Trump administration has defended third-country deportations as necessary since the home nations of some of those who are targeted for removal sometimes refuse to accept them.
In a brief to the Supreme Court, opponents of lifting the restrictions argued that the lower court ruling did not fully block all third-country deportations, “it simply requires them to do so lawfully.”
Trump’s solicitor-general, John Sauer, meanwhile, told the court that the rapid deportation to third countries was “an essential tool to remove certain aliens, including some of the worst criminal aliens.”
The lower court ruling “created substantial logistical problems” with removals, he said.
An AFP investigation found that the US has offered multimillion-dollar deals and threatened visa restrictions in a bid to get “third countries,” especially in Africa, to take such deportees.
Once in these countries - and outside US jurisdiction - deportees have been subject to abuse by local guards, indefinite detention, or quickly re-deported to their home countries.
Congress has made it US policy not to deport people to countries where their lives would be in danger or they could be subject to torture. AFP

Russia says domestic light industry now accounts for 45% of market

Russia says domestic light industry now accounts for 45% of market
Domestic light-industry products now make up 45% of the Russian market, Russian Industry and Trade Minister Anton Alikhanov said on September 29 at the BRICS+ Fashion Summit in Moscow.
According to the minister, that figure is close to the current target of 50% set out in Russia’s Light Industry Development Strategy through 2035. He added that in the updated version of the strategy, which is expected to be approved by the end of 2026, the target share is likely to be raised to at least 60%.
The minister said the clothing manufacturing segment is now entering a phase of market saturation. Production growth, which began after the departure of global brands from Russia, turned into a 3% decline in 2025.
“We are reaching a plateau,” Alikhanov said.
He noted that the market niches vacated by international brands had been filled partly by Russian producers and partly by imports from what Moscow describes as “friendly countries.”
Even so, foreign-made goods still dominate the Russian market overall. In the minister’s view, one reason is that around half of Russian brands are concentrated in narrow niches, including makers of high-tech clothing, as well as ethnic and regional labels.
Speaking about broader technological trends, the minister said the Russian market is largely keeping pace with global developments, particularly in the changing balance between natural and synthetic materials.
“As far as technological trends are concerned, our market is broadly moving in step with the international one: there is a transformation and a reduction in the consumption of natural fabrics and fibers,” he said. “Thirty years ago, half the market was cotton and 39% synthetics. Now cotton accounts for 25–26%, while synthetics have risen to 60%.”
Russia, he added, still remains heavily dependent on supplies of synthetic materials, including polyamides and polyesters. At the same time, he said Russian producers have opportunities to expand output of viscose and lyocell, an artificial cellulose fiber made from wood.
To support those sectors, the government is relying on a new national project called “New Materials and Chemistry.” Enterprises in the field can also apply for support from the Industrial Development Fund and the cluster investment platform, according to the minister.
“After the start of sanctions pressure, we also introduced support measures for equipment leasing. Next year, we hope to double financing in order to meet the demand of all manufacturers,” he said.
The comments came during the BRICS+ Fashion Summit, which is being held as part of Moscow Fashion Week and has focused on industrial development, local production, technology, and the future of the fashion market in BRICS and other emerging economies.

OpenAI Gets Sued Over the Hugging Face Hack
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
19:05:00 UTC
04:05:00 KST

A legal nonprofit sued OpenAI in a California court on Tuesday over the company’s agents escaping a testing environment and hacking the open source AI platform Hugging Face. “OpenAI’s actions straightforwardly violated California law,” the suit alleges.
The suit was filed by Legal Advocates for Safe Science and Technology (LASST) and the law firm Gerstein Harrow in California Superior Court in San Francisco, where OpenAI is headquartered. It alleges that OpenAI’s agents violated California’s Comprehensive Computer Data Access and Fraud Act (CDAFA) by breaching Hugging Face over the summer. The suit, which comes amid ongoing disclosures across the industry of agents going rogue, claims that OpenAI should be held responsible for the activity given a California AI law in effect since January 1 that says “it shall not be a defense … that the artificial intelligence autonomously caused the harm to the plaintiff.”
“We think it’s extremely important that existing laws are enforced to hold AI companies accountable for the harm they’re causing,” Tyler Whitmer, founder of LASST, tells WIRED. “Especially when that harm is caused by autonomous agents, because we see that as an obvious, extremely risky thing in the world that’s very new.”
OpenAI did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
On Monday, Florida attorney general James Uthmeier filed for a temporary injunction against OpenAI to block development of models without independent oversight, amid a lawsuit Florida brought in June against OpenAI and its CEO, Sam Altman. OpenAI “asked the government to tie them to the mast. Well, Florida is answering their cries for help,” Uthmeier said in a statement.
Given that the whole point of AI agents is that they can be empowered to take actions on a (human) user’s behalf, AI developers and safety researchers have long foreseen that unintended “agentic” activity would be a concern as machine learning development progressed. Protections built into mainstream, consumer AI systems have largely prevented mass rogue activity so far, but rapidly advancing capabilities in general, as well as situations where guardrails are suspended (such as in the Hugging Face case where OpenAI had removed some model restraints for testing), have led to an apparent uptick in rogue agent activity.
As governments weigh AI regulation amid both existential safety questions and economic and national security considerations, researchers and people around the world have increasingly called for accountability mechanisms for AI. And from a legal perspective, experts have largely emphasized that questions of responsibility, liability, and culpability can only be answered through precedent set by cases working their way through courts.
“After the Hugging Face incident was disclosed, we actually did a bunch of work trying to educate regulators and civil society organizations about the hack. And we were kind of wondering, is anyone going to do anything about this in court?” Whitmer says. “There are structural reasons why we think Hugging Face, which is the obvious potential plaintiff to do something here, is not doing anything. So given that it didn’t seem like anyone else was going to do anything about this, we moved forward. As these systems scale and as things get crazier, AI really could be catastrophically harmful.”
LASST and Gerstein Harrow brought the lawsuit under California’s Unfair Competition Law, which requires that LASST allege both how its work and resources were impacted and diverted as a result of the Hugging Face incident, as well as unlawful activity by OpenAI.
The suit does not seek financial damages, and instead asks the court for injunctive relief such that OpenAI would be barred from developing AI agents that can autonomously hack other entities, plus legal fees and “any other relief deemed just and proper.”

Tom Cruise Bloviates His Way Through the Aggressively Unfunny Digger
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
19:02:13 UTC
04:02:13 KST

Sometimes great movies are complicated movies. But not all complicated movies are great, and some directors can’t distinguish between the act of making a meaningful picture and pulling off an elaborate parlor trick. Digger, the eighth feature film from Alejandro G. Iñárritu, is pure, empty-headed trickery, a drab-looking gewgaw with a million moving parts and nothing to say, even if it desperately claws at profundity every minute. Greed is evil! Big oil is killing the planet! Human beings are in a pickle! You can believe all these things are true and still find Digger pathetically unpersuasive; it’s so thematically clumsy, even within the ostensible razzle-dazzle of its filmmaking, that it comes off as liberalism’s worst enemy. If human civilization really is nearing its end, assaultive bores like this one aren’t helping.
Tom Cruise, his face nearly unrecognizable beneath cookie-dough prosthetics, plays Texas oil tycoon Digger Rockwell who, as the movie opens, is desperately trying to keep his beloved but bedraggled long-haired emotional-support cat alive. We can see it isn’t a real cat; it’s sort of an animatronic thing, a bit of theatrical engineering, standing in for the real thing. Even so, Digger’s pathetic attachment to this creature is supposed to be funny, or somewhat touching, or something—it’s hard to say what, but we do know that Cruise sure is doing a lot of acting around this limp assemblage of metal, plastic, and faux fur. The ancient thing, barely a plot device, will eventually die and is nearly forgotten.
Meanwhile, Cruise’s Digger pads around his palatial digs in silk PJs and cowboy boots, alternately fulminating and rhapsodizing about nothing in particular, his overwritten eccentricities laid bare for indiscernable reasons. His mansion home is classic old-money-meets-new: tapestries and boars’ heads adorn the walls, and giant picture windows look out upon dreamy gray vistas. Actually, nearly everything in Digger—shot by the enormously gifted cinematographer Emmanuel Lubezki, who should perhaps be tested for cataracts—is grayish, from the interiors to the cloud-strewn skies to the characters’ skin. The movie is only pretending to be fun; its antic joylessness will more likely wear you down.
In case you haven’t guessed, Digger is an environmental parable. Early in the picture, Digger receives advance warning of a cataclysmic world event, resulting in the deaths of hundreds of thousands of people. His ruthless quest for oil is the cause of this calamity, but even with his insider knowledge, he does nothing to stop it. Digger’s nervous, well-meaning environmental adviser, played by Riz Ahmed, knows of his boss’s guilt but doesn’t know how to spin it. Later, Digger will face an angry tribunal of world leaders who demand that he explain his actions. He both wows them and angers them with a disarmingly honest speech about how everyone loves oil. It is, after all, the language of freedom. Digger’s point is that Americans specifically, with our need to traverse long distances in our gas-guzzling vehicles, sometimes just to get to the grocery store, are complicit in the sins of big oil, and he’s not wrong. The problem is that he’s so water-is-wet right that his alleged barnburner of a speech is nothing but a scolding rant. It doesn’t so much rev you up as beat you up.
Another alleged surprise: Digger isn’t real—he’s a character in a play (what we’re seeing is a tech rehearsal), and Cruise is merely playing the actor playing him. Iñárritu is a wily one, all right. With the “reality is just a construct” black comedy Birdman, he (almost) fooled us into believing the whole movie consisted of just one shot. While making The Revenant, he subjected his actors to grueling conditions, presumably thinking that allowing them to nearly freeze to death would make his gritty survival tale more realistic. That approach doesn’t empower actors; it insults them. They're professionals who are being paid to act, not to be brutalized.
Digger was cowritten by Iñárritu, Sabina Berman, Alexander Dinelaris Jr., and Nicolás Giacobone, from a story by Iñárritu, Berman, and Jez Butterworth, a too-many-cooks equation if ever there were one. The movie has the peculiar distinction of being both all over the place and laser-focused on its dumb premise; too bad there isn’t an Oscar for that. The play-within-a-movie conceit is just an excuse to show off enormous, elaborate sets-within-the-set: One of the massive picture windows in Digger’s mansion becomes a frame for a stand of miniature trees, tended to by stage-hand giants; it's a cool effect—and yet, so what? There are quite a few actors here you’ll recognize, including an ashen-looking John Goodman—he plays the president of the United States, and his chief function is to boom loudly about the “cancer of the asshole” from which he suffers. Jesse Plemons plays a member of the play’s audience, a man with a secret and a very bad haircut, though he has only a few brief scenes. Occasionally, Sandra Hüller drifts through the movie as if searching for another, better picture that might actually give her something to do. For those who enjoy gazing into cavernous nostrils, there are lots of grotesque low-angle closeups. These performers deserve combat pay.
Through the whole of this aggressively unfunny, boneheaded farce, Cruise’s Digger stomps and swaggers, bellows and bloviates. He doesn’t speak his lines, he flings them, like unguided missiles in a cafeteria food fight. The ugly prosthetics are perhaps intended to suggest that Cruise has no vanity—he’s perfectly willing to look older and pudgier than he really is, as long as it proves to everyone once and for all that he’s a great actor as well as just a hugely bankable movie star. But acting to prove a point is the antithesis of acting; the point is to do the job, not advertise what a great job you’re doing. That’s the overarching problem with the movie as well. Iñárritu and his star aren’t telling us a story; they’re selling us, relentlessly, on the genius of the movie they’ve made. This is reverse-engineered awards bait, a movie that insists it’s digging for the truth, when all it’s really doing is shoveling.

Iraq’s sovereignty should not be defined by a single day
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
19:01:39 UTC
04:01:39 KST

Iraq’s sovereignty should not be defined by a single day
TEHRAN – Freedom without the means to defend it is only a promise and sovereignty without the power to protect it is only a symbol.
This is the situation facing the Iraqi people following the government’s announcement that September 30, 2026, will be designated as a national day known as “Sovereignty Day.” Baghdad has also declared four days of public holidays, from Wednesday through Saturday, to mark the event.
On the surface, the occasion appears to mark a legitimate national milestone. At its core, however, it raises an ambiguity that deserves the attention of both Arab and Iraqi leaders.
It is self-evident that sovereignty, both in political science and in the experience of nations that have endured the struggles of liberation, is not defined by a day proclaimed from a podium. It is measured instead by principles that people embraced before their governments did.
Chief among them is the departure of the last foreign soldier from Iraq’s territory and the sole authority of national security forces to defend its land, sea, and air. They also include freedom in political and economic decision-making from outside pressure, and the right of the people to choose their own path rather than accept imposed alternatives.
When these conditions are met, a date becomes a symbol worthy of celebration. When they are not, any day given this name remains little more than a title without substance.
At the heart of the debate in Iraqi political and media circles is not the name of the day itself. It is the attempt to link it, either openly or indirectly, to the question of disarming the resistance factions.
Critics argue that this is a methodological error before it is a political one. The literature and historical experience of states that emerged from occupation link sovereignty to the departure of foreign forces and the independence of national decision-making. They do not define it as the disarmament of the forces that helped achieve that independence.
In Iraq’s case, the weapons of the resistance were never used to rebel against the state. Rather, they were used first to defeat al-Qaeda and later Daesh, helping to clear Iraqi territory of a transnational terrorist threat. Their role also extended beyond Iraq’s borders, supporting other resistance fronts in the region, above all the Palestinian cause.
A similar question was raised during a meeting that brought together political and military leaders, Popular Mobilization Forces leaders, and the prime minister. The discussion focused on the rationale and timing of any move against the weapons or leadership of the resistance. It also considered the strong social support these forces enjoy among Iraqis and the potentially difficult-to-control reactions that could follow.
At a meeting attended by prominent military and political figures directly concerned with the matter, participants discussed the view that restricting or confiscating weapons did not reflect a genuine popular demand in Iraq. Rather, they saw it as a response to external pressure, including threats to restrict Iraqi funds.
This account was reportedly conveyed by people close to the decision-makers themselves, not only by opponents of the policy. This raises a fundamental question. Who is actually setting the agenda for “Sovereignty Day”?
The debate over sovereignty and disarmament in Iraq cannot be understood in isolation from the wider regional context. The region is experiencing an ongoing confrontation between Washington and Tel Aviv on one side and the Axis of Resistance on the other. Any discussion of disarmament in Baghdad must therefore be understood in the context of this broader conflict.
Nor is this debate new. It is part of a long struggle over the balance of military and political power in West Asia. For decades, Washington, Tel Aviv, and their allies have sought to weaken the capabilities of resistance factions opposed to the Zionist regime by targeting their leaders and positions across the region.
This shows that the real struggle is over influence and weapons, rather than the slogans repeatedly invoked to frame it.
The Israeli regime entered an unprecedented strategic crisis after October 7, 2023. The conflict was no longer, as it had been during the previous six rounds of fighting in Gaza, limited to a single geographic area. Instead, it expanded to include supporting fronts in Lebanon, Iraq, Yemen, and Iran.
Washington and its allies, therefore, faced a regional crisis with several interconnected fronts. In response, they adopted a common approach of treating the weapons of resistance forces in each country as a purely domestic matter, framing the issue in terms of sovereignty and state-building.
In Lebanon, calls to hand over weapons are made in the name of completing state sovereignty, even as Israeli aggression continues unabated.
In Gaza, bombardment and destruction continue, while the weapons of the Palestinian resistance forces remain a central factor in any future settlement.
In Yemen, military pressure on Ansarallah continues, while Iran resists sustained political, economic, and military coercion.
This leaves little doubt that the issue goes beyond Iraq’s internal affairs and is deeper than a debate over the strength of the state.
In Iraq, many fear that any hasty move to address the issue of resistance weapons could trigger internal strife or confrontation between the official security forces and forces that defeated Daesh and openly supported the Palestinian cause.
The recent experience in Syria may offer an instructive lesson. Following the political transformation in Damascus, the Israeli regime launched widespread attacks on Syrian army weapons depots and defensive systems. This highlights that stripping a state of its weapons can leave it more exposed and weaken its ability to defend itself. Disarmament can also become part of a broader effort to reshape the balance of power within the country.
A legitimate question naturally arises. Do foreign forces leave other countries of their own accord? Or does their departure usually come after armed resistance, widespread public opposition, or sustained protests and political pressure, as seen in numerous liberation struggles throughout modern history?
Had the matter been left entirely to foreign powers, it would be difficult to imagine them willingly abandoning the bases they established. American forces, for example, remain stationed at military bases in Japan and South Korea decades after the circumstances that originally justified their presence.
This confirms that foreign military presence is shaped by broader American strategic interests rather than being determined solely by the host country’s wishes.
The American announcement of the withdrawal or redeployment of its forces in Iraq should not be seen as an act of generosity toward Baghdad or the peoples of the region.
Rather, it should be understood as a response to the real risks faced by American forces, whether from Iran or other resistance fronts. These risks were among the key factors that led Washington to reconsider the nature of its military presence in the region.
If “Sovereignty Day” is to carry any genuine meaning, it should mark the beginning of a broader national project to complete Iraq’s sovereignty. That means regulating arms, pursuing development, and securing full control over its land, sea, and air. It should not become a ceremonial occasion whose significance ends when the official celebrations are over.
Ultimately, completing this national project requires concrete steps that go beyond celebratory rhetoric.
These include ending the Turkish military presence on Iraqi soil. All armed anti-Iranian terrorist groups should also be removed from Iraqi territory without exception. The Peshmerga forces should be integrated into the General Command of the Armed Forces in accordance with the Iraqi Constitution.
Iraq must also have an advanced national air-defense system capable of protecting its airspace, which has been repeatedly violated. Finally, the American trusteeship over Iraqi funds held at the Federal Reserve should come to an end.
This would restore Iraq’s independent control over its economic and financial decisions. If these requirements are fulfilled, rather than simply proclaiming a date as “Sovereignty Day,” Iraqis from north to south will be able to celebrate it with genuine justification, not simply as a matter of courtesy.
Iraqi resistance leaders have warned decision-makers in Baghdad that sovereignty built at the expense of those who paid for it with their blood could ultimately become a calamity for those who pursue it.
The Americans have repeatedly contributed to internal instability. Now, they are mobilizing their forces and proxies so that they can later claim, as they did in 2011: “Look at what happened after we withdrew. This is the result: chaos, disorder, and bloodshed.”
The international community would then legitimize their return. At that point, “Sovereignty Day” would risk becoming just another episode in Iraq’s troubled history, remembered more for the headlines than for any lasting achievement.

Iran National Orchestra opens Iran Cultural Week at Moscow’s Bolshoi Theater
TEHRAN- The National Orchestra of Iran, conducted by Homayoun Rahimian and featuring vocalist Mojtaba Asgari, opened the Cultural Week of the Islamic Republic of Iran in Russia with a concert at Moscow’s historic Bolshoi Theater on Monday evening.
The performance brought Iranian music to the Bolshoi’s stage, one of Russia’s best-known cultural venues, in an event attended by Iran’s Minister of Culture and Islamic Guidance Seyyed Abbas Salehi, Iran’s Ambassador to Russia Kazem Jalali, Russian Culture Minister Olga Lyubimova, as well as artists, cultural officials and Russian audiences.
The concert presented a selection of Iranian compositions alongside a work from the Russian classical repertoire, creating a musical dialogue between the two countries’ traditions.
The program opened with “Adam,” composed by Fardin Khalatbari to lyrics by Afshin Yadollahi. It was followed by “Naghmegar-e Eshq,” composed by Ali Jafarian with lyrics by Bijan Taraghi.
The orchestra then performed “Concerto for Tar and Orchestra” by Behzad Abdi, bringing the distinctive sound of the Iranian tar into an orchestral setting. The program continued with “Chelleh-ye Eshq,” another collaboration between Khalatbari and Yadollahi.
A performance of Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky’s “Swan Lake” subsequently added a familiar work from Russia’s classical musical heritage to the Iranian program.
The concert concluded with “Iran-e Ostovar” (“Strong Iran”), composed by Rahimian with lyrics by Hassan Rahimi, giving the closing section of the performance a distinctly national character.
Asgari’s Iranian vocal performance formed another central element of the concert, complementing the orchestra and presenting an important dimension of Iran’s traditional and contemporary musical expression to the Moscow audience.
The broader cultural program is being held in Moscow, St. Petersburg, Kazan and Astrakhan, bringing together 168 Iranian artists and cultural figures and covering fields including music, visual arts, handicrafts, theater, cinema, animation, video games, literature and manuscripts.
The Iranian National Orchestra is also scheduled to perform in other Russian cities as part of the program.
The orchestra will continue its Russian program in Kazan, extending the musical component of Iran’s cultural events to another major Russian city.

President Donald Trump has stressed self-regulation over government rules at a major gathering of artificial intelligence executives and government officials at the White House as Congress intensifies calls for stronger industry oversight.
Trump also indicated he would officially rename the technology "super intelligence" instead of artificial intelligence in government documents "because it's not artificial," he told reporters on Tuesday.
Asked by reporters if he believes no regulation of AI is necessary, Trump said: "Well, there's a belief that there should be tremendous self-regulation. And we automatically have regulation with the Department of Justice, the FBI, and all of that. But the self-regulation is very important."
Trump said the tech executives gathered at the White House to discuss had signed a "morally binding" commitment to build adequate safeguards on the fast-moving technology.
"They're going to police themselves," Trump said after the meeting.
The lunch meeting brought together some of the world's most influential tech leaders including Elon Musk, Jeff Bezos, Mark Zuckerberg, Satya Nadella of Microsoft, Sundar Pichai of Google and Jensen Huang of Nvidia.
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and OpenAI President Greg Brockman also attended.
Trump called meeting with the AI bosses as "very productive" and "extremely friendly", adding, "The one thing that we all have in common is we love our country and we love the world, and we want to make sure it's a safe place."
He said when he met last week with Chinese President Xi Jinping, Xi "acknowledged these are the most brilliant people."
AI and midterms
The gathering occurs as attitudes to AI sour in Washington, with lawmakers increasingly under pressure from voters to curb or slow AI development over fears it could displace workers and upend society.
Those concerns gained force from a run of incidents in which OpenAI's autonomous systems slipped out of their constraints, beginning with a July breach of Hugging Face — a widely used platform for sharing AI models.

The firm announced on Monday it was canceling the release of its latest model, known as Astra 6.1, after internal testing by the ChatGPT-maker revealed it did not meet safety standards.
Trump, advised by Huang and his former AI czar David Sacks, has urged unfettered AI development to outpace China and fuel a US economy increasingly dependent on AI-driven growth.
The issue of data centres, the vast computing facilities the technology requires, has emerged as a flashpoint in midterm election races in both parties, with more and more communities worried about rising electricity bills and the strain on water and land.
Trump has dismissed opponents of these data centers, saying communities against them "want to end up being backwards and poor" and that China "could not be happier" with the backlash.
The AI debate has created unusual political bedfellows: Senator Bernie Sanders appeared this month on the same Washington stage as former Trump strategist Steve Bannon to call for a rethink of the AI race.
'Right balance'
Meeting attendee Mike Johnson, who leads the Republican-controlled House of Representatives, signaled that the gathering was focused on striking what he termed "the right balance" between innovation and some form of oversight.
"We do not need a moratorium. We do not need to jump in and hyper-regulate this, because we'll lose the race to China," Johnson said in a Monday interview with Fox Business Network.
Major AI companies, particularly Anthropic and OpenAI, have issued stark public warnings about uncontrolled development of increasingly powerful systems — even as they develop and deploy this same state-of-the-art technology.
Those concerns intensified after a former employee of both companies went public with warnings that the industry is moving faster than safety reviews allow.
Anthropic warned investors of potential existential risks to humanity in the prospectus for its highly anticipated initial public offering, the Financial Times reported on Tuesday.
Anthropic is aiming for an IPO as early as November.
Trump has repeatedly characterised these warnings about existential risks as overblown and opposes curbs on the sector.
With midterm elections in November, lawmakers from both parties have drafted multiple bills to better govern AI.
Some would require companies to disclose more about how their systems work and what safeguards they employ.
But with the House on recess through early November and senators soon to head home to campaign, Congress is all but certain not to pass comprehensive AI legislation before the vote.
