Exclusive: Zomlot says public drove UK Labour shift on Palestine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
18:10:19 UTC
03:10:19 KST

Breadcrumb
Exclusive: Zomlot says years of public pressure drove UK Labour Palestine shift
Palestinian Ambassador to the UK Husam Zomlot has welcomed Labour’s shift on Palestine, telling The New Arab that the government has finally acknowledged that the British public “were right and they were wrong”, as Prime Minister Andy Burnham recommitted the UK to securing a two-state solution.
Burnham, who took office 10 weeks ago, used his conference speech on Tuesday to back the Palestine policy set out by Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband a day earlier, pledging that his government would be “principled in our leadership in securing a two-state solution for Israel and Palestine”.
The remarks followed Miliband’s acknowledgement on Monday that pro-Palestine activists “were right” to protest Israel’s war on Gaza, marking a shift in tone after sustained pressure on Labour over its approach to Israel and Palestine.
On the sidelines of the Labour conference in Liverpool, Zomlot told TNA that Miliband’s speech had “brought a great deal of unity in the party” and expressed hope that the rhetoric would now translate into government policy.
“I hope this is a moment of unity and clarity of the direction for Palestine,” he said, adding that the government’s policy shift “came a bit late, but at least they have acknowledged that the British people were right and they were wrong.”
Palestine has been a key issue for Labour since it came to power in 2024, with activists demanding tougher action against Israel over its war on Gaza, which has killed more than 73,000 Palestinians.
Zomlot credited sustained public pressure with helping drive the shift, saying support for Palestine had come first and foremost from the British public.
“The solidarity with the Palestinian people has been primarily by the people, and now finally governments are converging, and this reminds us of South Africa and the anti-apartheid movement,” he told TNA.
The Palestine Solidarity Campaign also responded to Burnham’s commitment by urging the government to put Palestinian rights at the centre of any political settlement.
James Tuite, a campaigns officer for the group, told The New Arab that ensuring those rights were upheld was “what the British government needs to be working towards to ensure”.
Burnham also recommitted the UK to supporting Ukraine and said his government would “stand up to threats wherever they come from, whether Russia, Iran, or anywhere”.
Fending off Reform
Alongside his foreign policy commitments, Burnham used the speech to set out a series of domestic policies as part of his efforts to draw “a line on a decade of division”, while addressing the electoral challenge posed by Reform UK.
Electoral reform featured prominently, with Burnham addressing a political landscape in which Reform had been polling above 30 percent and in first place before his premiership.
Although he did not name Reform explicitly, Burnham warned: “We will all have failed in our public duties if we carry on as we are and open the door of Number 10 to a divisive government on less than 30% of the vote.”
He announced that a national commission on electoral reform would be established and promised that electoral reform would become a manifesto pledge for Labour at the next general election.
Burnham also used the issue of migration to reopen the debate over the UK’s relationship with the European Union, telling delegates: “We have to be honest. Brexit hasn’t given us control.”
While backing his government’s efforts to tackle small-boat crossings and migration, Burnham also addressed rising anti-migrant sentiment in the country.
“We will always be grateful, and we thank them, for those people who come here, and contribute to our country. Thank you to them,” he said.
Burnham said he would use an upcoming summit with the EU to lay out several options for a long-term partnership with the bloc and seek a national consensus on which one to pursue.
Other issues raised in the speech included plans for the UK to lead globally on artificial intelligence, build a new education system that brings greater parity between academic and technical skills, reform social care and bring water into public control.
Burnham also defended the union of the four nations that make up the UK, challenging Scottish First Minister John Swinney’s claim that he would be the last leader of the United Kingdom.
He ended by urging Labour members to rally behind his government, saying it was “time to draw a line, to move beyond a decade of drift and division, to bring a spirit of unity and positivity to our country”.

Manchester City found guilty of serious financial breaches, to appeal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
18:08:57 UTC
03:08:57 KST

Manchester City were found guilty of serious breaches of Premier League financial rules during a nine-season period, with the club announcing it would appeal the landmark ruling.
An independent commission on Tuesday found City committed breaches between the 2009-10 and 2017-18 seasons, including arranging “sham” contracts with commercial partners, misstating accounts and concealing the true state of their finances from auditors and football regulators.
It found the arrangements artificially increased revenues and reduced costs by more than $1.2 billion, allowing the club to appear compliant with financial regulations. It concluded City would otherwise have substantially breached Premier League and UEFA spending limits.
City were also found to have breached their obligations to cooperate with the Premier League investigation, with three of four related allegations upheld. The commission said the club had made efforts to frustrate the investigation.
Premier League chief executive Richard Masters described the case as the most significant disciplinary proceeding in the competition’s history, saying the findings established that City had systematically broken rules for nearly a decade.
A sanction has not yet been determined and will be considered at a separate hearing. Premier League rules allow penalties including fines, points deductions and other sporting sanctions.
Manchester City said they were “disappointed and surprised” by the ruling and maintained their innocence, arguing that the decision contained “clear material errors” of law, principle and fact.
The club confirmed it would pursue available appeal avenues. It has until Oct. 2 to formally challenge the findings.

Palestine on Tuesday called on companies worldwide to review their relationships with businesses included in the updated UN human rights office's database of businesses involved in activities linked to illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied Palestinian territory.
Palestine's permanent representative to the UN in Geneva welcomed the rights office's latest update, which lists 214 companies, including 61 newly added businesses.
"It is abundantly clear at this juncture that many enterprises of the 214 among the list are Israeli companies that have links with different companies in many countries around the world," Ibrahim Khraishi told the UN Human Rights Council.
"Any enterprises cooperating with these Israeli enterprises need to review those relationships," he said.
The rights office said the updated database covers 214 companies from 11 countries involved in specified settlement-related activities.
The Palestinian envoy welcomed decisions by companies that have withdrawn from settlement-related activities, including some that abandoned previously signed contracts, and called on the UN rights office to update the database annually.
In the update, five previously listed companies were removed after the office found reasonable grounds to believe their involvement in the specified activities had ceased.
Israel was not present in the room when the update was presented to the council and did not exercise its right of reply as the country concerned.
Meanwhile, Spain's permanent representative to the UN in Geneva accused Israel of "systematically violating those fundamental rights of the civilian population, submitting them to suffering an intolerable dehumanization with military campaigns, aggressions by settler gangs, destruction of homes, of key infrastructure, and the livelihoods in a context of total lack of legal security."
He urged Israel to comply with UN Security Council resolutions, cooperate with UN human rights mechanisms and fulfill its responsibilities as the occupying power.
"We reiterate our call to the government of Israel to withdraw from all occupied Arab territories, including from the Golan Heights, and to withdraw their military forces from all of Lebanese territory," he said. "Israel must immediately reverse measures aimed at the de facto annexation of the occupied territories."
The two-state solution, according to the envoy, is "the only means for achieving a just, lasting peace."

Anthropic Says It Discovered a Crispr-Like System. Now What?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
18:03:01 UTC
03:03:01 KST

Tech executives have long touted the potential for their AI models to accelerate the pace of biology discoveries. Last week, they announced one. In a September 23 announcement, Anthropic claimed that its large language model Claude had identified an enzyme system with properties “reminiscent of Crispr,” the Nobel Prize-winning gene-editing tool.
According to Anthropic, about 950 Claude agents running simultaneously found the interesting genetic sequences in 21.5 hours. “I sincerely compliment Anthropic for telling the world about their discovery,” says Fyodor Urnov, a gene-editing expert at the University of California, Berkeley and director for therapeutic R&D at its Innovative Genomics Institute. (IGI is collaborating with Anthropic, but was not involved with the new discovery.)
Other scientists are less enthusiastic about the finding, which is the first to come out of a research group formed by Anthropic earlier this year. “The experiments are still in the queue. The PR is already live,” says Le Cong, a professor at Stanford University focused on integrating AI into genome engineering research.
Anthropic, which has set up a wet lab for drug discovery, has been clear that the finding isn’t the end of its work. (“We don’t yet understand what this system does,” the company said in an X post, “but only a handful of known systems share its features, and all of them are able to cut, copy, and paste DNA.”) One physical experiment was included in a technical report, which has not been peer-reviewed. However, a lot more needs to be done to determine the significance of this discovery. It remains unknown whether this enzyme system can be used as a gene-editing tool and, if so, whether it’s a useful gene-editing tool.
“Let's say we are on Santa Monica Beach and trying to scan through all the sand to find a diamond,” Cong says. “AI found this thing that looks very shiny, and then you have to go back to the lab to know—is it glass? Is it a diamond?”
Claude found this shiny object after researchers at Anthropic prompted it to search through huge genomic databases for “interesting new examples” of reverse transcriptases, proteins that copy RNA into DNA. This is the opposite of the normal process in our cells, in which DNA is transcribed into RNA, but is used by other organisms in a variety of biological functions, including inserting segments of DNA.
Claude agents initially identified more than 200,000 possible reverse transcriptases, according to Anthropic, and, after picking out several thousand that appeared to be new, narrowed the scope even further, eventually finding an “unusual” reverse transcriptase family containing a long region of repeat DNA sequences that resemble Crispr. Anthropic is calling this system ART, short for array-associated reverse transcriptases. The system is found in jumbo phages, large viruses that infect bacteria.
“I can see by eye a tandem repeat array … that's a Crispr-like … repeat array?!” an AI agent wrote. The agent also acknowledged that this system could be a retron, as noted in the technical report. Crispr and retrons are both bacterial immune systems, and while retrons have some utility in gene editing, they’re not the same multi-tool Crispr is. It’s therefore not too surprising Anthropic’s blog post played up the Crispr comparison.
Seth Shipman, associate investigator at the Gladstone Institutes, doesn’t think what Anthropic found is a new Crispr system, but says the discovery is still interesting. “The novel thing is how they found it, not what it is,” he says. His lab has used retrons to make gene-editing systems, so it is possible to use retrons in this way.
Identifying new reverse transcriptases can take months of mining genome databases manually, so Shipman says the fact that Anthropic was able to do this in a day is impressive. But he cautions against attributing the discovery entirely to an AI model. “I think we have to be careful about saying that Claude autonomously discovered something, because there are scientists involved in the study,” he says.
In fact, this same reverse transcriptase was previously identified by Jason Gill, a microbiologist at Texas A&M University, and his colleagues in a 2021 paper on jumbo phages. What’s perhaps new is that Claude identified repeats around it that hinted the enzyme might be part of a Crispr-like system.
“These models are good at finding patterns, better than a person staring at it with their eyeballs can,” Gill says. “A person could do all this but you have to already have a hypothesis in mind.” He adds that ART appears to have no “obvious relationship” to any known Crispr system, and it’s on Anthropic to prove that it actually has gene-editing activity.
Cong credits the scientists for finding the perfect kind of problem for Claude to tackle, given its pattern-seeking abilities. It’s possible the model could be used for similar large-data projects, but that doesn’t mean Claude will suddenly be accelerating all sorts of discoveries in the life sciences.
What kinds of information this model was trained on is also not something the scientific community can evaluate, which makes these findings unusually opaque in an era where major journals require scientists to freely publish their code in the name of reproducibility. This has also led a researcher who had been studying these exact enzymes to become suspicious that the model was trained on his work, since he’d shared yet unpublished findings with the public version of Claude. (“Claude was,” Anthropic told the New York Times, “not trained on any user transcripts, and our molecular biology team has no such access, either.”)
Even if Claude did identify the next big thing in gene editing, it would still take human scientists testing out that hypothesis in the lab to prove it. In a post on X about the discovery, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei mused, “Eventually it may even be possible for Claude itself to safely perform the experiments by autonomously controlling lab equipment.” Even if this does prove possible, it will be in a fairly distant future. (The idea, of course, raises many questions about safety and oversight, and Amodei quickly followed up this thought by mentioning that Anthropic’s labs are at the lowest biosafety levels, and thus don’t contain anything greatly harmful to humans.)
Answers in this area don’t come quickly. It took 25 years from the initial discovery of Crispr sequences in bacteria in 1987 until Jennifer Doudna and Emmanuelle Charpentier demonstrated it could be a programmable tool to cut DNA in 2012. And while Crispr is now ubiquitous in labs and is being tested in dozens of clinical trials to treat cardiovascular conditions, cancers, autoimmune diseases, and rare disorders, there is only one drug on the market so far that uses the technology, approved in late 2023. It’s a testament to the long arc of scientific progress—and the difficulties of translating promising basic science findings into medicines.
The limits of Anthropic’s finding also point to a more fundamental issue. What made Crispr revolutionary was that scientists identified a biological system that was previously unknown. It remains to be seen whether any AI model is capable of finding something useful without knowing exactly what it’s looking for.
“If you have an AI that only trained on knowledge from before people ever discovered Crispr, and then that AI actually discovered Crispr, that seems to be a better setup to test an AI scientist,” Cong says.

Royal Navy navigation interface work to go to OSI Maritime
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
19:00:46 BST
03:00:46 KST

The Ministry of Defence intends to award OSI Maritime Systems a two-year contract worth £15 million including VAT to design, build, install and assure replacement interface units connecting the Royal Navy’s electronic chart system to its combat systems, placing the work directly on the grounds that no other company could do it, the department stated in a transparency notice.
The notice, identifier 2026/S 000-091457, was published on 28 September by the National Armaments Director Group and gives a value of £12.5 million excluding VAT. The earliest date the contract can be signed is 15 March 2027, with estimated dates running from 1 April 2027 to 31 March 2029.
What is being bought is the plumbing rather than the system itself. The Warship Electronic Chart Display and Information System, known as WECDIS, is the digital charting and navigation system fitted to warships, and the two units covered here connect it to the wider systems aboard. Both have to work with an upgraded WECDIS already being procured from the same company under a separate transparency notice published in November last year.
According to the department, the interfaces also have to integrate with the Electronic Chart Precise Integrated Navigation System and the Warship Automatic Identification System already installed across the affected platforms, all of which are supplied, supported and assured by OSI. Only that company holds the intellectual property rights, technical drawings, design knowledge, safety assurance evidence and specialist expertise needed to produce replacements compatible with the existing architecture, the notice states, and there are no reasonable alternatives.
The company currently supplying the interface units was approached about continuing, and according to the notice, the equipment support package it offered, which included an update to the interface components, did not represent value for money and would not have delivered the obsolescence recovery the department needs, so it will not be taken forward, and the notice does not name that supplier.
The award is being made under Section 41 of the Procurement Act 2023, relying on the justification at paragraph 6 of Schedule 5 covering a single supplier for technical reasons, and the notice is published under the defence and security special regime. The department states that it assessed alternative procurement approaches before settling on this route and concluded that OSI was the only viable supplier able to meet its technical, operational, interoperability and safety requirements.
OSI Maritime Systems is a Canadian company based at Burnaby in British Columbia, and is recorded in the notice as not being a small or medium-sized enterprise. Its navigation systems are in service with a considerable number of NATO and allied navies, and the company has supplied the Royal Navy’s electronic charting for years, which is the reason the technical case for going direct reads as it does.
Transparency notices of this type are published before a direct award is made rather than after, so that the market can see both the intention and the reasoning while there is still time to raise concerns. The notice records that a conflicts assessment has been prepared, flags the requirement as particularly suitable for voluntary, community and social enterprises, and lists the supplier as not being one.

Lula adapts Bad Bunny's 'What Happened to Hawaii' amid US tensions ahead of Brazil's tight vote
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
18:00:31 UTC
03:00:31 KST

With elections just days away, Brazil's President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva's campaign has adapted a song by Puerto Rican artist Bad Bunny to talk about national sovereignty and external pressures.
"They want to take the river, and the beach too. They want the rare earth minerals," goes the reworked Portuguese version of "Lo que le paso a Hawaii" (What Happened to Hawaii) by Bad Bunny, posted by Lula on his social media accounts.
Brazilians will vote in a nail-biting first-round presidential election on Sunday, pitting Lula, 80, against right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, son of far-right former president Jair Bolsonaro.
Lula has made sovereignty a key plank of his campaign, amid pressure from US President Donald Trump, a Bolsonaro ally who has backed several right-wing candidates in Latin American elections.
Washington has slapped punitive tariffs on Brazil and has expressed keen interest in its massive reserves of critical minerals.
With nearly seven million views on social media, the campaign jingle inspired by the Puerto Rican star calls on people not to "let go of the Brazilian flag."
It ends with Lula declaring: "Brazil has only one owner: the Brazilian people."
Flavio Bolsonaro's campaign has often featured United States flags and images of Trump.
'Brazil does not belong in anyone's backyard'
Bad Bunny's song addresses the loss of local control through the impact of tourism, gentrification and displacement — using Hawaii as a cautionary tale for Puerto Ricans.
The singer included the tune in his setlist at the Super Bowl halftime show in February, described by Trump as "an affront to the Greatness of America."
A source from Lula's Workers' Party, requesting anonymity, said Bad Bunny had not granted rights for the song's use. The artist's press office did not respond to an AFP news agency’s request for comment.
"Bad Bunny is an artist who recognises our worth... he stood on the world's biggest stage to reaffirm that we are all America," said Warlen Pereira, a 30-year-old accountant, during a Lula campaign event in Sao Paulo.
Lula has warned Trump against "meddling" in his country's elections and last week told the UN General Assembly that "Brazil does not belong in anyone's backyard."

Desk setups that encourage an expansive posture may boost risk-taking
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
18:00:01 UTC
03:00:01 KST

A recent study published in British Journal of Psychology suggests that people’s physical posture, even when influenced naturally by their environment, can affect their mood and willingness to take risks. The findings indicate that environments forcing individuals into a more upright, expansive position might subtly encourage riskier decisions compared to settings that cause them to hunch over.
The concept of embodied emotion suggests that adopting the physical expressions of an emotion can trigger the experience of that emotion. For instance, power poses involve making the body expansive and upright to signal dominance, while contractive postures involve hunching and taking up less physical space to signal submission.
Early research claimed that deliberately holding expansive body postures boosts feelings of dominance and leads to riskier decisions, according to a widely cited 2010 study. However, major replication efforts, such as a high-profile 2015 replication, failed to find any change in risk-taking from deliberate power posing. This sparked a debate over whether the original findings were genuine or simply the result of people guessing what the experimenters wanted them to do.
Subsequent research showed that subtly guiding people into specific postures without explicitly telling them how to pose still alters their mood and cognitive performance, as seen in a 2021 study. Relatedly, a study covered by PsyPost in 2024 found that naturally standing more upright is associated with higher levels of social dominance orientation. This progression led researchers to ask a new question: can an incidental manipulation of posture, where the physical environment naturally nudges someone into a stance, influence risk-taking behavior without them knowing it?
The research, led by Soren Wainio-Theberge of McGill University, aimed to test this question. The researchers recruited 198 participants, mostly young women, and randomly assigned them to two different experimental groups. An additional 113 participants, recruited as part of a different project, were included to serve as a control group.
The study utilized an incidental posture manipulation, meaning that instead of instructing participants to sit a certain way, the researchers altered the physical environment. Participants sat at an adjustable table to complete a computerized task on a tablet. For the expansive group, the table was raised and the tablet was placed on a stand slightly above eye level, prompting an upright posture. For the contractive group, the table was lowered to near knee level, forcing participants to hunch over to see the screen.
To measure risk-taking, participants completed the Balloon Analogue Risk Task. In this task, participants earn virtual money by pumping up a digital balloon. Each pump adds virtual money to a temporary pot, but if the balloon pops, the money for that round is lost, requiring participants to decide when to cash out and bank their earnings or take the risk of another pump.
The researchers also recorded participants with a video camera to objectively measure their actual neck angles, ensuring they were genuinely adopting the intended postures. Finally, participants completed questionnaires about their mood and feelings of pride before and after the task.
The environmental manipulation successfully changed participants’ postures without most of them realizing it. Video analysis confirmed that those in the expansive group sat with a more extended, upright neck angle compared to the hunched posture of the contractive group. Most participants later reported having no idea that their posture was being manipulated by the setup.
In terms of behavior, the expansive group exhibited higher levels of risk-taking. As the experiment progressed, participants in the expansive group chose to pump the balloons more times before cashing out compared to those in the contractive group. This increase in risk-taking translated to slightly higher overall earnings for the expansive group, averaging 701 virtual dollars compared to 645 in the contractive group, without an increase in the number of balloons that actually popped.
When comparing the results to the control group, who completed the task at a standard desk setup, the researchers noticed that the expansive group drove the behavioral differences. The expansive group took more risks than the control group, while the contractive group behaved similarly to the controls. Physical posture also influenced emotional states, with a more upright neck angle predicting a stronger sense of self-reported pride after the task.
These results stand in tension with a 2017 study covered by PsyPost, which found that deliberate power posing had no beneficial effects on risk-taking in real-world situations. However, the new study induced posture subtly through environmental setup rather than instructing participants to hold deliberate poses, which may account for the differing behavioral outcomes.
As with all research, there are a few things to keep in mind. The study relied primarily on young, female university students from a single Western country. This specific demographic means the findings might not naturally apply to older adults, males, or people from other cultural backgrounds where social dominance is expressed differently.
Allowing participants to adopt postures naturally in response to their environment also created physical variability. In the contractive group, some people dropped their heads to look at the screen, while others leaned forward from the hips. This inconsistency makes it harder to pin down exactly which physical movements drive the changes in mood and behavior, suggesting a need for future studies to track body mechanics in greater detail.
The study, “Manipulating posture implicitly through environmental constraints influences mood and risk-taking behaviour,” was authored by Soren Wainio-Theberge and Jorge Armony.

Israel faces growing hostility around the world, going beyond its policies - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
18:00:00 UTC
03:00:00 KST

Israel is obsessively demonized and singled out for alleged human rights violations by global media outlets and international forums. Concurrently, there is a burgeoning sentiment that denies the Jewish nation’s right to self-determination and statehood.
The underlying causes of this hostility toward the Jewish state are multifaceted, deeply rooted, and mutually reinforcing.
First, Israel’s reality is characterized by a state of protracted conflict. Over the past three years, the nation has faced persistent aggression from terror armies along its northern and southern borders, while Iran has launched missile strikes against Israeli population centers – explicitly articulating its objective to eliminate the Jewish state.
As with all wars, Israel’s defensive counteroffensives generate distressing imagery that shapes public perception. Despite a shifting global security landscape marked by rising threats from Russia and China and a subsequent push for rearmament, the use of military force remains unpopular across much of the world.
Furthermore, the complexities and destructive consequences of modern warfare in densely populated civilian areas remain widely misunderstood.
Consequently, Israel has been unjustly accused of orchestrating starvation in Gaza and committing genocide, overriding the reality of its military’s unprecedented operational efforts to mitigate collateral damage and to facilitate the delivery of vast quantities of humanitarian aid – much of which was subsequently misappropriated by Hamas.
Second, the pervasive animosity directed at the Jewish state possesses a profound theological foundation. Within Christianity and Islam – the world’s two largest religions, which collectively encompass over half of the global population – doctrines are predicated on the Jewish rejection of their respective paths to salvation. These theological frameworks have generated centuries of overt antisemitism.
While it is certain that not all Christians and Muslims harbor antisemitic views, their respective cultural traditions remain permeated by these historical motifs.
In Christianity, the concept of deicide aligns with the historical condemnation of the Jewish rejection of Jesus as the savior.
Similarly, Islamic tradition critiqued the Jewish refusal to recognize Muhammad as a prophet. Although Jews were classified as “People of the Book” rather than infidels, they were nonetheless relegated to the subordinated status of dhimmitude, rendering them second-class citizens within Muslim-majority societies.
While various Christian bodies have made modern efforts to reform internal attitudes toward Judaism, their long-term efficacy remains ambiguous.
Conversely, comparable theological revisions in Islam are almost nonexistent. Furthermore, the modern resurgence of radical Islamism has fortified anti-Jewish sentiments among Muslims, stressing the view that Jewish statehood is a religious sacrilege.
Third, Israel’s unique historical narrative elicits significant skepticism among non-Jews. Zionism, the Jewish national movement, represents an unusual trajectory wherein an ancient people, expelled from its ancestral land, returned to reestablish its state after a two-millennium Diaspora. When juxtaposed against the contemporary Palestinian narrative, the Zionist history frequently fails to persuade observers who lack historical depth. Proponents of Zionism are often forced to explain the complex history of the region, including the fact that a substantial proportion of the Arab population in Palestine arrived via migration only during the 19th century.
Moreover, global public opinion remains largely oblivious to the historical record of Palestinian Arab leadership consistently rejecting all suggested territorial compromises, responding instead with enduring violence.
Justifying Israel’s legitimacy requires a historical literacy that the general public often lacks. Today, Israel finds itself entangled in a tragic conflict with a very hostile population often perceived by outsiders as indigenous victims of oppression.
This dynamic is exacerbated by a postcolonial guilt within parts of the West, which is subsequently projected onto the Arab-Israeli conflict; the establishment of Israel is viewed through a colonialist prism, positing that Western imperial powers implanted a Jewish polity in the Levant to secure regional hegemony.
This perspective has been widely adopted across the Muslim world, reinforcing existing religious hostility and the belief that Israel is a transient, modern version of the Crusader state, destined for collapse.
Fourth, Western societies increasingly exhibit post-nationalist attitudes that are critical of nationalist particularism. This trend is particularly evident among younger Europeans, who see themselves primarily as Europeans rather than citizens of a specific nation-state. This transnational preference is sustained by multicultural ideologies that tend to obscure national identities.
A distinctly nationalist project
In stark contrast to this trend, Israel remains a distinctly nationalist project. Within progressive and leftist intellectual circles, nationalism has been increasingly delegitimized, often conflated with jingoism and reactionary conservatism.
Furthermore, certain critics seek to reduce Jewish identity strictly to a religious category, thereby denying the validity of its national manifestation.
Fifth, the radical Left, which has long maintained hostility toward Zionism, has gained significant global influence.
This ideological shift is visible within European socialist and social-democratic parties; for instance, the Labour Party in the United Kingdom has adopted anti-Israel policy positions.
In the United States, the administration of president Barack Obama served as an ideological precursor to the ascendance of the progressive wing within the Democratic Party, a faction increasingly critical of Israeli policies compared to traditional elements of the American political mainstream.
This broader polarization of domestic politics across Western nations has empowered political extremes on both sides, each harboring distinct forms of animosity toward Israel.
Sixth, there is a consolidation of the “red-green” alliance – an alignment between the political Left and Islamist factions. This alliance has emerged as a potent political force, particularly in Western Europe, where expanding Muslim minorities exert growing electoral and political influence.
Because these factions oppose the global projection of American power and values, their hostility is naturally extended to Israel, which is correctly identified as a staunch American ally.
Furthermore, widespread international disapproval of political figures such as US President Donald Trump has further degraded Israel’s diplomatic image by association.
Seventh, the collective memory of the Holocaust is experiencing a natural generational decline. The historical sentiments of guilt and sympathy regarding Jewish suffering are weaker today than in the immediate postwar era, leaving public consciousness vulnerable to deeply entrenched anti-Jewish biases.
Regrettably, these historical sympathies are occasionally replaced by a perverted rhetoric that frames Palestinians as victims of Nazi-like Israeli actions.
The Palestinians have conducted public diplomacy campaigns designed to institutionalize a narrative of victimhood.
This global effort to cultivate hostility toward Israel has been heavily subsidized by Arab states – most notably Qatar.
Eighth, opponents of Israeli policy frequently cite domestic Israeli critiques. Furthermore, Diaspora organizations such as “Jews for Justice in Palestine” and advocacy groups like J Street in the United States align themselves with campaigns critical of Israeli policy.
Conversely, on the opposite end of the ideological spectrum, the controversial rhetoric and positions of radical right-wing Israeli factions, with a representation within the present Israeli government, provide external critics with ready pretexts to erode the legitimacy of the state.
In conclusion, hostility toward Israel is a pervasive global phenomenon that mirrors the historical permanence of antisemitism. Consequently, shifts in Israeli policies can alter this reality only marginally.
While navigating an exceedingly difficult diplomatic landscape, Israeli public diplomacy must remain committed to projecting the state as a rational and moral actor amid the geopolitical instability affecting portions of both the Middle East and the West.
Ultimately, strategic messaging must consistently emphasize that Israel’s existential struggle serves the national security and civilizational interests of the Western world.
The writer, a professor emeritus in political studies at Bar-Ilan University, is the founder and senior researcher at the Jerusalem Institute for Strategy and Security.

Morocco's king appoints first woman PM following election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
17:53:36 UTC
02:53:36 KST

Breadcrumb
Morocco's king appoints first woman prime minister following election
King Mohammed VI appointed Fatima Ezzahra El Mansouri on Tuesday as Morocco's first woman prime minister after her liberal-centrist party came out on top in a September 23 parliamentary election, the royal palace said.
The king asked El Mansouri to form a new government, the palace said in a statement.
El Mansouri’s Authenticity and Modernity Party (PAM) was created in 2008 by an adviser to the king and has since positioned itself as a counterweight to the Islamist Justice and Development Party (PJD) by advocating social modernisation and secular-leaning views.
Morocco is a constitutional monarchy where the king retains sweeping powers over foreign policy, defence and other key portfolios.
Under Morocco's constitution, the king appoints the head of government from the political party that wins the largest number of seats in the House of Representatives.
PAM, which was the second-largest member in the outgoing coalition, moved up to the top spot, bolstered by the recruitment of Fouzi Lekjaa, Morocco's football federation chief and two-time government budget manager, who joined weeks before the vote.
El Mansouri, a lawyer who was housing minister in the outgoing government and Marrakech mayor, will lead talks to form a coalition government and submit a list of cabinet members for the king's approval.
'No red lines'
The incoming government will oversee the last stages of a $20-billion push to get ready for the 2030 World Cup, which Morocco will co-host with Portugal and Spain.
It will also implement economic policies aimed at addressing widespread youth discontent, an issue highlighted by a mass border rush on the Spanish enclave of Ceuta in July and deadly Gen-Z-led protests last year.
PAM won 97 seats, followed by its partners in the outgoing government, the liberal-centrist National Rally of Independents (RNI) with 66 seats, and the conservative nationalist Istiqlal with 65.
During the campaign, PAM had ruled out staying in a coalition with the RNI — the two had traded blame over policy shortcomings including a failure to halt rises in food prices.
But El Mansouri said on Thursday she would have no "red lines" when it came to negotiations. "We have turned the page," she said.
Abdelilah Benkirane, former prime minister and leader of the PJD, which won 54 seats, said the party would stay in opposition.
Three leftist parties took smaller shares of the seats.
Turnout, closely watched as an indicator of trust in elected institutions, fell to about 38% from around 50% in the previous elections five years ago, when the moderate Islamist PJD was dealt a crushing defeat after a decade in power.
In recent years, King Mohammed VI had appointed a female adviser and Morocco has had women in senior institutional roles. The outgoing government had four women ministers.

Trump administration ‘must be changed’: Iran’s IRGC appeals to US voters
Iran’s military has issued an open letter accusing Trump of lying to US citizens about the state of the ongoing war.
Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) has made a direct appeal to Americans, saying the United States government under President Donald Trump “must be changed”.
In a lengthy open letter (PDF) released on Tuesday, the IRGC tells Americans to “wake up” and “wrest control back from corrupt politicians”.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Iranians stock up on food and medicine as fears of new US fighting grow
- list 2 of 3Iran downplays possible role in Houthis’ recent Yemen victories
- list 3 of 3US-Iran talks in New York: What’s the latest?
The message comes five weeks before the midterm elections in the US and one day after the US-Israel war against Iran hit its seven-month mark.
“Now is the time, as the American political system is at its weakest,” the IRGC said.
Addressed to “the honorable people of the United States of America”, the letter accuses the Trump administration of misleading Americans about the war, Iran’s nuclear programme and who controls the Strait of Hormuz.
It also declares Iran the victor in the war, arguing that the US has failed to meet any of its stated goals, including curtailing Iran’s nuclear programme.
“The United States and Israel expended thousands of bombs and missiles, striking government and residential buildings, dozens of less-advanced and lower-tier weapons-manufacturing facilities, and a number of decommissioned military installations,” the letter said.
“Yet, aside from damaging several buildings tied to Iran’s nuclear industry and a limited number of air-defense sites, they failed to achieve any of their declared objectives.”
The letter is careful to distinguish the US government from its people, and it seeks to draw parallels between the concerns of US voters and Iranians.
It argues that “the nations of Iran and America are both, each in their own way, victims” of the “corrupt politicians” in the White House. “We share the same pain,” the letter said.
The letter is not Iran’s first attempt to reach Americans directly. Since the war began on February 28, Iran-linked media and online networks have used artificial intelligence (AI) to generate Lego-themed videos, memes and other short-form content in English to push Tehran’s message about the war.
The letter also offers an explanation for the “Death to America” slogan sometimes used in Iranian politics, insisting it is aimed at the US political establishment, not the American people.
“‘Death to America’ is a prayer for the eradication of the diabolical ruling elite whose seat of power is the White House,” the letter said.
‘Big lies’
Speaking to reporters on Tuesday, IRGC spokesperson Hossein Mohebbi echoed the letter’s message, accusing Trump of being an “inveterate liar” and telling Americans “big lies” while in office.
He also argued that US citizens are largely unaware of the “harms” of the Trump administration’s campaign.
“I feel that the American people are unaware of this reality,” Mohebbi told reporters on Tuesday. “If they were aware of these realities, they would definitely think differently, and they would definitely put pressure on their administration.”
Al Jazeera reached out to the White House for comment but had not received a response by the time of publication.
Trump has repeatedly cited the threat of nuclear weapons as one of the reasons for launching the war against Iran. But Iran denies seeking a nuclear weapon and has accused Trump of lying about its uranium enrichment programme, which it says is for civilian energy purposes.
“The enemy [US] knows that Iran is not after nuclear weapons,” Mohebbi said.
Mohebbi also pushed back against US assertions that Iran has lost much of its leverage over the Strait of Hormuz, a key waterway for the global fuel and fertiliser trade. Since the start of the war, Iran has restricted traffic through the strait, and the US has responded with a blockade.
“The fact that the Americans might manage, at great expense, considerable trouble and high risk to sneak a small vessel through the Strait of Hormuz under cover of darkness … does not mean the Strait is open,” Mohebbi said.
However, oil exports through the strait have been recovering, averaging about 13.2 million barrels per day over the past week, about 77 percent of their pre-war level, according to data from Kpler, a trade analytics firm.
Trump has repeatedly argued that Iran is “losing badly”, and he recently dismissed an Iranian proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz as “unacceptable”.
Both US and Iranian officials spoke separately with mediators on Monday as part of renewed efforts to end the war. Tehran said a day earlier that diplomacy was the only way to resolve the conflict.
But speaking to the United Nations General Assembly last week, Trump weighed whether to “annihilate” Iran.
“I have a big decision to make,” Trump said. “Will a deal be made with Iran that lets them rebuild and create a far greater country than it ever was before, maybe one of the greatest in the Middle East or even the world? Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly?”
He speculated that a deal might arise “right after the election” on November 3. The midterm races will determine which political party controls the US Congress — and whether Trump will face legislative roadblocks in the final two years of his second term.

Has Netanyahu's postponement of a state commission of inquiry into October 7 backfired? - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
17:48:21 UTC
02:48:21 KST

For Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, postponing a state commission of inquiry into October 7 may have looked like the sound political move.
Netanyahu’s stated argument in the aftermath of the massacre was that the time for a national inquiry would come after the war. That argument had a certain practical appeal. A country fighting on several fronts has urgent demands on its political and military leaders’ attention. An inquiry into the greatest security failure in Israel’s history would be long, difficult, and divisive.
It was also politically convenient. Why open the door to testimony, documents, and potentially damaging findings while trying to hold a coalition together through a war? Why allow an independent commission to establish a public record that might place at least part of the responsibility for October 7 at your doorstep? What politician with an eye on reelection would welcome that?
And, somewhat counterintuitively considering the anger in the country following the attack, Netanyahu appeared to have his eye not only on remaining in power but on running again. A commission of inquiry that produced damaging findings before an election could only hurt his chances.
Netanyahu, against considerable odds, has now made it to the end of his term. The election is less than a month away, and no state commission of inquiry has been established to examine the decisions that preceded the Hamas attack. If part of the calculation was to prevent its findings from shaping the next election, that part worked.
Or did it?
Postponing inquiry does not end questions
The difficulty with postponing an inquiry is that postponement does not put an end to the questions. It leaves them hanging, waiting for someone else to answer them. And that is what is happening now, in the final weeks of the campaign.
Reports that leaders in Egypt and the United Arab Emirates warned Netanyahu of danger from Gaza before October 7 have thrust the days and weeks before the attack back into the limelight. Netanyahu has denied receiving such warnings. The accounts remain contested, as do crucial questions about what, precisely, was said, how specific the warnings were, and whether any information reached Israel’s security agencies through other channels.
Meanwhile, a public confrontation has erupted between Netanyahu and former Shin Bet chief Ronen Bar. Netanyahu has accused Bar of knowing of warning signs during the night before the attack and failing to inform him. Bar denies that accusation. He says he warned Netanyahu of danger before October 7 and has called for the release of documents that he says would establish what the prime minister knew. The two are making claims about different points in the period leading up to the attack, and each is challenging the other’s account.
What is taking place now is not a commission weighing all the evidence, examining the documents, and questioning witnesses. It is a political argument conducted through statements, selected documents, media reports, and threats of lawsuits. The public is left to judge sharply conflicting claims without access to anything near a full record.
And that is the potential boomerang in Netanyahu’s strategy. An independent inquiry before an election could have damaged him. Without it, the campaign is full of speculation about what did and did not transpire before the attack.
Every new disclosure opens another question that triggers a response. Instead of containing October 7 as an issue, the failure to establish what happened has allowed it to return repeatedly, each time with a new set of allegations. And this is now dominating the agenda.
The timing could hardly be worse for the prime minister. Netanyahu wants to shift the election from who failed to protect the country on October 7 to who fundamentally changed the Mideast since then and who can protect Israel now: who stood up to Iran, who prosecuted the wars against Hamas and Hezbollah, and who can navigate a hostile international environment. His argument rests on his experience, his resolve, and the threats still facing the country.
Netanyahu’s remark at Tel Nof Airbase on Tuesday – that Israel’s adversaries may attempt an attack before the election – has stirred controversy. The warning may well reflect a genuine threat. It also reinforced the argument he wants voters to consider: that the danger is not over, and that his experience makes him the leader best equipped to confront it.
The reports about the period before October 7 pull the discussion in the opposite direction. They ask what the country’s most experienced prime minister understood about the threat that materialized on his watch, and what exactly he did with the information available to him.
That question does not absolve the IDF, the Shin Bet, or anyone else of responsibility. Their failures were profound, and a serious inquiry would have to deal with them as well.
No one account is widely accepted
But the prime minister cannot make questions about his actions before October 7 go away by pointing to failures elsewhere. He has ultimate political responsibility for the security policy his government pursued. The issue now is not whether he personally knew the date and hour of Hamas’s attack. It is what warnings reached him, what they conveyed, what decisions followed, and whether the government’s view of Hamas made it less willing to recognize a growing danger.
There is an irony here. A state commission might have given Netanyahu a forum to challenge the claims against him. It could have demanded relevant documents, questioned witnesses, and established whether the accounts emerging now are accurate, exaggerated, or wrong. It might also have found much that supported his argument about failures in the security agencies.
Instead, no account is widely accepted across the political divide. Netanyahu didn’t want a state commission and advanced a different mechanism, one whose composition and mandate would be shaped by politicians. His supporters argue that a commission appointed through the usual process would itself lack public trust.
None of this means that the latest reports will change the election result. Many voters formed their views of Netanyahu long ago; others will judge him on the wars that followed October 7, the economy, military service, or the available coalition alternatives. And an earlier commission, had one been established, might have produced headlines still more difficult for him than those appearing now.
But if politics played a part in the decision to delay, the apparent advantage was clear: get to election day without the findings of a state commission hanging over him. Netanyahu has done that. What he could not do was ensure that the questions themselves would fade.
He now faces the election with the facts of what preceded October 7 still bitterly contested – and with those arguments playing out in public, weeks before the vote. Whether that proves more politically costly than the inquiry he resisted is something voters will decide on October 27.

Ra’am, Joint List appeal election bans as petitions target Otzma Yehudit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
17:47:44 UTC
02:47:44 KST

Ra’am and the Joint List have appealed their exclusion from the October 27 election, while separate High Court petitions filed Tuesday seek to overturn the Central Elections Committee (CEC) decision to allow Otzma Yehudit to run.
Together with the mandatory Supreme Court review of the committee’s decisions to disqualify MK Ofer Cassif and Balad chairman Sami Abu Shehadeh, the filings placed the major election-disqualification disputes before the High Court.
The cases have reached the court through several legally distinct routes. Ra’am and the Joint List are appealing decisions against entire lists. The decisions against Cassif and Abu Shehadeh were transferred automatically because a committee vote barring an individual candidate cannot take effect without Supreme Court approval.
The Democrats and the Zulat Institute, meanwhile, filed High Court petitions challenging Otzma Yehudit’s approval. The Democrats are also contesting the rejection of their attempt to disqualify National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir and MK Tali Gottlieb.
Tuesday was the statutory deadline for election appeals. The Supreme Court must deliver its rulings in the ordinary election proceedings by Sunday. The Otzma petitioners are seeking intervention within the same compressed timetable, although their cases were filed as High Court petitions rather than statutory appeals.
Democrats, Zulat pushed for court intervention following disqualification vote
The Democrats and Zulat asked the High Court to intervene after the committee voted 19-10, with one abstention, against disqualifying Otzma Yehudit.
Both petitions face an immediate procedural obstacle. Under the law, only the attorney-general, the committee chairman, or at least one-quarter of the committee’s members may appeal the approval of a list. Neither petitioner secured the required support.
Zulat argues that the High Court should nevertheless exercise its broader constitutional authority to review the committee’s decision.
The Democrats’ petition challenges two separate decisions. It asks the court to require the committee to explain why Otzma Yehudit should not be barred or, alternatively, why Ben-Gvir and Gottlieb should not be individually disqualified.
Sohlberg did not consider the allegations against Ben-Gvir and Gottlieb, ruling that the request could not proceed because it had not obtained the signatures of one-third of the committee’s members as required for an application to disqualify an individual candidate.
The petition acknowledges that The Democrats lack both the signatures required to initiate the individual cases and the one-quarter support required to appeal the approval of a list. It argues that the High Court should make an exception because the case against the list was heard by the committee, the party is represented on the committee, and the allegations rely partly on court decisions and formal positions issued by the attorney-general.
The petition’s central argument is that senior Otzma candidates have used government authority and parliamentary immunity in ways that undermine the rule of law, civil rights, and the separation of powers.
Regarding Ben-Gvir, it cites court decisions and attorney-general opinions concerning alleged political interference in police operations, investigations, and appointments.
Regarding Gottlieb, it cites her assertion in civil proceedings that court orders did not apply to her because of parliamentary immunity; her call for demonstrators to go to the Beit Lid military base on the day protesters breached its outer barrier; and her refusal to report for questioning over the publication of a Shin Bet (Israel Security Service) employee’s identity. Gottlieb was subsequently indicted over that publication. The charge has not been decided.
The petition’s racism argument cites support by several Otzma candidates for Amiram Ben-Uliel, who was convicted of murdering three members of the Dawabshe family, and alleged identification with the outlawed Kach movement.
It also relies on Otzma’s “Disengagement Plan 710,” which calls for a government ministry to facilitate what the party describes as voluntary migration from Gaza. The petition argues that its numerical targets make it a plan to remove a population defined by nationality and residence.
Otzma Yehudit disqualification opposed by Attorney-General Gali Baharav-Miara
Attorney-General Gali Baharav-Miara opposed disqualifying Otzma before the committee. She described the evidence as deeply troubling and said it brought the list dangerously close to the prohibited territory, but she concluded that it did not amount to the “critical mass” required for disqualification.
Ben-Gvir and Gottlieb have rejected the applications as politically motivated.
Ra’am’s appeal argues that the three applications against it – filed by Otzma Yehudit, Likud, and the Choosing Life Forum – relied largely on allegations and evidence considered in previous unsuccessful disqualification proceedings.
The applications sought to link Ra’am with the southern branch of the Islamic Movement, Aid 48, and other associations accused of transferring assistance to entities connected to Hamas. Ra’am argues that these are indirect organizational links and that the applicants did not produce clear evidence that the list itself supports armed struggle.
It also argues that much of the material consisted of media reports and internet publications rather than evidence concerning the current list, its platform, or its candidates. Ra’am cited its participation in the Bennett-Lapid coalition and the addition of former police major-general Yoav Segalovich to its slate as evidence of its present political course.
Baharav-Miara opposed Ra’am’s disqualification, saying the evidence did not meet the Supreme Court’s stringent standard. Eighteen committee members nevertheless voted to bar the list, with one abstention.
The Joint List has also appealed after the committee voted 18-5, with one abstention, to disqualify it. The list has called the decision political persecution directed at Arab representation.
The committee voted 19-5, with two abstentions, to bar Cassif on the grounds that he rejects Israel as a Jewish and democratic state and supports armed struggle against it.
Cassif argues that the statements and political activity cited against him, including support for international proceedings and sanctions against Israel, cannot be equated with support for armed violence.
He also alleges a procedural defect, saying Likud improperly combined its request against him with its request against the Joint List. He argues that the committee’s decision to separate the hearings prevented him from answering claims directed at the list rather than at him personally. Baharav-Miara opposed his disqualification.
The court will also review Abu Shehadeh’s disqualification on Thursday. Baharav-Miara and State Attorney Amit Aisman urged the justices on Tuesday to approve it on the ground of support for armed struggle, focusing primarily on an article he wrote on October 8, 2023, while the Hamas attack was still unfolding.
Abu Shehadeh maintains that the article did not endorse the attack and was written before its full scale was known. The committee voted 30-4 to disqualify him, with Sohlberg also supporting the decision, bringing the result to 31-4.
The court will hold two hearings before the same nine-justice panel on Thursday, first reviewing Abu Shehadeh’s disqualification and then considering Cassif’s case, together with the Joint List’s appeal. Ra’am’s appeal was not included in the Thursday schedule previously announced.
All the cases arise under Section 7A of Basic Law: The Knesset, which permits a candidate or list to be barred for rejecting Israel as a Jewish and democratic state, inciting racism, or supporting armed struggle by an enemy state or terrorist organization.
Supreme Court precedent treats disqualification as an exceptional measure requiring clear, convincing, and unequivocal evidence of a dominant and sustained objective. The court has not yet decided whether that standard has been met in any of the current cases.

Israeli opposition parties formed three joint working teams Tuesday to coordinate their campaign to remove Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu from power in the Oct. 27 election and prepare a common platform for a new government.
The five-party opposition alliance notably excluded Arab parties from the joint initiative ahead of next month’s general election, seen as crucial for both Netanyahu’s government and the opposition.
On Saturday, opposition leaders Yair Lapid, Gadi Eisenkot, Naftali Bennett, Avigdor Lieberman, and Yair Golan agreed to form a "change bloc” to coordinate their election efforts.
Opinion polls indicate that neither Netanyahu’s bloc nor the opposition bloc would secure the 61 seats needed to form a government in the 120-member Knesset.
The opposition could potentially form a government with Arab parties, but most Jewish party leaders reject such an alliance, while the government has also sought to exclude Arab parties.
In a statement Tuesday, the opposition said it had decided to "establish joint working teams to ensure victory in the election and form a stable Zionist government that works for the state.”
The term "Zionist government” is generally used for a coalition made up of parties that embrace Zionist ideology, whether from the right, center or left, and focus on what they regard as the national interests of the Jewish people, effectively excluding Arab parties from such governments.
"In 28 days, Israeli citizens will go to the polls to participate in the upcoming decisive election and determine the path Israel will take in the coming years,” the statement said.
Netanyahu has led the current government since late 2022. It has been described as the most right-wing government in Israel’s history.
Criticizing Netanyahu, the opposition said the election comes "after years of internal polarization, lies, failures and loss of trust.”
"It is our responsibility to form a Zionist government that works for the state, puts Israel back on the right track and unites the country,” it added.
The opposition said that following Saturday’s meeting of party leaders, "three joint working teams were formed to strengthen cooperation, coordinate preparations to win the election and lay the groundwork for forming a Zionist government that works for the state.”
The first team is tasked with increasing voter turnout, while the second will be responsible for drafting the guiding principles of the next government and an action plan for its first 100 days.
Among the issues it will address are "equality in sharing the burden” of military service and universal enlistment, establishing an official commission of inquiry, limiting the number of terms a prime minister may serve and advancing the adoption of a constitution for Israel.
Israel has no formal constitution despite its establishment in 1948. Instead, it relies on a series of Basic Laws amid longstanding disagreements over the state’s identity and whether it should be defined primarily as "the state of the Jewish people” or "a state of all its citizens.”
Israel rejects the establishment of a Palestinian state along the June 4, 1967 borders with East Jerusalem as its capital, as stipulated in relevant UN resolutions under the two-state solution.
"The third team will be responsible for media coordination and combating disinformation and smear campaigns,” the statement said.
The opposition party leaders have not agreed on who would head a future government if they are able to form one after the election.

NATO sets out plan to make allied forces quantum ready
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
18:45:40 BST
02:45:40 KST

NATO has published a public summary of a quantum technology roadmap intended to speed up the adoption of quantum computing, communication and sensing across the alliance and allied armed forces, and to guard against the disruption those technologies could cause in the hands of others, according to NATO.
Allies approved the roadmap on 30 July, with the summary released on Tuesday. It builds on the alliance’s Quantum Strategy of 2023 and concentrates on the three branches of the field, alongside how each interacts with other dual-use technologies including artificial intelligence, space and next generation communication networks.
Delivery runs through the Transatlantic Quantum Community and its industry network, working with industry and academia. That body met in Washington on 24 and 25 September, where according to NATO the discussion covered how advances in quantum computing could affect secure communications, critical infrastructure, intelligence, strategic stability and decision making in a crisis, along with what the convergence of artificial intelligence and quantum means for defence.
The same meeting looked at positioning, navigation and timing, and at sensing, in light of the Questor 26 experimentation campaign run earlier this month at La Spezia by the NATO Centre for Maritime Research and Experimentation together with the industry network.
A sufficiently capable quantum computer would break the public key cryptography that protects most military and civil communications, which is why encrypted traffic intercepted today is worth storing against the day it can be read, and why allied governments have been migrating towards post-quantum algorithms. Quantum sensing runs the other way, offering navigation that does not depend on satellite signals at all, which matters a great deal to forces operating where those signals are jammed or spoofed as a matter of routine, as they now are across the Baltic and the Black Sea.
The Transatlantic Quantum Community welcomed Belgium and Bulgaria at the Washington meeting, bringing it to 24 allies alongside six partner nations. The Netherlands took the chair in May for a year with Canada as vice-chair, and the body, established in 2024, is an informal and non-binding grouping of experts drawn from national governments, industry, academia, funding bodies and research institutions rather than a decision-making forum.
Britain has been working the same ground nationally for some years, and the Ministry of Defence and the Defence Science and Technology Laboratory have run quantum navigation trials at sea and in the air over recent years, and the National Quantum Strategy commits public funding across the decade with defence as one of the intended beneficiaries. The Royal Navy’s experimentation vessel XV Patrick Blackett has been used for trials of this kind.
The full roadmap summary is published on the NATO site alongside the announcement, and the alliance gives no figures for what the work will cost or timescales for when any of the capability is expected to reach the field.

PM-RAHAT provides care to 25,000 crash victims (PTI file photo)
NEW DELHI: In the past eight months, nearly 25,000 road crash victims have been treated under PM-RAHAT, govt’s cashless scheme, and in nearly 13,000 cases, hospitals have been reimbursed for cost of treatment, a top road transport ministry official said Tuesday.Speaking at a roundtable on “Rethinking Urban Speed” organised by Road Safety Network, additional secretary in road transport ministry Mahmood Ahmed said that the scheme has helped save lives. The scheme under Motor Vehicles Act makes it mandatory for hospitals to treat road crash victims for free treatment up to Rs 1.5 lakh per victim, subject to a cap of seven days from the date of crash. Different studies suggest that 50% of lives can be saved by providing quick medical care to road crash victims.Mahmood highlighted the need to strengthen electronic enforcement of traffic rules considering that there is a tendency to break rules and deployment of manpower to detect this can never be sufficient. “Unless there is a certainty of punishment, the deterrence will never come,” he said. The official said the system would work only if violations were detected and followed through.Experts and govt officials at the workshop observed that India’s growing vehicle-safety capabilities cannot substitute for controlling speeds on urban roads, where pedestrians, two-wheeler riders and cyclists remain exposed to crash and their severity is directly linked to speedChairman of newly set up National Road Safety Board (NSRB), Nitin Gokarn, said the nature of Indian urban roads compounds the problem as different users, including pedestrians, two-wheelers, cars, trucks, and others use the same space.
It’s worse in congested areas where pedestrians have no option left than walking on the main road because pedestrian facilities are absent. What adds to their risk are wrong-side driving, inadequate medians and poorly lit road infrastructure.
Gokarn said at times when segregation of vulnerable road users is not possible, there are cars and bikes on roads that can reach speeds of 240 kmph and 100 kmph. This makes them vulnerable and more so when the speed is higher, he said.Experts, at the meet, shared examples such as Paris which has a maximum speed of 30 kmph or less on 89% of its urban road network; Brussels-Capital Region has 86%. They added that speed management in Indian cities needs to move beyond the setting of speed limits and focus on the interaction between road design, enforcement, local conditions and the behaviour of road users.Prof Bhargab Maitra of IIT, Kharagpur said that speed management provides an immediate opportunity to improve road safety. “Speed management is doable, implementable and workable in the short term. It is not merely about reducing speed limits; it requires the right combination of engineering, enforcement and context-based speed regulation. Aligning road design, speed limits and operating speeds, while prioritising pedestrians, cyclists and two-wheeler users, can help make our urban roads safer and more inclusive,” he said.

NEW YORK, Sept. 29 (Xinhua) -- U.S. consumer confidence index deteriorated sharply in September, driven down by surging energy costs and persistent price pressures, according to survey results issued by The Conference Board on Tuesday.
The Conference Board Consumer Confidence Index fell 6.7 points to 81.9 in September, down from 88.6 in August, marking the lowest level since April 2014. This also marks a notable acceleration in household pessimism after two consecutive months of softening sentiment.
Both components of the index declined. The Present Situation Index, which tracks consumers' assessments of current business and labor market conditions, retreated 7.9 points to 109.3.
The Expectations Index, which measures consumers' short-term outlook for income, business and labor market conditions, dropped by 5.9 points to 63.6, marking its third consecutive monthly decline.
"The Consumer Confidence Index deteriorated notably in September, following two prior months of softening," said Dana M. Peterson, chief economist at the board.
Peterson said consumers' views of current business conditions turned negative for the first time since September 2024, while perceptions of the labor market also worsened. Looking ahead, consumers expected both business conditions and the labor market to weaken over the next six months.
Consumers also expressed growing concern about prices. References to the high cost of goods and services, particularly oil and gas, rose to new highs in September amid a surge in fuel costs, according to The Conference Board.
U.S. diesel prices hit a record average of about 6.53 U.S. dollars a gallon on Sept. 22 and remained above 6.40 dollars on Tuesday, compared with about 3.68 dollars a year earlier, according to the American Automobile Association.
On Friday, the University of Michigan Surveys of Consumers found that its Consumer Sentiment Index fell to 48.1 in September from 51.7 in August, down 7 percent month-on-month and 15 percent from January. ■

China Focus: China to implement mortgage interest subsidies to unlock housing demand
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
01:38:04 CST
02:38:04 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 29 (Xinhua) -- China will implement interest subsidies for housing loans starting Oct. 1, 2026, as part of efforts to help reduce home-buying costs and better unlock the housing demand of residents.
With a tentative implementation period of one year, the fiscal authorities will provide an annualized subsidy of 1 percentage point for eligible first-time homebuyers, according to a notice jointly issued by the Ministry of Finance, the People's Bank of China and the National Financial Regulatory Administration on Tuesday.
This is the first time the central government has offered interest subsidies on commercial housing loans.
This interest subsidy policy is focused on first-time homebuyers. The floor area of each purchased unit must not exceed 120 square meters, and the purchase price must not surpass 1.5 million yuan (about 222,516 U.S. dollars).
Under this policy, the maximum amount of interest-subsidized loans can reach 1 million yuan, and the subsidy period can extend up to five years.
According to estimates, for a long-term 1-million-yuan commercial personal mortgage, the subsidies could help borrowers reduce cumulative interest payments by nearly 50,000 yuan.
By defining housing price, floor area and loan category, the policy aims to precisely benefit target groups and help lower-income families reduce their monthly mortgage burdens, the departments said.
The policy focuses on first-time buyers with essential needs, supporting families in purchasing small and medium-sized, and relatively low-priced homes, according to the departments.
The policy is expected to reduce the mortgage burden for new urban residents, newly employed college graduates, and urban wage-earning families, said Luo Zhiheng, chief economist at Yuekai Securities.
In recent years, China has introduced supply-side measures to support the development of the real estate market, including supporting the issuance of new special-purpose bonds for land reserves and supporting local governments in purchasing existing commercial housing for use as affordable housing. This time, the focus has shifted to the demand side, further expanding policy efforts through fiscal-financial coordination.
Industry insiders believe that interest subsidies can reduce home-buying costs, accelerate the destocking of new homes, and ease the funding pressure on real estate developers.
The policy clearly demonstrates strong support for rigid home-buying demand, or first-home demand, and will in turn influence subsequent replacement and upgrading demand, said Yan Yuejin, deputy director at E-house China R&D Institute.
Li Yujia, chief researcher at the Guangdong Housing Policy Research Center, said the interest subsidy policy will reduce the cost of residents' mortgage loans and improve their willingness to take on leverage, thereby restoring the financial accelerator effect of the real estate sector.
Data released by the National Bureau of Statistics earlier this month showed narrower year-on-year declines in home prices across major Chinese cities in August, pointing to further signs of stabilization.
In August, Chinese authorities deepened reforms to the housing provident fund system, and refined regulations on commercial housing sales and property financing.
The package of policies is working in a coordinated manner from both the supply and demand sides, aiming to improve market expectations, restore residents' willingness to buy homes, and promote the steady and healthy development of the real estate market, experts said. ■

"The major cause is the torrential rains in Togo. It has been raining in Hohoe for months now, but not to this magnitude. It has rained continuously, so the load from Togo that joined the Hohoe rains led the river to overflow, causing what we are seeing," Tsekpo told local media.
Some of those affected are reported to have been temporarily accommodated in nearby classrooms while authorities work to find more suitable shelter.
"The flooding has displaced more than 3,000 residents, and over 700 affected people are now sheltering in classrooms," according to the MP.
He added that the situation remained unstable, as water levels continued to rise despite the end of heavy rainfall. He called for sustained emergency support as authorities work to provide shelter and protect residents in the affected communities. ■

And the idea is to allow students to use AI, not penalize them but rather focus on supporting them on how to use AI."
University of Bristol President and Vice-Chancellor Evelyn Welch said attitudes toward AI varied across cultural contexts, while universities also faced a need to establish shared standards.
"There is quite a different set of anxieties that we can see depending on the cultural contexts. But that doesn't mean that we don't all have to come up with some common standards," she said.
THE World University Rankings 2027 will be released on Wednesday, with the latest edition covering higher education institutions in 118 countries and territories. ■

EV charging costs less than half of diesel fuel costs in Europe: analysis
