BRUSSELS, Sept. 29 (Xinhua) -- Electric vehicle (EV) drivers in Europe pay, on average, less than half as much per kilometer to charge as diesel drivers pay to refuel, according to the Brussels-based environmental group Transport & Environment (T&E).
An analysis released Tuesday by T&E called on Europe to accelerate its transition to EVs and opposed across-the-board cuts in fuel duties. It recommended targeted support for low-income households, together with windfall taxes on energy firms to fund public transport and vehicle scrappage schemes.
"We are at a critical moment in the diesel crisis. Prices are already sky high for citizens and businesses and if the U.S. blocks exports of diesel, there is a real risk of a genuine shortage of supply," said Antony Froggatt, senior director at T&E.
"Electrification is the only way to ensure this is the last oil crisis. But we need short-term measures as well," he said.
The analysis showed that diesel drivers now pay 32 euros (36.4 U.S. dollars) more to fill a 50-liter tank than at the start of the year, with about 16 euros of the increase due to higher refinery margins.
Estimates by the European Central Bank (ECB) show that the margin rose from about 0.10 euro per liter in February to 0.41 euro per liter around Sept. 14.
The comparison covers refueling and recharging costs only. It is based on average consumption of 6.9 liters per 100 km for diesel vehicles and 20.2 kilowatt-hours per 100 km for battery electric vehicles, with electricity priced at 0.343 euro (0.39 U.S. dollar) per kilowatt-hour.
T&E said its charging-cost estimate, which takes into account the correlation between electricity and gas prices and the delayed pass-through to household electricity prices, is likely an upper bound.
An earlier T&E analysis showed that six of the eight major oil companies it studied, including BP and Shell, more than doubled their profits in the European Union (EU) in the second quarter of 2026 from a year earlier.
A T&E study published Monday found that battery-electric heavy trucks have a lower total cost of ownership than diesel ones in six of nine major EU markets. These six markets account for 46 percent of new heavy truck sales in the bloc.
EU Commissioner for Energy and Housing Dan Jorgensen wrote to member states asking them to consider implementing energy-saving measures in response to potentially high gas prices.
T&E said the European Commission should not focus on gas alone, arguing that oil and diesel are at the sharp end of the energy crisis. ■

GQEBERHA, South Africa, Sept. 29 (Xinhua) -- China's zero-tariff policy for qualifying South African exports has significantly driven demand for dry bulk commodities moving through South Africa's deep-water Port of Ngqura, including chrome, magnetite, iron ore, and corn, a port official said Tuesday.
Xola Mkontwana, business strategy manager at the Port of Ngqura, said the port has recorded "exponential growth" in commodity throughput destined for the Chinese market since the implementation of the trade policy.
"There was an exponential market in terms of demand from China," Mkontwana told journalists during a media tour of the adjacent Coega Special Economic Zone (SEZ) in South Africa's Eastern Cape Province.
He highlighted that the tariff preferences have significantly enhanced bulk operational volumes across the regional logistics hub. "The zero-tariff has assisted the throughput for bulk across the port system because there's chrome and magnetite, iron ore, and also corn," Mkontwana added.
The zero-tariff treatment for qualifying exports from South Africa and 19 other non-least developed African countries officially took effect on May 1, 2026. Running through April 30, 2028, the two-year non-reciprocal framework expands duty-free access for African goods to the Chinese market, provided exporters comply with rules of origin and standard customs regulations.
The initiative fulfills commitments made under the Forum on China-Africa Cooperation framework to promote balanced bilateral trade and support industrialization across the African continent.
Addressing the drivers behind the surge in Chinese orders, Mkontwana pointed to expanding industrial and infrastructure activity in China alongside favorable price realizations for South African mining and agricultural enterprises.
"It's the companies that they're actually developing on that side. It's the market that is there and the price that is good for the miners and owners," he noted.
Located approximately 20 km northeast of Gqeberha, the Port of Ngqura is South Africa's newest deep-water commercial port and serves as a critical maritime gateway connecting Eastern Cape minerals, agricultural produce, and automotive manufacturing to global shipping lines.
South Africa remains China's largest trading partner in Africa, with bilateral trade dominated by mineral products, raw materials, and agricultural goods. As South African producers seek to expand export destinations, China's preferential tariff framework provides key momentum for economic diversification, job creation, and increased logistics activity across South Africa's supply chains. ■

China Focus: China outlines sci-tech priorities for 2026-2030 to underpin high-quality development
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
01:37:31 CST
02:37:31 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 29 (Xinhua) -- China will strengthen basic research, tackle core technologies and speed up the industrial application of research results during the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030) to better support high-quality development, officials of the Ministry of Science and Technology said on Tuesday.
At a press conference held by the State Council Information Office, Minister of Science and Technology Yin Hejun said China's total R&D spending exceeded 3.92 trillion yuan (about 582 billion U.S. dollars) in 2025, or 2.8 percent of GDP. This amount exceeded the average among the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) members for the first time.
China has ranked first in the world for many consecutive years in international patent applications under the Patent Cooperation Treaty (PCT) and in papers published in high-level international journals, Yin said.
China ranks ninth among 60 countries in overall national innovation capability, according to the National Innovation Index Report 2025 released by the Chinese Academy of Science and Technology for Development.
Looking ahead, basic research will be organized in areas such as mathematical theory and applications, control of states of matter, synthetic biology, the materials genome, controlled nuclear fusion and intelligent scientist systems, Yin said.
He also called for faster application of artificial intelligence (AI) in scientific research to lead a shift in how research is carried out.
Paramount core technologies are another important priority, Yin said. China will push for progress along the entire innovation chain in key fields such as integrated circuits, machine tools and high-end instruments, and step up R&D in frontier technologies including AI, quantum technology, biotechnology and brain-computer interfaces.
Sci-tech innovation should also deliver more quality products and services that improve people's well-being, he said, with tasks laid out in areas including environmental pollution control, resource recycling, agricultural biological breeding, innovative drug development, high-end medical equipment and responses to population aging.
On turning research results into real-world productivity, Zhang Guangjun, vice minister of science and technology, said China will break the stereotype of producing results first and considering their application later on. Policies will instead direct research to where demand lies and ensure that results, once achieved, can be put to use, so that scientific and industrial innovation are planned in tandem and support one another, he said.
Zhang also called for stronger enterprise-led collaboration among industry, universities and research institutes, with innovation resources such as projects, platforms, data, talent and funding channeled to enterprises. Proof-of-concept and pilot-scale testing platforms will be built to help technologies mature and upgrade faster, he said.
Venture capital has played a vital role, with investors increasingly backing early-stage and small companies, taking a long-term view and focusing on hard technology, said Qiu Yong, vice minister of science and technology. New funds raised in the equity investment market exceeded 1 trillion yuan in the first half of 2026, up 49 percent year on year, he said, citing statistics from relevant institutions.
Universities are adjusting their disciplines to meet urgent national needs, he said.
China will continue to build Beijing and the Beijing-Tianjin-Hebei region, Shanghai and the wider Yangtze River Delta, and the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area into international sci-tech innovation centers, Yin said. The three centers account for 58.8 percent of the country's R&D spending and 81.1 percent of its PCT international patent applications, and are helping drive innovation in surrounding provinces and municipalities and across the country.
R&D spending in the Beijing-Tianjin-Hebei region has reached 4.48 percent of regional GDP, with major sci-tech achievements emerging in fields such as AI and biomanufacturing, Yin said.
The Yangtze River Delta accounts for nearly 30 percent of the country's basic research spending, with corporate spending on basic research up 38.3 percent year on year in 2025. It has witnessed key breakthroughs in areas such as integrated circuits and quantum technology, he said.
The Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area draws on Guangdong's industrial innovation strengths and the science and education resources of Hong Kong and Macao, Yin said. Guangdong, Hong Kong and Macao have jointly built 35 laboratories, and produced 14,000 papers under international collaboration. ■

IISc team uses blue light to switch on cell division; may aid cancer research
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
17:31:58 UTC
02:31:58 KST

BENGALURU: Scientists from IISc’s Department of Microbiology and Cell Biology (MCB) have found a way to use blue light to switch on a key part of the machinery that helps cells divide, and have used it to restore cell division in cells from which a crucial structure had been removed.The finding could help scientists understand how cells divide and, eventually, identify new targets for drugs against diseases such as cancer. The study has been published in EMBO Reports. And their new technique may also help further cancer researchCell division is a tightly controlled process. Before a cell splits into two, its genetic material has to be copied and then pulled apart accurately. This is done by the mitotic spindle, a network of thread-like structures that attaches to the genetic material and separates it.The centrosome, a small structure inside the cell, helps organise this spindle. It’s made up of more than 200 components, but which are essential has remained unclear..The IISc team has developed a technique called Light-Induced Spindle Activation (LISA), which allows them to switch on Aurora A, an enzyme involved in building the spindle, by shining blue light on it.Aurora A normally becomes active at the centrosome, where it gathers into clusters.
Scientists had believed that a protein called Cep192 was needed to help activate it. LISA showed that Aurora A can instead be artificially clustered and activated using light, without Cep192.Researchers adapted an existing technique called LARIAT, which uses light to make proteins cluster together. They attached Aurora A to a light-sensitive plant protein called CRY2 and introduced it into human cells.When blue light was shone on the cells, CRY2 interacted with another protein, CIB1, causing Aurora A molecules to cluster. This, in turn, triggered the formation of microtubules, the tiny structures that make up much of the spindle.“This provides a novel way to trigger and activate an artificial Aurora A kinase complex – Aurora A fused to light-sensitive plant proteins, which is sufficient to induce microtubule nucleation,” Vignesh Olakkal, a PhD student in Sachin Kotak’s lab and first author of the study, said.Researchers then asked whether the technique could actually compensate for a missing centrosome. They chemically removed centrosomes from human cells, which normally causes problems during cell division. They then introduced the light-controlled Aurora A system.When blue light was applied during cell division, Aurora A clustered and triggered the formation of microtubules. The cells were able to rebuild their spindles, effectively rescuing the division defects caused by the loss of centrosomes.
The technique may also help in cancer research. Aurora A is overexpressed in many solid tumours and is already targeted by some drugs. But because the enzyme acts on several different proteins, it can be difficult to determine exactly which of its functions should be blocked.“In many solid tumours, Aurora A kinase is overexpressed, and that’s why there are drugs targeting it. But Aurora A kinase has multiple targets. Now, with our strategy, we can find out what the Aurora A kinase-specific targets are, independent of the centrosome, as far as microtubule nucleation is concerned. Then we will hopefully be able to find other targets of Aurora A kinase and design drugs,” Kotak said.
Chethan Kumar is a Senior Assistant Editor with the Times of India. Aside from specialising in Space & Science, he has reported extensively on varied topics, with special focus on defence, policy and data stories. He has covered multiple elections, too. As a young democracy grows out of adolescence, Chethan feels, there are reels of tales emerging which need to be captured. To do this, he alternates between the mundane goings-on of the Common Man and the wonder-filled worlds of scientists and scamsters, politicians and soldiers. In a career spanning nearly 18 years, he has reported from multiple datelines — Houston, Florida, Kochi, Hyderabad, Chennai, Sriharikota (AP), NH-1 (J&K Highway), New Delhi, Ahmedabad, Raichur, Bhatkal, Mysuru, Chamarajanagar, to name a few — but is based out of Bengaluru, India’s science capital that also hosts the ISRO HQ.

Ukraine runs first supply mission with amphibious robot
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
18:30:39 BST
02:30:39 KST

Ukrainian troops have carried out what is described as the first logistics mission using a domestically developed amphibious uncrewed ground vehicle, covering more than 40km over land and water to deliver rations and ammunition to positions, according to the Ukrainian Ministry of Defence.
The mission was flown, or rather driven and swum, by personnel from one of the separate mechanised brigades of the Armed Forces of Ukraine. The department said the vehicle retained the cross-country mobility of a conventional ground robot on land and could transition to water within seconds before continuing.
Water is the reason the capability exists in the first place, and according to the ministry, rivers, canals and marshy ground along the front complicate or entirely block routes for ordinary uncrewed ground vehicles, while resupply from the air is not always the better answer. Putting both modes on one platform removes the need to plan around obstacles or to hand a load between systems partway along a route.
The vehicle was refined over several months in cooperation with the units that would use it, drawing on real missions, operational experience and the particular characteristics of front-line terrain. Development was supported through grant funding from Brave1, the Ukrainian defence innovation cluster, which introduced a dedicated amphibious uncrewed ground vehicle track within its grant programme in June.
The ministry stated: “We are expanding the capabilities of robotic systems so that Ukrainian service members have more technological tools to carry out combat missions.”
Ground robots have moved quickly from novelty to routine in Ukrainian service. The department has previously reported that its forces more than tripled their use of uncrewed ground vehicles for logistics and casualty evacuation, work driven by the same pressure that has reshaped so much of the war, namely that the last few kilometres into a position are watched continuously by drones and that anything moving along them in daylight is liable to be struck.

There the British teams talked in strikes by F-18 Super Hornets against area denial systems including surface-to-air missiles, work that falls under the suppression of enemy air defences. Completing it leaves the battery fully certified to support operations at very high readiness.
M Company forms Special Operations Maritime Task Unit 9 and concentrated on maritime interdiction. According to the Royal Navy, task units of this kind are built to deploy worldwide from hubs ashore or from ships, working alone or folded into a partner force, and each can field one force protection team and two boarding teams, with scout snipers, uncrewed systems, dive teams, explosive ordnance disposal and electronic warfare added as required.
The training began with the two sides exchanging tactics before moving on to close-quarters battle objectives, with teams inserted by helicopter in darkness to take compounds, and more than twenty missions were run across various scenarios.
Attention then turned to the water, where an assault team conducted a vessel takedown at night covering explosive and mechanical methods of entry alongside close quarters marksmanship. In the final week the commandos embarked on USS Arlington for a last mission against an American target vessel, with two Black Hawk helicopters putting a combined British and American team onto the ship to seize it.
Both forces hold Arctic responsibilities for their respective countries, and the Royal Navy says the integration work moves to colder conditions this winter.
42 Commando is based at Bickleigh outside Plymouth and is the Royal Marines unit specialising in maritime operations, including boarding and interdiction work. 148 Battery, part of 29 Commando Regiment Royal Artillery, provides forward observation and joint fires support to the commando force and its members qualify as joint terminal attack controllers, which is what allows them to direct strikes by other nations’ aircraft.
The Commando Force has been the subject of considerable investment, with Wes Streeting restating from the Labour Party conference platform this week that half a billion pounds is going into the force and its drone equipment as it helps defend NATO’s High North.

Ethiopia blames regional rivals as risk of conflict spillover rises

Ethiopia blames regional rivals as risk of conflict spillover rises
Addis Ababa’s accusations against neighbours raise fears that its conflict could spill over into the region.
As renewed fighting spreads across northern Ethiopia, the government has accused Eritrea, Sudan and Egypt of backing armed opposition groups, raising fears that the conflict could draw in regional powers.
Over the weekend, Ethiopian army chief Birhanu Jula attributed his country’s unrest to those he called Ethiopia’s “historical and contemporary adversaries”.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Ethiopia’s army promises restraint amid fears of new civil war
- list 2 of 3Ethiopia accuses Sudan, Egypt of backing Tigray rebels as fighting rages
- list 3 of 3Fighting in Ethiopia intensifies: What’s the latest?
Birhanu accused Eritrea of being the go-between linking these external powers – including Sudan and Egypt, which he explicitly named – with armed groups inside Ethiopia.
Eritrea, Sudan and Egypt have all rejected the accusations. Speaking to Al Jazeera, Egyptian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Nader Zaki said that Egypt’s foreign policy was founded on “full respect for the sovereignty, unity and territorial integrity of states, and noninterference in the internal affairs of other countries”.
Zaki added that Egypt “is fully committed to the rules of international law and the Charter of the United Nations, and rejects any practices that would undermine regional security and stability”.
Major-General Samir Farag, the former head of the Egyptian Armed Forces’ Morale Affairs Department, also told Al Jazeera that the accusations against Egypt were false. “It has not been Egypt’s policy to interfere in the internal affairs of any state in the region,” he said.
Sudan’s military also dismissed the accusations as “baseless” and levelled its own charge of destabilising behaviour at Ethiopia, accusing it of supporting the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), which has been fighting the Sudanese Armed Forces since 2023. Ethiopia has denied those allegations.
Troubled relations
Ethiopia’s relations with the countries it has accused have already been strained by other disputes that predate the latest fighting.
Relations between Cairo and Addis Ababa have remained tense as a longstanding dispute over the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD) remains unresolved. Competition between the two has increasingly extended to regional security, the Red Sea and the Horn of Africa.
Sudan’s relations with Ethiopia are similarly troubled. Since the outbreak of the Sudanese civil war, Khartoum has accused Addis Ababa of providing training, supplies and the use of Ethiopian territory to the RSF.
Eritrea had fought alongside Ethiopia against rebel groups in the latter’s Tigray region during a war between 2020 and 2022, but relations between the two neighbours have since soured, with Eritrea alarmed by Ethiopia’s attempts to gain access to the Red Sea.
Against that background, some analysts and Ethiopian opposition figures say that Addis Ababa is pointing the finger at foreign conspiracies in a bid to rally support behind its national army.
Mohamed Selim, deputy chair of the Egyptian parliament’s African Affairs Committee, told Al Jazeera that he believes the accusations were an attempt to shift attention from Ethiopia’s domestic problems by creating an external enemy and seeking to unify the internal front.
Amani al-Tawil, director of the Africa Programme at the Al-Ahram Centre for Political and Strategic Studies, similarly described the accusations as “an understandable attempt to escape from internal crises”.
She questioned why Egypt would choose this moment to intervene militarily in Ethiopia, given the two have been in dispute over GERD since 2011.
Al-Tawil said the breadth of the new opposition alliance in Ethiopia – seven groups representing disparate ethnic groups and regions announced the coalition last week – presented a challenge to Addis Ababa.
Spillover concerns
The renewed fighting in Ethiopia has spread across Tigray and into neighbouring Amhara and Afar.
Mohammed Hussein, the chairman of the Prosperity Party Afar Region Branch Office – the ruling party in Ethiopia’s Afar region – told Al Jazeera that the three regions together have a population of more than 38 million, according to his estimate, and include areas near the borders with Djibouti and Eritrea, raising fears of a regional war.
Ammar Arki, a writer focusing on Horn of Africa affairs, told Al Jazeera that Ethiopia had, at various stages, blamed Sudan, Egypt and Eritrea for contributing to instability inside Ethiopia.
He said the latest accusations could be interpreted as an attempt to redirect some domestic attention towards an external threat and build support around the federal government.
But Arki warned that the longer Addis Ababa continued to explain its internal crisis in terms of an “external conspiracy”, particularly if neighbouring states responded in the same way, the greater the risk that Ethiopia’s conflict could move beyond Ethiopia’s borders and become regional.

Morocco's king appoints first woman prime minister following election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
17:22:38 UTC
02:22:38 KST

Morocco's king appoints first woman prime minister following election
RABAT, Sept 29 - King Mohammed VI appointed Fatima Ezzahra El Mansouri on Tuesday as Morocco's first woman prime minister after her liberal-centrist party came out on top in a September 23 parliamentary election, the royal palace said.
The king asked El Mansouri to form a new government, the palace said in a statement.
El Mansouri’s Authenticity and Modernity Party (PAM) was created in 2008 by an adviser to the king and has since positioned itself as a counterweight to the Islamist Justice and Development Party (PJD) by advocating social modernisation and secular-leaning views.
Morocco is a constitutional monarchy where the king retains sweeping powers over foreign policy, defence and other key portfolios.
Under Morocco's constitution, the king appoints the head of government from the political party that wins the largest number of seats in the House of Representatives.
PAM, which was the second-largest member in the outgoing coalition, moved up to the top spot, bolstered by the recruitment of Fouzi Lekjaa, Morocco's football federation chief and two-time government budget manager, who joined weeks before the vote.
El Mansouri, a lawyer who was housing minister in the outgoing government and Marrakech mayor, will lead talks to form a coalition government and submit a list of cabinet members for the king's approval.
'NO RED LINES'
The incoming government will oversee the last stages of a $20-billion push to get ready for the 2030 World Cup, which Morocco will co-host with Portugal and Spain.
It will also implement economic policies aimed at addressing widespread youth discontent, an issue highlighted by a mass border rush on the Spanish enclave of Ceuta in July and deadly Gen-Z-led protests last year.
PAM won 97 seats, followed by its partners in the outgoing government, the liberal-centrist National Rally of Independents (RNI) with 66 seats, and the conservative nationalist Istiqlal with 65.
During the campaign, PAM had ruled out staying in a coalition with the RNI — the two had traded blame over policy shortcomings including a failure to halt rises in food prices.
But El Mansouri said on Thursday she would have no "red lines" when it came to negotiations. "We have turned the page," she said.
Abdelilah Benkirane, former prime minister and leader of the PJD, which won 54 seats, said the party would stay in opposition.
Three leftist parties took smaller shares of the seats.
Turnout, closely watched as an indicator of trust in elected institutions, fell to about 38% from around 50% in the previous elections five years ago, when the moderate Islamist PJD was dealt a crushing defeat after a decade in power.
In recent years, King Mohammed VI had appointed a female adviser and Morocco has had women in senior institutional roles. The outgoing government had four women ministers. REUTERS

No explosive devices found in vehicles near Fairford just petrol
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
18:19:30 BST
02:19:30 KST

No improvised explosive devices were found in the three vehicles examined after five men were arrested close to RAF Fairford at the weekend, although a quantity of petrol was recovered, according to Counter Terrorism Policing.
Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor, head of National Counter Terrorism Policing, gave the update on Tuesday evening. “Those vehicles have been subject to extensive examination, with the support of military assets and forensic experts, and we can confirm that no improvised explosive devices were found. However, a quantity of petrol was recovered,” he said.
He also set out what prompted the response in the first place. “A police response was activated in the early hours of Sunday morning due to a range of information received, including a call from a member of the public about several vehicles acting suspiciously close to RAF Fairford,” he said, thanking those who had contacted police with information and saying the events of recent days had reaffirmed the part the public plays.
The investigation has extended well beyond Gloucestershire in the days since. “As part of the investigation, we have searched properties in London which I can confirm have concluded,” Taylor said. The scenes around the airfield are being reduced and the assistant commissioner said he anticipated closing them down completely by Wednesday, which he described as an important step towards restoring normality for the local community.
The five men were released on police bail on Monday, a development Taylor acknowledged had not been universally expected. “They remain under investigation and must adhere to strict conditions while we continue our work. The safety of the public is at the forefront of our investigative decision making, and this was certainly the case yesterday,” he said. “I understand why this development will have come as a surprise to many, but I’d like to reiterate that it was investigative decision, and one which is grounded in experience and careful consideration of policing powers.”
Counter Terrorism Policing has released only limited details of those arrested, all five of whom are British nationals resident in London, one aged 25 and the others aged between 23 and 24, with four living in the borough of Westminster and one in Camden, and none of them has been named.
The men were arrested on Sunday morning on suspicion of offences under the Explosives Act and later of preparation of a terrorist act under Section 5 of the Terrorism Act, after Gloucestershire Constabulary declared a major incident and evacuated properties in the village of Whelford next to the airfield. Taylor said on Monday that investigators were keeping an open mind on whether the current international situation had any bearing on the case, and that they were considering the possibility of activity by proxies or by individuals knowingly or unknowingly working on behalf of a foreign state, as we reported.
He thanked the community near the airfield, Gloucestershire Police, and what he called many partners in Britain and the United States supporting the investigation.
Fairford is a United States Air Force forward operating location whose long runway has made it the standing European base for American strategic bombers, and B-1B Lancers have been operating from the airfield. The base moved to its highest force protection condition before the arrests were made.
The investigation continues, and anyone with information has been asked to contact the police.

China’s AI strategy ‘paradox’ really isn’t one
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
17:14:51 UTC
02:14:51 KST

China’s AI strategy ‘paradox’ really isn’t one
Artificial intelligence is becoming a defining force in economic development, international competition, and national security. While striving to develop more powerful AI systems, China also seeks to determine how they should be governed, shared, and secured in a rapidly changing world.
A technology shaping China – and the world
By June 2026, the number of users of AI products in China had exceeded 500 million, underscoring the technology’s growing reach in one of the world’s largest digital economies. Together with the US, China is a key engine of AI development and innovation. Its domestic choices and international initiatives have consequences well beyond its borders.
At the BRICS summit in New Delhi, Chinese President Xi Jinping advanced proposals for more inclusive AI cooperation, industrial development, and technological exchange. At the same time, State Security Minister Chen Yixin set out a national security perspective that places AI at the center of strategic competition and calls for stronger safeguards.
China’s AI policy combines the pursuit of international openness with domestic security governance. Understanding how Beijing seeks to reconcile these objectives is essential to understanding its ambitions for AI – and the emerging global order around it.
Xi’s BRICS vision: AI as a shared opportunity
Xi’s proposals at the New Delhi summit place AI cooperation within a broader effort to connect technological development with economic growth and international inclusion. The emphasis is on widening access to the capabilities, skills, and industrial networks that make AI economically useful.
China has proposed taking a pioneering role in establishing a BRICS AI open-source community, supporting cooperation on the development and application of large language models, and organizing specialized seminars and training courses. The stated objective is to build an open ecosystem in which countries can exchange knowledge and expand their capacity to develop and use AI.
This approach is particularly relevant for emerging economies. Access to AI requires not only the availability of software, but also computing infrastructure, technical expertise, investment, and the ability to adapt technologies to local needs. Open-source collaboration and skills development can help accessibility, although they cannot by themselves eliminate disparities in resources or technological capabilities.
Xi’s digital industry cooperation initiative extends the same idea into the infrastructure and skills underpinning the digital economy. China has proposed a BRICS digital ecosystem cloud platform, alongside digital skills training, technological exchange, and industrial alignment.
A third proposal focuses on AI-enabled new industrialization. Here, the objective is to deepen cooperation in research and development, practical applications, and industrial and supply chains.
Taken together, these initiatives present AI as a means of expanding productive capacity. For BRICS members, the proposals raise practical questions about how to share expertise, develop compatible infrastructure, and translate technological cooperation into tangible industrial outcomes.
Chen Yixin’s warning
Xi’s international cooperation agenda coincides with a more security-focused assessment from Chen Yixin, China’s minister of state security. In an article published during the summit, Chen described AI as a central arena of global scientific and technological competition and a new front in strategic rivalry among major powers.
Chen’s argument begins with a dual imperative: innovation must be the primary driving force, while security must remain a bottom-line requirement. In this framing, AI is simultaneously an engine of economic and social transformation and a technology capable of changing the conditions of national security.
His assessment identifies several interconnected risks. AI-generated content, including deepfakes and automated online activity, could affect political security by enabling the rapid production and dissemination of misleading information. Chen also warns that AI may transform cyber operations, making it easier to identify vulnerabilities, develop malicious software, and automate elements of complex attacks.
Another concern is the potential for AI-assisted data collection and analysis to amplify espionage and information-security risks. Chen points to the possibility of sensitive government data, commercial secrets, and personal information being gathered or exposed through intelligent crawling, data mining, and profiling.
He also identifies structural challenges: concentration of technological capabilities could deepen inequalities between countries, while AI-driven decision-making could strain existing systems of social governance. In the military sphere, he argues that AI is helping move warfare toward an increasingly intelligent era, with implications for sensing, decision-making, and targeting.
These concerns are not confined to China. Cybersecurity, data protection, misinformation, military applications, and the concentration of technological power are subjects of international debate. What distinguishes Chen’s article is the way it brings them together under a comprehensive national security framework.
From principles to institutions
Chen calls for AI security to be integrated into other key areas of national security, supported by stronger cross-sector cooperation and improved capacity to identify and anticipate emerging risks. He also calls for an AI safety supervision platform, expanded risk assessment and monitoring, and greater investment in fundamental research and core technologies, including computing chips, development frameworks, and application software. His article advocates strengthening AI infrastructure while reducing vulnerabilities associated with dependence on critical technologies.
Chen advocates the implementation of China’s Cybersecurity Law and Counter-Espionage Law, alongside further development of rules addressing AI research, applications, data protection, algorithmic security, and accountability. He also emphasizes public communication and national security awareness.
These measures reflect Beijing’s view that AI governance cannot be separated from overarching questions of technological self-reliance, data control, and national security, and that when it comes to AI, innovation has to be inseparable from oversight.
A global governance agenda
China’s domestic security priorities sit alongside an international agenda that predates the New Delhi summit. Its 2023 Global AI Governance Initiative calls for people-centered development, international cooperation, respect for national sovereignty, and broader access to AI technologies. It also advocates risk-based governance, privacy and data protection, human oversight, and greater representation for developing countries.
The initiative supports discussions within the United Nations framework on establishing an international institution for AI governance. Chen’s article echoes several of these themes, describing AI as an international public good and calling for cooperation that helps Global South countries strengthen their technological capabilities and bridge the global intelligence gap.
China recently released its AI Safety Governance Framework 3.0, following earlier versions issued in 2024 and 2025. The updated framework revises risk classifications and adjusts technical and governance measures in response to emerging challenges.
Making openness and security compatible
China’s international and domestic AI agendas may seem to be contradictory, but a country can support international technology exchange while seeking to protect sensitive data, strengthen infrastructure, and manage risks. The challenge is determining where legitimate safeguards end and restrictions on cooperation begin.
For China, the task is to demonstrate that its security framework can support innovation and international engagement without unnecessarily constraining them. For its partners, the task is to assess how cooperation will work in practice: what technologies will be accessible, how data will be protected, and how shared initiatives will be governed.
BRICS member countries have different development priorities, regulatory systems, and strategic interests. A common AI ecosystem will require practical arrangements that accommodate those differences while delivering measurable benefits.
A defining question for the AI era
Xi Jinping’s BRICS proposals and Chen Yixin’s national security assessment capture two dimensions of China’s AI strategy: expanding the technology’s reach internationally while strengthening its governance at home.
AI cooperation could widen access to technological capabilities and support industrial development. Security governance could help address genuine risks involving cyber operations, sensitive data, and increasingly autonomous systems. Yet both agendas also raise questions about implementation, institutional accountability, and the balance between openness and control.
China’s approach will be judged by the practical outcomes it delivers: whether cooperation is genuinely inclusive, whether safeguards are effective and proportionate, and whether international partners can participate on mutually understood terms.
The underlying proposition is that artificial intelligence need not be treated as a domain of zero-sum competition. When innovation is prioritized and security requirements are treated as non-negotiable, the technology can be steered toward benefit for all.

ShinyHunters suspect also investigated for alleged murder orders

Although Dutch authorities have not publicly identified the man, his former employer, Amsterdam-based cybersecurity company Neo Security, said his name is Pepijn van der Stap.
Reuters has not been able to reach Van der Stap or identify a lawyer or representative.
He was arrested in a dramatic police raid amid escalating concern over ShinyHunters, a hacking group known for large-scale data breaches and extortion, and its recent theft of what it said was terabytes of sensitive personnel data from US FBI servers.
At least some of the data includes employees' intelligence assignments and medical records, Reuters has reported.

Bessent said on Saturday that he had sent envoys around the world to pressure countries to economically isolate Iran, hailing the new restrictions targeting the country's airlines and banks.
Iranian airlines had suspended their flights to Iran as of September 23, while Iraqi Airways halted its flights to neighbouring Iran in March near the start of the Middle East war "in order to safeguard the safety of flights and passengers", the transport ministry said.

Police recorded 229 antisemitic incidents between January and August, an 8% increase over the corresponding period last year.
Mamdani increases NYC hate crime prevention budget by $26 million
Mamdani said his administration had increased hate crime prevention funding by $26 million, or more than 800%, compared with last year. The strategy includes $6.4 million for community organizations working to prevent hate-motivated violence.
The city will also revive an interagency security working group disbanded in 2024, bringing together agencies including the NYPD and Department of Transportation to identify threats before attacks occur.
Cultural investments include $2 million for the Queens Holocaust Memorial Garden and $2.5 million for the Brooklyn Center for New Jewish Culture.
"Jewish New Yorkers should feel cherished and celebrated in the most Jewish city in America," Mamdani said.
On his first day in office, Mamdani revoked an Adams executive order adopting the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance's working definition of antisemitism. The definition includes examples addressing certain forms of anti-Zionist rhetoric, including denial of Jewish self-determination.
He also rescinded an order restricting city agencies from participating in boycotts or divestment targeting Israel, along with a directive requiring police to examine regulations governing protests outside houses of worship. Mamdani retained the Mayor's Office to Combat Antisemitism.
Seven major New York-area Jewish organizations criticized the reversal of the IHRA and boycott orders. Mamdani defended the decision, arguing that some Jewish organizations had concerns about the definition and pledging to fight antisemitism through prevention and community engagement.
The newly announced strategy does not adopt a replacement definition of antisemitism. The administration maintains that existing hate-crime and anti-discrimination laws provide a basis for enforcement without a single codified definition.
Mamdani concluded his announcement by appealing to New Yorkers to protect their Jewish neighbors.
"Our safety is bound up together," he said. "That is the work we are undertaking at City Hall, and I am asking every New Yorker to join us."
Ofir Akunis, Israel's consul general in New York, criticized Mamdani in a Tuesday X post, saying that "money can't buy values," and calling on the NYC mayor to readopt the IHRA definition of antisemitism.
"Until you recognize that your language against the Jewish State, which you don’t recognize as the homeland of the Jewish people, is the fundamental reason for the rise of antisemitism in New York City, it will continue to increase."
"Truly combating antisemitism requires readopting the IHRA Working Definition of Antisemitism, which you overturned as the first decision of your administration on day one," he said. "To truly fight antisemitism would be to call for your supporters to stop shouting “from the river to the sea” and “globalize the intifada,” have them condemn the October 7th massacre, and instead of supporting Hamas, declare that they are a terrorist organization."

Lindsay Clancy returns to court for hearing after murder case mistrial ruling
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
17:10:31 UTC
02:10:31 KST

Lindsay Clancy returned to court on Tuesday, as her lawyers sought to head off a retrial by having a judge find the Massachusetts woman not guilty of murder for the killing of her three young children in 2023.
Judge William Sullivan in Plymouth, Massachusetts, took up the issue after declaring a mistrial on September 4, which occurred after a single juror prevented the 12-member jury from reaching a unanimous verdict on whether to convict Clancy or find her not guilty by reason of insanity.
Plymouth County District Attorney Timothy Cruz's office has in the weeks since been silent on whether it plans to retry Clancy, 36, on first-degree murder charges, which carry a life sentence.
No one at Clancy's trial disputed that she strangled her three children with exercise bands on January 24, 2023, in the basement of their home in the Boston suburb of Duxbury. She then cut herself with a knife and jumped from a second-story window in an attempt to end her own life, leaving her paralyzed.
Defense lawyer Kevin Reddington during her first trial sought to convince jurors that she did not understand what she was doing was wrong and that she had been in the throes of postpartum psychosis when she killed Cora, 5; Dawson, 3; and 8-month-old Callan.
Total, complete lack of evidence
During Tuesday's hearing, Reddington told Sullivan that there was a "total and complete lack of evidence" at the trial to prove she killed the children and knew what she was doing was wrong.
He said non-lawyers had trouble understanding the idea that someone could admit culpability while maintaining a lack of criminal responsibility. That was leading many members of the public to call Clancy a "demon" and call for her execution, he said.
"This is coming from politicians, from President Trump all the way down," Reddington said.
Several jurors have in televised interviews stated that but for the one holdout juror, they had been prepared to find her not guilty by reason of insanity, known in Massachusetts as lack of criminal responsibility.
If found not guilty on those grounds, she would be committed to a state psychiatric hospital for evaluation. Her commitment would then be subject to regular review by the court.
Prosecutors have several options before them, including trying to reach a plea deal or retrying Clancy on lesser second-degree murder charges, which would give her the option to waive a jury trial and proceed before a judge.
Clancy's lawyers file series of motions to head off retrial possibility
Clancy's lawyers have filed a series of motions seeking to head off the possibility of a retrial by urging Sullivan to declare her not guilty and bar a retrial on the grounds that there was no reason to declare a mistrial and that it would as a result violate her right to avoid being tried twice for the same crime, known as double jeopardy.
They say jurors had been clear in notes delivered to the judge that the holdout had been refusing to apply the court's instructions on how to determine if prosecutors proved their case beyond a reasonable doubt, and that the juror should have been dismissed rather than allowing the case to be retried.
Her attorneys have also asked Sullivan to allow them to review normally confidential records about the jury and the holdout and question him about his truthfulness during the jury selection process and his cellphone use.
Sullivan said he would take up that issue and several other motions during a November 2 hearing. The holdout's lawyer, Edward Paltzik, told Fox News in an interview that aired on Monday that his client, Michael Desronvil, "had zero doubt" and "rigidly applied the reasonable doubt standard."

Russian daily casualties highest since war began
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
18:04:48 BST
02:04:48 KST

The Ukrainian General Staff recorded 2,090 Russian casualties, killed and wounded, in the twenty-four hours to 28 September, the highest daily total it has reported since the full-scale invasion began in February 2022, according to British Defence Intelligence.
In its daily update on the war, the Ministry of Defence organisation set the figure against the rest of the record. Three previous daily totals above 2,000 were recorded during 2024, and the fourth-highest, of 1,960, came earlier this month on 16 September.
British Defence Intelligence stated: “The casualty rate has remained high since the summer, highly likely as Russia maintains its intensity in the fortress belt region, particularly in the vicinity of the Ukrainian stronghold of Dobropillia.”
The fortress belt is the line of fortified towns in Donetsk oblast running through Sloviansk, Kramatorsk, Druzhkivka and Kostiantynivka, built up since 2014 and the principal obstacle to any Russian advance across the remainder of the region. Dobropillia sits to the west of that line, north of Pokrovsk, and became a focus of fighting after Russian forces pushed a narrow salient towards it, which Ukrainian units then worked to cut off.
Casualty figures in this war have to be handled with care whichever direction they come from. The Ukrainian daily total counts killed and wounded together without separating them, covers the whole front rather than any one sector, and is compiled by one of the belligerents. Western estimates of total Russian losses have generally been produced separately and with wide margins, and the British assessment has for some time been that Russia continues to accept losses at a rate it can sustain in manpower terms while taking ground at a pace measured in fields rather than towns.
What the figure does indicate, if the trend holds, is the cost of the tempo Russia has chosen to maintain through the autumn rather than pausing to reconstitute, with the highest and fourth-highest daily totals of the entire war now both falling within the past fortnight.
British Defence Intelligence has published updates on the war since shortly after the invasion began, releasing them through the Ministry of Defence account most days, and the format has settled into a short set of observations drawing on open sources alongside its own material. The updates carry the probability language deliberately so that readers can distinguish between what the organisation knows, what it assesses and how confident it is in the assessment.

Netanyahu is embracing Israel’s isolation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
17:00:00 UTC
02:00:00 KST

Benjamin Netanyahu’s address to the United Nations General Assembly last week sounded more like a speech marking the end of an era than one opening a new chapter. Perhaps behind it was an awareness that this could be the last time he stands on that podium as Israel’s Prime Minister.
With the approach of Israel’s elections, set for October 27, Netanyahu’s political future has become inseparable from the way he addresses Israelis and the world. Yet his speech appeared directed primarily at his electoral audience at home, with little regard for the international community.
Netanyahu did not come to New York to offer a new political vision, propose a way out of the war, or present a vision for the region’s future. He came above all to defend his standing in Israel and his conduct of the war, while recasting Israel from a state facing growing international criticism into a purported victim confronting a hostile world. The question was thus turned on its head: instead of asking what Israel was doing to Palestinians and to the region, the focus became what the world was doing to Israel.
The sight of dozens of delegations walking out of the hall as he entered provided a striking image of the very predicament Netanyahu sought to deny. Rather than treating it as a sign of growing political isolation, however, he incorporated it into a narrative of “heroism”. The more others walked out, the more steadfast he appeared in his own telling. And the louder the criticism became, the more determined he was to present himself as the leader who stands alone but refuses to bend.
Israelis united against the world
When political options narrow, military force and confrontational rhetoric can serve as substitutes for a political way forward. The aim was less to convince the world that Netanyahu had a plan to end the conflict than to demonstrate that he could still defy the world and reject its demands — and ultimately settle the conflict by force.
At the same time, the speech was clearly directed at Israelis. Netanyahu spoke of unity, resilience, and courage, of Israel standing against its enemies, invoking the image of a leader who protects his people and knows how to confront the world. This is what led some analysts to describe it as an electoral speech rather than a diplomatic one.
Netanyahu was not trying to convince the world that Israel had changed; he was trying to convince Israelis that Israel did not need to change. The speech sought to move the narrative from accusation to victimhood, from isolation to heroism, and from accountability to persecution.
But the image of a united Israel he presented sits uneasily with the country’s internal reality. Israel’s divisions did not begin on October 7. The war was preceded by a profound crisis over the nature of the state, democracy, the judiciary, religion, society, and identity. These divisions have deepened around Netanyahu’s project and that of his allies. Presenting himself as the leader who unites Israelis against the world, therefore, overlooks the fact that his own policies have been part of the internal struggle that has divided Israeli society.
This is the deeper political meaning of the false heroism in the speech: an attempt to turn isolation into evidence of strength, the absence of a political solution into proof of steadfastness, and the world’s rejection of Israeli policies into evidence that those policies are justified.
What should Palestinians take from this?
Simply, that force may impose new realities, but it cannot by itself turn them into lasting legitimacy. Palestinians should not compete with Israel over power, but consolidate their existence and national rights as a political and legal reality grounded in self-determination, freedom, and equality. That requires moving beyond reaction, strengthening unified national institutions and resilience, and speaking to Israelis and the world in a language aimed at ending the conflict rather than denying the other side.
Between the end of Netanyahu and a new image of Israel
Perhaps the absence of a meeting between Netanyahu and Donald Trump during this visit was more than a matter of protocol. The meeting was not on the U.S. president’s schedule at a time when Netanyahu is fighting an electoral battle and facing growing international isolation. It would be an exaggeration to turn that absence alone into a judgment about his political future. But the question remains legitimate: did it reinforce Netanyahu’s sense that his political era is approaching its end, and that Israel itself is paying the price for conflating the state with his government and its policies?
Netanyahu has increasingly blurred, in both his rhetoric and political practice, the distinction between the Israel he claims to represent and himself as the person who represents it. At this moment, the new Israel exposed by war and international isolation appears more starkly before the world: a state attempting to protect its old image through force, even as the gap widens between that image and what the world sees in its policies — occupation, settlement expansion, genocidal war, ethnic cleansing, and the denial of Palestinian rights. The construction of ever more “iron walls” may not be enough to conceal this image forever.
If this was indeed Netanyahu’s final address to the General Assembly as prime minister, he wanted to leave the podium with the image he had chosen for himself: a leader standing alone but refusing to bend, confronting the world while insisting that his people stand united behind him.
Yet his speech revealed another image: a leader trying to turn isolation into heroism, force into a substitute for politics, and the denial of the Palestinian people’s rights into a reality imposed through brute power. Perhaps this is the clearest irony of all: he sought to present himself as the leader whom the world could not isolate, yet, unwillingly, he may have contributed to deepening Israel’s isolation.

AI generated
KYIV - Ihor Malchevsky focused solely on his family as he peered over the edge of his third-floor office window, thick black smoke billowing behind him after a Russian drone smashed into the historic building setting it ablaze.
“My thoughts were about just one thing: how to rescue myself from this situation,” said the 69-year-old, a deputy department head at Ukraine’s National Academy of Sciences in central Kyiv which was hit on Sept 28.
Malchevsky concentrated on his wife, two adult children and seven grandchildren. His fear of heights did not get in the way as he clambered onto a ledge outside the window to avoid the smoke and fierce flames.
Images of Malchevsky and a colleague trapped in the burning Tsarist-era building fuelled fresh anger at Russia’s escalating strikes on Ukraine’s capital Kyiv and other cities.
Moscow, in recent weeks, has broadened its deadly attacks to target consumer logistics, businesses and data centres. Ukraine has struck oil and defence infrastructure in Russia, as well as online retailers.
The Sept 28 attack, which killed one person and wounded several others, was one of an increasing number of daytime strikes on central Kyiv using jet-propelled drones that Russia has developed to outpace Ukrainian air defences.
Chaotic scenes
Speaking to Reuters a day later, Malchevsky recalled the chaotic moments after the drone tore into the ornate yellow building just steps away from the National Opera and German embassy.
“The first seconds you don’t understand - then the mind switches on and begins analysing what happened,” he said in an interview at his home outside Kyiv.
Below, sirens and car alarms wailed as bystanders shouted and flames roared through the building.
After tense moments clinging to the side of the building, as dozens of onlookers watched with bated breath, Malchevsky gingerly descended a ladder that rescuers had pitched against the building.
Reaching the sidewalk largely unscathed, the mild-mannered Malchevsky sat stunned in a park across the street, gulping down water to clear the smoke from his throat.
Family members raced to the scene to greet Malchevsky, who called them shortly after his rescue.
His daughter, Kateryna Moskaliuk, 37, recalled the emotional moment she first saw her father smudged in soot.
She smiled with relief, but expressed dismay about countless other Ukrainian families affected by more than four years of war.
“What is all this for?” Moskaliuk asked.
Ukraine should fight on
Ukrainians are expecting another winter of fierce Russian attacks on the country’s energy grid, amid dwindling supplies of critical air defences.
Malchevsky - whose grandchildren jokingly compared him to “Spider-Man” after seeing the footage on YouTube - said Ukraine should fight on to weaken Russia, despite attempts to revive US-backed peace talks.
A US official said on Sept 29 that Russian President Vladimir Putin’s envoy Kirill Dmitriev held “constructive” talks with his American counterparts.
“It’s a senseless exercise,” Malchevsky said. REUTERS

California recognises Eid al-Fitr, Eid al-Adha as state holidays
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
16:56:56 UTC
01:56:56 KST

Breadcrumb
California formally recognises Eid al-Fitr, Eid al-Adha as state holidays
California has formally recognised the Islamic Eid al-Fitr and Eid al-Adha festivals as state holidays, making it the second state of the United States to do so.
Authored by Assembly member Matt Haney, Assembly Bill 2017 (AB 2017) now allows state and school employees to observe both Eids by using existing personal holiday credits or available leave.
The legislation also permits K-12 schools and community colleges to close for Eid, provided such closures are established through locally negotiated arrangements.
Many states, cities and school districts recognise Eid locally, but not as statewide holidays. Washington state was the first one to officially recognise the two festivals as state holidays in 2025.
Eid al-Fitr marks the end of the holy fasting month of Ramadan, and Eid al-Adha honours Prophet Ibrahim's (Abraham's) willingness to obey God by sacrificing his son.
Eid al-Adha, the most important event in the Muslim calendar, coincides with and marks the culmination of the annual Hajj pilgrimage in Mecca, home to Islam’s holiest mosque and site, the Kaaba.
The California chapter of the Council on American-Islamic Relations (CAIR-CA) welcomed Governor Gavin Newsom’s signing of AB 2017, saying it addresses a longstanding challenge for the state’s more than one million Muslim residents who are often forced to choose between practicing their faith and showing up to school or work.
"For far too long, Muslim students and employees in California have had to make the difficult choice between participating in observances essential to their faith or falling behind on their academic or professional obligations. AB 2017 removes these structural barriers and aligns state policy with the values of inclusion, equity, and respect for cultural diversity that define our state," it said in a statement shared on its website.
CAIR, the United States' largest Muslim organisation, said the passage comes at a time of increased Islamophobia in the country, saying it recently documented a 183% increase in incidents targeting mosques and Islamic centres from May to July compared to the same three-month period last year.
"Officially recognising these holidays sends the necessary and powerful message that California values and protects its Muslim community in the face of growing hostility".
In May, a shooting at the Islamic Centre of San Diego by two gunmen killed a security guard and two community members outside the mosque.

In a significant move, two officials from the Ministry of Home Affairs have been apprehended on corruption charges linked to FCRA registrations.
NEW DELHI: Two officials of the ministry of home affairs (MHA) were arrested on Tuesday following a tipoff by the ministry that they had reached out to an association, seeking illegal gratification in return for facilitating its pending registration under the Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act 2010.MHA, for which the two accused were working as senior accountant and accountant, has initiated legal as well as departmental action in the matter. Both officials face suspension in view of the corruption allegations and their arrest.While one of the officials is presently posted in the MHA’s foreigners division, the other had earlier served in the same division. The latter is currently posted in a pay and accounts office. “Acting on specific information received by the MHA, the special cell of Delhi Police, in coordination with the central agencies, apprehended two govt officials in New Delhi on September 28, 2026,” the home ministry said in a statement on Wednesday.
Stating that the MHA has zero tolerance against corruption, the ministry shared that the preliminary questioning of the two arrested officers indicated that they were in contact with certain associations for facilitating their registration and renewal in lieu of illegal gratification.
“Further investigation is in progress,” it added.The ministry emphasised that human interface in FCRA applications had more or less been eliminated, with all FCRA-related services delivered online through the dedicated FCRA portal. “No intermediary, agent or individual is authorised to facilitate any FCRA service,” said an MHA spokesperson, in a clear message to associations in the process of getting themselves registered under FCRA or seeking prior permission to receive foreign contributions.

'White House oppressing both Iranians and Americans'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
16:46:14 UTC
01:46:14 KST

'White House oppressing both Iranians and Americans'
IRGC letter to American people urges break from US war policies
TEHRAN — The Islamic Revolution Guard Corps (IRGC) has published a 26-page open letter to the American people this week, urging them to break with the foreign policy of their government and to reconsider what they have been told about U.S. wars in West Asia.
The letter is addressed to scholars, students and media workers. It says the American public is not the target of Iran's resistance. Rather, the target is a political class that turns war into a business and uses the country's power against people in the region and at home.
"The men enthroned at the White House oppress both Iranians and Americans," the letter states.
The letter is signed by the IRGC's public relations office and circulated in English and Persian. Its central message is that Americans have been misled about Iran and about their own government's role in the region.
Much of the document calls on Americans to separate themselves from the "U.S. war machine." It asks university communities to refuse research and media work that helps plan or justify attacks that kill civilians. It says silence in the face of such policies makes Americans complicit in decisions taken in their name. "This is not a call for hostility toward Americans, but for them to hold their own leaders accountable," the letter reads.
The letter then lists historical grievances that it says explain the hostile nature of Iran-U.S. ties. It begins with the U.S.-orchestrated 1953 coup in Iran, which installed a dictator and created the roots of decades of hostility. It points to the Iran-Iraq War, which it explains was an American-backed effort to destroy Iran's new government through Saddam Hussein. It also cites the 1988 downing of Iran Air Flight 655 by the USS Vincennes, calling it a crime that was rewarded instead of punished.
The letter adds that these policies continue through sanctions, covert operations and support for armed groups opposed to Iran. It asks Americans to "test that record against what they have been told about Iran by their own media and politicians."
On its designation as a "terrorist" organization by the U.S. government, the IRGC rejects the label as a political tool used by Washington to isolate and silence its opponents. It says the American people should see the IRGC "not as a threat but as the main line of defense against Western and Zionist domination." Iran's resistance is regional and defensive, the letter says, while U.S. power is expansionist and driven by interests outside the region.
The document is written from the position of an Iran that, it says, has survived a major military aggression launched by the United States and Israel on February 28, 2026. The letter devotes several pages to that aggression. It says the war failed to break Iran's will or change its course, and that the "outcome has exposed the limits of American military power in the region."
From that experience, the IRGC draws a larger conclusion: the United States is a declining power, and Iran's doctrine and worldview have already won a moral and strategic victory.
"It is perfectly clear which of the two leaders God supports," the letter says, contrasting Iran's leadership with a "self-enriching" elite in Washington.
The IRGC also accuses American politicians of treating foreign wars as financial opportunities. It notes that some trade stocks based on the outcomes of conflicts. It says the same leaders who speak of democracy and human rights have little concern for the Americans who bear the costs of war. That charge, the letter says, should unite Americans and Iranians rather than divide them.
The closing section is a warning. "America's crimes have turned the world into a powder keg that is ready to explode," the letter states. It says the American public has the power and the responsibility to stop a course that is unsustainable and dangerous for West Asia and for the United States itself.
The letter ends by invoking the Golden Rule, found in the Talmud and the Gospels, and calls on Americans to demand immediate change before more conflict spreads.

LONDON, Sept. 29 (Xinhua) -- The European Union (EU) has paid an extra 100 billion euros (about 113.3 billion U.S. dollars) for the same volume of fossil fuel imports since the start of the U.S.-Iran war, EU Energy Commissioner Dan Jorgensen said Tuesday.
He was speaking at a meeting of the bloc's energy ministers in Dublin, in Ireland, which currently holds the rotating presidency of the EU.
According to the Financial Times, Jorgensen told journalists that the EU had not received "one extra molecule of gas or oil" - despite paying so much more.
Noting that rising global energy prices were hurting Europe's industries and consumers, Jorgensen said, "We are entering a winter that currently looks so challenging that we want to eliminate any uncertainties that can be eliminated."
His remarks came after U.S. President Donald Trump threatened to impose a ban on diesel exports last week, pushing up already high prices for refined oil products. Nevertheless, U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright later expressed skepticism about the merits of a full diesel export ban, and Jorgensen said he was happy about this.
Meanwhile, Irish Energy Minister Darragh O'Brien said he had spoken with U.S. administration officials during meetings at last week's United Nations General Assembly, and a 90-day diesel export ban was unlikely to happen.
EU member states are currently discussing measures to prepare for a winter of high energy prices. Jorgensen has urged member states to consider ways to cut demand, continue filling gas storage facilities to at least 80 percent of capacity, and adopt "targeted and temporary" measures to address high prices. ■

Feature: Doolittle Raid fragment returns to China, completing shared China-U.S. wartime history
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
00:43:50 CST
01:43:50 KST

HANGZHOU, Sept. 29 (Xinhua) -- A small piece of metal from a Doolittle Raid bomber during World War II was reunited on Monday with fragments from its sister aircraft, reviving memories of a heroic rescue that has linked China and the United States for more than eight decades.
The fragment from B-25 bomber No. 8 was donated by George Retelas, a descendant of a Doolittle Raid participant and a representative of the USS Hornet Museum in California, to the Doolittle Raid Memorial Hall in Quzhou, east China's Zhejiang Province.
On April 18, 1942, a group of 16 U.S. bombers took off from the USS Hornet and bombed Japan in retaliation for the attack on Pearl Harbor.
After the raid, 15 planes heading for an airport in Quzhou ran out of fuel and crashed in various localities in east China. B-25 bomber No. 8 was the only one that diverted to the Soviet Union.
Chinese villagers risked their lives to rescue the parachuting airmen and helped them evacuate to safety. Of the 75 airmen aboard the planes, 64 were rescued by the Chinese people.
Their rescue, however, came at a tremendous cost. Many locals were suspected of sheltering the Americans, and some were tortured or even killed by Japanese soldiers.
In China, the Doolittle story has long been regarded as a symbol of the friendship forged between the Chinese and American peoples during their joint fight against fascism.
Today, the memorial hall in Quzhou preserves fragments from 11 of the 16 bombers, while the wreckage of five others was not found. China has designated the memorial hall as a new national patriotic education base.
"The fragment enriches this unique collection," said Tong Lijuan, director of the memorial hall, noting that the memorial hall will properly preserve and document the artifact, conduct further research and put it on display at an appropriate time.
Tong added that it will help tell the story of how Chinese and American people worked together during World War II to resist fascism and safeguard peace.
Retelas' connection to the raid runs deep. For him, the return of the fragment represents both a piece of history and a part of his family story.
His grandfather was a U.S. Navy sailor who helped load bombs onto the USS Hornet before the mission.
"My grandfather and those men in Alameda couldn't believe that they were part of history," Retelas said, adding that they would only learn later that the bombers were preparing for the first U.S. air strike on Japan after the attack on Pearl Harbor.
"That mission meant so much to Americans at that time because it boosted morale. At that point in World War II, it seemed like there was no hope. And the success of the Doolittle Raid gave people hope," he said.
Decades later, while volunteering at the USS Hornet Museum, Retelas discovered a 16mm film reel donated by a descendant of one of the Doolittle Raiders. The footage captured the Raiders training with their B-25 bombers before the mission.
Around the same time, he received an invitation to travel to China.
"What if we could exchange? What if we could create a cultural exchange to bring our two countries a little bit closer through the shared memory and sacrifice of our two peoples?" he recalled.
That discovery led him to Quzhou for the first time in 2025. He brought the film to the Doolittle Raid Memorial Hall as part of a cultural exchange and was given a fragment from B-25 No. 9, Whirling Dervish, recovered in China.
The visit changed his perception of China.
"China had always been a mystery to me as a place. But now I've found myself falling in love with the people," he said. "I know what that friendship felt like when those Doolittle Raiders were rescued by Chinese people. They must have had that same feeling of affection."
Back at the USS Hornet Museum, Retelas came across a plaque containing a fragment from B-25 bomber No. 8. The piece had been recovered in Russia in the early 1990s and eventually entered the U.S. museum's collection.
Knowing that Quzhou held pieces from several other bombers that reached China, he saw an opportunity. "So why not complete the collection?" he said.
The donation closed a circle that began with his grandfather more than 80 years ago. "As a grandson of a sailor who helped load those bombs and to be here, now, eight decades later, to help bring those aircraft back together in a very sentimental way, is very heartwarming," he said.
During his visits to Quzhou, Retelas also befriended local volunteers who helped recover fragments from Doolittle Raid bombers.
"They're like a version of me I see over in China," he said. "Seeing someone that you see a little bit of yourself in across the Pacific brings that ocean closer."
Retelas is working on a documentary called The Great Doolittle Raid Rescue, focusing on descendants, witnesses and volunteers who have helped keep the story alive. He hopes the film will reach wider audiences on both sides of the Pacific.
The 16 U.S. bombers that left the Hornet in 1942 could not be physically reunited, as the whereabouts of five remain unknown.
But for Retelas, the small fragment from bomber No. 8 has already brought together something else: a family memory in California and a wartime story preserved in China. It also carries the weight of shared history and the friendship across the Pacific. ■
