The cabinet of Madhya Pradesh has sanctioned horizontal reservations for ex-Agniveers aiming to join various uniformed services, such as the police force.
The Madhya Pradesh cabinet has approved a 20% horizontal reservation for former Agniveers in several uniformed services and cleared schemes and projects worth more than Rs 24,500 crore, the state government said.The decisions were taken at a cabinet meeting chaired by chief minister Mohan Yadav at the state secretariat.The reservation will apply to recruitment for police constables, the Special Armed Force, jail guards, forest guards and excise constables. It will be available across the General Category and reserved categories, including Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes and Other Backward Classes.Under the approved policy, former Agniveers will receive 20% horizontal reservation in police constable recruitment, while Home Guards will get 10% and ex-servicemen 5%.For the Special Armed Force, the allocation will be 20% for former Agniveers, 10% for Home Guards and 5% for ex-servicemen. In jail guard recruitment, 20% will be reserved for former Agniveers, 15% for Home Guards and 5% for ex-servicemen.The same allocation will apply to forest guard recruitment. For excise constable posts, former Agniveers will receive 20% reservation, Home Guards 10% and ex-servicemen 5%.The cabinet approved Rs 5,329.17 crore for payment of honorariums to around 76,000 guest teachers over five years, from 2026-27 to 2030-31.
It also cleared Rs 348.7 crore for school uniforms and Rs 3,245.8 crore for health centres and drug control, according to the official cited by PTI.The cabinet approved the construction of the Damoh-Katni four-lane road at a cost of Rs 4,470.30 crore and allocated Rs 3,580.22 crore to the Rural Development Fund.It also approved the continuation of major irrigation projects in Banda, Datia, Neemuch and Sagar, along with the Kanh Diversion Project in Ujjain, ahead of the Simhastha Kumbh Mela in 2028.The Rs 348.7-crore allocation for school uniforms will be transferred directly to the bank accounts of parents or students enrolled in government schools from Classes 1 to 8 during the 2026-27 academic year.The government also plans to use guest teachers to fill vacant posts in government primary, secondary, high and higher secondary schools. Madhya Pradesh currently has around 76,000 guest teachers, the official said.
Under the Centre’s Agnipath scheme, Agniveers serve in the armed forces for four years, including six months of training. The scheme provides for retaining 25% of each batch in the Army, Navy and Air Force, while the remaining personnel are released after their tenure.

Syrian city of Douma bans grooms from their own wedding parties
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
16:23:06 UTC
01:23:06 KST

Breadcrumb
Syrian city of Douma bans grooms from their own wedding parties
Grooms in the Syrian city of Douma have been banned from entering women-only wedding celebrations, with local authorities threatening legal action against men who turn up at their own brides' parties.
The decision by Douma City Council in the Damascus countryside prohibits "the groom entering women's celebrations in the halls of Douma city", according to a copy of the order published by the council.
It means that even the groom himself cannot enter the women's section of a wedding celebration.
In socially conservative parts of Syria, weddings are usually segregated by gender. However at the end of the women's party the groom usually enters to meet the bride and take her home.
The council warned that anyone violating the ban could face legal measures, although it did not specify what those measures would be or what penalties could be imposed.
The order was approved during a council meeting on 22 September but emerged publicly on Monday, prompting debate over why a local authority was regulating who could attend private wedding celebrations.
The council has not publicly explained the reason for the ban or when it will come into force.
Syrian fact-checking platform Ta'akkad said it contacted the council asking about the reasoning behind the decision, its legal basis, how broadly it would be applied and what action could be taken against those breaking the rule.
It had received no response by the time its report was published.
The decision has also prompted questions over whether local councils have the legal authority to regulate social customs in this way.
The council cited Syria's Local Administration Law No. 107 of 2011, but critics have questioned whether the powers it grants local authorities extend to imposing restrictions on private social practices.
The Syrian Observatory for Human Rights said the decision had divided opinion, with supporters viewing it as a way of organising weddings and protecting the privacy of women-only celebrations.
Opponents, however, questioned both the council's authority to impose the restriction and how it could threaten legal measures without clearly defining either the offence or the punishment.
The Douma decision is not the first attempt by a local authority in the Damascus countryside to regulate men's attendance at women-only weddings.
In May, the local council in Badda issued a broader order banning men from entering women's wedding halls, including the groom and male relatives of both the bride and groom.
Unlike the Douma decision, the Badda order explicitly invoked religious considerations, saying the restriction was intended to prevent mixing between men and women.
The latest controversy comes amid a wider debate in post-Assad Syria over the extent to which local authorities should be able to regulate social behaviour and customs.
For grooms planning weddings in Douma, however, the immediate implication is simpler: when the women's party begins, even the man getting married may have to wait outside.

Bennett’s B’Yachad party is one of the leading parties in the opposition bloc seeking to replace Netanyahu in the October elections.
“I am here today at Hostages Square, which symbolizes the terrible failure of the October 7 government, which has yet to be investigated. Everyone who was part of this failure must immediately step down,” Bennett said.

The former prime minister has vowed that, if he is part of the next government, he will seek to establish a state commission of inquiry to investigate the government’s failures surrounding October 7.“Everyone is focused on the warnings Netanyahu ignored before October 7, but when the next disaster happens, no one will be able to say they were not warned about this one.”
“The IDF is on the verge of collapse. The chief of staff has raised 10 red flags, saying the IDF is short 20,000 combat soldiers, but Netanyahu is ignoring them and dismantling the IDF,” he added.
Bennett said that he has gone into the field and spoken with officers and soldiers who told him that the shortage of combat soldiers “is already costing us soldiers’ lives.”
“They say soldiers are being wounded and killed by drones because there are not enough observers and snipers to protect them. The long reserve-duty rotations are wearing down the soldiers’ operational readiness, and that too is costing us casualties,” he noted.
Bennett also said that during combat, “they are forced to abandon positions they have already captured because there is no one to hold the ground, and then they have to recapture them at the cost of bloodshed.”
“Voting for the draft-evasion coalition is a direct vote against IDF soldiers and against those who serve.
Bennett: 'We will enlist everyone'
“We will enlist everyone, stop funding draft evaders, and strengthen the IDF,” he added.

The IDF has repeatedly warned of an urgent manpower shortage after three years of war.
In March, IDF Chief of Staff Lt.-Gen. Eyal Zamir said the IDF could soon collapse if no solution was found for the manpower shortage.

Seventeen prominent Michigan Jewish Democratic elected officials, party leaders, and activists publicly signed on to the “Nonnegotiable Michigan” campaign, urging on Tuesday Democratic US Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed to affirm foundational commitments regarding Jewish safety, identity, and Israeli statehood.
The growing roster of signatories includes University of Michigan Regent Mark Bernstein, State Representative and founder of the Michigan Democratic Jewish Caucus Noah Arbit, former state representative Ellen Cogen Lipton, and former Keego Harbor Mayor Rob Kalman, alongside several local council members, township supervisors, and executive board members of the Michigan Democratic Jewish Caucus.
This expanding backing follows the initial launch of the campaign earlier this month by Michigan rabbis, cantors, and synagogue lay leaders. Nonnegotiable Michigan noted that these prominent Democrats joined the effort three weeks after its debut, after receiving no public response from the El-Sayed campaign addressing requests from Jewish Democratic voters.
Campaign centers on five commitments
The campaign centers on five core commitments: affirming that Jewish safety, including the safety of Zionist Jews, is nonnegotiable; recognizing the right of Jews to define their own identities; supporting Jewish sovereignty in Israel; welcoming the full participation of Jews in American political life; and providing an affirmative vision for a better future in the Middle East.
Nonnegotiable Michigan emphasized that the initiative is designed as an invitation for candidates to engage with Jewish voters rather than an ultimatum or an endorsement in the US Senate race. However, participants expressed frustration over what they described as a lack of engagement from El-Sayed as Election Day approaches, pointing to past rhetoric of concern to the community.
In a letter sent last week to former vice president Kamala Harris before her visit to Michigan, Nonnegotiable Michigan faith leaders detailed their concerns regarding the Senate nominee.
“Dr. El-Sayed has had every opportunity to meet our request to support our basic needs,” the leaders stated in the letter. “So far, he has declined even to respond. He has called Israelis ‘bloodthirsty’ – language that echoes the centuries-old blood libel used to justify violence against Jews.”
Demand that El-Sayed state plainly that safety of Zionist Jews is nonnegotiable
The campaign further presses the candidate on these concerns, stating that “The organizers urge El-Sayed to state plainly whether the safety of Zionist Jews is nonnegotiable – without any ifs, ands, or buts – and whether he aspires to dismantle Jewish sovereignty and self-governance in the State of Israel.
Nonnegotiable Michigan leaders are also asking El-Sayed to publicly reject and walk back rhetoric that stigmatizes and incites violence against Jewish Michiganders, that invokes longstanding anti-Jewish tropes and stereotypes, casts Jewish political participation as nefarious or corrupt, or scapegoats Israel and Jews for the suffering of Michiganders.”
This campaign follows an incident last week in which El-Sayed evaded an audience member’s request to condemn Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) and declined to comment on Iran, telling the crowd that the United States should not be involved in foreign regime change wars.
El-Sayed’s election campaign team did not respond to an emailed request for comment by time of publication.

The initiative, which The Atlantic noted is "still in its early stages," would "promise to advance several of Trump's goals at once."
"It would help reintegrate Russia into the global economy and broaden Trump's talks with the Kremlin beyond the intractable war in Ukraine, which his envoys have failed to end after more than a year of diplomacy...create a path for the US to sign lucrative deals involving Russian oil, diesel, rare earth minerals, and other commodities, [and] as a bonus, the release of prisoners on humanitarian grounds could bolster Trump's case for his long-coveted Nobel Peace Prize," the report said.
However, this approach "is likely to outrage the Ukrainians, Europeans, and even many of Trump's allies on Capitol Hill," the report noted.
This is because "any potential business deal between the US and Russia would risk funneling money to the Russian military even as it continues to terrorize Ukraine and threatens a wider war against US allies in Europe," the report added.
Earlier in September, Trump signed a law co-authored by the late senator Lindsey Graham that authorized the president to "impose severe sanctions on Russia and its trading partners," the report highlighted.
Coale used his successful experience negotiating with Belarus, Lukashenko
Coale, who proposed the strategy, was formerly Trump's envoy to Belarus, Russia's closest ally. During his talks with Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko, Cole achieved the release of hundreds of political prisoners from Belarusian jails in exchange for easing sanctions and promising to buy potash fertilizer.
Trump has therefore given Cole his "blessing" to do the same with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said during his visit to New York for the United Nations General Assembly that he would try his best to "block" any attempt to lift sanctions on Russia before the war ends, but "it's difficult."
However, Trump's envoys do not see a way to conduct business with Russia without first achieving at least a partial ceasefire in Ukraine, one of the negotiators told The Atlantic.
"Economic ties usually result in normality," Coale told The Atlantic, adding that, in his view, such deals could help bring the Ukraine-Russia War closer to a ceasefire by easing tensions between Russia and the West.
The White House has nominated Coale to serve as the special presidential envoy for hostage affairs, with full ambassadorial rank and privileges, pending Senate confirmation, the report noted.
"The president and his team remain committed to continuing to play a constructive role in ending the war between Russia and Ukraine, and he remains optimistic that we'll ultimately get a peace deal done," a White House official said when asked to comment on Coale's mission.
According to the report, Coale plans to coordinate his efforts with Trump's special envoy Steve Witkoff, who has met with Putin at least seven times since the start of the war.
Most recently, on September 5, Putin expressed gratitude to Witkoff and Jared Kushner for their attempts to negotiate a peace deal following meetings in the Kremlin.
"I'd like to tell you that we find it comfortable to work with you, and, of course, we have a very high level of trust doing this work," Putin told them.

As US leaves Iraq definetly, Baghdad sees withdrawal as 'symbol of sovereignty' - analysis

ISIS invaded Iraq in the summer of 2014. It swept across the Sunni cities of Iraq, preying on the anger among locals who resented then-premier Nouri al-Maliki. Maliki was close to Iran and was thought to be suppressing Sunni Arabs.
The Islamic State conquered the city of Mosul in June 2014, and in August, it began massacring the Yazidis in what would become an eventual genocide. It went on to decimate Iraq’s military. Thousands of military vehicles, many of which were supplied by the US, fell into ISIS’s hands.
Iraq asked the United States for help. The US left Iraq in 2011, but the Obama administration nonetheless wanted to help. Thus, three years after its departure, the US returned to Iraq, this time to join the fight against ISIS.
Today, over a decade later, the US is leaving Iraq again. The Iraqi News Agency (INA) reported: “September 30 represents a significant historic milestone in Iraq’s path toward completing its national sovereignty and strengthening the independence of its political and economic decision-making.”
Iraq is treating this like a victory over America. Instead of thanking the US for its help, Iraq is treating the US like it’s the problem, not ISIS.
INA noted: “The importance of this step extends beyond its security and political dimensions to highlight the state’s ability to capitalize on this transition to improve the economic environment.
“Experts and lawmakers see the success of this phase as dependent on the ability to uphold the rule of law, provide a secure environment for investors, and undertake structural reforms that strengthen the confidence of domestic and foreign capital in the Iraqi economy.”
Why does Iraq think the US leaving is good?
Why is it like this? The US assisted, trained, and equipped the Iraqi army. US soldiers fought ISIS and helped Iraq recover. Only just recently, Iraq’s prime minister was in the US, seeking energy investments and other deals. So why is the coalition deemed the problem, instead of getting the applause it deserves?
Iraqi Parliament member Nasser Turki told INA that “September 30 represents an important historic day, marking the withdrawal of all foreign forces from Iraq, and this will have a positive impact on attracting foreign investment opportunities.” He added that “the state’s strategic plans will focus on working in the service, economic, industrial, and agricultural sectors while taking into account the interests of its people.”
The Security Media Cell, a confab of Iraqi security news that is also official and run by Lt.-Gen. Saad Maan, said: “Sovereignty Day represents a new chapter in Iraq’s relations with the countries of the world, based on shared interests in accordance with Iraq’s vision and the interests of its people. It reflects the ability of the state and its institutions to assume responsibility for protecting the country and confronting security challenges, thereby strengthening citizens’ confidence in the security and military institutions.”
Meanwhile, The National in the United Arab Emirates noted that the US and Iraq signed a deal to transfer diplomatic and logistical facilities at Baghdad airport to the Iraqis. This site had often been targeted by Iran and Iran-backed militias. In fact, Iran has attacked Iraq more than 1,000 times, primarily targeting the Kurdistan Region. Iranian-backed militias in Iraq executed over 600 attacks against other groups.
Iran's influence in Iraq also impacts withdrawal
Another angle to America’s withdrawal from Iraq is Iran. Iran still believes the US has far too much influence in Iraq. Iran wants the US away from Iraq and the Gulf, and will view its departure as a win.
Rudaw Media reported that Hossein Shariatmadari, representative of Iran’s supreme leader, accused Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi on Tuesday of accepting and implementing US sanctions against Iranian airlines.
Rudaw also noted that the “Kurdistan region’s Peshmerga Affairs Ministry on Monday warned that the planned withdrawal of US-led coalition forces from Iraq on September 30 comes at a ‘sensitive time,’ as Baghdad and Washington proceed with a joint agreement to end the military mission in the country, including operations in the Kurdistan region.”
Meanwhile, Iranian-backed militias have hinted at their increased role. This comes as they’re supposed to be disarming. However, Hezbollah “warned Monday that it would shoot down ‘hostile’ aircraft violating Iraqi airspace after the US-led Global Coalition completes its military withdrawal from Iraq this week,” Rudaw said.
Currently, the Kurdistan Region appears to lack some of the defenses the coalition had provided in the past. It’s still unclear how many of their air defenses remain. In the past, Baghdad has refused to provide the Kurdistan Region with air defenses. Thus, the US’s departure has left many Kurds feeling concerned.
North Press media wrote that “Kurdish leader Masoud Barzani warned of the repercussions and dangers of the withdrawal of US and international coalition forces from Iraq, according to Kurdistan 24.”
It remains to be seen what comes next. However, Iraq depicting the US’s withdrawal as a victory points to its failure to value America’s contributions. It is unclear what Iraq will do after the US has left its shores, and when – or how – Iran could take advantage of it.

From ruins, regrowth: Artists answer October 7 with humanity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
16:15:18 UTC
01:15:18 KST

An exhibition at the Bible Lands Museum, born of a Jerusalem Biennale open call, gathers artists who had to find their way back to the studio after the massacre, and asks whether a people, like a tree, can grow again.
Six artists have contributed their own views of life, death and humanity to mark the third anniversary of the October 7 massacre. Curated by Yael Boverman-Attas, the exhibition "As Humankind," which opened to the public on September 24, has brought life back to the Bible Lands Museum's garden in Jerusalem.
In the weeks after October 7, some of the artists now showing in the garden could not make anything at all.
"It just shut your mouth," Galit Shvo, one of the featured artists, told The Jerusalem Post. "I couldn't work."
The exhibition took shape during the Israel-Hamas War, when Dr. Risa Levitt, the museum's executive director and acting chief curator, approached Boverman-Attas, an artist, designer, curator and researcher, with a vision for a show in its garden, "which is so beautiful," the curator told the Post. A call for works for the Jerusalem Biennale followed. Boverman-Attas gathered a group of artists, applied, and was accepted.
"Since then, it was a kind of journey that we went through," the curator said. "I think the war actually brought a new way to look at art."
Some of the pieces were made years before the war and are now being seen from a new perspective, while others were built on site. According to the curator, a single idea connects them.
"In every piece of art that I chose for this exhibition, I could see the growth," she said. "We were searching for an optimistic message. We were searching for hope, and we were searching for regrowth."
The title "As Humankind" comes from a poem and a verse in Deuteronomy that compares humankind to a tree, a comparison that holds "in many senses," Boverman-Attas said. "One of them is their ability to grow, to regrow after the disaster," she told the Post.
Trees cut from a single plate
Shvo's folded iron trees stand among the garden's plantings. The series grew out of four years of sketches and a fascination with branching.
"It's a process that started four years ago, in all kinds of sketches, and my interest in bifurcation and splitting," Shvo told the Post. "It's an algorithm that is mutual to trees, to growth, and also to a nuclear explosion, a chain reaction."
Asked what about October 7 had inspired the work, Shvo pushed back on the premise. "They didn't inspire me," she said. "The only thing I could do was work with children."
With the help of volunteers, Shvo cut small trees that the children folded, painted, and wrote on, "especially kids that were away from home." Only months later, when invitations to exhibit arrived, did she return to the studio and begin creating "other variations of splitting, of growing algorithms."
"It really took me a lot of time to find myself again in this horrible situation and start working," Shvo said.
Four rooms, a broken heart
Tel Aviv artist Sharon Pazner, a trained architect, built the exhibition's largest ruin out of the wreckage of her own studio.
The piece, Four Rooms, began with the footage of destroyed homes that emerged after October 7. "I thought I'd make a piece called Four Rooms, like the four rooms of our heart," she told the Post. "Like a broken heart and a broken house."
The material came from a crisis of faith in her own work. "I was so traumatized, as we all were, but I was thinking that to be an artist after such a tragedy was kind of absurd," she said. "It was kind of depressing, because I thought I could never create again."
Each brick in Four Rooms was cast individually in fresh concrete and embedded with fragments of earlier works she had come to see as irrelevant, along with small objects she had cast in her studio and pieces of broken industrial blocks.
"To overcome the pain and the feeling of art being irrelevant, first of all, I had to make my art relevant," Pazner told the Post. "My art couldn't be the same after the 7th of October."
For Boverman-Attas, the work reads as an archaeological site. The four-room plan echoes an ancient Israelite building form, while the bricks hold fragments of dolls and objects linked to Pazner's activism during the war. "If you take a very close look, it seems like they're all kind of crashed into the ruins," the curator said. "She's asking us to feel and to look at the details."
Reaching for the apple
Not every work in the garden was made in response to the war. Eva Avidar's figure straining toward an apple on a tree was made about a decade ago, as the artist tried to come to terms with "my new body, the new me."
The sculpture captures a single instant of desire. "I wanted to feel this extreme pleasure of sweetness in the mouth," Avidar told the Post, describing the moment when "the tree that was holding the apple disappears, and only the essence of the bite is the experience."
The curator saw something else in it after October 7. "I felt that she's really talking about the war, about how we all ache, how we all feel the pain and how we are all trying to achieve the fruit of Eden," Boverman-Attas said.
The figure's pose, she noted, is impossible. "If she bites the apple, it will fall. If she tries to hold it, she will lose her balance. And I felt that this is so much how we feel about the situation, so fragile, so on the edge, and so full of hope to try and make things better."
Relics for a distant future
Gabriel Klasmer, primarily an abstract painter, is showing a figurative sculpture made from an unlikely material: compressed shopping bags, bound with tape and wrapped in cling film.
"Living especially in Israel, you accumulate lots of plastic bags very quickly from all the shops," Klasmer said. "This is a very discarded material. But on the other end of it, it is a very highly sophisticated material."
The work, Klasmer said, touches "a very deep human aspect, but it's also a very political aspect."
Between life and death
Max Epstein carves with archaic tools: axes, knives and fire. For 17 years he has co-run a community animation studio where children and teenagers make films and develop "their own voices."
His newest work here, whose title translates roughly as Roadside, draws on the ancient Greek herm, a roadside marker topped with the head of a god, which the Romans later turned into portraits of a territory's owner.
"For me it was important to create a portrait of a man who is [suffering] from inside, physically and mentally," Epstein told the Post, "and to try to point to the border between the suffering and the silence before, and the silence after death."
"Art has no right to escape from the world," Epstein said. Most of the works in the garden, he added, are dealing with "the current period, which has a lot of pain."
Reflecting on what art means after October 7, Pazner offered an optimistic view. "I see this work as an optimistic work, first of all, because it exists, because I could make art again," she said. "But more importantly, I wanted to show that despite the many losses we have, they're still here with us. We haven't forgotten them, but we must continue."

‘New path’: UK’s Burnham promises huge expansion of public services
UK prime minister tells his first Labour Party conference ‘fundamental rethink’ needed to set Britain on right course.
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham has promised to put the United Kingdom on a new path of equitable growth during his first Labour conference speech as leader of the country and party.
Covering a range of topics including healthcare, pensions, electoral reforms, affordable housing and publicly-owned utilities, Burnham on Tuesday said it was time for the UK to opt for drastic change and reject a slow and painful demise.
“Britain has been on the wrong path for a long time,” Burnham told delegates, adding that he was “ready to do things my predecessors wouldn’t”.
“I will make a break with the direction of the past 40 years and put Britain on a new path, build a new economy and a new politics. That is the case I make to you today,” he said.
Burnham, who replaced Keir Starmer as the UK prime minister in July, said there was a “sense of the powers-that-be pulling against the people, not with them”.
“More of the same isn’t good enough,” said the former mayor of Manchester, where the party conference was held. He added that it was time “to break the mould today”.
Social reforms
This year’s Labour Party conference brought together legislators and party members alongside trade unions and businesses in one place.
“This country isn’t where any of us would want it to be,” Burnham said.
Much of Burnham’s speech addressed the need for social reforms with a focus on caregivers and healthcare, including building a “National Care Service … free at the point of use”.
He said it will be “a person-centred, high-quality” service where “everyone contributes and everyone is covered” and care “is about people not profit”, does not erode savings and gives “proper recognition” to care workers.
There was also talk of adjusting the so-called “pension triple lock” that sets state pension rises. He said changes will be made by April 2030, after the next general election.
Burnham said low-income pensioners would not pay income tax in the current Parliament. The planned changes meant pensioners would receive annual rises to their state pension without additional care charges, “so that pensioners will always share in the rising prosperity of the nation”.
He also spoke on the need to make housing more affordable, confirming his party’s intention to make it easy for young people to own a home by reducing the deposit needed to buy property.
There was also mention of returning control of utilities, such as water and electricity, back to the public, by scrapping “[former Prime Minister] Margaret Thatcher’s ideological ban on public ownership of water companies”.
On electricity, Burnham announced a new publicly-owned “Great British Grid” that will “challenge the private sector operators” to “increase competition, drive down costs and speed up delivery”, and make it easier to connect to the electricity grid.
Russia, Iran ‘threats’
Burnham’s speech also focused on foreign policy issues, saying he will “stand up to” Russian and Iranian “threats”.
“I will be steadfast in my support for Ukraine and stand up to threats wherever they come from, whether Russia, Iran, or anywhere,” he said.
On Israel, the occupied West Bank and Gaza, Burnham praised his foreign secretary’s approach, since assuming office in July.
“We will be principled in our leadership in securing a two-state solution between Israel and Palestine, as [Foreign Secretary] Ed Miliband has done,” he said.
Al Jazeera’s Milena Veselinovic, who was listening to the British prime minister at the conference, said Burnham’s speech was laced with “a lot of fiery rhetoric”.
“Britain finds itself in a very dire position when it comes to finances,” said Veselinovic, adding that there is immense pressure on Burnham’s new government as it prepares to introduce its first budget at the end of October.
The UK annual consumer price inflation (CPI) reached 3.1 percent in the 12 months to August, ticking up from 2.9 percent in July, according to the Office of National Statistics.
Veselinovic said Burnham is aware he may have to “pay a political price for all the reforms he’s promising”, but that he also understands, “somebody has to rip out the plaster on that because the costs are too high”.
‘Remarkable speech’
Danny Sriskandarajah, the chief executive officer of New Economics Foundation, said Burnham delivered “a remarkable speech”.
“Andy Burnham has this knack to be able to come across as authentic, as genuine,” Sriskandarajah told Al Jazeera.
Burnham, Sriskandarajah said, “was tearful at moments”.
“He was honest about what challenges Britain faces. But he also generates a sense of hope which I think is much needed,” he said.
Sriskandarajah said the challenge for Burnham will be to fund the promises he made in the speech.
“All of these things that he wants to do will cost money, which means they’ll have to raise those resources somewhere,” he said.

Kataib Hezbollah threatens to bring down Iraqi govt over Iranian airline ban

The Kataib Hezbollah warning came after several countries began restricting Iranian airlines from operating at their airports as sweeping new US sanctions targeting Iran's aviation sector came into force on 23 September.
"We warn Iraqi Prime Minister Ali Falih al-Zaidi and those behind him that any government that does not work in the interests of the people will be brought down by all means," Kataib Hezbollah’s security official Abu Mujhaid al-Assaf wrote in a social media post.
"If the air blockade on Iran continues after the first of next month, our people will take a clear position, which could include closing the border crossings of countries participating in the blockade of the Iranian people," continued al-Assaf. All four Iraqi airports that had been operating flights to and from Iran suspended them, significantly expanding restrictions first imposed in Baghdad.

The Iraqi state news agency INA said that only Iraqi Airways would now operate flights to and from Najaf.

Kataib Hezbollah was not officially given seats in al-Zaidi’s cabinet, as al-Zaidi agreed to exclude militia-aligned actors from his government to secure international support and avoid immediate US sanctions, ending months of political stalemate in Iraq.
While Kataib Hezbollah is officially part of Iraq’s state-funded security apparatus through the Popular Mobilisation Forces, it enjoys a large level of autonomy.
Iraq has long played a delicate balancing act in its relations with Washington and Tehran, which both still yield significant political and military influence in the country.
The US backs al-Zaidi’s government and is pressuring it to disarm Iran-backed factions and bring all arms under state control. While most groups have agreed to surrender their weapons and integrate with the state, Kataib Hezbollah has refused to disarm.
When the US-Israel war on Iran broke out, deadly US-Israeli airstrikes hit bases belonging to Iran-backed militias in Iraq which in turn targeted US interests, including Washington’s embassy and bases hosting US forces.

Rail in today’s world – full of challenges
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
16:12:26 UTC
01:12:26 KST

After years of Polish road hauliers dominating European markets, the time may have come for Polish rail companies to play an increasingly strong role in European logistics as well. We talk about the opportunities and challenges of today’s rail market with Marcin Witczak, President of the Management Board of Laude Smart Intermodal.
Can Polish rail companies make a stronger entry into the European freight market and, over time, play a role comparable to that of road transport firms? Which transport directions in Europe are the most promising? Where do we see bottlenecks?
Absolutely, yes. The European Union still allows several countries to effectively restrict market entry. That does not serve the markets, and the customer pays for it by buying a more expensive, lower-quality service. I am referring to Belgium and France, among others. For Poland to become a leader, it should have financial support from institutions such as PFR, BGK or ARP to fund the outlays needed to enter foreign markets. I am not only thinking of acquisitions. I also mean the purchase of rolling stock, licence fees and investment in our own terminals abroad.
For Laude Smart Intermodal, being a leader means above all delivering the most innovative solutions. Meeting that challenge requires enormous outlays. In rail, nothing can be done “at half the cost”. Every investment here means really big money, and the vast majority of rail companies cannot generate such funds on their own.
To sum up: as a country and as a logistics sector, we have the necessary potential, technical capacity and infrastructure in Poland. But to make a stronger push onto European rail routes, we need solid capital backing. And we are not talking about hundreds of millions here, but billions of zlotys. I am convinced, however, that this money would be sensibly invested.
In a word, can Europe’s railway lines take on more freight in the coming years?
Definitely. Rail infrastructure in the European Union is ready for it. As it is renovated and expanded, it will cope with more trains and more cargo. What is missing, both in Poland and in Europe, is the ability to run longer trains on a much larger number of routes. I mean trains at least 750 metres long.
Before we charge onto European routes, we have to deal with a potential threat hanging over our railways from “stray Russian drones”. We are talking about terminal security. Is Laude planning or considering protection of its Zamość terminal against such drones?
That in turn raises the question of whether we, as carriers, can protect ourselves against threats during transport in the border zone. That is the first point. Going a step further: are we considering using drones ourselves to counter threats to our terminals?
So let us start at the beginning, with our terminal in Zamość. The Laude terminal is located in a closed zone that is already protected today by the authorities appointed for that purpose. State services are responsible for protecting critical facilities, and they have the right tools, training and knowledge. The private sector has no access to weapons or military technology and no way of buying them. In any case, I am not sure that allowing companies to take independent action involving weapons would be the most sensible solution.
I would like to stress that drones should already be patrolling rail routes today, just as they patrol critical infrastructure.
A question has come up in public debate: since the Russians are systematically destroying Ukrainian rolling stock, mainly locomotives, can Poland help Ukraine in some way? Are there equipment reserves that could be handed over or sold to Ukraine?
Realistically, there are no such reserves. What I can see is handing over the entire LHS rolling stock fleet and quickly replacing it with new stock. LHS is preparing to renew its fleet anyway, but I don’t think it planned to transfer its existing stock to Ukraine. That is why the whole process is moving rather slowly. Still, I think nothing prevents us from looking at this strategically and deciding to hand over the broad-gauge locomotives and wagons we have to our Ukrainian partners. On our side, we would need to shorten, as far as possible, the approval procedures, for example for diesel locomotives on the only broad-gauge line in use in Poland.
Of course, supporting our eastern neighbours with locomotives would be crucial. It is a realistic solution, but we are talking about a minimum of two years to implement it. With political will, though, that period could probably be shortened very considerably. This matters because, to my knowledge, Poland does not have even a dozen or so broad-gauge locomotives, let alone several dozen, set aside in deep reserve. Nor do I really see any possibility of buying them on the open market.
I see sense in joint action on this by Poland and the Baltic states, including Finland. They are in a better position because they still run on broad gauge, so they have the right facilities. Such action, supported by simpler procedures and shorter testing periods, would be a step towards real help for Ukraine. Cooperation with these countries would also strengthen the resilience of the whole region to potential disruptions. This is a war, and we have to think outside the box. I encourage exactly this approach; otherwise we stand no chance. The purchase of new equipment could be subsidised from the Solidarity Corridor programme.
Finally, let us not forget that we all hope and expect that one day not only our wagons and containers, but also our locomotives and entire trains will run into Ukraine. So we too will need locomotives adapted to broad gauge.

Brief exposure to uplifting YouTube clips eases depressive feelings
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
16:00:56 UTC
01:00:56 KST

A new study suggests that watching short, uplifting videos online can reduce momentary feelings of depression. Participants who viewed hopeful video clips experienced increased positive emotions and greater motivation compared to those who watched merely pleasant content. The research was published in Psychology of Popular Media.
Depression affects millions of people globally, ranging from mild daily struggles to severe mood disorders. Despite this widespread burden, a large portion of those individuals never receive formal treatment. Barriers such as limited access to healthcare, financial constraints, and social stigma keep many from seeking traditional face-to-face therapy. This gap in care leaves a pressing need for accessible, low-cost methods to support emotional well-being in daily life.
Psychological research often focuses on positive emotions as a way to buffer against depressive feelings. Theories suggest that positive emotional states broaden a person’s cognitive flexibility, helping them build psychological resilience over time. A specific concept called hope theory breaks this future-oriented motivation down into two distinct parts.
The first is agency thinking, which is the internal motivation or drive to pursue goals. The second is pathway thinking, which involves the ability to create specific plans or strategies to reach those goals. Depression often diminishes both of these capacities, leaving individuals feeling helpless and unmotivated.
Yanhan Zhao, a psychology researcher at Beijing Normal University, led a team to investigate whether everyday digital content could tap into these specific cognitive mechanisms. Zhao and colleagues wanted to see if brief exposure to media tailored to elicit hope could improve mood more effectively than general positive entertainment. They focused on video-sharing platforms, which offer a vast, free library of emotional content that people already use to regulate their daily moods.
To conduct the experiment, the researchers first needed a systematic way to identify hopeful videos. They started with a pool of 236 public YouTube videos and used computer software to analyze the emotional tone of viewer comments. Rather than relying solely on the visual content of the videos, the team looked for content that generated specific reactions from the audience.
Using an established psychological model, they categorized hope as a combination of anticipation and trust. Videos that generated high levels of these two emotions in the comments were classified as hopeful. These clips often featured narratives of personal growth, overcoming adversity, and goal pursuit.
For comparison, the team identified a second set of videos that were generally positive but lacked the specific themes of hope. These control videos focused on humor, entertainment, and pleasant daily experiences without any explicit forward-looking narratives. The researchers selected a final pool of thirty hopeful videos and thirty non-hopeful positive videos to use in their experiment. Expert psychologists reviewed the final selections to verify that the videos matched their intended categories.
The study included 385 adult participants recruited online. The researchers started with a larger pool of volunteers but excluded those who failed attention checks or completed the task too quickly, ensuring the final data represented genuine engagement. Before watching any videos, participants completed questionnaires measuring their baseline levels of depression. They also answered questions to determine their general, long-term tendencies toward hopefulness, establishing a baseline for both their agency and pathway thinking.
The researchers then randomly assigned each person to watch either the hopeful videos or the positive control videos. Participants watched two videos from their assigned category, mimicking a natural browsing experience that lasted around ten minutes. Immediately after viewing the content, the participants filled out a second round of questionnaires. These surveys assessed their current momentary feelings of depression, their immediate positive and negative emotions, and their current state of hopefulness.
The researchers observed measurable differences between the two groups. Participants who watched the hopeful videos reported lower momentary depression scores than those who watched the standard positive videos. This benefit occurred consistently regardless of a person’s baseline depression level. The videos helped individuals with severe depression just as much as they helped those with mild or subclinical symptoms.
By analyzing the survey responses, the team identified how the hopeful videos altered the participants’ mindsets. The videos successfully elevated general positive emotions, which in turn contributed to the drop in depressive feelings. This boost in positive emotion accounted for a quarter of the overall reduction in momentary depression.
The hopeful content also sparked a distinct rise in state agency thinking. This means participants felt a temporary boost in their motivation and internal drive to pursue goals. This motivational shift accounted for about fifteen percent of the relief from depressive symptoms. The hopeful videos produced a direct benefit on mood that extended beyond these measured emotional and cognitive shifts, highlighting the unique impact of hope-oriented media.
While the videos improved motivation, they did not increase state pathway thinking. Participants felt more driven, but they did not feel any more equipped to formulate concrete strategies for their goals. The researchers suggest that pathway thinking might represent a more stable psychological trait. Generating concrete plans likely requires longer-term, skill-based interventions rather than a brief emotional boost.
The intervention also failed to alter negative emotions. While participants felt more positive and motivated, their underlying negative feelings remained unchanged. Negative emotions often involve persistent cognitive patterns, like repetitive worrying or rumination. A short video clip might elevate positive feelings without directly dismantling those ingrained negative thoughts.
The research relies entirely on self-reported questionnaires, which can sometimes fail to capture the full depth of a person’s emotional state. People might answer questions in ways they believe the researchers expect, introducing potential bias. The experiment also only tested a single, brief viewing session.
It remains unknown if repeated exposure to hopeful media over days or weeks could produce lasting benefits. Future studies could explore whether combining this accessible digital mood regulation with other psychological treatments offers stronger, more durable results for those struggling with depression.
The study, “Brief Exposure to Hopeful YouTube Videos Reduces Depressive Symptoms: Evidence From a Preliminary Study,” was authored by Yanhan Zhao, Danni Wang, Yang Yang, and Zhijin Hou.

Dare to try: A visibly rewarding creative journey into Disney
HKMU student turns a winning Disney design into a dream opportunity
[The content of this article has been produced by our advertising partner.]
Inside Chloe Tong Tsam-yu’s sketchbook is a world of her own making, populated by characters with distinct personalities and stories to tell. A Creative Advertising and Media Design student at Hong Kong Metropolitan University (HKMU), she grew up immersed in adventure and fantasy, from Disney classics to fictional worlds that sparked her imagination. She hopes to one day turn that passion into a career by building her own brand of original characters.
When she heard that Hong Kong Disneyland was running an illustration contest last summer, with an internship as the top prize, she threw her hat into the ring — and came out on top.
The character that found her
During her internship with the Hong Kong Disneyland merchandise team, Chloe and her colleagues created a fresh themed line of products, including plush key chains, water bottles, postcards, pouches and T-shirts. She proposed Stitch as the main character because the story of the alien and his young Hawaiian friend Lilo had moved her deeply since childhood. In the tale, Lilo is isolated for her quirky, free-spirited ideas. For Chloe, Stitch’s name also suggests an image of mending: he enters Lilo’s life, ends her loneliness and becomes her companion. It struck a deep chord in Chloe, whose own childhood was spent absorbed in fantasy worlds, struggling to find kindred spirits and to be understood.
“I came up with the line ‘Stitch Up the Spring’ as a nod to his name. The key that unlocks spring has gone missing, and Stitch sets off to look for it and bring spring back to the forest.”
From storyboard to meeting room
Justin Chan Wai-yin, Merchandise Operations Integration Manager at Hong Kong Disneyland Resort (HKDL), explains that HKDL staged its first tertiary illustration contest last year to mark the resort’s 20th anniversary, inviting art and design students from selected institutions to showcase their talent. He was glad to have Chloe on board.
“She was a little shy at the start of the internship, but as her confidence grew, she ended up presenting her own product line to dozens of colleagues at the department meeting.”
Chloe says she carries a lesson acquired from her HKMU programme: ideas alone are not enough — you have to know how to execute them, to make them “land”. During her internship, the timing was right. Her coursework had taught her the relevant design software, letting her apply what she had learnt straight away.
Learning from the workplace
She admits that self-doubt crept in along the way. “The suit I’d designed for the character — would people like it? I went to my colleagues for advice, took their suggestions on board, and broke down my idea into specific details to work out which elements could stay.” In the end, Chloe settled on a bow tie for Stitch — a touch that added personality.
After the internship ended, Hong Kong Disneyland offered Chloe a part-time role to continue developing a career in design. The experience has confirmed her resolve to build a life as a designer of original characters. To classmates with dreams of their own, she offers a word of encouragement: “You have to try — only then will you be seen.”

A medieval remedy could offer ideas for beating antibiotic resistance
It was harder for bad bugs to evolve resistance to the potion than to typical antibiotics
A look one thousand years into the past is revealing clues about how to develop the bacteria-fighting drugs of the future.
A concoction from a 10th century medical manuscript damaged cell membranes, altered the expression of disease-promoting genes and interfered with interbacterial communication when added to bacterial cultures, researchers report September 3 in mSphere. What’s more, three kinds of harmful bacteria developed resistance to the medicinal mixture much more slowly compared with conventional single-molecule antibiotics.
“The difference is remarkable,” says Omar El-Halfawy, a microbiologist at the University of Regina in Canada who was not involved in the research.
This impaired ability to develop resistance may occur because the medieval medicine affects several bacterial targets, says Freya Harrison, a microbiologist at the University of Warwick in England. For bacterial colonies to survive, “they’ve potentially got to mutate multiple targets, and that’s difficult.”
Bald’s Leechbook
The modern adaptation of the 10th century recipe (shown) involves combining garlic, onion, bovine bile and wine, then brewing the pungent mixture in a brass vessel for nine days.
Currently, antibiotic-resistant infections kill more than 1 million people each year. But humans have been battling the minuscule enemies that cause diseases like plague, leprosy and tuberculosis for millennia. Sometime in the 10th century, Anglo-Saxon scribes compiled several sometimes-dubious treatments into a medical text known as Bald’s Leechbook.
In 2015, Harrison and a team of microbiologists and historians brewed a remedy from the Leechbook, called Bald’s eyesalve, in the lab. They mixed garlic, onion, bovine bile and wine in a brass vessel, then allowed it to stand for nine days. In laboratory tests, Bald’s eyesalve displayed surprisingly effective antimicrobial activity against both Staphylococcus aureus and its drug-resistant form, MRSA.
This time, the scientists set out to determine how the eyesalve affected pathogens, measuring how the brew altered gene expression in bacterial cultures. After eyesalve treatment, hundreds of S. aureus genes were expressed differently, including ones related to cell membrane composition and disease-causing potential.
The remedy also damaged bacterial membranes, a possibly lethal maneuver. Furthermore, very low concentrations of the eyesalve reduced S. aureus’ ability to create hardy antibiotic-resisting colony formations called biofilms. It also inhibited bacterial cell communication, which pathogens use to coordinate activities and become more harmful.
Finally, the team dosed cultures of S. aureus and two other pathogens with increasing concentrations of the eyesalve or commonly used antibiotics to see how quickly resistance developed. After two weeks, the microbes often flourished despite exposure to eight to sixteen times the amount of the traditional antibiotic that had stymied their growth at the beginning. In contrast, they could only tolerate slightly higher eyesalve concentrations.
Harrison says she’s not expecting people to whip up their own batches of eyesalve to treat infections. “It would be really impractical to do that, and also potentially really unreliable and dangerous because it’s going to be so variable.”
Instead, she says, researchers could recapitulate the eyesalve’s multipronged attack in a clinically suitable way with a lab-made cocktail containing a handful of the potion’s active ingredients. “Somewhere in there, there’s this combination of molecules that’s responsible for most of this effect — so, can we find out what they are?”

LIVERPOOL, England - Prime Minister Andy Burnham risked reopening the bitter division over Britain’s departure from the European Union on Sept 29 by vowing to seek a consensus on closer ties with the bloc.

“Brexit has done more harm than good,” Burnham told the Labour Party Conference on Sept 29, setting out the November summit with the EU as the next step in rebuilding ties in a bid to improve growth and prosperity.

====================================================================================================

How the War is Changing the Geography of Iran’s Influence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
15:55:00 UTC
00:55:00 KST

On Sept. 10, Israel destroyed Hezbollah’s underground command center and weapons stores beneath the Ali al-Tahir ridge in southern Lebanon, about 10 miles from the Lebanon-Israel border. The loss deprived Hezbollah of a fortified position and dealt another blow to Iran’s most important regional ally, which has lost senior commanders and much of its arsenal over the past two years.
Farther south, another part of Iran’s regional network was gaining ground. In Yemen, the Houthis seized territory along the Red Sea coast, bringing them closer to controlling the approaches to Bab al-Mandab, the passage connecting the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden.
The fall of Bashar al-Assad in Syria in 2024 and Hezbollah’s weakening have diminished Tehran’s influence in the Levant. Yet the wider war has created opportunities for Iran and its partners, particularly around the waterways indispensable for trade and energy exports. Thus, Tehran is losing influence in one arena while acquiring new sources of leverage in another.
Iran’s efforts to control passage through the Strait of Hormuz are only one part of the picture. The Houthis’ expanding reach in the Red Sea gives Tehran’s partners leverage over a strategic waterway, while Iran-aligned armed groups in Iraq can threaten oil pipelines built to bypass these maritime chokepoints.
For Iran’s neighbors, even the routes meant to provide an escape from one danger are exposed to another. Tehran remains under enormous military and economic pressure, but its setbacks in its traditional centers of influence have not ended its ability to impose costs elsewhere.
From the Mediterranean to the Red Sea
In 2014, Yahya Rahim Safavi, a senior adviser to Iran’s then Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei, was at a conference of Iran-Iraq War veterans that was broadcast live on state television. He spoke of Iran’s growing reach through Syria and Lebanon. Iran’s “strategic depth” had stretched to the Mediterranean coast and just to the north of Israel, he declared. Hezbollah’s arsenal and the supply corridor through Syria were central to Iran’s “forward defense,” a strategy intended to deter adversaries and keep conflicts away from Iranian territory.
The foundations of that strategy have since been severely weakened. Assad’s removal cost Tehran one of its few state allies and disrupted its ability to resupply Hezbollah, while Israeli operations diminished the group’s capacity to retaliate on Iran’s behalf. Subsequent attacks on Iran itself by Israel and the United States demonstrated the consequences: its regional partners could no longer be counted on to prevent a direct war.
But Iran has been adapting. Even while fighting its own direct war with the U.S., Tehran has worked to develop other sources of regional leverage. On Jun. 8, Esmail Ghaani, commander of the Quds Force, the overseas operations arm of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) announced a “new security belt” extending from the Strait of Hormuz to Bab al-Mandab and from “the Persian Gulf to the Red Sea.” His statement pointed to a growing emphasis on the ability of Iran and its partners to threaten maritime transit across both waterways.
The Houthis’ capture of Mokha, a port city on the Red Sea coast, and Perim Island, which lies within Bab al-Mandab, gives them a stronger foothold at the southern entrance to the Red Sea. These positions could allow them to monitor passing vessels more closely and deploy weapons near the shipping lanes.
They do not need to halt all traffic to exert influence over the passage. Although the Houthis claim they are targeting only Saudi-linked vessels, the threat of attack alone has driven up insurance costs and forced shipping companies to choose longer routes.
The Houthis have their own agenda and should not be treated as an Iranian proxy acting on Tehran’s instructions. Their domestic motivations remain important: their campaign against rival Yemeni factions aims to consolidate their dominance and attacks on Saudi Arabia seek to force Riyadh to reduce its involvement in Yemen, lift what the Houthis consider a “siege,” and recognize them as the country’s ruling power.
Still, the ties between the Houthis and Tehran have deepened since Oct. 2023, and Iranian support has been central to the development of Houthi military capabilities. Some reports suggest Tehran has sent IRGC commanders, military advisers, and missile and drone equipment to Yemen to strengthen the Houthis’ ability to threaten Red Sea shipping.
Overall, the Houthis increasingly see the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran as a threat to the wider “Axis of Resistance” to which they belong; this translates into a close strategic relationship, even though Tehran may not direct every Houthi operation. As the Houthis see it, supporting Tehran serves both Iran’s and their own interests.
These interests are reinforcing one another. Iran’s disruption of Hormuz has increased the strategic importance of Red Sea export routes, giving the Houthis greater leverage over Saudi Arabia and forcing the kingdom to shift exports back to Hormuz, where—despite a recent significant uptick in traffic—passage remains uncertain. From Iran’s perspective, the goal of pressuring Saudi oil exports is to raise the costs of war for Washington and the global economy, giving President Donald Trump another reason to think twice before escalating the campaign.
Between Hormuz and Bab al-Mandeb
For Saudi Arabia, the interaction between Hormuz and Bab-al-Mandab fronts creates a vulnerability. While it is true that “shuttle runs” through the strait have helped Gulf oil exporters get their goods out and eased market pressure, shipments remain at risk of Iranian disruption.
As with the Houthis and Bab al-Mandab, Tehran need not close the strait entirely: intermittent attacks can sustain uncertainty and raise shipping costs. Given Houthi advances in Yemen, diverting exports to Red Sea ports is not necessarily a safer option. Riyadh can shift between routes but cannot entirely evade the risk of disruption.
The vulnerability extends inland. A recent drone attack launched from Iraq damaged three pumping stations on Saudi Arabia’s East-West Pipeline and forced a shutdown. Although the pipeline has resumed partial operations, the message was clear: attacks on this alternative route cannot be ruled out.
Among some Iranian strategists, the attack was also interpreted as a broader warning against building pipeline routes to carry Iraqi oil toward Europe through Turkey and Syria: diverting oil away from the straits would not necessarily put it beyond the reach of Iran and its partners.
The attack was widely attributed to an Iran-backed militia, even though the Islamic Resistance in Iraq—an umbrella grouping of Iran-aligned factions—denied involvement. Since the war began in February, the IRGC reportedly has mobilized smaller cells of Iraqi Shiite fighters operating under its command, giving Tehran a more direct role in operations from Iraqi territory.
There may well not be a unified chain of command across the Iranian, Yemeni, and Iraqi fronts, yet attacks from Iraqi territory must be seen as part of a broader campaign, adding to both Houthi pressure in the Red Sea and Iranian disruption in Hormuz. The cost to Baghdad is high, as it is unable to prevent armed factions from launching attacks that expose Iraq to retaliation and undermine its relations with Gulf neighbors. The resulting tensions could also serve Tehran’s interest in limiting its Gulf rivals’ influence in Iraq.
Together, these developments help explain Tehran’s defiant posture, as it feels it can threaten Saudi exports in numerous ways and thereby heighten the economic costs of the war for the United States and its partners.
This has strengthened the argument within the Iranian leadership that they should hold firm and, with time, improve their bargaining position in potential negotiations with Washington. The problem with this argument is that mounting costs for its adversaries do not necessarily mean Iran can afford a prolonged confrontation.
The costs of waiting
Trump’s campaign has so far failed to force Iran to accept American terms, while giving Tehran and its partners new opportunities to threaten the global economy. The longer the confrontation continues, the greater the likelihood that Tehran will respond by deepening military coordination with its non-state partners and escalating attacks, directly or through them. In this sense, Washington should have an interest in reaching a settlement before such cooperation becomes more entrenched and the confrontation spreads further.
But Tehran risks drawing the wrong conclusion from this dynamic. Recent developments may encourage Iranian leaders to demand more and offer less, believing that mounting economic costs will eventually force Trump to retreat. But such a scenario is far from being inevitable. Washington might instead respond with further attacks or tighter enforcement of the blockade. Each side would then treat the other’s refusal to concede as reason to intensify pressure, prolonging an uneasy standoff while making an agreement even more difficult.
Iran would be wrong to assume that time will improve its position. Its economy continues to bear the costs of the blockade, and disrupting its neighbors’ exports does nothing to finance its own recovery. Saudi Arabia will resist any arrangement that leaves its access to global markets dependent on Iranian and Houthi restraint. If Riyadh concludes that a negotiated deal would formalize that dependence, it could shift toward more open support for American military and economic pressure on Iran.
Saudi resistance to a planned Oman meeting among Iranian and Gulf officials earlier this month already points to limitations in Iran’s strategy. An emerging Iran-Oman agreement over the Strait of Hormuz ostensibly offered a basis for negotiations over maritime passage, but Gulf governments—and notably Riyadh—resisted arrangements that, in their eyes, would legitimize Iran’s unacceptable claim to control transit in the waterway.
Although their vulnerability gave them an urgent reason to seek an agreement, it also led them to resist a deal on terms that would entrench Iran’s dominance. Their refusal to attend showed that Iran’s ability to disrupt their trade has not translated into acceptance of Iranian terms.
Iran’s expanding regional reach, both directly and through its partners, strengthens its position in negotiations. But it also makes it all the more necessary to reassure its neighbors. A settlement will remain difficult as long as Tehran expects those neighbors to accept lasting uncertainty over their legitimate maritime rights in exchange for relief from the immediate threat of disruption.

China Focus: AI, other technologies to play bigger role in cultural heritage protection
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
23:54:07 CST
00:54:07 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 29 (Xinhua) -- China will expand the use of artificial intelligence (AI), satellite remote sensing, drones, 3D modeling and virtual reality as part of a new five-year plan aimed at protecting and preserving cultural heritage.
The cultural heritage protection and inheritance plan for the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030), issued by the General Office of the Communist Party of China Central Committee and the General Office of the State Council, proposes upgrading equipment for cultural relics conservation and strengthening technical support for the protection of historic buildings, grottoes, ancient murals, rock art, earthen sites, ancient books and archival materials.
Home to more than 760,000 immovable cultural relics and about 108 million pieces (or sets) of state-owned movable cultural relics, China is using technology to help survey, monitor and protect its vast cultural heritage resources.
The growing use of AI and other digital technologies is also changing how cultural heritage is protected, with experts noting a shift from simply recording and monitoring sites toward earlier risk detection.
A recent example is Wenwu-01, China's first remote-sensing monitoring satellite dedicated to cultural heritage protection, which was launched in June.
The satellite is designed to monitor changes in the environment surrounding heritage structures, using high-resolution imaging and an AI recognition model to detect changes such as abnormal construction activities. It can also provide long-term monitoring of risks including landslides, floods, wind-sand erosion and land subsidence.
A SYSTEMATIC APPROACH
The plan sets out 33 major tasks for cultural heritage protection and inheritance from 2026 to 2030, placing technological innovation within a systematic framework that also covers archaeological work, intangible cultural heritage, museums and international cooperation.
It aims to bring archaeological work forward in the development process, particularly where construction may affect underground cultural heritage. The plan requires archaeological surveys before major development projects and calls for integrated protection of cultural relics and their historic settings.
China now has 45 elements inscribed on UNESCO's lists and register of intangible cultural heritage, including silk craftsmanship, acupuncture and tea-processing techniques. More than 100,000 items are recognized on national, provincial, prefectural and county-level intangible cultural heritage lists.
Therefore, the plan places particular emphasis on their preservation. It calls for stronger protection and inheritance of traditional festivals, crafts, opera, folk arts, music, dance and traditional sports, while encouraging contemporary forms of expression and new settings for experiencing traditional culture.
The plan further calls for deeper international cooperation on cultural heritage, including bilateral cooperation, joint archaeological projects and international exhibitions on Chinese civilization.
It also encourages efforts to trace and facilitate the return of Chinese cultural relics lost overseas, while strengthening cooperation with UNESCO and other international organizations and multilateral mechanisms. ■

China further refines VAT credit refund policy to better target key sectors

00:54:02 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 29 (Xinhua) -- China has further refined its value-added tax (VAT) credit refund policy to sharpen its focus on manufacturing, technological innovation and green development and make tax incentives more targeted. In the year since the measures took effect, 281.8 billion yuan (about 41.8 billion U.S. dollars) in refunds have been issued, the State Taxation Administration said Tuesday.
Manufacturing, scientific research, software and environmental protection sectors accounted for 212 billion yuan of the total, with their combined share rising to 75.2 percent from the same period before the new policy took effect, the tax authority said.
Manufacturing alone received 191.4 billion yuan, accounting for 67.9 percent of the total, with its share rising 20.2 percentage points from the comparable period before the policy took effect.
VAT credit refunds allow eligible businesses to get refunds for input VAT they have already paid, rather than carrying the credits forward to offset VAT payable on future sales. By bringing forward the timing of the refunds, the policy gives businesses more funds for technological upgrades and investment in innovation.
China has continued to refine its VAT credit refund policy in recent years. In August 2025, the Ministry of Finance and the State Taxation Administration announced that, starting in September, eligible businesses in manufacturing, scientific research and technical services, software and information technology services, and ecological protection and environmental governance would be allowed to apply for full monthly refunds of end-of-period excess VAT credits.
The policy adjustment puts greater emphasis on supporting manufacturing, technological innovation and green development, while also making the policy more targeted, said Liang Ji, director of the public revenue research center at the Chinese Academy of Fiscal Sciences.
The move came as China moved to establish a more stable, long-term mechanism for VAT credit refunds, following earlier measures introduced in response to changing economic conditions.
The tax authority said it would continue to improve the long-term refund mechanism and refine related services to ensure that policy benefits reach businesses. ■

Asian Games | Feature: Five years on, China's Wang finds a different way to win

by sportswriters Zhang Can and Liu Yichun
TOKYO, Sept. 29 (Xinhua) -- Three gold medals in three events made Wang Zongyuan's return to the Tokyo Aquatics Center a triumphant one.
But five years after winning his first Olympic title in this very pool, the Chinese diver's Asian Games campaign has been about more than adding three more golds to his collection. It has offered a glimpse of what has changed in the young champion who once took the world by storm.
Wang completed his gold-medal sweep at the Aichi-Nagoya Games on Tuesday, following victories in the men's synchronized 3m springboard and 1m springboard with a successful defense of his men's 3m springboard title.
"It was a challenge for me to compete in three events and fight for three gold medals, especially as I get older," Wang said after his third victory. "I'm very happy that I managed to push through and accomplish the goal, although the overall performance was not perfect."
That last sentence may say more about Wang than the three gold medals themselves.
In Tuesday's 3m final, Wang remained in control from the opening dive, but he was not immune to mistakes. His fifth dive, a back 3 1/2 somersaults in tuck position, earned 68.40 points, his lowest score of the final. He recovered with 85.50 on his last attempt to finish with 494.40.
Wang later admitted that he had felt the strain of competing in three events.
"I didn't hesitate in the final. I tried to be more confident, relaxed and decisive," he said. "But in the later rounds, I could clearly feel that my physical reserves were not enough."
For Wang, learning to recognize and manage such moments has become part of growing older in the sport.
Five years ago, when he stood on the same pool deck as a 20-year-old Olympic champion, Wang described himself as someone who simply went all out.
"Five years ago, I was a young athlete who was just starting out. I went all out and competed without holding anything back," he said after winning the synchronized 3m springboard title. "After five years of growth, I feel more mature and more stable. I have gained experience and learned from different competitions."
Perhaps no change is more obvious than the way people around him now address him.
There was once "Xiao Wang," or the younger Wang, the fearless rising star. Now he hears "Lao Wang," or the older Wang, a playful nickname reflecting not only his years on the national team but also the role he has gradually taken on among younger teammates.
Wang sees that evolution as part of his journey.
"From the time I first stepped onto the international stage until now, I feel that I've become more mature. I can adjust and control myself more quickly during competitions," he said. "All these experiences and lessons have helped me grow."
He is also quick to share the credit.
"I couldn't have become the calm and steady 'Lao Wang' I am today without my country, my team, my coaches and my teammates," he said. "Their encouragement and support have allowed me to keep moving forward."
Wang's relationship with diving began long before the Olympic titles and nicknames.
In 2008, he was a young boy watching the Beijing Olympics on television while training in gymnastics. He spent two years in gymnastics before switching to diving after the Games.
Growing up in Xiangyang in central China's Hubei Province, along the Han River, Wang had always been drawn to water. His parents enjoyed swimming and often took him into the water when he was young.
When he had to choose between gymnastics and diving, the decision came easily.
"I really liked water," Wang recalled.
What began as a childhood attraction eventually became an Olympic career. Wang has spoken of the 2008 Games as the moment when the dream of competing at the Olympics was first planted in his mind.
His childhood idol was Chinese diving champion He Chong. Years later, Wang had the opportunity to talk with his former idol and learn from his experience.
Now Wang increasingly finds himself on the other side of that relationship.
That role was on display Tuesday with younger teammate Zheng Jiuyuan, his partner in the synchronized 3m springboard. Zheng made two major errors in the individual 3m final but fought back to take silver, scoring 93.60 points on his final dive, the highest single-dive score of the competition.
Wang was impressed by the way Zheng responded.
"He made a big mistake on the first dive, but became more relaxed in the following rounds and performed his movements more freely," Wang said. "I think this was valuable experience and a lesson for him, helping him find a better balance between excitement and control."
Zheng has described Wang as someone he learns from, and the two have developed a close partnership in training and competition. After they won the synchronized 3m title on Saturday, Wang told Zheng: "Believe in yourself, surpass yourself, and then let's win Olympic gold together."
In 2021, Tokyo marked the arrival of a young Olympic champion. Five years later, the same city has seen Wang complete a three-gold sweep at the Asian Games and emerge as a more experienced diver, teammate and guide.
Yet Wang is not looking back on his career as something already complete.
"Later, the person you become will definitely thank the person you are now for working hard and striving," he said.
For now, his direction is clear.
"See you in Los Angeles," Wang said. ■

GENEVA, Sept. 29 (Xinhua) -- Artificial intelligence (AI) is driving a rebound in venture capital and R&D spending, while a new generation of deep-science startups is turning frontier research into new industries, said the World Intellectual Property Organization's (WIPO) on Tuesday.
WIPO's Global Innovation Index 2026 (2026 GII) shows that Switzerland, Sweden, the United States, the Republic of Korea and Singapore lead the 2026 rankings. China, India, Vietnam, Türkiye, the Philippines, Morocco and Indonesia have climbed quickly over the past decade.
According to the report, global R&D expenditure grew by more than 3.3 percent in real terms in 2025 and is expected to reach 3.4 trillion U.S. dollars in 2026. Corporate R&D rose 5.8 percent in 2025 to a record 1.5 trillion U.S. dollars, driven by software, AI and defense-related research.
Venture capital funding for innovative startups grew by 28 percent to 510 billion dollars in 2025, the strongest gain since 2021. But investment is increasingly concentrated, with AI accounting for 53 percent of global venture capital deal value even as deal numbers fell for a fourth consecutive year. African startups raised about 3.2 billion dollars in 2025, up 40 percent.
Deep-science startups are booming. More than 30,000 have been created since 2000, nearly 10 times the 2010 figure, and their share of venture-backed startups reached 16 percent in 2025. Together they are worth 7.6 trillion U.S. dollars, up 23 percent from 2024. The United States leads with 12,752 firms, followed by China (3,466) and the United Kingdom (2,133). Growth since 2020 has been fastest in Central and Southern Asia, Latin America and the Caribbean, and Sub-Saharan Africa. These ventures span semiconductors, robotics, quantum computing, life sciences, space and advanced materials.
"AI is opening new technological frontiers across all fields of science," said WIPO Director General Daren Tang. "Our 2026 GII report shows that a new generation of deep-science startups is translating breakthroughs into products and transforming fields such as life sciences, space, robotics and clean energy."
Published annually, the WIPO GII ranks 139 economies on their innovation ecosystems using 79 indicators. ■
