Nvidia's record buyback shows chipmaker's stock is too cheap for CEO Huang to resist
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
13:09:30 UTC
22:09:30 KST

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is putting his company's money where his mouth is.
When the chipmaker announced a record stock repurchase on Monday, its share price was, by one key metric, at its cheapest level in a decade. Huang told CNBC's Jim Cramer last month that, "Buying back Nvidia stock is a tremendous opportunity."
Nvidia's price-earnings ratio for fiscal 2028, which begins this coming February, sits at just 14.5, below all of its megacap peers other than Micron. Its average current P/E ratio over the past five years is 62.9, more than double where it is today.
The constricted multiples for the world's most valuable company, now worth more than $5.5 trillion, reflect the sustained historic rate of profitability growth for the chipmaker powering the artificial intelligence boom. The stock is up 23% this year, topping the Nasdaq, but it's not keeping up with expected earnings growth.
Analysts on average expect Nvidia to hit net income of close to $385 billion in fiscal 2028, up 60% from the prior year and more than fivefold over a three-year stretch.
So on Monday, Nvidia said it's authorized an additional $150 billion to its share buyback program. That's on top of an $80 billion repurchase plan announced in May, when the company also boosted its quarterly cash dividend to 25 cents per share from 1 cent.
The latest buyback is a "clear-cut message" that management thinks its stock is undervalued, said Karan Ramchandani, managing director at Post Oak Group, in an interview.
"If you look at the P/E ratio, the earnings are scaling up faster than the share price," Ramchandani said. "It's a very healthy mark of a company looking at their own stock buybacks as the best investment they could do in the coming year."
The stock rose almost 2% on Monday, when the company also announced new software and hardware solutions to control AI agents.
'Growth value stock'
Nvidia is stepping up its capital return plans as its revenue and cash flow explode because of demand for the company's graphics processing units used to build and run AI models and services.
The company has signaled continued growth through early 2028, telling investors in August that it sees 70% sales growth in its fiscal 2028, which implied Nvidia will do hundreds of billions more in sales than Wall Street had previously forecast.
Huang told investors at a Goldman Sachs conference earlier this month that Nvidia was "misunderstood" and implied that it should be more highly valued both for its growth as well as its value measured by future earnings.
"We are the world's first and only growth value stock," Huang said. "People are trying to figure out which one we are. We are both."
Nvidia previously said it planned to return about half of its free cash flow to investors through share repurchases and buybacks. Its share count could drop by 4% if the chipmaker spends its entire current authorization.
"We're going to generate a lot of cash in the coming years," Huang said on CNBC's "Squawk Box" on Monday. "As we generate more cash, we'd like to be able to return it back to shareholders."
Gene Munster, managing partner at Deepwater Asset Management, told CNBC's "Fast Money" on Monday that investors appear worried that growth rates will slow after a monstrous few years.
"It's just really hard for investors to get comfortable that that's going to continue," Munster said. "That downward slope of growth rate, that's the reason why it trades at that compressed multiple."
Nvidia's fiscal 2028 P/E ratio puts it behind behind Apple (35.5), Alphabet (22.6), Microsoft (21.7) and Amazon (23.2) as measured for a similar period. It's also less highly valued than its primary AI data center chip rivals including Broadcom (18.2), Advanced Micro Devices (38.2) and Intel (54.7). None of Nvidia's rivals are forecasting 70% sales growth next year.
Broadcom's silicon business is built around developing custom chips with companies such as OpenAI and Google. AMD competes with Nvidia in GPUs, but with a small fraction of the market share. Intel makes central processors and has dabbled in AI chips, but doesn't have a competitive product to Nvidia's GPUs.
Ben Reitzes, an analyst at Melius Research, has a buy recommendation on the stock and said it "deserves to be higher given its growth rate."
"Buying back stock in a bigger and bigger way is going to really help it solve that problem and get a better valuation," Reitzes told CNBC's "Closing Bell" on Monday.
UBS analysts said in a note Monday that Nvidia's stepped-up stock repurchases could add 8 cents per share to the company's calendar 2027 earnings, which it estimates at $17.16.

Ukraine’s F-16s have downed over 3,150 Russian targets
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
13:08:58 UTC
22:08:58 KST

- Ukrainian F-16 pilots have shot down more than 3,150 aerial targets, including 666 cruise missiles and about 2,500 drones, Ukraine's Air Force commander said.
- Ukrainian officials and Lockheed Martin discussed a possible move to the newer F-16 Block 70/72.
Ukraine’s F-16 pilots have shot down more than 3,150 Russian aerial targets, including 666 cruise missiles and about 2,500 drones, the commander of Ukraine’s Air Force said during a meeting with Lockheed Martin.
Lt. Gen. Anatolii Kryvonozhko gave the figures when a Ukrainian Air Force delegation he led met with representatives of the U.S. company, the Air Force said. He said Ukrainian F-16s have also flown more than 650 strikes against Russian ground targets. Kryvonozhko said the pilots are getting the most out of the jets despite a limited supply of weapons, using several different types of munitions.
The Ukrainian Air Force did not say when or where the meeting took place, or over what period the kills were counted.
Conor McGuire, who leads F-16 capability development at Lockheed Martin, praised how Ukrainian pilots and ground crews have operated and fought with the jet, and said the company intends to help Ukraine improve the capabilities of the F-16s it already flies, according to the Air Force. The two sides also discussed the possibility of Ukraine moving to newer versions of the Fighting Falcon, including the F-16 Block 70/72.
The Block 70/72 is the latest production model of the F-16, built by Lockheed Martin in Greenville, South Carolina. It adds an AN/APG-83 active electronically scanned array radar, which can track more targets at longer range than older radars, along with new cockpit displays and a longer structural service life. Ukraine currently flies older F-16s donated by European countries, which were upgraded in the 2000s but were not built new for Ukraine.
The first F-16s arrived in Ukraine in the summer of 2024, supplied by the Netherlands, Denmark, Norway and Belgium. Ukraine has used them mainly to intercept the Russian cruise missiles and Shahed-type attack drones that target its cities and power grid, often firing guns and short-range missiles at drones to save more expensive weapons. Ukraine has also lost several F-16s and pilots in combat and accidents since the jets entered service.
Ukraine is also looking beyond the F-16. In October 2025, it signed a letter of intent with Sweden for up to 150 Saab Gripen E fighters, and in November 2025 it signed a similar agreement with France for up to 100 Rafales. Neither deal has produced deliveries so far.

Ms Rachel warns disabled Gaza children face 'torture' under Israeli siege
Renowned children’s entertainer Ms Rachel has called for urgent action over the plight of Palestinian children with disabilities in Gaza, warning that starvation and Israel’s restrictions on medical supplies are putting already vulnerable children at further risk as Israel’s genocidal war on the Palestinian territory approaches its third year.
In an Instagram post on Monday, the content creator and activist condemned the Israeli government for the “torturing [of] babies, toddlers, children and teens with disabilities”, as Israel’s war and siege continue to devastate Gaza’s healthcare system and restrict access to essential humanitarian and medical supplies.
“Starvation of children with preexisting medical conditions is a form of torture,” she added.
Ms Rachel, whose real name is Rachel Accurso, also highlighted information shared by Tareq Hailat, Director of Global Patient Affairs at the Palestine Children’s Relief Fund (PCRF), about children awaiting medical evacuation from Gaza.
In a separate Instagram post, she drew attention to two-year-old Hashem Abu Mustafa, a Palestinian toddler who was “starving due to medical conditions” while his family had been waiting for his evacuation from war-torn Gaza since 2024.
“Silence is not okay during a genocide,” she stressed in a video shared on social media.
Her latest intervention comes amid mounting warnings over the impact of Israel’s blockade on Palestinians with disabilities and serious medical conditions, as rights groups demand the immediate and sustained entry of humanitarian and medical supplies into the devastated enclave.
A June report by UN investigators found that Israel’s war had caused a “severe orphan crisis”, while wounded Palestinian children “face a lifetime of disability”.
The crisis extends beyond shortages of medicine and treatment. The New Arab recently revealed that more than 900 wheelchairs donated by two Australian charities for wounded and amputee children in Gaza have been blocked by Israel from entering the enclave, leaving the shipments stuck in storage in Jordan since 2025.
The restrictions have particularly serious consequences for Palestinians living with disabilities and the tens of thousands recovering from injuries sustained during the war, many of whom require mobility aids, medical equipment and continued rehabilitation.
Israeli rights group Gisha also reported earlier this year that Israel had arbitrarily classified essential items, household goods and medical supplies as “dual use” since the start of the Gaza war on 7 October 2023, restricting their entry into the territory.
The shortages come amid a much broader humanitarian crisis. Last month, UN Secretary-General spokesperson Stephane Dujarric said 94 percent of Gaza’s 2.1 million Palestinians required shelter and basic household assistance.
Citing the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA), Dujarric also highlighted continuing reports of Palestinian civilians, including children, being killed and injured by Israeli air strikes, shelling and gunfire.
“More than four out of five families face critical or catastrophic [living conditions] in their current shelters which lack fuel, energy and essential household items,” he said.
The restrictions have severely affected Palestinians’ ability to sleep, cook, bathe and store food and water, while leaving families without adequate lighting or the means to cope with extreme heat and cold, according to Dujarric.

Yemen health system near collapse, WHO warns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
13:05:31 UTC
22:05:31 KST

Yemen's latest conflict escalation is pushing its already fragile health system towards a "breaking point," with casualties and displacement rising while essential services face mounting pressure, the World Health Organization (WHO) has warned.
Annette Heinzelmann, WHO regional emergency director for the Eastern Mediterranean, told journalists in Geneva on Tuesday that 4,481 casualties, including 838 deaths, have been reported since August 6, citing data from the health ministry in Aden.
More than 180,500 people have been displaced across 10 governorates, while over 3,600 Yemenis have crossed into Djibouti since September 10, nearly half of them children. Humanitarian partners are preparing for 5,000 to 10,000 arrivals in the coming weeks.
Heinzelmann said nine health facilities or assets have been damaged, forced out of service, closed or directly attacked in Taiz, Lahj and Al-Hodeidah.
Emergency obstetric and newborn care has also been suspended at two hospitals in Marib and Ras Al-Arah as staff and capacity have been redirected to trauma care.
Even before the latest escalation, only around 60 percent of Yemen's health facilities were fully functional, she said.
Disease outbreaks are compounding the crisis, with more than 22,000 suspected measles cases and 128 deaths reported this year, alongside 7,784 suspected cholera or acute watery diarrhoea cases and 9,604 dengue cases.
WHO has secured only $2 million of the $9 million required for its response, while stocks of some lifesaving supplies, including trauma kits and essential medicines, have already run out at its Aden warehouse.

Russian Tu-95 crashes on takeoff after engine failure
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
13:01:11 UTC
22:01:11 KST

- A Russian Tu-95MS strategic bomber crashed in the Amur region on Sept. 29, killing six of seven crew members.
- The bomber went down after an engine failure on takeoff, according to Russian military sources; early reports misidentified it as a Tu-154.
A Russian Tu-95MS strategic bomber crashed in the Amur region of Russia’s Far East on Sept. 29, killing six of the seven crew members on board.
The bomber went down near the village of Krasnoyarovo after an engine failure during takeoff, according to sources in the Russian military. The sole survivor was taken to hospital. A large fire broke out at the crash site.
Initial reports in Russian media, first published by the Telegram channel Baza, identified the aircraft as a Tu-154 belonging to the Russian Defense Ministry’s Ukrainka air base, with seven people on board. Footage and photos from the crash site that appeared later show the distinctive tail fin of the Tu-95, and the engine sound heard on video matches the Tu-95’s four turboprop engines with counter-rotating propellers.
The Tu-95MS, known by NATO as the Bear-H, is a Soviet-era long-range bomber that carries cruise missiles under its wings and has been used throughout Russia’s full-scale war to launch Kh-101 missiles at Ukrainian cities. The aircraft normally flies with a crew of seven.
Ukrainka, near the Amur River, is Russia’s main base for Tu-95MS bombers in the Far East. It was one of the intended targets of Ukraine’s Operation Spiderweb in June 2025, when drones hidden in trucks struck Russian strategic bombers at several air bases. The truck carrying drones toward Ukrainka caught fire in the Amur region before reaching the base.
Engine trouble has brought down Tu-95s from Ukrainka before. In June 2015, a Tu-95MS caught fire and ran off the runway there during its takeoff run after one of its engines exploded, killing crew members and leading Russia to ground its entire Tu-95 fleet. A month later, another Tu-95MS from the base crashed in the Khabarovsk region after three of its four engines failed in flight, killing two of the seven crew.

As America shifted left under Trump, emotional hostility widened the partisan gap
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
13:00:51 UTC
22:00:51 KST

Over the course of Donald Trump’s first presidential term, American public opinion generally shifted in a more liberal direction, driven primarily by left-leaning and independent voters changing their minds on specific issues. At the same time, emotional animosity between the two major political parties intensified, a shift that appears connected to the widening gap in policy preferences. These findings were recently published in American Politics Research.
Political scientists often track changes in public opinion using a concept known as the public mood. This mood tends to operate like a thermostat. When a conservative administration is in power, the public typically reacts by moving to the left, and when a liberal administration takes over, the public usually shifts to the right.
Beneath these broad swings, there is also a phenomenon called partisan divergence. This refers to the growing gap between Democrats and Republicans on specific policy issues, such as health care, taxation, and immigration. Over the past few decades, the two parties have moved further apart on these topics.
This policy divide has been accompanied by a rise in affective partisanship, which is the emotional dislike or hostility that voters feel toward the opposing party. Theoretical models help explain how these factors interact. For instance, a 2024 study covered by PsyPost demonstrated that a stronger connection between political disagreement and personal dislike tends to drive people into two opposing ideological camps.
Understanding how public opinion shifts requires looking at individual voters. The authors of the new study note that a study covered by PsyPost in 2023 found that party identification remained remarkably stable between 2011 and 2020. This indicates that when the public mood changes, it is often because people who already identify with a party are changing their minds on issues, rather than simply switching their party allegiance.
The research was conducted by Alan Yang, a senior lecturer at the School of International and Public Affairs at Columbia University, and Robert Y. Shapiro, a professor in Columbia’s Department of Political Science and School of International and Public Affairs. “We were interested in whether the election of an ‘untraditional’ Republican president in 2016 may have upended or accelerated past patterns of opinion change, partisan divergence, and ‘affective partisanship,'” the researchers told PsyPost.
Because Donald Trump’s platform did not always align with traditional conservatism, it was an open question whether the expected liberal reaction would occur. The authors wanted to see if partisan gaps continued to widen, and whether the emotional animosity of the era played a role in how individuals changed their minds on policy issues.
To explore these questions, the researchers analyzed data from the 2016-2020 American National Election Study (ANES) and the 2016-2020 General Social Survey (GSS). Both datasets are uniquely useful because they use panel designs, meaning they surveyed the exact same individuals at multiple points in time. This setup allows researchers to track whether an individual actually changed their answer from one election year to the next.
The team examined 32 specific policy questions from the ANES and 40 questions from the GSS. These questions covered a wide range of topics, including government spending, racial equality, immigration, foreign affairs, and social issues like abortion and gay rights. The researchers tracked how responses changed between 2016 and 2020 across the entire sample and within specific political groups.
To measure affective partisanship, the surveys used a feeling thermometer scale. Respondents were asked to rate their feelings toward Democrats and Republicans on a scale from 0 to 100 degrees, with higher numbers indicating warmer, more positive feelings.
The analysis indicates a noticeable overall shift in a liberal direction between 2016 and 2020 across many policy areas. For example, support for keeping or increasing welfare spending, providing more government services, and expanding immigration levels grew substantially. “We found an (expected) liberal rebound in aggregate opinion after the election of a Republican president, which was an open question given that Donald Trump was not a mainstream conservative Republican,” the researchers noted.
However, this overall shift masked a growing divide between the political parties. The partisan divergence continued to expand, and it did so asymmetrically. The liberal shift in the broader public mood was driven almost entirely by Democrats and Independents adopting more progressive positions on issues like government spending and racial equality.
In contrast, Republican opinions generally remained stable on these issues, or moved slightly to the right on specific topics like scientific research and alternative energy. The findings are in line with research covered by PsyPost in 2026, which found that widening issue divisions were largely driven by the left shifting in a more progressive direction. It is worth noting a slight measurement difference, as the previous study clustered respondents purely by their policy beliefs, whereas the new study measured divergence between self-identified partisans.
The emotional temperature of the country also shifted notably. Overall affective partisanship increased, but the most dramatic changes occurred among Republicans. Between 2016 and 2020, Democratic panelists maintained a steady level of warmth toward their own party and cooled by roughly four degrees toward Republicans.
Republican panelists, on the other hand, grew over 10 degrees warmer toward their fellow Republicans and cooled by about eight degrees toward Democrats. The gap between how much Republicans liked their own party versus the opposing party grew by nearly 19 degrees, which was a much larger jump than the three-degree increase observed among Democrats.
When the researchers looked at individual changes, they found that these short-term increases in emotional polarization predicted changes in actual policy preferences. For both Democrats and Republicans, individuals whose partisan animosity intensified were more likely to change their minds on specific high-profile issues. At the individual level, the researchers found that an “increased affective partisanship level was associated with Republican partisans moving rightward and Democratic partisans moving leftward across a number of highly salient policy preferences during the period of the first Trump presidency.”
For example, voters who developed stronger negative feelings toward the opposing party were more likely to adopt their own party’s typical stance on issues like immigration, the environment, and racial justice.
As with all research, there are a few things to keep in mind. The study looks at a relatively short four-year window that was dominated by a highly unusual political environment and the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic. It is hard to know whether the specific dynamics of the Trump presidency will continue into future election cycles.
The relationship between emotional animosity and policy opinions is also highly complex. The data shows an association between the two, but untangling which one causes the other is a challenge. People might develop stronger negative feelings toward the opposing party because they disagree on policy, or they might change their policy views because they want to distance themselves from a party they dislike. Both processes likely happen at the same time.
To see if these dynamics persisted after Trump left office, the authors plan to expand their timeline. “We see as a next step for us and others to extend this analysis to 2020 to 2024 using the available panel data for this period,” Yang and Shapiro said.
The study, “Individuals and Public Opinion Change: The Liberal Rebound, Continued Partisan Divergence and Affective Partisanship 2016–2020,” was authored by Alan Yang and Robert Y. Shapiro.

In the wake of the flood, could Nepal avert the next disaster?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
13:00:00 UTC
22:00:00 KST

Wednesday, August 26 began as a regular day for Prakash Pyakurel, a 43-year-old shopkeeper in the bustling town of Dhunge Bazaar in the northern belt of Central Nepal. Then sometime around 9:10 a.m. came the muffled crackle of a police loudspeaker. The words were “impossible to hear” over the noise of the town, he says.
Pyakurel took a couple of minutes to piece together that the announcement was calling for evacuation. He lost time closing the shop before sprinting home to alert his parents and daughter. In their living room, just a few hundred meters from the Trishuli River, they spent more vital minutes arguing over whether to head for higher ground.
It was too late. At 9:15 a.m., a towering wall of water and debris surged in, forcing the family to the second floor. Then the third, and finally the fourth. Trapped at the top of their home, they could only pray as the flood obliterated the town around them. “We had lost all hope,” Pyakurel says.
After more than an hour of terror, the Pyakurels narrowly survived. Their “miracle green house,” as it came to be called in videos that went viral on social media, somehow remained standing. Thousands of others in towns along an almost 100-kilometer-stretch of the river weren’t as lucky.
Though the rock-ice avalanche that caused the Himalaya flash flood in late August occurred at 8:37 a.m. local time, many people downriver had only a few minutes of warning or less before the debris flow arrived. The flow destroyed four river gauge sensors before they could signal an alarm. Local authorities who learned of the flow by word of mouth scrambled to send SMS alerts and to reach riverbank towns with handheld megaphones. “The police officer [who made the announcement] was swept away by the floodwaters himself,” Pyakurel says.
The initial avalanche released an energy that equaled an atomic blast, and the resulting debris flow killed at least 1,400 people with more than 5,000 still missing as of September 24. Scientists are calling it one of the most catastrophic geohazards in recorded history.
But despite the magnitude of the event, it didn’t have to be so deadly.
Survivors and scientists say that the fragility of Nepal’s early warning systems and the lack of coordinated community responses probably upped the number of lives lost. The disaster is spurring conversations about how Nepal should prepare for future glacier-related failures. Such events are becoming increasingly common across high mountain regions including the European Alps, Andes, Karakoram and the Himalaya. But because of its high slopes and steep valleys, says Christian Huggel, a geographer at the University of Zürich, “everything is much bigger in the Himalaya.”
The challenges of prediction
Predicting an event like Nepal’s rock-ice avalanche in advance is “likely impossible,” says Ashim Sattar, a cryosphere scientist at the Indian Institute of Technology in Bhubaneswar. Because events of such magnitude are rare, there isn’t a lot of existing data to go on.
Satellite images taken weeks before the avalanche show signs of cracks opening up, but those cracks are nothing special. “There are probably hundreds of cracks opening in the Himalaya,” Huggel says. It’s not clear which cracks pose a serious risk.
Most current glacier monitoring in the Himalaya focuses on the threat of a glacial lake outburst flood, or GLOF. An influx of meltwater is increasing the size of highland lakes, which can suddenly burst and flood downstream villages. A mix of satellite monitoring, which can track the size of lakes, and on-the-ground field stations can warn of such hazards in advance. “If glacial lakes are forming rapidly, scientists can detect that a few weeks before possible outburst,” Huggel says. Even here, though, only 21 of some 40,000 glacial lakes across the Himalaya are actively monitored via on-the-ground stations.
Rock-ice avalanches are harder to predict, largely because it is difficult to study the fracture zone hidden beneath the surface and thus to know what volume of material will break off.
Despite these challenges, scientists have managed some similar avalanche predictions. In May 2025, a massive glacier collapsed in southwestern Switzerland, triggering an ice and rock avalanche that destroyed the village of Blatten. The possibility of the avalanche, which ended up being a tenth the size or smaller of the Nepal avalanche, was recognized by a local hazard observer who was assigned to monitor the mountains and knew them well.
“He observed something strange as the mountain seemed to move and alerted the local and district authorities,” Huggel says. They brought in various sensors and monitoring systems to measure the movement of the slope and executed a quick evacuation around a week in advance of the failure, saving hundreds of lives.
Whether similar local hazard observers could have spotted a potential disaster in Nepal and called on the necessary resources for early evaluation is far from clear. The terrain is difficult to access, and its location near the border between Nepal and China adds a layer of political complexity. “Monitoring these slopes is nobody’s job,” says Kshitij Dahal, a hydrologist at the University of Kansas in Lawrence who is originally from Nepal. Most of the monitoring in Nepal is reactive rather than anticipatory, he adds.
Are early warnings possible?
Without the ability to predict such catastrophes, early warning systems are the primary line of defense. In the Himalaya, river gauge sensors are commonly deployed to warn of coming floods. These sensors monitor the water level in the river and send out an alarm if there is a substantial rise.
But these sensors, including the ones installed in Trishuli River, are primarily used for monsoon season flooding, when the water level tends to increase gradually. They transmit flood data every 10 minutes. Nepal’s flood hit with such sudden intensity that sensors located between nine and 100 kilometers from the avalanche site were wiped out before they could report high water.
Other technologies are available or in development. Early warning systems that rely on seismometers might offer a workable solution. After Nepal’s massive earthquake in 2015, Basanta Raj Adhikari, an engineering geologist at the Tribhuvan University in Kathmandu, Nepal, and his team installed six seismometers along Bhotekoshi River in a nearby valley of Central Nepal.
Placed a couple of kilometers above the riverbank, the sensors were intended to assess how long it took for the landscape to become stable again after such a major geological event. In July 2016, when a glacial lake in Tibet burst open, the resulting flood destroyed hydropower stations, highways and buildings — and produced distinct seismic signals picked up by those Bhotekoshi River sensors. Adhikari thinks that if such systems are set up to operate in real-time, they could detect and warn of floods in advance.
Researchers studying seismic signals after historic and deadly flooding in western Germany’s Ahr Valley in 2021 also determined that seismic monitoring could have provided an early warning. The signals revealed details about the likely height of the water, the velocity of the sediment, the spread of the flood and the types of debris. Inexpensive seismic stations can cost somewhere around a couple thousand dollars, the researchers say, with some citizen-science seismographs available for costs below $500.
Putting eyes on the landscape is another approach. Ólafur Stitelmann, a geomonitoring expert at the Zürich-based company Geoprevent, deploys tools that can scan and monitor glaciers for deformations of millimeters per day or per hour. Some of these tools, including interferometric radars, camera systems and satellite-based navigation sensors, were used to assess the ice before the Blatten collapse, and they could form the basis of early warning systems.
Stitelmann’s team is now working to deploy high-resolution cameras, weather stations, lake level sensors and water temperature sensors at two sites at risk from GLOFs in the state of Sikkim, India. Once a day, the data is sent via satellite to local authorities who can analyze conditions and take timely action if needed.
Yet early warning systems are far from plug-and-play solutions, and they are too costly to deploy en masse. What works in the Alps may not automatically work in the Himalaya, in part because these systems need to be integrated into the local infrastructure. “If you have very good sensors but suddenly don’t have power to turn it on, then it’s worthless,” Stitelmann says. Similarly, there needs to be a network available to transmit the data that can trigger the warning. And every step needs to have backups, he adds.
It is important to have more than one sensor, says Huggel, who would complement any seismic stations with wire-based sensors stretching across the river. Installing backup sensors at different elevations could also buy crucial time if primary riverbank stations are wiped out.
Such dream systems are expensive, ranging from tens of thousands of dollars to costs in the millions for a multi-sensor set of stations when the necessary infrastructure and backups are included, Stitelmann says. When the World Bank financed the setup of an early warning system downstream of a glacier lake, Tsho Rolpa in Nepal, in 1998, the cost was over a million dollars.
In the case of Nepal, officials are discussing some relatively simple steps. One is putting backup sensors on the cliffs, since systems on bridges were quickly wiped out. Another is changing the design of river gauges so they transmit data once the water reaches a threshold level, rather than after a 10-minute interval.
Community awareness
Even if the technology works perfectly, there are social aspects to consider, including who decides when an alarm is issued, what message is delivered and how, and who coordinates evacuation. False warnings are also a problem, because people who have received them before may not trust that the next warning is genuine. “Technologies alone are no magical solutions,” Stitelmann says.
After GLOF events in the village of Lunana in Bhutan in 2019 and 2023, Sattar and his team interviewed residents about the community response. Although an automated siren had been installed in the region, it wasn’t triggered in either case. Locals instead relied on environmental cues including the sound of the river, ground vibrations and phone calls from friends and family to evacuate.
Locals also reported being aware of the potential danger because of past flooding and ongoing government outreach. Sattar’s team also learned that disaster response could have been improved if the community had regular mock drills and if families prepacked evacuation bags with medicines, food, lights and warm clothes in case of an emergency.
In Nepal, many people probably lost their lives because of confusion and lack of awareness, says Pyakurel, the Dhunge Bazaar shopkeeper. For most, it was the biggest flood that they would have encountered in their lifetime. In July 2025, a glacial lake in Tibet burst open, leaving nine dead and 20 missing in Nepal, but it didn’t affect this area as dramatically. “Last year’s flood barely touched the bridge, so [we] assumed this flood wouldn’t reach high ground,” he adds.
The disaster highlights the need for better education about the potential dangers and preparation so people can act quickly, says Sattar.
Stories of survival also offer insights into what matters most in an emergency. On the morning of August 26, Rajendra Dawadi, a principal at the Tribhuvan Trishuli Secondary School, received a verbal warning from another school staffer about rising waters upstream. Even without official confirmation, he acted instantly. He asked to ring the school bell, instructed teachers to evacuate classrooms, and called drivers carrying buses with students to head to higher ground — saving more than 900 students.
It wasn’t a sophisticated system that made the difference in this case, but a quick decision to evacuate. “I thought that even if the warning turned out to be wrong, the worst it would cost us was one day of study,” Dawadi told the New York Times. “But taking it lightly could mean the loss of hundreds of lives.”

Settlers set Palestinian homes and cars on fire in West Bank rampage
Dozens of Israeli settlers rampaged through villages in the occupied West Bank overnight into Tuesday, attacking Palestinians and setting fire to homes and cars.
Around 100 settlers raided Jalud, south of Nablus, shortly after midnight on Monday, targeting the homes of the Toubasi family, Middle East Eye reported.
The family had been forced out of their home in July following repeated settler attacks aimed at taking over the property.
They returned to the house hours before Tuesday’s attack after an Israeli court ordered the army to secure their return.
Settlers then arrived in large numbers and set fire to two homes belonging to the Toubasi family, forcing them to flee again.
Mahmoud Toubasi, the owner of one of the houses, said the family was shocked by the extent of the destruction and vandalism when they returned.
The fire destroyed the house, damaged its contents and left it uninhabitable, he said.
Local media reported that Israeli forces eventually arrived but did not intervene to stop the attack. Instead, they provided protection to the settlers, according to the reports.
The Toubasi family was forced to evacuate the house again at gunpoint, the reports added.
The army also clashed with some settlers as it sought to disperse the large crowd.
Army officials said “rioters” had blocked roads, set tyres on fire and thrown stones at troops, injuring three officers.
Israeli President Isaac Herzog condemned the clashes between settlers and the army as a “moral stain and an attack on the rule of law and our most basic values as a nation”.
He did not mention the attacks on Palestinians.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said the “small number of rioters does not represent the law-abiding settler community”, while also not referring to the violence against Palestinians.
Elsewhere in the occupied West Bank, settlers set fire to a house and several vehicles during an attack on the village of al-Mughayyir, northeast of Ramallah, overnight.
Large numbers of settlers also entered Beitunia and the Jaryout Road west of Ramallah under the protection of Israeli forces.
According to local sources, settlers attacked passing vehicles and pelted some with stones, creating an atmosphere of fear among residents.
In occupied East al-Quds (Jerusalem), dozens of settlers attacked two Palestinian men at Damascus Gate late on Monday, with footage of the assault later posted online.
The footage showed Israeli youths pushing the two men to the ground and kicking them.
Occupied East al-Quds has been crowded with Israelis marking the Jewish holiday of Sukkot in and around the Muslim Quarter of the Old City, including areas surrounding Al-Aqsa Mosque.
Dozens of Palestinian shops have been ordered to close by Israeli forces to allow Jewish rituals to take place in the Old City’s alleyways, while Palestinian residents have been forced to remain indoors.
Violence by Israeli settlers against Palestinians has long been a feature of life in the occupied West Bank and East Jerusalem, but it has intensified sharply since the start of Israel's genocide in Gaza in October 2023.
Settlers carry out near-daily attacks on Palestinian towns and villages, including arson, vandalism, physical assaults and forced displacement, often under the protection of Israeli forces. More than 1300 Palestinians have been killed in the occupied West Bank since 2023.
Earlier this year, the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory described the escalation in settler violence against Palestinians as unprecedented and sustained.
The commission said the Israeli government supports the attacks through financial backing, logistical assistance and military protection.
“Violence by settlers is the direct outcome of Israeli policies that support, enable and protect their actions,” said Srinivasan Muralidhar, chair of the commission.
According to the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA), more than 1,600 settler attacks resulting in Palestinian casualties, property damage or both were recorded between the beginning of January and September 14.
That amounts to an average of 6.7 attacks a day, compared with five per day in 2025, when 1,836 attacks were recorded. Around 1,500 attacks were recorded in 2024, compared with 1,291 in 2023 and 853 in 2022.

Georgia's historic wooden mosques face neglect and disappearance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
12:57:00 UTC
21:57:00 KST

Breadcrumb
'I'm afraid they will be forgotten': The fight to save Georgia's disappearing wooden mosques
Bats dart overhead, rotting floorboards groan underfoot, a solitary string of prayer beads dangles by a boarded window. Yet amid the decay, the expert craftsmanship that went into Gulebi mosque is still evident in the faded reds and blues of its ornate interior and the intricate patterns carved into its minbar.
"It breaks my heart that even in my lifetime I might experience the vanishing of this mosque," says Lia Dekanadze, a young activist from Adjara, an autonomous republic in south-west Georgia, bordering Turkey.
She first came here five years ago, and even in that short time, she has noticed a distinct deterioration: the once-vibrant turquoise door dulled by the elements.
Gulebi is one of more than 50 historic wooden mosques dotting the hillsides of Upper Adjara.
Built between 1817 and 1926, some remain well-maintained and active places of worship to this day. But many others are in urgent need of repair or have been left abandoned, and activists say their neglect reflects a wider failure to value the culture and history of Muslims in Georgia.
In a predominantly Orthodox Christian country, Adjara is something of an outlier.
The Caucasus nation is the world’s second-oldest Christian state, after its neighbour Armenia.
The Orthodox Church has become a cornerstone of national identity, particularly in the decades since the collapse of the Soviet Union.
Today, some 82% of Georgians practise the faith.
However, in Adjara, Islam arrived four centuries ago with the Ottoman Empire, and to this day, around a third of the population is Muslim.
Over a cup of tea in his office in Khulo, a small town in mountainous Upper Adjara, local mufti Aslan Abashidze guides The New Arab through the contours of the region’s history.
"Although there was Ottoman influence at the time, people lived as families, and these places of worship, the mosques, were built with the resources of the local population," he says.
Crafted from timber plentiful in the forested highlands, they mirror the forms of the region’s traditional wooden houses, giving them a character uniquely rooted in Adjara.
Mosque construction stopped in the early Soviet period, and in the 1930s, religious sites closed as the state intensified its campaign against religion.
The minarets were even severed from many mosques.
"They repurposed them as shops or warehouses," Abashidze explains. "While the interior design might have been partially ruined, the physical structures themselves were preserved because of their utility."
A heritage under threat
When the Soviet era ended, life returned to some of the mosques.
Ghorjomi Mosque, for example, is the heart of the community in one of Khulo’s largest villages, its well-kept interior a kaleidoscope of colour.
But for many others, after surviving the purges of the Soviet era, neglect and a lack of resources are the modern threats.
"These mosques are literally disappearing very rapidly," says Giorgi Rizhvadze, a researcher from Khulo.
As wooden structures, the mosques are particularly vulnerable to the elements, and Adjara’s snowy winters and humid summers can take a heavy toll.
Many of the mosques also have ageing electrical systems, adding another risk.
Last year alone, two were destroyed by fire. The exact cause remains unclear, but electrical faults are suspected in at least one.
Renovations are expensive, often beyond the means of rural communities.
Villages also increasingly suffer from depopulation, with landslides and limited economic prospects forcing many to leave for Batumi, the regional capital.
As communities shrink, so too do local resources.
Authorities have pledged to rebuild Satiskhuri, one of the mosques that burnt down last year and renovations were recently finished on two others.
But Rizhvadze and Dekanadze have long been frustrated by what they see as the slow pace of progress.
During the pandemic, they created an NGO with a group of friends from the region to tackle issues facing rural communities.
Solidarity Community, as it was known, drew up maps of Islamic heritage sites, conducted a survey to assess their condition, and put pressure on the local government to implement necessary interventions.
"Before our campaign, there was not a lot written about it," says Rizhvadze, explaining that in the capital, Tbilisi, people often had little to no knowledge about the region’s unique architectural heritage.
The group also had a broader ambition: to change the way history is told in Georgia and whose narratives are included in its national story.
"Islam is portrayed as something very foreign," Dekanadze says, explaining that people often associate Islam with communities that came to Georgia from Azerbaijan or Chechnya, while Georgian Muslims in Adjara are frequently overlooked.
Even more harmfully, a small but vocal ultranationalist fringe promotes exclusionary narratives that question or outright deny the possibility of being both Muslim and Georgian.
And at a state level, although governments may acknowledge the religious pluralism guaranteed by Georgia’s constitution, their engagement with it remains shallow, according to Rizhvadze.
"I think in the end, it's a big issue of government policy towards minorities, especially Georgian Muslims, because they don't do anything in particular to promote the culture, to promote what Georgian Muslims did for Georgian history."
Muslims on the margins
Without positive, inclusive narratives, Muslims and the issues facing them in modern Georgia are often sidelined.
For everyone The New Arab spoke to, one example stood out. In Batumi, the regional capital of Adjara and Georgia’s second city, worshippers are often forced to pray in the street.
The city has just one mosque, and its capacity is insufficient for the city’s size, especially as it's a travel destination for travellers from Turkey and the Middle East.
Permission has been granted to build a new one, but bureaucracy has long stalled the start of construction.
Last year, Solidarity Community’s work championing religious pluralism was brought to an abrupt end. As Georgia sank into political chaos, they stopped operations.
Daily protests have been ongoing in Georgia for almost two years, ignited by the government’s announcement that it would pause EU integration talks.
The decision was a catalyst that mobilised hundreds of thousands, but dissent had already been brewing over the Foreign Agent law, which sought to restrict organisations receiving donations from abroad.
These laws, which the government claims are aimed at ensuring national sovereignty, but Amnesty International calls a "crackdown on civil society", have been tightened again and again, forcing many civil society groups out of action.
Unable to access foreign funding and unwilling to register as "foreign agents" and face the stigma and restrictions that come with it, Solidarity Community had to suspend its activities.
It was the only NGO dedicated to tackling the issues facing the highlands’ rural communities.
"When we advocated for them, the mosques entered into the public discourse, but now due to the ongoing very difficult social and political situation in the country, they’re not even a topic of debate," Dekanadze says as she walks down the long winding path leading from Gulebi Mosque.
"I’m really afraid that with time they’ll be forgotten."
Gulebi Mosque has long since fallen out of use, and nowadays, the village is predominantly Christian.
But Dekanadze insists that, regardless of modern use, these buildings should be treasured as an important part of the community's and the country's history.
"They fascinate me because I see this collective labour, and I also know these mosques were not only a place of worship, but also somewhere that the community would gather and make important decisions," Dekanadze says.
"It’s the indifference to these communal traditions that really breaks my heart and disappoints me, not as a Muslim, but as a human being who cares about cultural preservation."
The region may no longer suffer the active repression it once experienced, but neglect is also corrosive.
And now, against the backdrop of the current political turmoil, there are fewer resources and avenues for advocacy for both the practical preservation of these sites and the promotion of inclusive narratives that celebrate Muslim heritage and living culture in Georgia.
Poppy Askham is a freelance journalist based in Tbilisi, regularly filming features for the Associated Press (AP). Her text and photo reporting has been published by outlets including New World Magazine, Index on Censorship and The Kyiv Independent

How Greece and Greek-administered Southern Cyprus risk their sovereignty by aligning with Israel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
12:48:39 UTC
21:48:39 KST

Türkiye, Greece and Greek-administered Southern Cyprus are neighbours in the Eastern Mediterranean, and their relations have long been marked by tensions over a range of unresolved issues.
With little progress towards resolving these disputes, friction is likely to persist. Greece and the Greek Cypriot administration have succeeded in internationalising some disputes with Türkiye, making a lasting settlement harder, while their growing military alignment with Israel risks further complicating relations.
The Türkiye-Greece relationship is burdened with several chronic disputes that must be settled before normalisation is possible.
Both countries currently hold six nautical miles of territorial waters in the Aegean. Greece wants to extend them to twelve, citing the law of the sea, while Ankara regards such a step as a casus belli because it would cut Türkiye off from waters it now uses.
Closely linked to this is the dispute over the continental shelf and exclusive economic zones (EEZs). The two sides have never agreed on how to delimit their maritime boundaries.
Ankara rejects Greece's position that islands close to the Turkish coast should generate maritime zones in the same manner as the mainland, arguing that this would disproportionately restrict Türkiye's continental shelf.
They also disagree over sovereignty over small Aegean islands and islets, which both claim. Greece further asserts a national airspace (FIR) of ten nautical miles even though its territorial waters extend only six, an evident inconsistency.
In addition, the Lausanne (1923) and Paris (1947) treaties provide for the demilitarisation of several Eastern Aegean islands and the Dodecanese, yet Greece has stationed troops and weapons on them.
The Cyprus question
Türkiye does not recognise the Greek-administered Southern Cyprus as representing the entire island because of the unresolved Cyprus conflict. When the Republic of Cyprus became independent in 1960, the Greek majority (80%) and the Turkish minority (20%) shared power, generally at a 70/30 ratio.
The Greek side considered this arrangement unfair and tried to forcibly reduce the Turks to minority status.
The dispute escalated into violence, and a coup backed by the Greek military junta ousted Makarios and declared the island united with Greece. Turkish forces intervened and divided the island, with the north becoming a home for Turkish Cypriots. The Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus (TRNC) was proclaimed in 1983.
International efforts to resolve the Cyprus problem followed. The 2004 Annan Plan, which envisaged two federal states under a single sovereign Cyprus, might have solved it, but the Greek side rejected it.
Although the EU said it would not admit the Greek-administered Cyprus until the issue was settled, the country became a member just a week after the rejection.
One last dispute worth noting concerns Cyprus's offshore gas and maritime zones. The Greek-administered Southern Cyprus claims exclusive ownership of any oil and gas found in the island's waters, whereas Türkiye insists that Turkish Cypriots have equal rights to these resources.
At present, none of the major or minor problems between Türkiye, Greece and the Greek-administered Cyprus has been resolved.
The two Greek states have exploited their EU membership to have the Union adopt their disputes with Türkiye as its own, so maritime zones, the continental shelf and Cyprus's unity now involve Brussels as well. Greek veto power and pressure within the EU are clearly one reason Türkiye's accession process has slowed.
Yet no step against Türkiye is as dangerous as a military alliance with Israel. Israeli officials have called Türkiye an enemy since the fall of the Assad regime and have openly threatened to attack it.
As part of an effort to contain Türkiye, Israel, the Greek-administered Southern Cyprus and Greece agreed at their tenth trilateral summit in December 2025 to strengthen security, defence and military cooperation, including maritime security and the protection of critical infrastructure, with US backing.
They have also built trilateral defence cooperation covering joint training, military intelligence sharing, naval and cyber security, and interoperability of their armed forces. Israel and Greece signed a €750 million PULS rocket artillery deal in April 2026 and a €3 billion "Achilles Shield" agreement in August 2026. On the Greek Cypriot territory, Israeli defence systems and intelligence facilities are already in place.
Türkiye says this alliance is meant to contain it, and Israeli PM Benjamin Netanyahu has hinted at the same. Athens and Nicosia have not named Türkiye directly, but their remarks make the intention plain.
Both Greece and the Greek-administered Southern Cyprus carry a historical fear of Türkiye.
Having lived for centuries under Ottoman rule, Greek states and society have developed a lasting suspicion of Turks.
Security or dependency?
The 1974 military intervention in Cyprus, Ankara's casus belli response to Greece's plan for twelve-mile waters, and Türkiye's expanding domestic weapons production seem to have alarmed them further.
Besides spending tens of billions of dollars on arms, the Greek side has found a partner in Israel to counterbalance Türkiye.
However reassuring the arms buildup and the new alliance may appear, they are hardly a way to settle disputes with Türkiye, and they put the two states' sovereignty at risk by tying them to Tel Aviv.
First, Greece and the Greek-administered Southern Cyprus have purchased sophisticated Israeli systems, including Barak MX air defence, PULS rocket artillery and anti-tank missiles. Such heavy dependence gives Israel leverage over how and when these weapons can be used, not to mention the possibility of arms and component embargoes.
Second, the alliance risks dragging them into Israel's wars. In 2024, Hezbollah threatened the Greek-administered Southern Cyprus over Israel's use of its territory.
If Israel uses Greek and Greek Cypriot soil to gather intelligence or strike Turkish targets, both states would become potential targets in wars that are not theirs.
Third, military and energy partnerships with Israel may weaken the Greek Cypriot side's incentive to compromise on a settlement, thereby entrenching the island's division.
Israel would also probably hold the upper hand in cooperation with them on oil and gas exploration and on undersea cable and pipeline networks.
Fourth, with Israel isolated by most of the world, closer ties with Tel Aviv are unpopular among the Greek public, according to media reports. The governments' alignment therefore opens a gap between them and their voters.
Fifth, Israeli analysts openly, and the Israeli government implicitly, portray Greece and the Greek-administered Southern Cyprus as a counterweight to Türkiye. In effect, Israel is saying it uses them as tools against Türkiye.
Ankara is aware of this, and if a confrontation breaks out, the two states would hardly be able to stay out of it.
There also seems to be an Israeli campaign to provoke Greeks and Greek Cypriots against Türkiye: in recent months Israeli media have carried analysts urging Greeks to defend their Aegean claims and to expel Turks from the island.
Such writing plainly aims to stir the Greek public into action. Israel would seem to want a Greek-Turkish war or, failing that, access to Greek and Greek Cypriot airspace and bases against Türkiye, since its other approaches are largely shielded.
Finally, about 25,000 Israelis are reported to live in the Greek-administered Southern Cyprus already, and thousands more live on Greek islands, reportedly in private communities separate from the local population.
If such enclaves grow, questions of parallel security arrangements and legal jurisdiction could eventually arise, amounting to a state within a state and diluting sovereign authority.
While Greece and the Greek Cypriot administration have longstanding disputes with Türkiye, aligning with Israel instead of pursuing direct negotiations is neither plausible nor wise, as it risks heightening tensions with Ankara and facilitating a greater Israeli presence in the region.
Greece and the Greek Cypriots urgently need to reconsider, since the price of their latest choice, allying with Israel against Türkiye, could be higher than ever.

Why Has the Maldives Inserted Itself Into the Chagos Sovereignty Dispute?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
12:46:00 UTC
21:46:00 KST

It is official government policy under President Mohamed Muizzu that the Maldives has the strongest claim to the Chagos Islands. His is the first Maldivian administration to assert sovereignty over the archipelago, located in the central Indian Ocean and home to the joint U.K.-U.S. military base on Diego Garcia.
In doing so, Muizzu has inserted the Maldives into the long-running dispute between the United Kingdom and Mauritius over sovereignty over Chagos.
Chagos was administered as a dependency of British Mauritius from 1814 until 1965. That year, three years before Mauritius gained independence, Britain separated the archipelago from Mauritius to create the British Indian Ocean Territory (BIOT) and establish the military base on Diego Garcia. The Chagossian population was then brutally expelled to make way for the base.
The separation ran counter to decolonization principles barring the dismemberment of colonial territories before independence.
Mauritius has objected ever since and, in recent years, has seen international law and global public opinion turn in its favor. In 2019, the International Court of Justice concluded that Mauritius’ decolonization had not been lawfully completed and that Britain should end its administration “as rapidly as possible.” That same year, the United Nations General Assembly overwhelmingly endorsed that position by 116 votes to six.
Mounting pressure eventually led Britain to negotiate with Mauritius, culminating in a 2025 treaty that recognized Mauritian sovereignty while retaining Diego Garcia under a 99-year lease arrangement. Yet the deal remains stalled amid British political opposition and U.S. concerns over the base’s security and continued operation.
Amid these negotiations, the Muizzu administration has asserted that neither the U.K. nor Mauritius has the strongest claim to Chagos, the Maldives does. It therefore opposes any transfer of sovereignty to Mauritius while its own claim remains unresolved.
Muizzu raised this objection in letters to the U.K. government in November 2024 and January 2026, with then Deputy Prime Minister David Lammy in December 2025, and again in a September 2026 letter to Prime Minister Andy Burnham seeking talks.
The government’s case is nebulous. It rests principally on a 16th-century document in which the exiled Sultan Hassan IX claimed title to the “seven islands of Pullobay,” identified in the Maldives with Foalhavahi, or Chagos. The government also cites Maldivian folklore, alleged centuries-old gravestones bearing Dhivehi script, and the islands’ proximity to the Maldives.
The claim also has no precedent in Maldivian diplomacy. In more than 60 years since independence, no previous administration has claimed sovereignty over Chagos.
Previously, Maldivian concerns centered on maritime boundaries, as the Maldives’ EEZ overlapped with waters claimed on the basis of Chagos. Malé kept its position on Chagos sovereignty ambiguous, dealing with either the U.K. or Mauritius depending on which better served its interests. It entered delimitation talks with the U.K. in 1992 and joined Mauritius in a 2011 communiqué opposing the U.K.’s marine protected area around Chagos, which restricted fishing.
The claim of sovereignty over Chagos itself has its origins in the politics surrounding the 2023 presidential election. Opponents of then President Ibrahim Mohamed Solih began conflating the Maldives’ EEZ dispute with Mauritius with the separate issue of sovereignty over Chagos.
The controversy began after it emerged that Solih had written to Mauritian Prime Minister Pravind Jugnauth in August 2022, recognizing Mauritius’ sovereignty over Chagos. This reversed the Maldives’ earlier position as one of only six countries to oppose the 2019 United Nations General Assembly resolution endorsing the ICJ opinion in favor of Mauritius’ claim to Chagos.
Solih’s shift appears to have reflected the growing international legal recognition of Mauritius’ claim. During maritime delimitation proceedings initiated by Mauritius before the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea (ITLOS), the Maldives argued that the case could not proceed while sovereignty over Chagos remained disputed between Mauritius and the U.K.
ITLOS dismissed that objection, treating sovereignty over Chagos as settled in favor of Mauritius.
Once Solih’s letter became public, however, the dispute turned sharply political.
His opponents argued that recognizing Mauritius’ claim weakened the Maldives’ case before ITLOS. Although the tribunal’s final ruling in April 2023 awarded the Maldives slightly more of the disputed maritime area than Mauritius, the opposition portrayed the outcome as a loss of Maldivian territory.
The rhetoric escalated when the EEZ dispute became entangled with a new sovereignty claim. Former President Mohamed Nasheed, then locked in an internal struggle with President Solih within the ruling MDP, argued that the Maldives itself had a claim to Chagos and that Solih had betrayed Maldivian interests by recognizing Mauritius’ claim. Former President Abdulla Yameen and the opposition Progressive Party of Maldives (PPM) soon adopted the same position. Neither, however, had advanced such a claim while in office.
It was in this political context that Muizzu inherited the issue and turned it into government policy. After Yameen was barred from contesting the 2023 election, Muizzu led the PPM-People’s National Congress (PNC) coalition to victory on a nationalist platform built around defending Maldivian sovereignty.
Alongside the “India Out” campaign, he pledged to recover the Maldives’ “lost” maritime territory. In office, that rhetoric hardened into policy. Muizzu rejected the final ITLOS judgment on the maritime boundary and became the first incumbent Maldivian administration to assert sovereignty over Chagos itself.
Muizzu has formally withdrawn Solih’s 2022 letter supporting Mauritius’ claim and promised to submit evidence supporting the Maldives’ claim to Chagos to relevant international bodies. He has also created a new government office to oversee territorial boundaries and related disputes.
Perhaps most dramatically, in February the government deployed Coast Guard vessels and drones across the full 200-nautical-mile zone it claims, including waters awarded to Mauritius by ITLOS, and intercepted Sri Lankan fishing vessels there. Despite the theatrics, the ITLOS judgment on the maritime boundary is final and not subject to ordinary appeal. Repeating such deployments in waters assigned to Mauritius would therefore risk turning a settled legal dispute into an international incident.
Nor do these actions advance the Maldives’ separate sovereignty claim over Chagos, which has so far gained no international traction. The U.K. has shown little inclination to entertain it, reiterating that Chagos sovereignty remains a bilateral matter between the U.K. and Mauritius and does not concern the Maldives.
Mauritius, meanwhile, suspended diplomatic relations with the Maldives in February 2026.
For now, then, the claim’s clearest impact is domestic rather than international. It allows Muizzu to place Chagos within a broader political narrative about defending Maldivian sovereignty and recovering territory supposedly lost by previous governments. Internationally, however, the claim has yet to alter either the legal or diplomatic landscape surrounding Chagos.

Activist Sarah Cotte vows to support Palestinian resistance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
12:43:15 UTC
21:43:15 KST

Breadcrumb
Activist Sarah Cotte: I will not back down from supporting Palestinian resistance
Sarah Cotte has defied all attempts to deter her from supporting the Palestinian people's right to armed resistance, despite facing nearly three years of legal proceedings that ended with two trials over the same charge: expressing support for Hamas.
Friday, 18 September, marked the end of an ordeal experienced by the young activist, who supports the Palestinian people and opposes Israel and the Zionist movement.
The ordeal began with a campaign led by UK Lawyers for Israel, prompting British police and prosecutors to refer Cotte to the Central Criminal Court, which hears only major criminal cases.
After two trials, jurors acquitted Sarah Cotte , 22, of a charge that could have resulted in a 14-year prison sentence had she been convicted.
In an interview with The New Arab following her acquittal, Cotte said she did not feel a moment of regret despite the suffering she endured.
"I think it was absolutely worth the suffering that I experienced in the context of this case," she said.
She attributed this to being able to "affirm the political point, which is the right to armed resistance and armed struggle".
Despite attempts to portray Palestinian armed resistance negatively throughout the two trials, Cotte insisted that this was "a purely legal issue that should be supported, because oppressed peoples have this right".
A message to Zionists
Cotte criticised what she described as "the self-censorship that we impose on ourselves", as liberals do, in her view, when they "tend to impose censorship on others who express support for armed struggle, and on oppressed peoples so that they are not just victims but freedom fighters".
In this context, the young activist said the prosecution wanted to contribute to a campaign to criminalise those who support fighting for freedom.
She argued it was therefore extremely determined to secure a conviction and to show the rest of the British state, as well as Zionists and others, that it was dealing with pro-Palestine protesters with extreme strictness and severity.
Despite her position in the British state, Cotte praised the judiciary because it still relies on juries in criminal cases, and they had acquitted her twice.
The key point, for her, is that "the jury system works in a way that means a group of your peers, people like you, judge you".
"Most people in this country are horrified by what is happening in Palestine at the hands of the Israeli state, and they feel ashamed of the fact that Britain is complicit in it," she added.
However, she did not rely on this alone during her two trials.
Based on her experience, what also makes a real impression on the public and jurors is "being able to explain your political positions clearly using your own terms and your own language".
One of the lessons Cotte learned from her prosecution was that "regardless of how difficult what the state is trying to do is, when we fight, when we struggle, when we do everything we can, and use politics and our tactics as activists, we can win, and we are winning, and this is not limited to my case alone".
The enemy can be defeated
Another lesson is that, in cases such as defending the right to struggle for freedom, she believes there are no big or small victories.
She said her victory "seems like a small victory", but pointed out that she is one activist among similar people in Britain who are being criminalised.
She considered these victories "very important for giving the movement new energy and raising morale, and showing that the enemy is not too powerful to be defeated and that the enemy cannot crush us and silence us, but that we are capable of responding and confronting it".
Therefore, she explained that "the way I dealt with my case was not centred on me personally so that I could survive but was about being able to share my context, in which I carry out my political activism, and use this case as a platform to speak to people about what I believe in".
Cotte, who is of Ethiopian origin, arrived from France, where she holds citizenship, to Britain to study political economy and philosophy several years ago.
She became political and student activist at the School of Oriental and African Studies (SOAS), University of London, and known, along with many of her colleagues and peers at other universities, for defending the rights of peoples, including the Palestinian people, to fight colonialism, Zionism and occupation.
This brought her into conflict with the authorities and the Israeli lobby in Britain.
Despite what she has been through, she said she would "stay in Britain for a little longer" and does not intend to return to France now.
"I know that if I went back to my country, France, things would be similar, if not worse," she remarked.
She believes there is still an opportunity to continue what she describes as the struggle, saying, "It is important for me to continue fighting against the same people and the same state that I have been fighting."
She will therefore continue "confronting repression and defending, or helping to defend, some of our comrades who are being criminalised" because they want to support the Palestinian people's struggle.
A step to "restore credibility"
Cotte does not expect protests against what she, and many others in Britain, see as British complicity in Israeli crimes to decrease, even after the government of Andy Burnham announced sanctions, which are still being prepared, on "illegal" settlements in Palestine.
She described the language used by the government as "still clearly framed in the context of 'we are committed to Israel's security' and 'we are committed to fighting Israel's enemies who pose an existential threat to it, and this includes Iran, Hezbollah and armed resistance".
While she said she believed the expected sanctions "will, to some extent, have a tangible impact on the illegal settlements", she described them as "part of Britain's broader objective of saving the two-state solution, saving Israel from itself, and trying to save Israel's international reputation".
Regarding the two-state solution, which Britain says it is working to achieve to resolve the conflict between Palestinians and Israel, Cotte described it as "an illusion and a myth that Britain seeks to keep alive".
"We know that Israel will never allow a Palestinian state to be established, and it will always pose a threat to the Palestinian people," she added.
The possible and sustainable solution, which she argues should be fought for, is "one state; one secular, democratic Palestinian state with the right of return" for Palestinians displaced by Israel since its establishment on Palestinian land in 1948.
On domestic politics in Britain, Cotte said the move, namely the announcement of plans to impose sanctions on settlements, also seeks to "restore some credibility to the Labour Party, because this move is actually very electorally popular for the Burnham government".
Since joining SOAS, Cotte has been active in the Revolutionary Communist Group, which she sees as a useful framework for defending those criminalised for defending the rights of the Palestinian people.
In light of her experience, she advised activists, particularly young people, to join political organisations "after establishing their political positions" and not to work alone because she believes that "we can only work collectively".
"The only reason the campaign to defend me worked so well was that it was within a political organisation," referring to the communist group," she said.
She added that "any organisation is a good place to start" active political work and "it enables us to take a very disciplined approach to organising our campaign".
She warned that this approach "means that when the police were harassing us at protests, for example, everyone knew exactly what to do, what to say, what not to say, how to protect each other, and how to respond" to any situation.
Cotte's other advice to young people is: "Get out into the streets. A lot of things happen there; talk to people and meet them."

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Formosa Plastics Corp. and Taiwan Pulp & Paper Corp. plan to establish a US joint venture producing electronic-grade hydrochloric acid, CTEE reported Tuesday.
The venture, FTA Tech LLC, will build a facility at Formosa Plastics’ existing complex in Texas. Food-grade hydrochloric acid produced there will be further purified for semiconductor manufacturing.
The project aims to establish a local supply chain as semiconductor manufacturers expand production in the US. Formosa Plastics estimated that US demand for electronic-grade hydrochloric acid would grow at a compound annual rate of about 9.5% from 2026 through 2035.
Formosa Plastics and its US subsidiary will each own 25% of the venture, while Taiwan Pulp & Paper will hold the remaining 50%. FTA Tech will have capital of US$38.1 million, while total investment is estimated at US$129 million (NT$4.1 billion). Production is scheduled to begin in December 2028.
Hydrochloric acid is one of several high-purity chemicals used in semiconductor manufacturing, along with hydrofluoric acid, sulfuric acid and hydrogen peroxide. It is used to clean and etch wafers during production, according to Data Bridge.
Formosa Plastics has been expanding its semiconductor materials business through partnerships with Taiwanese specialty chemical companies. It has also teamed up with Chung Hwa Chemical Industrial Works to develop electronic-grade sulfuric acid in Taiwan.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan’s benchmark stock index fell on Tuesday as investors became more cautious following strong gains last week.

Declines in the market’s largest-cap stocks weighed on the index. TSMC closed unchanged at NT$2,475.
MediaTek lost 7.1% to NT$4,910. Foxconn ended flat at NT$250.5, Delta Electronics fell 3.93% to NT$1,835, and ASE declined 1.72% to NT$687, according to Anue.
High-priced stocks recorded notable declines. Of the 15 stocks trading above NT$3,000 per share, 14 closed lower, with seven falling more than 3%.
Petrochemical stocks were among the stronger-performing sectors, supported by a structural supply shortage in global refining markets and higher oil prices. Formosa Petrochemical gained 8.14%, while Nan Ya Plastics rose 3.78%. Formosa Plastics and Formosa Chemicals and Fiber closed higher.
Power semiconductor stocks also stood out against the broader market after reports that product prices could rise. Phoenix Silicon International and Episil-Precision gained more than 7%, while Mosel Vitelic and Vanguard International Semiconductor rose more than 3%.
Power semiconductors are key components in power conversion, handling functions such as voltage conversion while also protecting circuits against over-voltage. Major international suppliers, including Onsemi and Renesas Electronics, have announced plans to raise prices, benefiting Taiwanese suppliers, according to CTEE, Business Weekly, and MoneyDJ.
Several optoelectronics stocks recorded strong gains. Jochu Technology, Daxin Materials, Aiptek International, Onano Industrial, and General Interface Solution all reached the daily limit. The optoelectronics industry covers a wide range of products that use light and electronic technologies for applications such as light-based data transmission, sensing, and converting light into electrical signals, according to Money Weekly.
In contrast, the custom chip sector, which had performed strongly in recent weeks, saw profit-taking. In addition to MediaTek, Global Unichip fell 7.04%, while Alchip Technologies declined 2.25%.
Analysts said investors are watching oil prices and interest rates, two key international factors. Still, 45 stocks hit the daily limit-up while only two hit the lower limit, suggesting that investors were shifting between sectors rather than broadly reducing their market exposure, according to CTEE.
Analysts also noted that stock purchases made with borrowed funds have grown too quickly in recent weeks, raising the risk of greater short-term volatility. They expect the market to remain volatile at high levels in the near term.
For investment strategies, analysts recommended watching liquid large- and mid-cap AI stocks, as well as thematic stocks backed by earnings. For longer-term sectors, they said investors could continue to monitor TSMC and its advanced packaging and testing supply chain, along with semiconductor equipment, printed circuit boards, optical communications, thermal management, and other core AI-related supply chains.

Taiwan institute develops AI-powered drone inspection system
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
12:41:55 UTC
21:41:55 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Institute for Information Industry has integrated three technologies to improve inspections by drones and other unmanned vehicles, according to a recent press release.
Inspecting large areas such as ports, marine conservation zones and energy facilities can be time-consuming, while remote locations may lack adequate camera and network coverage. The system combines AI-assisted electronic fencing, digital twin technology and resilient networking.
For electronic fencing, coastal cameras use AI to detect and track vessels entering restricted waters, analyze their routes and alert authorities. The system also displays the vessels’ locations and related information on a digital twin platform.
The digital twin synchronizes information about operating areas, vehicles, equipment and network performance. It simulates changing mission requirements and network conditions to help operators adjust communications resources.
For remote connectivity, a resilient network integrates satellite, 5G, Wi-Fi and Ethernet connections. Drone relays and portable private networks can extend coverage to areas that ground equipment cannot reach and maintain communications if one connection fails.
The institute said the system could establish communications within two hours after disasters block roads, compared with more than eight hours for conventional equipment. Related drone systems have been used for inspections, supply deliveries, warehouse inventory, firefighting and biological pest control. The technologies could also support marine conservation, port inspections and energy facilities.
