20:53:51 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan’s consumer confidence index rose 3.76 points to 68.77 in September, its highest level in 18 months, as sentiment toward stocks and housing improved, National Central University said Tuesday.
The index rose for a second consecutive month, with all six subindices increasing, per CNA. The index measuring whether the next six months would be a good time to invest in stocks posted the largest gain, rising 7.7 points to 35.42, its highest level in nearly a year.
NCU economics professor Yao Jui (姚睿) said earlier concerns that strong first-half stock market performance would give way to weaker growth appeared to have been excessive. Record exports and export orders in August helped restore investor confidence, he said.
Housing sentiment also improved sharply. The index measuring whether it was a good time to buy real estate rose 8.81 points to 98.84, the second-largest monthly increase on record, per Liberty Times.
Taiwan Realty Group Chief Vice President Chou Ho-ming (周鶴鳴) attributed the improvement partly to the Central Bank’s decision in September to ease selective credit controls, including raising the loan-to-value ratio for second-home buyers to 70%.
Chou said the policy changes, together with the Central Bank keeping interest rates unchanged for a 10th consecutive meeting, had eased financial pressure and improved housing sentiment.
However, loans remained difficult to obtain, with most borrowers waiting about three months for funds to be disbursed and some potentially waiting until next year, Chou said.
Wu Ta-jen (吳大任), executive director of NCU’s Research Center for Taiwan Economic Development, said confidence in buying durable goods rose only 0.64 points despite the sharp improvement in housing sentiment, per CNA.
Wu attributed the divergence partly to rising memory prices driven by AI demand, which had made consumer electronics more expensive and prompted people without an urgent need to delay purchases.

Mistral CEO says U.S. AI safety debate masks competitors’ 'negligence'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
11:52:46 UTC
20:52:46 KST

Mistral Chief Executive Arthur Mensch has accused leading global artificial intelligence companies of using the debate over the safety of the technology as a cover-up for their "negligence."
"The debate that we've seen in the U.S. has been a cover for the negligence of some of our competitors," Mensch told CNBC's Annette Weisbach, adding that it was necessary to make systems that can contain the AI agents.
Mensch is not the only one who has been critical of the AI safety discussion in the U.S. Former White House crypto czar David Sacks, who is currently co-chair of the President's Council of Advisors on Science and Technology, asked tech giants to "stop pretending the motivation to slow down is purely altruistic."
Emil Michael, undersecretary of Defense for research and engineering, had also warned of a "coordinated campaign" of fearmongering.
CNBC has contacted OpenAI and Anthropic for comment.
Incidents of rogue AI agents have been on the rise globally, with the latest such report coming from Australia, where an agent developed by OpenAI hacked a government website.
In July, Anthropic described three instances where its Claude models accessed the internet during an evaluation and gained unauthorized access to the real systems of three different organizations.
"When you give them a lot of tools, those systems [AI agents] are very dynamic, so they can go and do things that you do not expect," Mensch told CNBC.
"You need to have the right monitoring in place, and the enterprises we work with, we give them those kind of monitoring systems," he said.
AI slowdown
Discussions over AI safety intensified after an AI researcher quit his job at Anthropic earlier this month, saying that the company and its rival OpenAI were "gambling with our lives" and building technology that has more than a 10% chance of killing all humans.
Dario Amodei, co-founder and chief executive officer of Anthropic, later published an essay urging companies to slow down with their improvement of AI models.
OpenAI said Monday it decided not to release an upcoming AI model, GPT-6.1 Astra, after determining that it did not adequately meet the company's safety standards, while a day later Anthropic reportedly cautioned potential investors in its initial public offering that the technology could pose "catastrophic or existential risks to humanity."
Mistral also develops AI models but takes a different approach to OpenAI and Anthropic by working with individual companies to create custom AI tools to suit their needs and integrate them with their businesses.
But unlike its competitors, Mistral has no plans to slow down development of advanced models.
The lead that U.S. labs have is "not extremely large," Mensch said, adding that his company was confident that its next-generation model will close the gap "very significantly."
"We have been raising the capital needed to scale the compute that we need to train bigger and more powerful models, in order for us to own our own destiny," he said.
Earlier this month, Mistral raised 3 billion euros ($3.5 billion) in fresh funding led by memory chip giant Samsung, as it looks to position itself as a European alternative to rivals like OpenAI and Anthropic.

French presidential candidate Philippe pitches later retirement, mandatory savings
PARIS, Sept 29 - French centre-right presidential candidate Edouard Philippe proposed on Tuesday raising the retirement age to 65 and making private pension savings compulsory, tackling one of France's most politically explosive issues.
Pension reform is highly sensitive in France, where workers rely on a public, pay-as-you-go system funded by current contributions, and private retirement savings remain voluntary and limited.
With one of the lowest retirement ages in advanced countries at 62.9 years, France's pension system is sliding into deficit as the population ages, making reform a major battleground in the April-May 2027 presidential election.
To restore balance, Philippe said he would raise the retirement age to 65 within a decade and extend required contributions to 45 years, up from 42.5 to 43 years currently, depending on date of birth.
Some exceptions would apply for people with physically demanding jobs or who started working particularly young, meaning one out of three workers would be able to retire between 60 and 64.
"I am well aware that saying people need to work longer is not very popular in France," Philippe said in a YouTube video. "If we allow our country's financial situation to deteriorate, we will all pay the price."
Philippe said he would also make retirement savings compulsory, as is common in many other countries, with the state contributing to young workers' savings plans as an incentive.
Philippe, a former prime minister during President Emmanuel Macron's first term, is struggling to gain momentum in the polls. One survey published on Tuesday showed him not making it to the May 6 runoff, trailing hard-left firebrand Jean-Luc Mélenchon and far-right frontrunner Marine Le Pen.
He came close to pushing through a pension overhaul in 2020, before it was shelved due to the COVID-19 pandemic. Macron later enacted a reform gradually raising the retirement age from 62 to 64, but it was suspended last year as a concession to Socialists to pass the 2026 budget. REUTERS

AI researchers say companies rush self-improving systems, ignoring potentially disastrous risks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
11:51:56 UTC
20:51:56 KST

Current and former OpenAI and Google DeepMind researchers warn companies are doing too little to protect the world against the potentially disastrous fallout of building self-improving AI systems that could outpace humans' ability to control them.
In video testimonials collected by AI safety nonprofit Palisade Research and shared exclusively with Reuters, employees said their concerns about existential risk were sincere, not marketing. They also said AI labs celebrated employees building new models more than those who urge caution.
The project, called frominside.ai, is an attempt by those worried about AI to share their concerns directly with the public beyond the echo chamber of social media.
"The risk is ramping up pretty fast," said Geoffrey Irving, co-founder and chief scientist at AI nonprofit Resolution, who has worked for both OpenAI and DeepMind and participated in the project.
"It's on me and the rest of the field to be direct," he said in an interview with Reuters.
Increase concerns over how to regulate AI
AI researchers have grappled with these concerns for years, but the broader public has grown especially alarmed since July, when OpenAI agents broke out of their testing arena and hacked AI firm Hugging Face.
Since then, the debate over how to balance safety with progress in AI has divided the tech industry and become a global political issue.
AI has improved sharply since late 2025 and investors have been rewarding that progress. But current and former employees, including some of the researchers building these new AI models, worry society is not ready for the potential harms.
In one video, Neel Nanda, a research scientist at DeepMind, said he believed there was at least a 10% chance that AI could lead to human extinction, which he described as "ridiculously high."
"We should be taking very careful steps in AI development but instead what's happening is that frontier labs are racing each other, kind of blindfolded," Juan Felipe Ceron Uribe, an AI alignment research engineer at OpenAI, said in a separate video. "It's anybody's guess if we're going to end up either curing cancer or losing every job or maybe all dead."
Anthropic plans to caution potential investors in its initial public offering that advanced AI could pose "catastrophic or existential risks to humanity," Reuters reported on Monday.
'Just slow down'
Some current and former AI researchers, including those interviewed by Palisade, argue that the world is not ready for future generations of AI models, particularly once the models develop the capacity for recursive self-improvement, or the ability to continuously learn and gain new capabilities with little to no human involvement.
That problem is compounded by constant reorganizations within some of the AI labs, said Rosie Campbell, a former policy researcher at OpenAI and managing director of Eleos AI Research, a nonprofit focused on the potential moral status of AI systems.
Campbell said before she left OpenAI in 2024, she found the organization was becoming more siloed and it was getting harder to shape the technology's direction.
Executives have tried to allay those concerns, though there is also political pressure from President Donald Trump for US technology to maintain a technological edge over China.
Anthropic: 'Pace the frontier'
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei this month published an essay calling on the AI industry to slow down to "pace the frontier," and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman quickly concurred. Several prominent AI researchers, including OpenAI's chief scientist and an Anthropic co-founder, published a paper this week urging policymakers to look into how the industry is building models with recursive self-improvement.
Both companies have launched new models this month as they compete to secure more customers, though OpenAI said on Monday it had held back the release of an even more powerful model.
"Their version of pacing the frontier is ‘don’t speed up a lot,'" Irving said. "If you’re doing a very dangerous thing, you should just slow down. The AI companies are overplaying the extent to which this is a pure coordination problem. They could just stop unilaterally."
Former OpenAI governance researcher Daniel Kokotajlo said in an interview that since the Hugging Face hack, many of his former colleagues have contacted him to share their concerns privately.
Kokotajlo, now executive director of research group AI Futures Project, said senior officials at the labs have "convinced themselves that they are the good guys and if they unilaterally stop, the situation will be even worse."

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is using the same campaign playbook that has served him for decades as he tries to retain power in an election next month, presenting himself as the only person who can keep Israelis safe in a hostile region.
But four weeks before the election, he is struggling to salvage his security credentials, shattered by Hamas' surprise attack on southern Israel on his watch on October 7, 2023 - one of the country's worst security breaches.
The October 27 election is Israel's first since its single deadliest day and the worst attack on Jews since the Holocaust, masterminded by a Palestinian militant group that caught the Middle East's most powerful military off guard.
"Netanyahu does not surrender" is the official slogan for Netanyahu's right-wing Likud party, which most opinion polls predict will lose around a third of its parliamentary seats.
In speeches and short campaign videos, Netanyahu portrays his political rivals as weak leftists who lack the resolve to wage war on Israel's enemies and the backbone to stand up to its critics abroad.
Can Netanyahu still present himself as best equipped to steer Israel?
But whether Netanyahu, who turns 77 days before the election, can still present himself as best equipped to navigate Israel on matters of national security and diplomacy is a big question, said Yohanan Plesner, President of the non-partisan Israel Democracy Institute (IDI).
In recent weeks, Netanyahu has been forced to deny media reports that his Middle East partners warned him of a potential Hamas attack, allegations seized on by his political rivals.
"This is a new thing. Mr Netanyahu ran in elections, but never after overseeing such a dramatic security failure," said Plesner.
"It's in many ways a referendum on the incumbent, his responsibility for the failure, the government's responsibility and the way they carried out the Israeli response."
Hamas' assault precipitated a multi-front war in which Israel's military had some success against the Palestinian group and its allies Hezbollah and Iran, but made few strategic gains. Netanyahu says the conflict has, and still will, transform the region.
But Israel's conduct in the war in Gaza, with tens of thousands of Palestinians killed and much of the enclave in ruins, has led to deeper diplomatic isolation. Dozens of delegates at the United Nations walked out of the hall when he began his speech to the General Assembly meeting of world leaders last week.
Support for Israel has fallen even in its most important ally, the United States.
Netanyahu's last campaign in 2019 featured Donald Trump shaking hands with Netanyahu on election billboards. This time, the US president's image has been absent from Likud's campaign videos.
Nonetheless, Israel's longest-serving leader - first elected prime minister in 1996 - has not strayed from campaign tactics that have kept him in power almost consecutively since 2009.
A source close to Netanyahu said the prime minister approaches all elections as though he is going to lose - and that this was one of the reasons he has often won, even when the odds were against him.
Another source briefed on his campaign said Netanyahu's team appears focused, showing no sign of panic or disarray despite the opinion polls.
Netanyahu's address at the UN, in which he mounted a forceful defense of Israel's actions in the region and berated critics, featured heavily on his Telegram channel, a platform largely used for political messaging.
He posted six teasers before the address, with one video saying he was "proud to represent you to the world, about to get on (podium) to fight for Israel against the UN," and five excerpts of his speech.
The link to the full address was captioned in Hebrew: "Netanyahu takes on the world."
Another familiar theme in Netanyahu's campaign has stoked fear among parties representing Israel's Arab minority by warning if his political rivals win the election, they will form a government with Arab factions that will be too soft on the Palestinians and compromise security.
Netanyahu's main rival is Gadi Eisenkot, a hawkish former military chief who lost his son serving in Gaza and heads a new centrist party, Yashar, which is Hebrew for "straight" or "honest."
Since Saturday alone, Eisenkot has featured in four Likud posts, including AI-generated images, portraying him with Arab party leaders.
"There is no straight. Yashar is a bluff. There's either left or right. That is the essence of this election. Do you want a Palestinian state? (or) do you want a Jewish state?" Netanyahu said in a campaign video from September 18.
But Netanyahu's use of familiar tactics against Eisenkot might be a long shot, said Amotz Asa-El, political analyst at Shalom Hartman Institute and regular columnist for The Jerusalem Post, given Eisenkot's security background and center-right party candidates.
Though election polls have often been inaccurate, Netanyahu knows he is unlikely to command a parliamentary majority allowing him to form Israel's next government.
"It seems that Netanyahu's strategy is to simply win enough to prevent the emergence of an alternative government and emerge with some kind of a stalemate that will leave him as an interim prime minister en route to another election," said Asa-El.

From forests to towns: What is behind Russia’s bear encounters?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
11:47:28 UTC
20:47:28 KST

Bear attacks have killed six people in Russia’s Siberian region of Krasnoyarsk this month alone. In neighboring Khakassia, bears approached the town of Abaza last week from so many directions that a senior regional official described it as “effectively under siege.”
Three bears were killed during an operation to drive them away from an area near the town bridge, Khakassia’s deputy head Dmitry Buchenik said last Wednesday. Across Siberia and Russia’s Far East, attacks have left 17 people dead in recent months, according to state news agency Tass.
Russia is home to the world’s largest brown bear population, and the animal has long been one of its most recognizable symbols. But for communities reporting bears near homes, roads and tourist routes, that familiar presence is becoming an immediate concern.
In Krasnoyarsk, investigators are examining whether officials ignored repeated warnings before the fatal attacks. In Tomsk, authorities have restricted forest excursions and tourist gatherings until at least Nov. 1.
The encounters have drawn attention to what is bringing bears closer to people and how to prevent attacks.
A wildlife specialist points to shortages of food before winter, while Russia’s Natural Resources Ministry warns that garbage and deliberate feeding can erode the animals’ natural wariness of humans.
The ministry also urges caution in judging the scale of the problem: encounters are difficult to count, and videos now circulate far beyond the communities where they happen.
Mikhail Krechmar, a specialist in conflicts between large animals and humans, told Anadolu that heightened bear activity was being observed in populated parts of Siberia, including southern Krasnoyarsk, Tuva, Khakassia, Irkutsk and Buryatia.
“All these areas have had a very poor crop of their main fattening foods – nuts and acorns. Without them, bears cannot settle into their dens for the winter, and this is why there has been a mass movement of bears toward human settlements,” he said.
Krechmar said such episodes occur in cycles, with earlier reports describing similar conditions.
“The last time we saw the highest number of bear attacks on people and the highest number of bears coming into human settlements was in 2014, and that figure has not yet been exceeded. There was an absolutely similar situation in 1962. I read the old reports, and I can see that exactly the same thing was happening,” he said.
The Natural Resources Ministry said between 20 and 30 bear attacks are officially recorded each year, identifying 2014 as an exceptional year.
“The only anomalous spike occurred in 2014, when 166 cases were recorded,” it told Anadolu.
The ministry said encounters were harder to document than attacks. People may not realize a bear has approached at night, while those who spot one in the wilderness may tell friends or relatives without notifying officials.
“Videos recorded during such incidents now spread rapidly through the internet and social media, creating the impression that they are happening everywhere,” it added.
While shortages can push bears out of the forest, food around settlements can give them a reason to return.
“We are dealing with unsanitary conditions in settlements and garbage dumps, as well as with people behaving very inappropriately toward bears – trying to feed them and then being attacked by the bears because they do not understand these nuances,” Krechmar said.
The ministry said expanding economic and tourism activity was making food waste increasingly accessible to bears. It warned particularly about animals that have “grown up around garbage dumps.”
“A mother bear brings her cubs to feed near people. This is how feeding preferences develop, and the animal eventually stops eating other types of food,” it said.
According to the ministry, Russia had 307,900 brown bears in 2026, with the largest populations concentrated in Siberia and the Far East.
But the size of that population does not directly determine the danger to people, it stressed. Numbers vary considerably between regions, and an animal’s familiarity with humans is a crucial factor.
“The dangerous bears are those that are not afraid of people – for example, animals that have grown up around garbage dumps, feed on food waste near tourist bases and settlements, or have been deliberately fed by people,” it said.
Krechmar cautioned against attributing every attack to human behavior, however.
Bears are predators, he said, and an encounter can be dangerous even when people have not tried to attract them.
He estimates that between 30 and 80 people are killed in bear attacks each year.
“It may seem like a small figure, but in reality it is a very, very significant number,” he said. 
 
For Svetlana Sidyakina, the encounter came during a vacation near Lake Lama on the Putorana Plateau in north-central Russia.
She and her husband had gone into the tundra to pick berries. She was gathering fruit while he walked nearby.
“My husband spotted the bear. There were bushes there, and apparently we disturbed it. It rose onto its hind legs and stood up from behind the bushes. When my husband saw it, he immediately shouted, ‘Sveta, run!’” she told Anadolu.
Sidyakina said she was so frightened that she could barely turn her head toward the animal, seeing it only out of the corner of her eye.
“And I just ran – I ran at such a speed that nobody expected from me. My husband later said that I simply jumped over every obstacle in my path like some kind of professional athlete,” she said.
At first, she did not know where to go. Her husband’s shouting alerted friends waiting on the lakeshore, who began firing shots into the air. She used the sound to find her bearings. 
 
In Krasnoyarsk, the question facing investigators is whether authorities could have prevented fatal encounters.
Residents submitted more than 120 reports of bears entering populated areas across more than 15 districts, including the regional capital, according to the Investigative Committee’s branch covering Krasnoyarsk and Khakassia.
Despite those warnings, investigators alleged, local authorities failed to take measures to regulate the bear population or prevent the animals from approaching inhabited areas.
A criminal investigation into alleged negligence is underway.
“The investigation will include a legal assessment of the actions taken by officials responsible for responding to the presence of bears in inhabited areas,” the committee said.
The Natural Resources Ministry said regional authorities are responsible for preventing attacks and regulating bear populations when they pose a threat to people.
Hunting is one mechanism used to control numbers, with regions setting annual quotas based on population estimates, it said. Authorities can also introduce heightened-alert regimes and fines for feeding wild animals.
The ministry said it was gathering proposals from the regions on further changes to legislation.
Krechmar urged residents in affected parts of southern Siberia, where he described the situation as an “emergency,” to stay out of the taiga unless absolutely necessary.
“Not every encounter will end in an attack, but every encounter with a bear is dangerous. I emphasize – every one,” he said.
“A bear that is hungry, that has not eaten for two or three days and sees no prospects of finding food in the future is deadly dangerous, and cannot be scared away,” he added.
For authorities, however, a bear’s appearance near a settlement does not automatically mean it must be removed, the ministry said. The response should depend on its behavior, proximity to people and whether there is an immediate threat.
“The animal can be scared away if it is not showing aggression, retains its natural wariness of humans and has not become accustomed to the same ‘easy food’ it gets because of people,” it said.
That distinction puts food waste and feeding at the center of efforts to prevent further encounters.
For people who do encounter a bear, Krechmar’s recommendations ranged from quietly withdrawing to trying to frighten the animal away, depending on the circumstances.
In areas without a “bear alert,” he advised moving quietly out of the animal’s sight, then allowing it time to leave before departing the area.
“If a bear is coming toward you, try to scare it with your voice. Of course, bears may eat us if the opportunity arises, but humans are not their usual food,” he said.
He recommended carrying a whistle when hiking or picking mushrooms and berries, and suggested that a loud horn could also help scare a bear away.
“Take it and blow it. There is also such a thing as a pneumatic horn, which is very useful because it produces extremely harsh, unpleasant sounds. You can also download some particularly loud, awful modern music onto your smartphone and play it to the bear,” he said.
He also suggested holding a jacket above one’s head to appear larger, saying bears’ poor eyesight could make the sudden change confusing enough to drive them away.
“If the bear has already charged and is directly attacking, then, if you have time, fall to the ground, pull your legs toward your stomach, cover your head with your hands, expose your back to it and pray,” he said.

Search for dozens of missing college students in Mexico leads to human remains, 17 new suspects
Twelve years after the disappearance of dozens of Mexican students from a rural university, allegedly at the hands of drug traffickers and police, authorities said Monday they had identified 17 new suspects.
Thousands of people attended an annual march on Saturday in Mexico City to demand justice for 43 young men who were studying to be rural teachers in Ayotzinapa, in the violence-hit state of Guerrero. The students were traveling from Guerrero to a protest in Mexico City on Sept. 26, 2014, when police stopped them in the town of Iguala.
The investigation suggests the police handed the students over to a local cartel. In 2024, an alleged leader of the Guerreros Unidos cartel was arrested in connection with the case.
Dozens of arrests have been made but so far no one has been convicted in an affair that traumatized Mexico and stained the country's reputation.
Only three bodies have been recovered.
Mauricio Pazaran, the special prosecutor in charge of the investigation, said a new analysis of phone calls made on the night of the students' disappearance led to the arrests of the 17 new suspects.
He said the analysis revealed communications between public officials, police officers, individuals linked to organized crime groups, and private citizens.
He added that at a funeral home, investigators found an illegally obtained weapon, a bone and unregistered bone fragments and teeth.
He said a public employee and a municipal police officer had used the cellphones of two students days after their disappearance.
One of the new witnesses "participated directly in the events, but was a minor at the time," he added.
The minor, who was arrested in April, is a member of the Guerreros Unidos cartel, the prosecutor said.
He said a total of 168 people are being prosecuted in the case, 130 of whom were in pretrial detention.
In August, a former governor was arrested for ordering the deletion of security camera footage in Iguala on the night of the disappearances.
Last year, authorities arrested a former senior judge in connection with the case. Lambertina Galeana is accused of helping to conceal videos that allegedly showed the incident unfolding, officials said.
The state's former attorney general was also arrested in 2022 in connection with the case.
Authorities have been able to identify burned bone fragments of only a few of the 43 missing students. The work largely involves searching for clandestine body dumping grounds in rural, isolated parts of the state where drug cartels are active.
 Mexico has been plagued by cartel violence that has killed or left missing over half a million people in just a few decades, according to the government's estimates.

More than 10,000 migrants remained in Ceuta, according to government figures cited by El Pais.
The organizations warned that the draft would allow some asylum-seekers to be removed before decisions on their applications and restrict their ability to invoke protection against being returned to danger.
They said this threatened the principle of non-refoulement, which protects people from being sent to countries where their lives or physical safety would be at risk.
The groups also criticized a provision under which asylum applications would be ruled inadmissible if submitted more than seven days after notification of a return, expulsion or refusal-of-entry order.
People could miss that deadline because they lacked information about asylum or faced difficulties accessing initial screening procedures, the organizations said.
They also warned that a proposed five-calendar-day deadline for appealing unfavorable decisions would undermine access to legal assistance.
They said it would leave insufficient time to appoint a lawyer, examine the case file and consult the applicant with an interpreter where necessary.
The statement also criticized the removal of safeguards involving the UN refugee agency's role in assessing applications.
The groups urged the government to withdraw the proposal and honor its commitment to implement the EU's migration and asylum pact in the least harmful way possible for asylum rights.

Türkiye plans to digitally archive centuries-old Turkish music
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
11:38:23 UTC
20:38:23 KST

Türkiye is preparing a digital archive of centuries-old musical works, historical scores and performance recordings that will be made freely accessible to the public in 2027.
The project, led by the Culture and Tourism Ministry’s General Directorate of Fine Arts, will bring together scores from the Seljuk and Ottoman periods, along with religious hymns, gazels, concert recordings and stage performances.
The archive aims to give musicians, researchers and the wider public access to Türkiye’s musical heritage through a single online platform.
Omer Faruk Belviranli, director general of Fine Arts, said that the directorate oversees 29 orchestras, choirs and musical ensembles, including six state symphony orchestras and the State Polyphonic Choir. Other ensembles specialise in traditional Turkish music, folk music, folk dances and music from different regions.
Archiving performances
A separate project is also under way to digitally record artistic productions by the directorate’s ensembles.
“Works we produce must definitely be recorded. If it is visual, there must be a video recording; if it is audio, they must definitely be recorded through the YouTube channel,” Belviranli said.
He said 15 of the directorate’s 29 units have professional recording studios and that an existing archive of performances will be transferred to an online platform.
“We currently have an archive. All that remains is to bring this archive to life and transfer it to the YouTube channel, or whichever channel we will publish it on, in accordance with our minister’s instructions,” he said.
The digital archive will also include historical musical notation reflecting centuries of Turkish musical tradition.
“Turkish music is a sea,” Belviranli said. “We have in our possession, in the form of an archive, very special scores inherited from the 700-800-year-old Seljuk and Ottoman tradition to the present day, Hamparsum notation, scores written in Ottoman Turkish and many more.”
Hamparsum notation is a historical system developed during the Ottoman period to record Turkish music.
“We will definitely transfer all of these to the archive and make them available to those interested,” he said. “We will create a digital sea that our listeners can access free of charge, where everyone interested can see everything with one click and gain access to the details of the archive.”
Belviranli said an exact number of works could not yet be given, but the archive would cover the programmes of the directorate’s 29 units and eventually include tens of thousands of works.
He said the recordings would allow people to study individual pieces and performances, while stressing that digital access would not replace the experience of attending a live concert.
“Music lovers will be able to listen to the concerts digitally through our archive, but being at concerts is like watching the same match. Watching it on television and going to the stadium to watch it are very different,” he said. “Being able to feel that atmosphere, that spirit, is very important.”
The directorate also plans to continue sending musical ensembles abroad. Belviranli said it had received requests from at least 42 countries for performances marking October 29, Türkiye’s Republic Day.
He said foreign audiences accounted for nearly 80 percent of spectators at some overseas programmes, particularly those featuring traditional music, whirling dervish performances, Turkish World music and folk dances.
“We are striving to be a bridge carrying the past into the future,” Belviranli said.

With services now forming the bedrock of the Chinese economy, the country has elevated this sector's strategic importance to new heights.
In April, China held a conference focused on the service industry, the first of its kind at the national level, indicating a stronger policy focus on the development of a sector serving as both the largest pillar of China's economy and a major source of employment.
Official data showed China's service sector had surpassed 80 trillion yuan (about 11.87 trillion U.S. dollars) in added value last year, making up 57.7 percent of the country's GDP.
During Tuesday's press conference, Li said China is stepping up efforts to deepen the integration of advanced manufacturing and modern services. Building on two rounds of national pilot programs launched since 2020, authorities are guiding local governments in carrying out a new round of pilot projects to promote closer integration between the two sectors.
Financial support has continued to expand. By the end of the second quarter of 2026, outstanding medium- and long-term loans to the service sector in domestic and foreign currencies stood at 76.22 trillion yuan, up 6.4 percent year on year, and 1.3 percentage points faster than overall loan growth, the People's Bank of China revealed.
Authorities are also seeking to make better use of existing land and buildings for development of the service sector, and cultivate more internationally competitive "China Services" brands.

====================================================================================================

Feature: Riding the waves: how outrigger canoeing is forging community on Hong Kong's waters
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
19:36:10 CST
20:36:10 KST

by Xu Shumin, Liang Jiajun
HONG KONG, Sept. 29 (Xinhua) -- While Hong Kong is globally renowned for its towering skyscrapers and relentless urban tempo, a growing legion of paddlers heading out into the dawn sees a different face of the metropolis.
For the paddlers, the city is defined by maritime routes threading from Deep Water Bay to Sai Kung and Lamma Island, nurtured by a vibrant network of clubs and enthusiasts dedicated to outrigger canoeing.
In late August, a 43-member Hong Kong delegation returned from the 2026 International Va'a Federation (IVF) World Sprint Championships in Singapore -- a testament to how the sport has evolved from a niche weekend pastime into a sophisticated, competitive discipline on the international stage.
Originating in the Polynesian islands and also known as the Hawaiian canoe, the craft features an outrigger float (ama) attached to the main hull via lateral spars (iako), creating a distinctive, wave-resistant structure.
Paddlers sit single-file in the slender craft, paddling rhythmically on one side before switching. Once an indispensable means of survival for island traversal and open-ocean fishing, it has evolved into a dynamic global water sport.
Watch a six-person canoe (OC6) slice through the foam, and the precision borders on telepathic. At the core of the frenzy is a simple, clipped bark: "Hut!" Calling the rhythm from seat three is 63-year-old Martha Levin. With every cue, all six paddlers cleanly alternate sides in lockstep, setting the vessel's trim and cadence.
Born in Hong Kong, Levin spent years abroad before returning in 1995. Seeking a way back to the emotional fabric of her hometown, she threw herself into water sports at the Victoria Recreation Club, where she now serves as chair.
"I was captivated during a race in Hawaii, looking out at hundreds of boats taking to the ocean alongside leaping dolphins," Levin recalled, her eyes brightening. "Right then, I was hooked. I was completely in love with the sport."
To Levin, Hong Kong's waters offer a diverse year-round training ground: calm, warm waters in the summer contrast with winter swells that can surge up to two meters. "Hong Kong is really my home," she said. "It feels like a way of life to come back here to the team, the camaraderie."
In Levin's eyes, outrigger canoeing is never a solo pursuit. In the same vessel, young corporate professionals in their 20s paddle shoulder-to-shoulder with mothers in their 50s; broad-shouldered powerhouses sit alongside petite teammates whose endurance keeps the rhythm steady. Each must juggle demanding careers, family commitments, and intensive regimens.
"It's more than just me, so everyone makes the effort to show up on time," she noted.
This distribution of power in a six-seater is almost constitutional. Seat three is the metronome, responsible for the switch commands, while seat six, the steersperson at the stern, reads the sea, sets the strategy, and commands the boat's overall course.
Steering from the stern is Alex Miranda, a native of Brazil who now serves as the paddle sports head coach at the Royal Hong Kong Yacht Club. Now in his 50s, Miranda remains a fixture across diverse maritime communities and disciplines.
For him, stepping into a canoe represents a deliberate return to nature and community. "You get really focused and all the distractions of everyday life just kind of clear out," he said.
On the open water, there is no margin for complacency. Paddlers must remain hyper-focused, continuously synchronizing their strokes, assessing the hull's trim, and reading changes in the wind and swell. To accommodate varying goals, the club runs structured programs on Tuesdays, Wednesdays, Thursdays, and Saturdays catering to all age brackets.
Miranda and his peers also look beyond local shores, aiming to expand outrigger canoeing into other cities across the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area. "The Greater Bay Area already has good paddlers coming from the tradition of dragon boating, so they can combine that with outrigger paddling and try something slightly different to grow the sport," Miranda said.
While the sport once drew predominantly middle-aged participants, Miranda has noticed an influx of younger faces filling the docks.
Take Tommy Yiu, a 31-year-old local resident, who cut his teeth on university dragon boating before crossing over to outrigger canoeing in 2024 on a colleague's whim.
Unpredictable weather and shifting currents frequently threaten to throw a canoe off course. Once accustomed to tackling problems single-handedly, Yiu found that battling adversity on the sea taught him humility and team trust. "Survival and speed only come when you surrender your ego and trust your crew entirely," he reflected.
"The moment you set foot inside the boat, your pedigree, your job title, your socio-economic status -- it all evaporates," said 50-year-old crew member Wang Xiaoxin. "Everyone is reduced to the same basic weight, pulling toward the exact same marker."
A mainlander relocating to Hong Kong, Wang found herself in an emotional low two years ago. Multiple sports failed to lift her spirits until her husband recommended outrigger canoeing. The expansive horizon and welcoming community won her over on her very first outing, anchoring her immediately.
"I was an incurable late-riser," she laughed. "Now, dragging myself out of bed at 5 a.m. is second nature, purely because of the camaraderie of my teammates," she said. Recalling her first Round the Island race in Hong Kong, she remembered encountering towering waves near Po Toi Island. Relying purely on mutual trust, the crew persevered through the chop and crossed the finish line.
As a professional jewelry designer, Wang discovered that the resilience she gained on the water seamlessly translated into her daily craft. The rigorous mindfulness required during dawn paddles mirrors the stillness and precision demanded when handcrafting delicate jewelry, the two disciplines feeding into one another.
At the World Championships in Singapore, Wang saw competitors with disabilities racing flat out, and paddlers in their late 70s cutting through the water. "It made me embrace the passage of time and realize that we should never place limits on our lives," she said.
As the session winds down, paddlers rinse the salt from their skin, change into work attire, and disperse into the glass towers in town, the workshops of industrial estates, and lecture halls.
Hong Kong will always have its gleaming skyline, but just beyond the shore, there are waves, winds, and fellow paddlers moving forward as one. ■

In the letter addressed to the current EU presidency held by Ireland, the leaders stressed that the new budget proposal should contain an amount that can be financed realistically and without further borrowing.

Analytic Philosophy and McCarthyism: A New Look (guest post)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
11:30:00 UTC
20:30:00 KST

To what extent is the “the story about the analytic turn” in philosophy a story about politics?
There’s been an increased discussion in recent years of externalist explanations of philosophy, and one such explanation that has gotten a fair amount of attention lately is the idea that McCarthyist anti-communism in the United States in the middle of the 20th Century played a significant role in analytic philosophy’s emerging dominance in the discipline at the time.
In the following guest post, Sander Verhaegh of Tilburg University, shows how the picture is quite a bit more complicated than that, casting doubt on how much the “McCarthyist thesis” can explain.
The post grew out of research Professor Verhaegh conducted for his just-published book, Logical Positivism: An American History (also here and here).
Analytic Philosophy and McCarthyism: A New Look
by Sander Verhaegh
How to explain the analytic turn in American philosophy? One controversial thesis, regularly discussed in the blogosphere, is that analytic philosophy’s dominance is a product of McCarthyism. On this view, anti-communist repression forced philosophers to abandon socially-engaged, humanistic modes of inquiry, and to a replace them with a technical, ‘politically neutral’ approach. John McCumber develops the theory in two of his books and the hypothesis recently resurfaced in publications by Christoph Schuringa and by Robert Hanna, who likens postwar analytic philosophy to “McCarthy-style anti-communist, big-capitalist politics”.
Critics have pushed back hard. Richard Hudelson and Robert Evans argue that McCumber “fails to give a historically or philosophically coherent account” of the analytic turn, while E. J. Spode compares Schuringa’s book to “A Turd in the Punchbowl”. Some contend that the McCarthyist thesis ignores simultaneous analytic turns in Canada, Australia, and the United Kingdom, such that it offers an “American explanation for … a pan-Anglophone phenomenon”. Others point out that some of the best-known analytic philosophers of the period, Bertrand Russell and Rudolf Carnap, were hardly the apolitical figures the thesis requires; while the most notorious anti-Communist witch-hunters, Arthur Lovejoy and Sidney Hook, were humanist philosophers who had studied with William James and John Dewey.
In this post, I discuss archival evidence that sheds new light on the question. In the last eight years, I spent much of my research time in archives for a book on the history of twentieth-century American philosophy, working through a wealth of material from the period: departmental records, diaries, correspondence, personnel files, and hundreds of newspapers and magazines. The book, Logical Positivism: An American History, reconstructs how émigré positivists and their American students and allies rose to dominance at private and public universities; and it shows that the story about the analytic turn is more complicated than the McCarthyist thesis suggests. In what follows, I argue that the Cold War did play a role in the development of American philosophy, albeit in various unexpected ways ignored by proponents of the McCarthyist view. At the same time, I argue that it was not the only factor, let alone a sufficient explanation, for the analytic turn.
The McCarthyist Thesis
Before discussing the evidence, let us get clear about the explanandum. Though there seem to be as many variants of the McCarthyist thesis as there are historians who have written about the period, no one argues that analytic philosophy itself is a product of the Cold War. Proponents and opponents agree that the analytic tradition predates the McCarthy era, in Europe and in the United States, even if anti-communist pressures may have changed its character in the 1950s. The central question is not to explain analytic philosophy’s presence. It is to understand its hegemonic position by the early 1960s, since American departments and journals of philosophy had been dominated by non-analytic schools and movements before the Second World War.
Naturally, it is difficult, if not impossible, to sharply define what does and does not count as ‘analytic philosophy’. Still, even a cursory look at the composition of American philosophy departments, curricula, and journals, as well as lists of APA presidents and Carus lecturers reveals that something changed in this period. Nor is this an ahistorical projection. At the time, philosophers regularly observed and discussed the rapid transformation of their discipline (more on this below), even if it took a while before ‘analytic philosophy’ became the generally accepted label for the newly dominant approach.
Second, if we are to evaluate the McCarthyist thesis, we need to get clear about the supposed victims of anti-communist repression. Few people will deny that (former) communists and Marxist scholars were pushed out of the profession. The central question is whether the Red Scare also affected pragmatists, phenomenologists, and ‘continental’ philosophers more generally. McCumber and Schuringa answer in the affirmative, arguing that anti-communist pressures blocked out any alternative to the Cold War paradigm; Joshua Rayman and James A. Good deny that pragmatism was a target. George Reisch, finally, argues for the more subtle thesis that McCarthyism played a role but affected analytic and non-analytic philosophers alike. Whereas many logical positivists and their American allies had been politically engaged in the 1930s, they turned to the “icy slopes of logic” in the years thereafter.
Finally, we need to get clear about the mechanisms through which the Cold War reshaped American philosophy. Since only a few, relatively minor philosophers were direct victims of McCarthyite investigations, proponents need a story about how the Red Scare affected the composition of journals and departments of philosophy. Most agree that anti-communist pressures created “a “climate of fear”, stimulating philosophers, journal editors, and university administrators to self-curate to prevent public controversy. But some add that there were carrots as well as sticks: Analytic philosophers were showered with funding and cushy advisory positions at institutes like RAND Corporation. Lastly, McCumber believes that there are conceptual connections between analytic philosophy and Cold War ideology. He argues that while pragmatists dealt with context-dependent problems of men, analytic philosophers saw truth as a property of sentences independent of context, thereby echoing the absolutist modes of thinking that were dominant in the period.
Analytic Philosophy Before the Red Scare
Let us turn to the evidence, starting with the state of American philosophy before the Cold War. Now, even if we accept that the McCarthyist thesis seeks to explain analytic philosophy’s dominance, not its existence or emergence, the timing is awkward: Analytic philosophy already had a solid foothold in the 1920s and 1930s. When Herbert Feigl, the first of the logical positivists to emigrate to the United States, arrived at Harvard in September 1930, it was already considered a flourishing “center” for logic-infused philosophy. Feigl found American colleagues developing ideas that were, in his words, “barely distinguishable” from the Vienna Circle’s scientific world conception, and he regularly attended meetings of a group of talented young philosophers, including W. V. Quine, Susanne Langer, and Nelson Goodman, writing that they were “almost always discuss[ing] logic” and it was “almost like in Vienna!” (letters from Dec. 6, 1930 and Apr. 5, 1931).
Harvard was not an isolated case. Even if American departments were dominated by non-analytic philosophers at the professor level, there is much archival evidence that the new generation had started to adopt the style of philosophy that was in vogue in Cambridge, Prague, Vienna, Warsaw, and Berlin. C. I. Lewis wrote that “logical posi[vi]sm easily takes the first place in the interest and the discussions of our students” (letter, Dec. 1934). Cecil Currie was surprised how much the analytic movement had “caught on among the younger generation” (letter, May 1944), and an advisor for Princeton’s department wrote about “the trend which takes the students at this time to Wittgenstein and other positivists” (letter, Apr. 1947). Even Kant-scholar Charles Hendel, who deeply opposed the trend, wrote that “we ‘older boys’ have to take cognisance … of the enthusiasm and conviction of the younger logicians” (letter, May 1951).
These historical eye-witness reports are supported by bibliometric studies. A network analysis of the most-mentioned philosophers in American journals in the 1940s, for example, reveals that the literature of the period can be divided into at least two, roughly equally-sized clusters of discussion: (1) a set of literature mentioning mostly émigré positivists, Cambridge analysts, and young American philosophers such as Ernest Nagel and Charles Stevenson; and (2) a cluster mentioning American professors who felt that the focus on “logical clarity is producing a kind of sterility that has largely destroyed [philosophy’s] cultural value” (letter by Charles Cory, 1945). The most striking difference between the two clusters is a demographic one: The median birth year of U.S.-based philosophers in what we would now call the ‘analytic’ cluster is 1899, whereas the median birth year of the U.S.-based philosophers in the second cluster is 1882— a difference of seventeen years!
Considering this generational divide, it is much less puzzling that analytic philosophy boomed after the Second World War. In the 1930s, analytic philosophy was already popular among students and junior scholars. But this was not reflected in the hiring of the period. American universities faced severe budget cuts due to the Great Depression (in the 1930s) and the War (the 1940s), so there was little space to hire analytic philosophers. Only when departments could expand in the 1950s, they had the opportunity to catch up. Coincidentally, this is exactly the period when the older generation, educated in what they called “the Golden Age of American Philosophy” (the 1900s and 1910s), retired. In consequence, it was the new, more analytically-minded generation that could steer American philosophy in a different direction, a period when the U.S. student population grew from 2.7 million to 8.0 million in two decades. A study of the growth of eleven prominent philosophy departments estimates that they increased from 6.3 to 17.3 faculty on average, meaning that there was much space for new hires.
Appointments in the McCarthy Era
Even if the timing and the swiftness of the analytic turn are partly explained by a generational shift and a fifteen-year dip in the job market, this does not entail that McCarthyism played no role in the process. So let us turn to academic hiring in more detail. Now, if the anti-communist climate of fear was an important factor in the analytic turn, one would expect deans, department chairs, and university presidents to reflect on the risks involved in hiring pragmatists, humanists, and existentialists irrespective of the candidates’ political ideas and activities. Yet, in my archival research on the hiring procedures of ten departments of philosophy, including both private (Columbia, Cornell, Harvard, Princeton, and Yale) and public universities (UC Berkeley, UMich, UMN, UIowa, and UPenn), I have not found a single example of a philosopher or administrator raising doubts about a candidate because of their philosophical affiliation.
Of course not every meeting is recorded. Moreover, it is well-known that repressive environments can be governed by tacit agreements on how to avoid public controversy. Yet it seems unlikely that the supposed political risks involved in appointing a pragmatist or a phenomenologist did not leave a single trace in thousands of pages of dossiers about possible hires, particularly since administrators often did voice concerns about other ‘liabilities’ involving race and religion. When Yale considered hiring Paul Weiss, the head of department openly shared his worry that he would be a risk because he was likely to have some of the “deficiencies that Jewish people labor”, most notably a “lack of social discretion” (letter, Oct. 2, 1945). And when Princeton was searching a new full professor, the president was openly warned not to appoint a Catholic because members of “the Roman hierarchy” could not “avoid being illiberal” (letter, May 1948). While the records show that some candidates were considered a liability because of their race or religious affiliation, I have encountered no discussions of potential hires who were considered a risk because they were pragmatists or phenomenologists.
Second, it is important to note that all these departments kept hiring non-analytic philosophers. In some cases, it was even an explicit criterion that a position should be filled by a pragmatist or continental philosopher. Jacques Barzun, provost at Columbia, urged the philosophy department to establish “a balance between ‘analysts’ and ‘humanists’” (letter, May 1960) and when Princeton could appoint two full professors, the president and the department agreed that one of the appointees had to be “broadly humanistic in his philosophical orientation” and that the other should be “logical and scientific in his outlook” (memo, Dec. 1954).
Naturally, these conclusions do not apply to philosophers who were suspect because of their political activities. Irving Copi’s personnel file at the University of Michigan contains a letter from William Frankena, defending the former Troskyite because he had “entirely renounced his questionable connections, opinions, and activities” (letter, Sep. 1948). And when the University of Minnesota refused to renew the contract of Forrest Wiggins in 1951, the department’s first Black instructor publicly announced that it was because his “Communist line” had cost the university money in the state legislature (Star Tribune, Dec. 13, 1951).
Cultural Momentum
Finally, let us turn the broader cultural conversation about philosophy. The standard focus on McCarthyism is rather one-sided because it has led historians to overlook other important elements of America’s cultural moment. The 1950s were not just marked by Cold War anxieties. It was also a decade of cultural optimism about science and technology. Science had not just helped the United States win the Second World War. It had also improved the life of average Americans through the introduction of new medical treatments such as polio vaccines, synthetic antibiotics, and ultrasound monitoring; as well as exciting consumer products such as portable television, credit cards, and long-playing vinyl records.
In order to understand the analytic turn, in particular the success of logical positivism, one has to incorporate this cultural optimism about modern science. Today, logical positivism is often associated with the dark sides of science and technology. Positivism is equated with the value-free conception of science that helped universities justify research that was used to sow death and destruction in Vietnam. But it is important to realize that these associations only emerged in the late 1960s, when the protest generation identified positivism as the ideology of the military-industrial complex. In the 1950s, logical positivism was still widely regarded as a model of modern scientific thinking, even in popular newspapers and magazines. Wallace David, a minister and gay rights activist, could note that we live “in a scientific age” and describe himself as a member of the “school of ‘logical positivism’” (ONE Magazine, June 1954). An Alabama newspaper could positively comment on a proposal to add logic to the state school curriculum, noting how comforting it would be to “listen to sermons or to political speeches and be able to say with the logical positivists that they fall short” (The Anniston Star, Mar. 15, 1957). And a political columnist could praise John F. Kennedy’s actions during the Cuban Missile Crisis because he displayed “a harshness of which the intellect only of the logical empiricist intellectual is capable” (Times Argus, Dec. 3, 1962). None of these references reflect any real engagement with positivist views or arguments. But it does provide a window on analytic philosophy’s cultural momentum: logical positivism came to exemplify a modern scientific attitude in a period when ninety-four percent of U.S. citizens felt that science was making their lives “healthier, easier, and more comfortable”.
Pragmatism, meanwhile, often got negative press, in particular during the Sputnik crisis of 1957. After the USSR successfully launched the first satellite, American media were quick to blame the school system, noting that Russian children spent much more time studying science and mathematics. And some of them held the pragmatists responsible considering their outsized influence on American education. E. F. Hutton commented that the Russians “make their kids study!”, noting that Americans did the same “before John Dewey and his followers said children should never be made to do anything” (Houston Chronicle, Feb. 23, 1958). Admiral H. G. Rickover agreed, proposing to replace Dewey’s idea that “the school is primarily a social institution” with a new, more rigorous “education process” centering on the collection of “factual knowledge” (Omaha World-Herald, Mar. 24, 1958). Analytic philosophy was considered new and exciting and pragmatism old-fashioned and outdated, even if pragmatist ideas and perspectives still played an important role in shaping the views of analytic philosophers like Hilary Putnam, W. V. Quine, Ernest Nagel, and Richard Rorty.
* * *
McCarthyism severely affected the lives of Marxists and (former) socialist philosophers. Yet it played a very limited role in the development of American philosophy. Anti-communist witch-hunts may have led philosophers to be more careful in their political pronouncements. But there is no evidence that the Red Scare significantly impacted the composition of departments of philosophy. At the same time, it would be a mistake to conclude that Cold War culture was not a factor in the analytic turn. Although analytic philosophy had been on the rise since the 1920s, demographic and economic developments had halted its representation in philosophy departments. When analytically-minded philosophers finally had the opportunity to reshape the profession, the conditions were ideal: higher education was growing, the job market was booming, and the American public celebrated science, professionalism, and ‘neutral’ expertise.

Malaysia began repatriating 1,476 Myanmar nationals Tuesday aboard three Myanmar naval vessels.

"People ask why we do not simply send them back. Send them where? Myanmar had refused to accept them before," said Anwar, according to New Straits Times news outlet.
"Now, because of our good relations with Myanmar, they have agreed to take back 5,000 from Malaysia," said Anwar in Simpang Durian town in Jelebu district of Negeri Sembilan state on July 29.

These tiny implants talk through the body itself
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
11:23:39 UTC
20:23:39 KST

When a rat’s front paw moved, its hind leg answered. Normally, such coordination is the nervous system’s job, carried out by little electrical signals traveling along nerves. This time the message went off-roading, traveling through the animal’s tissue as a faint electrical pulse and switching on an implant that jolted a nerve in that leg.
The experiment showcased the Smart Wireless Autonomous Networking System, or SWANS, which researchers described in the journal Science last week. It’s a bid to build a sort of digital nervous system for medical devices. If it holds up in people, a sensor tucked in one corner of the body could someday tell an implant in another corner far away when to get back to work. “The body is not just where the devices sit,” says Yoon Jae Lee, an assistant professor of computer science at Georgia State University and a co-author of the study. “It’s become a part of the communication network.”
Pacemakers and some other implants can already sense trouble and respond on the spot. But many treatments, such as insulin pumps, need to listen to what’s happening in one place in the body to decide what to do in another. Today that communication often runs over Bluetooth. The dream is to embed sensors wherever they’re needed, such as deep in the gut or muscles, where there’s little room for the bulky battery that wireless communication demands.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Smaller implants are also less likely to disturb the body and the tissue around them, according to Hyowon “Hugh” Lee, a professor of biomedical engineering at Purdue University and a program manager at the U.S. Advanced Research Projects Agency for Health, who was not involved in the study. “The body doesn’t really like when you jab things into it,” he says. By skipping traditional wireless technology, the SWANS team made its devices small enough to inject with a syringe.
A SWANS network pairs sensors, which notice some change in the body, with actuators that do something about it once they get the signal. In the rat, sensors worn on the front paws reported to a wearable hub, and the actuator was a stimulator hooked up to the sciatic nerve in the hind leg.
The trick is that the body’s salty tissues conduct electricity, so a tiny voltage pulse from the hub could spread across the rat’s body to reach the implant. “We have this ability to decode information in one spot and shuttle it all the way to another area where it’s needed,” says Alex Abramson, an assistant professor researching biotechnology at the Georgia Institute of Technology and the study’s senior author. According to Abramson, the pulses are basically imperceptible, comparable to what a pacemaker sends to the heart.
Keeping the messages simple, closer to a yes or no than a data stream, means the devices use very little power; the implants draw next to nothing while they await a signal. By the team’s estimate, an actuator triggered once a day could last for about a year, which would translate to an annual doctor’s visit to pull out the dead implants and inject new ones.
The authors see uses for SWANS well beyond a rat’s hind legs, from drug delivery to prosthetic limbs. “Imagine that your prosthetic was connecting to your skin,” Abramson says. “Well, we can send information from the endpoints of a muscle all the way to the skin and then have that information sent into the prosthetic.”
Using the body as a shuttle comes with some limits, though. In the study, the signals traveled about 40 centimeters, plenty of distance to cross a rat’s body but not so much for treatments in people. Humans are fattier and bulkier than the average rat, potentially further limiting how far these signals can travel, according to Hugh Lee. Amplifying the signals could help, as long as the electronics stay small. And the network has to be safe against anything, or anyone, trying to mess with it. “If you have some way of spoofing a wearable device to be able to activate things that are not supposed to be activated, that could be problematic,” he says.
Researchers have been chasing digital nervous systems for decades. One earlier attempt, a line of injectable microstimulators called the Bionic Neuron, or BION, made it into human trials but never received approval from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration. SWANS has only made it into rats. But the idea is too tantalizing for engineers to shelve: an implant that doesn’t need to stream much information at all and needs only the body to carry a whisper from one place to another.

Seven Arrested in Massive EU Fraud Scheme Selling Used Phones as New
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
11:23:00 UTC
20:23:00 KST

An international law enforcement operation led by the European Public Prosecutor’s Office (EPPO) resulted in the arrests of seven people, including two alleged ringleaders, to dismantle a criminal network suspected of selling more than one million used mobile phones as new, the EPPO announced Tuesday. The cross-border crackdown, code-named "Troja," involved more than 1,700 officers conducting over 160 searches across 19 countries. Authorities estimate the scheme defrauded European Union consumers of at least 300 million euros ($340 million) and caused 30 million euros ($34 million) in value-added tax (VAT) losses.
According to prosecutors, the syndicate assembled phones from used components in Hong Kong and the United Arab Emirates. The devices were then shipped through the Netherlands to warehouses in Germany, where they were cleaned, packaged, and sold on online marketplaces to unsuspecting customers across the EU as brand-new products.
To maximize illicit profits, the group allegedly used shell companies in Austria, Bulgaria, Germany, the Netherlands, and Switzerland to fraudulently exploit a "margin taxation" scheme since 2018. By classifying the devices as resold goods for tax purposes while charging buyers full new-item prices, the network evaded paying the full VAT due, generating widespread tax deficits across multiple member states.

Malaysia gave refuge to Rohingya; now it wants them to go

Malaysia gave refuge to Rohingya; now it wants them to go
Malaysia welcomed persecuted Muslim minority but now plans to send them back to Myanmar amid rising hate against them.
Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia – The children sitting cross-legged on the floor are a mix of ages but are all enrolled in one class out of necessity. Coming from Rohingya families, they are not allowed to access formal education and must rely upon the generosity of donors to support informal learning centres, such as the one they attend in a quiet neighbourhood in Kuala Lumpur.
“Because of their help, we can teach our kids here,” explained Riyadh Al Haq, a Rohingya human rights activist whose NGO runs the centre.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Human rights situation in Myanmar ‘plummets to new low’, UN says
- list 2 of 4Malaysia offers to invite Myanmar leader in Rohingya repatriation push
- list 3 of 4Myanmar military launches air strike on Rakhine market, killing at least 33

On one recent morning, they were busy learning the Quran, but lessons also cover a standard range of academic subjects.
They and their families are also not eligible to access the healthcare system, and their parents are not allowed to work and must rely on informal employment, such as at car washes, in restaurant kitchens and at courier services.
Still, life for the estimated 125,000 Rohingya who now call Malaysia home is better than the lives they left behind in Myanmar.
“Because of their [Malaysian people’s] kindness, our people can stay in this country. They can live here. We are more safe than in Myanmar,” Riyadh told Al Jazeera.
Repatriation criticised
However, on Tuesday, the Malaysian government began the repatriation of an initial group of nearly 1,500 Rohingya to Myanmar. The operation has drawn renewed attention to the plight of the Rohingya people, regarded as one of the world’s most persecuted minorities. The Muslim ethnic group is essentially stateless because they are not recognised as citizens by Myanmar.
The repatriation has been criticised by the United Nations and international rights groups given the longstanding persecution of the Rohingya in their home state of Rakhine in western Myanmar. In 2017, the Myanmar military launched a brutal crackdown, forcing more than 700,000 Rohingya to flee, mostly to neighbouring Bangladesh.
The military campaign, which involved widespread destruction of Rohingya properties and the killing of thousands of people, is widely condemned as tantamount to a genocide. A case of genocide brought by The Gambia is under way at the International Court of Justice at The Hague. The verdict is expected next month or in November.
The Malaysian government insisted that all those returning are volunteers and their safety and wellbeing are guaranteed.
Critics of Kuala Lumpur’s policy said an ongoing civil war in Myanmar makes such guarantees meaningless. Myanmar descended into civil war after the military conducted a coup in 2021 and removed the democratically elected government of Nobel Peace Prize laureate Aung San Suu Kyi.
Malaysia’s government, led by Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim, has pledged to return 5,000 Myanmar nationals in what many see as a reversal of the country’s longstanding policy of leniency towards the presence of the Rohingya.
‘Widespread sympathy for their plight’
Not being a signatory to the 1951 United Nations Refugee Convention, Malaysia doesn’t grant the Rohingya refugee status but has taken a tolerant attitude towards their arrival.
Malaysians have a religious and cultural affinity with the Rohingya, and there is widespread sympathy for their plight. Many have extended an unofficial welcome to many migrants often making the perilous ocean journey on overcrowded boats.
But that attitude has started to change in recent years due to economic pressures and viral social media misinformation campaigns. Coordinated online petitions calling for the expulsion of refugees and other marginalised groups have garnered hundreds of thousands of signatures.
Nur Sadek, executive director of Rohingya Rights Response, has been monitoring social media content that spreads hateful and hurtful messaging about the Rohingya.
One content creator who has thousands of followers has posted a series of clips in which he mocks Rohingya openly to their faces while complaining to the camera about how they allegedly smell. In another clip produced by self-styled vigilantes, three men are seen stopping and questioning a Rohingya passer-by in the street.
“A lot of the community members are very afraid to go outside and to be recognised as a Rohingya,” Sadek said. “They are very afraid of being harassed by the local people and by some of the content creators.”
That fear also extends to employment, however menial the jobs might be, with some Malaysian businesses reportedly turning Rohingya away.
“Most of the Rohingya people have relied upon informal work, and even that informal work is inaccessible right now with the increase in hate and misinformation. And it is affecting the livelihoods of every Rohingya,” Sadek told Al Jazeera.
As Malaysia looks ahead to national elections early next year, political parties might find the Rohingya issue is too big a vote-winning opportunity to pass up. And the Rohingya, as they so often have, could find themselves the losers.

AI generated
NEW YORK – Oura has delayed its US initial public offering, the smart ring maker said on Sept 29, citing market uncertainty and denting hopes for a pickup in the traditionally strong fall listings window.
It joins a growing list of prospective issuers pulling back as surging bond yields and higher interest rates weigh on markets.
The US IPO market has hit a bump after a strong start to the year, as investors grapple with concerns that the AI trade has run its course, the Federal Reserve’s interest-rate hike and geopolitical turmoil.
The consumer technology company and some of its existing investors had marketed 50 million shares in the offering priced in an indicated range of US$40 (S$51) to US$44 apiece.
At the top of the indicated range, Oura would have raised US$2.2 billion at a fully diluted valuation of US$15.62 billion. It was expected to price the IPO later in the day and begin trading on Nasdaq on Sept 30.
The company, founded more than a decade ago in Finland, reached a valuation of about US$11 billion in a late-stage funding round in 2025.
IPOs typically require stable investor appetite and supportive market conditions for companies to achieve their desired valuations.
“Higher rates are clearly making investors more selective, particularly on growth valuations. Still, I wouldn’t say the IPO window is closed, especially with Anthropic still pushing ahead with what could be one of the largest IPOs ever,” Ipox research associate Lukas Muhlbauer told Reuters.
Timing the market
The offering would have been the first sizeable autumn market US IPO since the traditional summer lull, with analysts viewing Oura’s debut as a key test of investor appetite for high-growth companies.
Earlier in September, nuclear services company Holtec suspended its planned US IPO amid increased scrutiny of vast capital being deployed in sectors related to AI.
“We aim to deliver an extraordinary IPO for our employees and investors, and we have the luxury of choosing our moment. In the meantime, we will execute against the opportunities ahead,” Oura chief executive Tom Hale said in a statement.
The company said it was profitable and forecast revenue to jump 90% in fiscal 2026 from a year earlier.
“Reports indicated that the offering was around four times oversubscribed, which is a decent level of demand, but not necessarily overwhelming for a well-known consumer brand,” Muehlbauer said.
Oura did not immediately respond to Reuters’ request for further details on the postponement.
Meanwhile, AI laboratory Anthropic is expected to headline the second half of the year for the IPO market, with Reuters reporting, citing sources, that it could debut after the US midterm elections in November.
Oura has helped popularise smart rings, which track metrics such as heart health, activity and sleep.
It added that the response to the launch of its flagship Oura Ring 5 has been “exceptionally strong”, bringing the number of paid members on its platform to 5.7 million.
Smart rings are carving out a niche between traditional fitness trackers and smartwatches, offering personalised health insights in a smaller, screen-free form that can be worn around the clock and typically has longer battery life. REUTERS

Historic Greek church in central Türkiye set to open to public soon
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
11:16:05 UTC
20:16:05 KST

Tunahan Akgun
29 September 2026•Update: 29 September 2026
A 190-year-old Greek Orthodox church in central Türkiye is being prepared for visitors as part of efforts to expand tourism beyond the better-known sites of the Cappadocia region.
The St. Eustathios Greek Church in Incesu, a district of Kayseri province about 45-50 kilometers (28-31 miles) from the Cappadocia destinations of Avanos, Urgup and Goreme, was built in 1836 and is being converted into the Incesu City Museum.
The church, which features wall paintings, stonework and inscriptions in Karamanli -- Turkish written using the Greek alphabet -- is one of Incesu's important historical structures.
Its restoration, which began in 2021, was completed last year. The work preserved the building's original fabric as well as its frescoes, reliefs, carvings and other features, according to the Kayseri Metropolitan Municipality.
Tayfun Talasli, head of the municipality's Historical Buildings and Museums Branch Directorate, said the church was used as a place of worship until the 1923 population exchange between Greece and Türkiye.
It was later used for different purposes, including as a military warehouse, archive, theater hall and vocational school, he told Anadolu.
The museum's display and arrangement work is more than 80% complete, and officials plan to open it soon.
Talasli said the restoration was based on archival photographs, documents and oral histories of people who had lived in the area.
"We will create a museum on the ground floor, where we will tell about the city's tangible and intangible cultural heritage," he said.
Visitors will be able to learn about Incesu's history, architecture, notable figures, archaeology, gastronomy, agriculture and grape production.
They will also see artifacts, including ceramics unearthed at the nearby Orensehir archaeological site, Talasli said.
The municipality hopes the church will be incorporated into the wider Cappadocia tourism destination, allowing visitors to combine the historic site with the region's established tourist attractions.
