Puja after paribartan: What is changing in West Bengal’s biggest festival
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
10:07:56 UTC
19:07:56 KST

One of the enduring memories of the Mamata Banerjee era in West Bengal will be the elaborate Durga Puja carnival, where handpicked baro pujos (marquee pujas) would parade along Red Road with tableaux before the CM and other dignitaries in an almost Republic Day-esque procession. It would often end with Mamata Banerjee doing an impromptu jig with the crème de la crème of the Bengali film industry.The carnival has been scrapped. Instead, a pre-Puja event will be held at the iconic Eden Gardens on Mahalaya, October 10, which Prime Minister Narendra Modi is expected to attend. These and many other changes are expected as West Bengal counts down to the homecoming of the Goddess.This year marks a significant break in Bengal's politics. The BJP government took office on May 9, making this its first Durga Puja in power in the state. And some changes are already in motion. Beyond the cosmetic, is Bengal's intrinsic style of celebrating Durga Puja going to change?The number of pujas continues to grow. As of September 24, 2,318 Durga Pujas had already registered on Kolkata's Sahaj single-window permission portal, including 270 new applicants, with more applications still expected. In 2025, the final tally of 2,936 applications was the highest ever. Across Bengal, the state power department expects the number of community pujas to cross 65,000 this year, an estimate based partly on demand for temporary electricity connections.
Durga Puja Carnival-has been scrapped
The barowari, or community-puja, tradition in Bengal is generally traced to late-18th-century Guptipara, although historians differ over the precise year and even whether the earliest community celebration there was Durga Puja or Jagaddhatri Puja. The word barowari is generally traced to baro yaar, or "twelve friends". From the patronage of zamindars to that of influential political leaders, Durga Puja's format has constantly changed, though it remains the cornerstone of Bengal's annual cultural calendar.
From ek-chalar thakur, where the divine family is presented within a single frame, to multi-part installations; from sabeki pratima, or traditional-style idols, to theme pujas; from sholar saaj to idols made from unconventional materials, creative people have continually found new ways to express their love and reverence for Goddess Durga.In the run-up to Mahalaya, Kumartuli, north Kolkata's famous idol-making quarter, draws growing crowds of photographers, selfie-seekers and curious visitors into its narrow lanes. The adjoining Kumartuli Ghat is now adding another attraction. A Rs 10-crore redevelopment of a 300-metre stretch of the Hooghly riverfront, with viewing areas, walkways and improved public facilities, is expected to add to the draw.
Change in Durga Puja patronage
The most visible change this year is in the patronage of Durga Pujas. For years, the names of influential Trinamool leaders were virtually interchangeable with those of Kolkata's marquee pujas. There was Sujit Bose's Sreebhumi, Arup Biswas's Suruchi, Firhad Hakim's Chetla Agrani and Partha Chatterjee's Naktala Udayan Sangha, among others.Along with these, many up-and-coming political leaders ensured that relatively unknown Durga pandals shot to fame with innovative themes. Often, hosting a large-scale Durga Puja became a proxy for growing political clout.That competition for spectacle and social ownership, however, long predates contemporary party politics. Kaliprasanna Sinha's 19th-century Hutom Pyanchar Naksha used Durga Puja to lampoon Calcutta's babu culture, its display, extravagance and social pretensions.At Sreebhumi Sporting Club, the extravaganza that became synonymous with former Trinamool minister Sujit Bose is being prepared by a new committee. BJP leader Kanak Debnath has become president, with the organisers promising to retain the puja's grandeur while ending prolonged road blockades.
Sreebhumi Puja in 2025
At Suruchi Sangha, for years associated with Arup Biswas and his brother Swarup, BJP MLA Sourav Sikdar is now secretary. Suruchi's new committee has replaced the Biswas brothers, although the transition was accompanied by protests from residents. At Tala Prattoy, which has been delivering extremely eye-catching themes over the last few years, much of the previous organising set-up has changed, with Sushanta Shibani Pal handling this year's theme.The organisational change is extending beyond individual clubs. A new statewide coordination platform, Paschim Banga Durga Puja Samannay Samiti, or West Bengal Durga Puja Coordination Committee, is taking shape, with Kartik Maharaj as chairman and BJP MLA Rudranil Ghosh as chief adviser. It could emerge as an alternative pole to the established Forum for Durgotsab, which represents hundreds of committees.The churn has reached venues old and new. Known for its elaborate Christmas and New Year celebrations, Park Street will host a Durga Puja at Allen Park for the first time this year. Without missing a beat, Kolkata Sanatani Sangha, fronted by BJP leader Shankudeb Panda, will be organising it.At Mohammad Ali Park, competing committees put up banners under different names after BJP councillor Meena Devi Purohit proposed renaming the historic venue Mahabali Park. The iconic Bagbazar Puja, meanwhile, landed in trouble over a deadlocked committee election before the courts sorted it out.The financial machinery behind Durga Puja is also being recalibrated. The Mamata Banerjee government introduced annual assistance to puja committees at Rs 10,000 in 2018 and increased it over the years to Rs 1.1 lakh in 2025. The new BJP government has announced Rs 1 lakh for 2026, while chief minister Suvendu Adhikari has appealed to big-budget organisers to leave the assistance for smaller celebrations that need it.During TMC rule, BJP leader Sajal Ghosh's Santosh Mitra Square was something of a 'rebel' puja, refusing to take grants. With power having changed hands and TMC virtually disintegrating, there are no such rebel pujas this time, at least publicly.Several prominent committees have agreed to forgo the grant, in line with the government's appeal. The BJP government has also asked electricity suppliers to provide free power to organisers; under the previous government, the waiver in 2025 was 80%.In Birbhum, BJP district president Uday Shankar Banerjee told puja committees that clubs taking the 2026 government grant must display the chief minister's photograph or face action, a claim promptly shot down by minister Dilip Ghosh.
Navratri tradition in Durga Puja?
It is perhaps on food that the focus will be most intense.In late August, Swami Nirgunananda, a member of the VHP's central advisory council, suggested that non-vegetarian food should be kept away from the immediate puja space, while acknowledging that Bengal's Durga Puja has never been exclusively vegetarian. VHP leaders subsequently clarified that there was no official or binding directive banning non-vegetarian food during Durga Puja.Days later, religious preacher Dhirendra Krishna Shastri, popularly known as Bageshwar Baba, went considerably further. He criticised the consumption of non-vegetarian food during Durga Puja, describing those who did so as pakhandis, or hypocrites.The remarks provoked criticism, including from within the BJP. State party president Samik Bhattacharya defended Bengal's food traditions, while Adhikari subsequently visited Kalighat temple and consumed traditional prasad that included fried fish, fish head and basanti pulao. At Suruchi Sangha, where BJP MLA Sourav Sikdar is now secretary, organisers have said mutton and hilsa will continue to be served at the Maha Navami feast. Many housing societies where community Durga Pujas take place have also affirmed that their Puja feasts aren't going to change and will remain largely non-vegetarian, barring Maha Ashtami.In large parts of north India, abstaining from meat during Navratri is commonplace. Critics of the BJP have expressed concern that such a food culture could gradually be pushed on Bengal. There is no evidence of any government plan to impose such a restriction. But the effect could be subtler than a formal ban.Some organisers are already drawing a firmer boundary around the immediate sacred space. Thakurpukur SB Park and Chaltabagan have announced restrictions on visitors entering while eating, while the new Allen Park puja will have no food stalls inside the park, TOI has reported previously.There is a perception that, at many pandals, egg-roll stalls and other non-vegetarian food outlets will be stationed farther away from the main arena where the Goddess will be placed.
To theme or not to?
Theme pujas have not been barred, but organisers have been asked to ensure that idols and themes do not hurt religious sentiments or undermine what the new government describes as Sanatani traditions. That has prompted some artists and organisers to tread more cautiously.However, social and experimental subjects continue this year too, including themes around care workers, gender identity and ecology. What is changing is the political vocabulary surrounding them. At the same time, several high-profile pujas this year are invoking patriotism, nationalism and Hindu cultural identity.There is no official census separating theme pujas from traditional ones.Santosh Mitra Square, whose committee is headed by BJP MLA Sajal Ghosh, has chosen Vande Mataram. New Town Sanatani Durga Puja, whose leadership includes chief ministerial adviser Subrata Gupta and Kartik Maharaj, is exploring what its organisers describe as the relationship between ancient Indian traditions and modern science.
Santosh Mitra Square in 2025 showing Operation Sindoor
The use of Goddess Durga as a political or nationalist metaphor is hardly new. In Bankimchandra Chattopadhyay's Amar Durgotsav (My Durga Puja), included in Kamalakanter Daptar, an opium-addled Kamalakanta looks at the Durga image on Saptami and eventually sees in her Bengal itself (Banga Janani, Mother Bengal), invoking the Goddess as an image of collective strength and awakening.Nazrul would later take the idea in another direction. In his Durga and Agomoni compositions, the rebel poet repeatedly invoked the Goddess as Shakti, or living power, rather than merely an image of clay. His 1922 poem Anandamoyeer Agamane used Durga's arrival as an anti-colonial metaphor so explicitly that the British prosecuted him for sedition.The VHP's Nirgunananda, though, has argued for a more explicitly religious ownership of the festival. At an August meeting with Puja organisers, he rejected the formulation that "religion belongs to individuals, but festivals belong to everyone", arguing instead that festivals primarily belong to followers of the faith, while people of other religions were welcome to visit.That marks a clear difference in outlook, which may well become one of the faultlines around Bengal's Durga Puja celebrations.
'Sharadotsav' coinage contested
Pandal-hopping has also traditionally been an easy way to get a crash course in political history.The Left Front's stalls, where the para-r communist kaku would be stationed selling books on Markshiyo Darshan, or Marxist philosophy, were hard to miss. Seeing them, the TMC also started its Jago Bangla stalls, though Didi, a skilled politician, never quite got the stamp of approval from Bengalis for her literary exploits.This year, though, the Left may face problems putting up some of those stalls.The name Sharadotsav, synonymous with Durga Puja, is facing questions. Chief minister Suvendu Adhikari has asked committees not to accommodate CPI(M) bookstalls that describe the festival as "Sharadotsav" instead of "Durga Puja", arguing that the terminology dilutes its religious identity.Interestingly, Rabindranath Tagore wrote Sharadotsav, a play celebrating the autumn season, way back in 1908, a point also raised by Left leaders in response to the controversy. A puja committee at Kamardanga in Tangra has gone further, announcing that it will not allow stalls run by CPI(M), DYFI, SUCI or other Left-wing organisations at its celebration. The committee has appealed to other organisers to follow suit, while CPI(M) has criticised the move.
How the calendar is changing
The Red Road immersion carnival, first held under Mamata Banerjee's government in 2016, has been discontinued. In its place comes a grand Mahalaya celebration at Eden Gardens on October 10, 2026, one week before Maha Shashthi on October 17. The programme is expected to feature traditional performers, thousands of dhakis, fireworks and a drone show. Prime Minister Narendra Modi is expected to attend and virtually inaugurate prominent Kolkata pujas from the programme. The Eden Gardens presentation aims to recreate important events and rituals associated with Durga Puja.Mahalaya holds a very special significance. Beyond tarpan, the ritual offering to one's ancestors, Birendra Krishna Bhadra's recitation in the Mahishasuramardini radio programme, which became associated with Mahalaya from the 1930s, has itself become a ritual. Hosting such a gala event on that day gives the new government a prominent ceremonial role at the opening of Bengal's Puja season.
Tarpan in Mahalaya
There are changes for ordinary pandal-hoppers too. The new government has said Puja pandals will not be allowed to be inaugurated before Mahalaya. Maha Ashtami will be a dry day, with liquor sales prohibited. DJs have been banned during Puja celebrations and immersion processions, while organisers have been instructed to avoid prolonged road blockades and complete immersions within the prescribed period.Even the appearance of Kolkata Police's crowd-management volunteers is set to change, with police floating a tender for orange T-shirts and caps to replace the familiar white-and-blue attire.There is not much clarity yet about how active the TMC will be during Durga Puja. But one thing Kolkata will surely be revisiting through reels is Mamata Banerjee's one-liners and gestures, from her suggestion that kash, the tall white kans grass associated with the Bengali autumn, could be used as stuffing for pillows to her symbolic chokhu daan.
File Image of Mamata Banerjee doing chokhu daan
What no government can legislate
So will Bengal's intrinsic style of celebrating Puja change? The answer may lie in how varied that style has always been.There has never been one compulsory Bengali Puja menu, or even one compulsory visual grammar. Mahendranath Datta, the younger brother of Swami Vivekananda, recorded striking differences between Durga images in Shakta and Vaishnava households. In Shakta homes, he wrote, Durga's lion had the conventional lion's face; in Gosain or Vaishnava homes, the lion had a horse-like face, apparently marking a distinction between the two traditions. On food too, practices differed. At Brahmin homes, guests could be served rice, five vegetable dishes, curd and payesh; in Shakta Brahmin households, he noted, fish was also permitted, while Kayastha homes served luchi.The traditions that have survived in Bengal's old family pujas are equally difficult to squeeze into a single dietary rule. The Sabarna Roy Chowdhury family continues to offer katla as Nabami bhog.
At Chorbagan Chatterjee Bari, fish is offered during the Puja days. At the Janbazar home of Rani Rashmoni's descendants, on the other hand, the Goddess receives vegetarian bhog even as non-vegetarian food is served to guests, reported TOI previously.There is no quick primer on how to be Sanatani across Bengal's myriad Durga Puja traditions. The pandals may change hands, and the colour of uniforms may change. But beneath the contest for ownership lies a diversity of practice too old and too deep-rooted.Perhaps the more things change, the more they stay the same.

FIFA has accused UEFA of conducting a “misinformation campaign” and seeking to influence its upcoming presidential election amid an escalating legal dispute over the abandoned FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE) project.
In a filing submitted Monday to the US District Court for the Southern District of Florida, FIFA opposed UEFA’s request for the disclosure of evidence and documents related to the project.
European football’s governing body accused FIFA President Gianni Infantino of “criminal mismanagement” and promoting what it called “a fraudulently off-market price” for his own benefit in connection with the FFE proposal.

Israel revokes aliyah of Jewish left-wing activists after initial approval
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
10:06:53 UTC
19:06:53 KST

Israel’s Population Authority (PIBA) has revoked the aliyah approval of two Jewish activists in their 20s, both active in pro-Palestine advocacy in the West Bank.
This was first reported by Ha’aretz on Monday, but The Jerusalem Post spoke with one of the individuals – British national Lawrence Shenkin – who said the details of the report are correct. The story of the other individual – an American woman – mirrors Shenkin’s.
These are believed to be the first known cases where halakhic Jews without criminal records have been denied the right to immigrate to Israel.
Shenkin grew up in a Modern Orthodox family in Golders Green. He was raised Zionist and has already lived in Israel for five years.
He moved to Israel at 18 to attend yeshiva, intending the stay and live in the country permanently. During this time, Shenkin joined the left-wing religious organization Bnei Avraham in 2023. As such, he has been involved in protecting Palestinian communities in the West Bank from alleged Israeli settler harassment.
In November 2025, on the cusp of finishing his university studies, he started the process of Aliyah.
He submitted all his files to PIBA and, in January, received an email saying, “Due to a change in the circumstances of your case, your ETA has been revoked.” In lieu of citizenship, an ETA is required to enter Israel.
Shenkin said he didn't think much of it, assuming the ETA revocation was a simple response to his Aliyah.
However, months went by, and he still hadn't heard any update on his Aliyah.
He then traveled to the UK to visit his family for Passover, and applied for a new ETA to return, which was again denied.
“I couldn’t really think of what was happening,” Shenkin told the Post. “Friends then told me that lots of left-wing activists have had their ETAs denied and had their ETAs revoked and that maybe it was related to that.”
He decided to stay in the UK and finish his Aliyah from there. In July, he received an email from the Jewish Agency congratulating him on his successful Aliyah.
Peace activists' aliyah denied over 'Section 40'
“I was elated. I sent my passport to the consulate to receive the visa because that’s what they said to do. “About three weeks later, I got an email from the Jewish Agency saying, 'Based on information received from the Population and Immigration Authority, and in accordance with Section 40 of the Entry into Israel Law, the approval of your eligibility for aliyah is currently under review by the Authority and is temporarily revoked.”
Shenkin’s lawyer said there is no Section 40 of the Entry into Israel Law. There is an amendment 40, which denies entry to people who denied October 7th or who call for the prosecution of Israeli soldiers, which Shenkin has not done.
“I was quite offended at the notion that it could be me. I’ve never done something like that ever at all,” he told the Post.
Shenkin’s lawyer informed him that Israel could not legally deny him Aliyah, given he is halachically Jewish, and has “never committed a crime.”
“I don’t know under what grounds they denied me.”
“I’ve been torn away from my homeland, which I love and whose welfare I’m only looking to contribute to. Israel is truly one of my greatest loves.”
Shenkin describes himself as a “very passionate religious Zionist.”
“I believe that, you know, there’s a mitzvah to be living in the land of Israel,” he said.
He, however, also believes that it is his religious duty to protect Palestinians from “settler violence” and “ethnic cleansing.”
He cited the Torah as commanding Jews to care for the welfare of the ger and the toshav.
“This is a Torah commandment, and the people who are committing this violence, often they’re wearing kippot and tzitzit and peyot; they are committing horrific acts that bring a terrible name onto Israel and onto my community of religious Zionists.”
Advocacy with Bnei Avraham
This informs much of his advocacy with Bnei Avraham.
“We’re a religious Jewish organization interested in creating a positive relationship between Palestinian communities and the religious Jewish community in Israel and in trying to prevent settler violence against Palestinians,” he said. I have been active with the group since late 2023, early 2024.”
“In 2025, our focus was on two villages that we had a connection with in the South Jordan Valley, Ras Ein al-Auja and Mu’arrajat. We would regularly go to these villages. And when settlers would come there, we went in principle, our hope was we were going to spend time with our friends who live in this village. These two villages no longer exist because they were ethnically cleansed as a result of settler violence. Every time we went every day, they suffered some kind of incident interaction with hilltop youth where they would get harassed, we would get harassed.”
“Violent incidents are very common. And so we would go because we wanted to stand in solidarity with them. And also we felt that as Israelis, oftentimes the police took us more seriously than they would take the Palestinians.”
He claimed that neither he nor anyone in Bnei Avraham “has ever been involved in a violent incident in the West Bank or a criminal incident in the West Bank of any type.”
“We are very careful about obeying the law and being respectful human beings,” he added.
When pressed by the Post on whether this activism and rhetoric may fuel the fire of anti-Israel hate and misconceptions around all settlers being violent, Shenkin said that idea is a “misrepresentation.”
“We were in the Palestinian village of Ras al-Ain. Okay. Where people not from that village came to invade private property and harass the people who lived on that property. These are people who have come and established an outpost with the goal of expelling the people there, explicitly the goal of coming to expel the people there. That is what they pursued and did.”
“If the state of Israel believes that non-criminal activity–activity that is in line with the biblical Torah commandments of caring for the welfare of non-Jews in the land of Israel–doing that in a way in a pacifistic way that does not involve violence, if they believe that–it is a serious offense that denies a person the rights that are codified in the Torah.”
“If that’s the case, it’s a total outrage, and that’s why this is a big story.”
Shenkin hopes that with public interest in the story it will be resolved.
“What’s happening here is anti-Zionist. After all, the whole promise of Israel is that any Jew can move there simply because they’re Jewish. And now there’s this new idea that you have to support a certain agenda, or else we don’t want you.”
PIBA told the Post that “The requests have been received and are being reviewed individually on their own merits. There is no freeze whatsoever.”
The Jerusalem Post was unable to reach the Jewish Agency for comment; however, the organization told Ha’aretz: “The Population and Immigration Authority is the government body responsible for implementing the Law of Return. In light of this, and for reasons of privacy, we cannot comment on the details of the cases.”

OPINION - The consensus of extremism in Israeli politics
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
10:04:12 UTC
19:04:12 KST

Daniel Levy is the president of the US/Middle East Project. He served as an Israeli peace negotiator at the 1993 Oslo-B talks under Israeli Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin and the 2001 Taba negotiations under Israeli Prime Minister Ehud Barak.
Israel’s upcoming election on Oct. 27 has been described in hyperbolic terms as unlike any before it, the most fateful, or perhaps even its last. The campaign, too, has been defined by mutual accusations between the government and opposition of betrayal, and fears that growing political incitement will spill over into violence. A spectator would be forgiven for believing that the differences between the diverging paths represented by the 11 viable Zionist and Jewish ultra-Orthodox political parties, split for the most part into two camps, would be vast. However, the options at the ballot box offer little alternative to a vision of permanent occupation and war that has become a blinkered and bloody national consensus.
Rather than being understood through left and right, the Israeli political map is defined by a central fault line: Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his political partners -- the far-right parties led by Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich and the ultra-Orthodox parties. Still on trial for three counts of corruption, Netanyahu is depicted as putting personal interest over national interest: his negligence in the run-up to Oct. 7, his exemption of the ultra-Orthodox from conscription at a time of manpower shortages, and his drive to strengthen the executive branch at the expense of the judiciary.
The lead actor in the opposition is former IDF Chief of Staff Gadi Eisenkot, whose Yashar party (meaning Straight or Honest) consistently polls above Netanyahu's Likud as the largest party. The remainder of the anti-Netanyahu Zionist opposition bloc is made up of Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid's Yachad (Together) party -- the two having led the only, short-lived, non-Netanyahu government of the last 17 years, from June 2021 to December 2022 -- as well as Yair Golan's centre-left The Democrats (the continuation of the old Labor Party together with Meretz) and Avigdor Lieberman's hard-right Yisrael Beiteinu.
These four parties have agreed to cooperate but have not agreed on their candidate for the premiership, and none of them are running on a platform of ending settlements, withdrawing from occupied territories, endorsing the two-state option, or repositioning Israel regionally (for instance, the occupation zones in Syria or Lebanon). They focus instead on questions of enlisting all citizens into the military (ending existing carve-outs for the ultra-Orthodox), reversing the Netanyahu coalition’s judicial overhaul, and properly investigating the failures of Oct. 7. To understand the remarkably limited scope of the alternative agenda proposed by the opposition is to understand the consensus that has emerged in Israel around an extremism that generated societal support for the genocidal campaign in Gaza. Therefore, in key respects, the opposition has largely replicated the hardline politics spearheaded by Netanyahu, Ben-Gvir, and Smotrich. The extent to which a rightward shift has crystallized, enabled by decades of international impunity, has crowded out space for a more pragmatic or realpolitik approach.
The opposition often criticizes the government for failing to turn military successes of the last three years into diplomatic initiatives. In so doing, it offers no critique of the military action itself -- even as evidence accumulates of the multitude of war crimes -- and there is no serious questioning of the military role in the West Bank, Lebanon, Syria, or the broader region.
What is more, while calling for diplomatic alternatives, the proposals on offer from the opposition also fall into the category of being zero-sum and unrealistic. None are proposing solutions that could plausibly be acceptable to Palestinians, Lebanese, Syrians, or any other self-respecting peoples of the region -- and these proposals would almost certainly lead back to the same dependency on the hard power of military force and American coercion.
At times, parts of the opposition even outflank the government from the right. They regurgitate visions of regional normalization without progress on the Palestinian front, and of continued pursuit, including via the military, of regime change in Iran. Moreover, key opposition leader Naftali Bennett has targeted Türkiye as Israel’s next main regional adversary to be confronted at all costs and has called for the formal designation of Qatar as an enemy state, with all that flows from that.
For all its shortcomings, there are nonetheless differences between this bloc and what is on offer from the current coalition of Netanyahu, the rest of the extreme right, and the ultra-Orthodox. Netanyahu’s Likud now largely resembles the Ben-Gvir and Smotrich factions, and there is a third party of the fascist right, recently established and running in this election, the Amcha Yisrael party led by retired IDF Brig. Gen. Ofer Winter, which is equally committed to territorial maximalism and the ethnic cleansing of Palestinians. Set against the policies of the existing Netanyahu coalition, it is worth acknowledging that the Zionist opposition bloc does offer apartheid rather than genocide. It is conceivable that an Eisenkot-led government formed by the opposition would ease some of the conditions in Gaza, including on the humanitarian front; would restrict some of the government’s excesses of Palestinian displacement and land confiscation in the West Bank; and might allow the Palestinian Authority to financially breathe. It might possibly even pursue a degree of de-escalation in the region. None of this constitutes a platform of peace, but it might ease some of the tension, radicalization, and suffering caused by Israel’s actions.
However, polling suggests that the election outcome remains unclear. While Netanyahu’s bloc is due to lose something like 10% of its parliamentary representation and significantly fall short of victory, the Zionist opposition bloc also fails to achieve the magic number of 61 seats needed to form a governing majority. This in itself paints a very telling picture. The balance of power is likely to be held by the non-Zionist parties, which overwhelmingly represent Israel’s Palestinian Arab citizens, who comprise approximately 20% of the population. They are largely represented by two political formations -- one of which, the United Arab List (UAL) led by Mansour Abbas, has taken a highly accommodating position toward Israel’s Zionist regime, even placing Yoav Segalovitz, a former senior police chief and parliamentarian from a Jewish Zionist party, as the number 2 on the party slate. The UAL and the Joint List -- the other slate representing the community and comprising three political parties -- are polling in the low double digits of seats combined.
Nevertheless, with the exception of Yair Golan’s Democrats, the other leaders of the Zionist opposition bloc have ruled out going into government with Abbas and the UAL. Eisenkot appears to have previously entertained the idea, but the zeitgeist and pressure have encouraged him to now openly reject it. And indeed, Eisenkot and the other anti-Netanyahu bloc parties have gone even further, supporting petitions to ban Arab parties and candidates in one form or another. This populist ritual, gaining momentum each election cycle, speaks to the limits of democracy under the actual existing regime of Zionism.
Under Israel's proportional representation system, horse-trading between different parties with different agendas is an inherent part of forming a coalition to govern. Netanyahu’s coalition managed to see out its full term. The current opposition bloc has far less discipline and unity than the coalition it is trying to unseat -- so any government it leads is likely to be unstable.
All kinds of outcomes currently look possible, including unity between Netanyahu’s Likud and part of the opposition, or a stalemate leading to a further round of elections with Netanyahu and the current government staying on in a caretaker capacity. If this election does lead to the permanent fall of Netanyahu, then what may be opening up is a period of ongoing political fluidity in which the current alignments come under enough strain that genuinely new ones become possible over time.
In the most optimistic scenario, space would then be created where the questions on the agenda are not primarily about who warned whom about Oct. 7 and how to better manage Israel’s international propaganda, but instead whether Israel has a different way forward for the Palestinians and the region that is not based on an ethno-supremacist regime, zero-sum outcomes, and domination. In other words, what is needed is a politics that goes beyond the current overreach and extremism (which this author considers doomed to eventually implode).
But that kind of change is only likely to become possible if meaningful, consequential, and ongoing pressure is exerted on Israel; if there is an end to the impunity that enabled the current Israeli extremist spiral; and if there is a different incentive structure and cost-benefit calculation for Israel’s treatment of the Palestinians, its commission of war crimes, and its project of regional hegemony.
There are some initial signs of that happening -- for instance, with the recent measures announced by Britain and some European nations, with Global South mobilizations to hold Israel accountable (such as the Hague Group), and with arms embargoes, such as those by Türkiye. If those are continued and deepened, there may be hope. But that also means understanding that the problem runs far deeper than Benjamin Netanyahu and a couple of his most vocal and violent ministers.

The brain is built from two separate sources, not one, new research suggests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
10:00:48 UTC
19:00:48 KST

The brain is often viewed as developing from a single starting pool of cells, but recent research suggests a different story. New evidence indicates that the brain actually arises from two distinct, parallel sets of early cells, one that builds the forebrain and midbrain and another that builds the hindbrain. These cells are restricted to forming specific regions from very early in development. These findings, detailed in a study published in Nature Neuroscience, point to an evolutionary strategy that has shaped nervous system development for hundreds of millions of years.
To understand how the brain forms, scientists study pluripotent stem cells. These are unique cells capable of developing into nearly any tissue in the body. During an early phase of embryonic development known as gastrulation, the basic body plan begins to take shape. At this stage, some stem cells become a tissue called the neural ectoderm, which eventually forms the brain, while other structures like the spinal cord arise from different early tissues.
Generating specific types of brain cells in the lab is a major goal in regenerative medicine. Scientists are particularly interested in the hindbrain, a region that manages vital body processes like breathing, swallowing, and sleep. Motor neuron diseases such as spinal muscular atrophy and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), which damage nerve cells in both the brainstem and spinal cord, are often fatal. A 2026 study found that stem cells guided to the same type of neuron through hindbrain-like versus spinal cord-like routes ended up with distinct patterns of gene activity, suggesting a cell’s developmental history leaves a lasting mark.
This highlights why researchers need an accurate roadmap of brain development. Historically, one popular model proposed that all brain regions emerge from a common pool of neural progenitor cells. A progenitor is an early, not-yet-specialized cell in the embryo that divides and gives rise to more specialized cells. Neural progenitors are the early cells whose descendants become the brain and spinal cord. While other early studies mapping cell fates hinted that cells might be dedicated to specific brain regions early on, they could not confirm if the cells were permanently committed to those paths or just following local chemical signals.
“We certainly didn’t expect to find that the brain comes from two different sources! In 1952, the trailblazing Dutch scientist Pieter Nieuwkoop proposed that the entire brain arises from a common source,” study author Kyle M. Loh of Stanford University told PsyPost. “This led to the prevailing model in the field. Therefore, finding two different brain origins surprised us.”
“I also want to emphasize that we built on important work by other scientists in the 1990s who also suggested that there are perhaps multiple origins of the brain,” Loh added. “The origins of the brain remain a longstanding question, with many twists and turns along the way, and we are excited to work with others to continue to explore this area.”
The research, led by Rayyan T. Jokhai, Carolyn E. Dundes, and Loh, aimed to resolve this debate. They wanted to see if the earliest brain cells are already restricted in what they can become. The team looked at both mouse embryos and human stem cells to track how these initial developmental decisions are made.
“The brain is one organ, but we found that it is built from two different sources while a baby is growing in a mother’s womb,” Loh explained. “These two pieces—the front part of the brain and the back part of the brain—are pushed together to create one integrated organ. For instance, a smartphone is built from many different pieces that come from different countries, but they are later connected to form one integrated unit.”
First, the researchers used a technique called genetic lineage tracing in mouse embryos. They applied a fluorescent tag to a specific group of early neural cells right as gastrulation was ending. This tag allowed them to track the exact locations of these cells and their descendants as the embryos continued to grow until just before birth.
The tagged cells, which expressed a specific gene called Gbx2, were almost exclusively found in the developing hindbrain. They were essentially absent from the forebrain and midbrain. This provided evidence that in a living embryo, this specific population of cells is already on a dedicated path to form the hindbrain.
To test if these cells could be forced to change their destiny, the team turned to human pluripotent stem cells grown in lab dishes. They exposed the stem cells to specific mixtures of chemical signals to mimic early embryonic development.
Using different chemical recipes, the researchers turned the stem cells into two separate types of early brain tissue within just two days. One recipe yielded anterior neural ectoderm, which naturally forms the forebrain and midbrain. Another recipe, which included the signaling molecules FGF and retinoic acid, produced posterior neural ectoderm, which naturally forms the hindbrain. The researchers then challenged these cells by exposing them to the opposite developmental signals.
The cells largely resisted the new instructions. When the anterior cells were given chemical signals meant to create a hindbrain, they mostly failed to make the switch. In the same way, the posterior cells could rarely be coaxed into becoming forebrain or midbrain cells. Both cell types generally held their identities even when the two were mixed together in the same dish.
To understand this stubbornness, the researchers looked at the cells’ chromatin, which is the way DNA is packaged and organized. They found that the anterior and posterior cells had markedly different chromatin landscapes. The genes required for forebrain development were accessible and ready for action in the anterior cells, while the hindbrain genes were locked away.
The most important takeaway is “that the neuroectoderm divides into two separate progenitor populations that diverge in their potential to generate different brain regions,” Eduardo Sequerra, a researcher at the Brain Institute at the Universidade Federal do Rio Grande do Norte who was not involved in the study, told PsyPost. He emphasized that this split happens “much earlier than the neural tube formation,” referring to the formation of the early embryonic structure that eventually becomes the brain and spinal cord.
“I am quite confident in their very interesting finding,” Sequerra said. “They joined in vivo developmental studies across different species with in vitro differentiation systems to show their hypothesis is solid in different ways.” In vivo means studies done in living organisms, such as embryos, while in vitro means studies done on cells grown outside the body, such as in a lab dish. Differentiation is the process by which an unspecialized cell, like a stem cell, turns into a specific cell type, such as a neuron.
This early division aligns with older clues in the field. “During the ’90s Nicole Le Douarin’s group performed a series of transplantation studies showing that the folding neural tube is divided into two parts,” Sequerra explained. He noted that one part sits above the notochord, a flexible rod of tissue that helps organize the developing embryo, and “cannot differentiate into anterior structures.” The other part, which lacks a notochord below it, “differentiates into the midbrain and forebrain,” he said.
“This article shows that the split into two populations occurs much earlier than the established notochord and neural folds stage,” Sequerra added, referring to the ridges of tissue on the embryo’s back that rise up and merge to form the neural tube. “This split possibly occurs when the future notochord-mesoderm cells are still migrating.” The mesoderm is the middle layer of cells in an early embryo, which goes on to form muscles, bones, blood, and other tissues.
Using this new knowledge, the research team successfully directed the posterior neural ectoderm cells to grow into specialized hindbrain motor neurons. These particular neurons are responsible for controlling muscles in the face and neck, including those necessary for swallowing. The lab-grown neurons showed spontaneous calcium activity and fired electrical impulses when stimulated, signs that they were functional.
“We are excited by the ability to create human hindbrain neurons in a Petri dish,” Loh said. “The hindbrain—the back part of the brain, otherwise known as the brainstem—controls life-sustaining functions such as sleep, wakefulness, consciousness, hunger, and so on. The ability to create human hindbrain neurons in a Petri dish may help us better understand these fundamental, life-sustaining processes, and diseases that impact them.”
“Both amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and spinal muscular atrophy are deadly diseases,” Loh noted. “In particular, spinal muscular atrophy is the #1 genetic cause of death in babies under 1 year of age. Both diseases kill hindbrain motor neurons that control muscles involved in eating, swallowing, and speech.”
“We cannot sample living motor neurons from a patient’s hindbrain to watch how these diseases attack these neurons. Growing these hindbrain motor neurons in a dish gives us a way to investigate these diseases,” Loh explained. “We hope to explore how amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, spinal muscular atrophy, and other diseases affect human hindbrain motor neurons, with the hope of using this system to discover and test potential treatments.”
“The development of a method to differentiate motor neurons in vitro has the potential to bring hope for those with neuromuscular disorders,” Sequerra said. However, he cautioned that this approach relies on studying patient-specific cells in a dish, rather than replacing damaged tissue in the body. “Of course it has the potential of becoming a way of studying specific patients’ motor neurons through iPSCs [induced pluripotent stem cells] but it definitely is not close to a stem cell therapy for regeneration.”
The researchers also examined the embryos of several other species, including macaques, chickens, zebrafish, and acorn worms. Acorn worms are small marine worms that burrow in the seafloor and are distant relatives of animals with backbones. The researchers found distinct anterior and posterior neural cell groups in all of them. This suggests that the mechanism of using two parallel starting populations to build a brain has been conserved across different species for roughly 550 million years.
“We hope to learn more about how the brain was built during evolution,” Loh said. “In humans, mice, and other types of animals, the two parts of the brain develop next to one another, even though they originate from different sources. However, other pioneering scientists discovered that jellyfish—which diverged from us 600 million years ago—have two separate nerve rings at different ends of the body.”
“Our speculation is that early during evolution, there was perhaps no ‘grand plan’ to create a single brain, but rather potentially two separate nervous systems were created,” Loh continued. “Later in evolution, these two nervous systems may have been pushed together to give rise to the appearance of one integrated brain. It is important to emphasize that this is only an idea, and it might change as scientists learn more.”
“The expansion of the midbrain-forebrain progenitor field was probably an important phenomenon in the vertebrate nervous system evolution,” Sequerra noted. Moving forward, he said “it will be nice to go deeper into the mechanisms for the segregation of the two populations in both vertebrates and invertebrate chordates, or even other deuterostomes.” Invertebrate chordates are animals without a backbone that still share key body features with vertebrates, such as a notochord at some stage of life. Examples include sea squirts and lancelets, which belong to the broader deuterostome group alongside vertebrates.
As with all research, there are a few things to keep in mind. Growing human cells in a plastic dish does not perfectly recreate the complex, three-dimensional environment of a developing embryo. The cells might behave slightly differently when isolated from the intricate chemical exchanges that happen naturally in the body.
Additionally, the researchers emphasize that their findings should not be misinterpreted as suggesting the brain lacks unity. “Some people reading our paper sometimes think it suggests the brain is two separate organs. More precisely, the brain is one organ, but it is built from two different sources,” Loh explained. “By the analogy, the heart is likewise built from two different sources: one source creates the right ventricle, and another source creates the three other chambers of the heart. But ultimately, all four chambers of the heart work together, similar to how different parts of the brain all work together to give rise to all the amazing things that the brain can do.”
In addition, while the lab-grown cells appeared strongly committed to their specific paths, other unknown chemical combinations might exist that could force them to switch identities. Testing this in living mammals is technically difficult and would require placing labeled progenitor cells into the wrong location in a growing mammalian embryo. Despite these caveats, the ability to predictably grow specialized hindbrain neurons offers a highly useful tool for studying fatal neurodegenerative diseases in the lab. These are diseases in which nerve cells gradually break down and die over time, such as ALS.
The study, “Two parallel neural ectoderm progenitors contribute to the developing brain,” was authored by Rayyan T. Jokhai, Carolyn E. Dundes, Hadia S. Ahsan, Rachel S. Kang, Rachel E.A. Salomon-Shulman, Arjun Rajan, Yoon Seok Kim, Liam J. Stanton, Christine Xu, Stephanie Do, Brennan D. McDonald, José Miguel Andrade López, Hugo A. Urrutia, Hannah Greenfeld, Alicia Wong, Yimiao Qu, Andrew S. Petkovic, Yi Miao, K. Christopher Garcia, Michelle Monje, Daniel E. Wagner, Marianne E. Bronner, Christopher J. Lowe, and Kyle M. Loh.

After 23 Years of Oversight, Oakland’s Police Reform Offers New Hope
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
10:00:05 UTC
19:00:05 KST

In the spring of 2014, civil rights lawyers John Burris and Jim Chanin invited me to Oakland, California, to serve as a subject matter expert. They represented a group of plaintiffs seeking justice in a city enduring an especially brutal version of a well-known story: a police department that many perceived as a hotbed of illegal tactics, violence, and discrimination directed largely at the Black community. As I heard one Oakland native put it at a public meeting shortly after I arrived: “People are damaged. People are heartbroken. People have fear. People are scared of the same people that’s supposed to protect them.”
Since revelations of a pattern of wrongdoing first came to light 23 years ago, the Oakland Police Department (OPD) has been under federal court oversight—the longest for any American city.
This week, a federal judge is expected to decide whether that oversight can finally come to an end, after years of progress toward reforms required by the court. Whatever the outcome, Oakland has undergone a substantial transformation over the past two decades. What changed over those years is a remarkable story about what can happen when we finally have the tools we need to see policing clearly.
A decade of body camera data
I’d been summoned to Oakland due to my work as a researcher focused on racial bias and inequality. The plaintiffs’ attorneys wanted to understand what was really happening between officers and civilians that might be contributing to systemic abuses and a breakdown of trust. The job for me and my team was to parse the data and try to quantify racial disparities. But we were also seeking clues about how those disparities took root, and whether anything could be done to address them.
We soon realized there was an all-too-familiar tension that arrest records, crime statistics, and other available data couldn’t solve—a problem of interpretation. The same disparities that community advocates saw as proof of officer bias were viewed by many police officers as proof of where crime was concentrated. The numbers told us what was happening. They were much less useful for helping us understand why. If we had any hope of uncovering the causes of those disparities—let alone finding solutions—we were going to need new tools.
As it turns out, as far back as 2014, Oakland was sitting on an extraordinary trove of data that contained everything we needed to know—it was just that nobody had thought of it as data before. Oakland had been an early adopter of police body-worn cameras, a rare technological innovation that consistently enjoys about 90% public approval. For over a decade now, police departments across the country have amassed troves of footage from these cameras, creating the most comprehensive record of interactions between officers and civilians in history. Yet the vast majority of that footage is never leveraged to improve those interactions.
That’s because we’ve largely treated body-worn cameras as a source of evidence: footage to be consulted only after a specific encounter goes horribly wrong. But those countless routine encounters where trust is built or broken, rights are upheld or violated, and officer training succeeds or slips have gone almost entirely unexamined. The reason for that is simple: humans could not possibly monitor and evaluate footage at that scale, let alone learn lessons from it in the aggregate.
But AI can.
Can AI improve policing?
Eager for a breakthrough to change the city’s trajectory—and compelled to reform by a federal monitor—Oakland granted Stanford researchers access to their body-worn camera footage. Our team of linguists, social psychologists, and computer scientists spent years building and refining a set of computational tools designed to analyze these videos at scale. Now, we can methodically measure the language of routine police interactions, identifying patterns across millions of encounters that no amount of manual review could surface.
Like a DNA sequencer or an X-ray machine, these insights let us see, for the first time ever, the actual makeup of a police encounter. We discovered linguistic signatures that could reliably predict, within the first 27 seconds of an encounter, which interactions were likely to escalate and which would conclude calmly. We were also able to map the “respect gap” that officers, including Black officers, imposed on Black drivers before the driver even spoke, finding consistent disparities in tone, word choice, whether officers explained the reason for the stop, and expressions of concern for a driver’s safety.
We brought our findings to the OPD and worked together with them to move from generic training to data-driven, surgically targeted reforms. Many were skeptical that our ideas—like requiring officers to briefly record the rationale for a stop before making it rather than acting on hunches—would do anything but drive up crime. But that skepticism evaporated when they saw what happened next.
After implementing new policies and trainings, stops of Black civilians in Oakland dropped by 43%—without any uptick in crime. In one pre-post study of a training designed to improve relations with the public, our footage analysis revealed a marked decrease in officer language that tended to trigger escalation, and a marked increase in language that built trust.
Over a 10-year period, the OPD continued to reform and refine its practices. And, in many respects, that effort paid off. For example, after the department implemented a foot pursuit policy to avoid chasing suspects into backyards and blind alleys, officer injuries dropped by 70%. And officer-involved shootings, which had previously averaged about eight per year, dropped to a total of eight over a five-year period.
Returning to Oakland
When I returned to Oakland not long ago, I found myself in an elevator with a fellow Black woman who worked for the police department. She told me that for years, the department would dismiss claims from community members about how they had been negatively treated, insisting that officers treat everyone professionally. “Data,” she said, “gave us a way to be heard”—a way for individual stories to become fodder for systemic change.
Currently, many new technologies, from Flock cameras to rogue chatbots, are being met with distrust and dread about surveillance, privacy, and safety—for good reasons. However, Oakland’s story offers another possibility: a concrete way for AI to actually improve life in our communities using the very cameras introduced to bring about reform. The city’s experience provides compelling evidence that turning body-worn cameras into the powerful accountability tools they were meant to be can help departments everywhere make police-civilian interactions safer and more respectful for everyone involved. It’s an approach that does not require the building of large AI data centers in neighborhoods across the country, and it doesn’t threaten to take away anyone’s job. It simply requires learning from the data that we already have—and that the vast majority of us feel is useful to have.
At a time when American policing is under enormous strain—with retirement at record highs, recruitment at record lows, officer wellness declining, and public trust in law enforcement diminished—the Oakland model delivers a ray of hope, even as it continues to battle to show the world it is capable of reform. And as more cities adopt this approach, I’m optimistic American policing could be transformed.

Flying Doesn’t Have to Be This Miserable
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
10:00:04 UTC
19:00:04 KST

When did flying become so expensive, cumbersome, and, in a word, miserable?
While the summer 2026 travel season has officially come to an end, the bite of high airline ticket prices has lasted far longer than anyone would hope. Higher fuel costs pushed up already-steep ticket prices by as much as 27% this summer. But pricey fares show no sign of abating. As we move into the fall season with Thanksgiving, Christmas, and New Year’s Eve just around the corner, The Points Guy estimates that fares will be anywhere from 9 to 18% higher than last year’s holiday-season tickets.
Even before the war in Iran drove oil prices higher, major U.S. airlines had already become experts at turning the screws on the flying public. The major airlines started charging for checked bags in 2008; nearly 20 years later, U.S. carriers raked in more than $7 billion in 2025 in bag fees alone. Charges for seat selection—windows, aisles, or even just the privilege of sitting further up in the economy cabin—are widespread, even as the seats and legroom have shrunk. And perhaps worst of all, air service has worsened in many smaller cities and at regional airports. This means fewer airlines competing against each other on fares and schedules, more flights with layovers, and in some cases, much higher prices on less-traversed routes.
The federal government has played an essential role in how we got here. While the 1950s to 1970s, known as the “golden age” of air travel, was certainly not perfect, American travelers benefited in many ways from the era of regulated competition. The federal Civil Aeronautics Board helped ensure that America had a stable, reliable air transportation system that served large and small communities alike and prevented the monopolistic exploitation of passengers.
But in 1978, in the name of reducing the government’s hand in the airline industry, Congress passed the Airline Deregulation Act, with the goal of injecting more competition into the air travel business. The theory sounded great: deregulate the airline industry, and the free market will make everything better. There will be dozens, perhaps even hundreds of new airlines. There will be more competition, lower prices, and no downsides for small communities, workers, or passengers. For a few years, this prediction even appeared to come true, but pretty quickly, the fundamental dynamics of the airline industry came roaring back.
Scale matters in the airline industry. Big airlines started undercutting small rivals, pushing them into financial crisis and bankruptcy. The big airlines then snapped them up, consolidating the industry more and more. Big airlines shifted toward hub-and-spokes systems, even creating “fortress hubs” where competition is minimal.
Today, for instance, Delta controls nearly 80% of flights in Atlanta, and American has approximately 90% of flights in Charlotte, N.C. Unleashed by pricing regulations, airlines were the pioneers of dynamic pricing, the practice of changing fares frequently for passengers. They then started “unbundling” their product to charge for every aspect of travel, from seats to boarding order. And now, with technology developing rapidly, the threat of AI-driven “personalized pricing” (read: even higher prices) is just a matter of time.
The good news is that we can have a system of air travel that is more reliable, resilient, competitive, and fair. It starts with acknowledging that the airline industry is essential infrastructure, and that it should be regulated as such.
For communities, that means ending the idea of “flyover country.” Air travel is transportation infrastructure, and small and regional airports with affordable fares are critical to the foundations of our national economy. Airlines also get a lot of benefits from the public. They should have a duty to serve the country in return. One way to solve the problem of the loss of service in smaller places would resemble the “draft pick” system in the NFL. The airlines would be like the teams and get a pick order, and smaller cities would be like the players who are drafted. Every airline would have to go through and pick cities until all of them are taken, and airlines would be required to provide consistent, affordable service.
We also need a more resilient system, one that can better withstand shocks from nasty summer rains, extreme heat, winter storms, or economic crises. Over and over again, we’ve seen taxpayer bailouts or bankruptcies as airlines fail to deal with crises. And over and over again, delays and cancellations cascade across the country due to weather at big hubs.
We should have a “rainy day” fund for airlines, paid into when the airlines are making huge profits. There should be caps on hub concentration, so airline networks are not so dependent on a small number of airports, and so the whole country isn’t beholden to a crisis in one city. And we need significant investment in the basic infrastructure of flying, too, from air traffic control to airport infrastructure. And for passengers, the answers aren’t difficult: Congress could set minimum seat sizes, ban personalized and dynamic pricing, and require transparent pricing.
Flying is an astonishing achievement of humanity. It has transformed our world in countless ways. We should all be grateful for how extraordinary it is to traverse the country in just a handful of hours.
But that doesn’t mean that we have to accept the indignities and unfairness that has emerged in this sector. In a democracy, we choose how our society functions. We can make sure airlines serve our national needs, without bailouts or crises. And we can make flying less miserable for all of us.

A few years back, I posted about the “Daily Logic” and “Daily Semantics” project of Josh Dever, professor of philosophy at the University of Texas at Austin.
The projects offer up mini-lessons in logic or semantics that anyone can subscribe to.
At the time, Professor Dever wrote, “The idea of each is that each day you get sent a little, roughly 200 word bite in the relevant area, so that you can gradually and painlessly(-ish) build up real expertise.”
Since that post, Professor Dever has added over 2000 more logic lessons and several hundred more semantics lessons to the services.
The lessons are pitched at roughly the “grad student new to the area” level.
Anyone can sign up for the lessons at the respective sites: Daily Logic and Daily Semantics.

Beats 360 Review: Customizable, Stylish, and Fun
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

Easily swappable ear cups and headband. Multiple cushion color and fabric options. Water-resistant. 32 hours of battery life with ANC.
TIRED
Lackluster midrange sound. No wired listening. Strong clamping makes for uncomfortable everyday wear.
The Beats 360, I'll admit, didn't click for me until I started thinking of them as over-ear workout headphones. As everyday headphones, I had a tough time ranking these, given the competition, but as gym cans, the Beats 360 are stellar.
It took me a while to come to this conclusion because working out with over-ear headphones has always kind of sucked. They shift around a lot, get warm and sweaty around your ears, and are way, way heavier than earbuds. That last part might not seem like a big deal, but if you’re running a half-marathon, a half-pound weight on top of your head starts to get annoying fast. This stigma made me ignore this attribute about the Beats 360 at first.
Still, the number of people I see working out (and running) with Apple AirPods Max, one of the heaviest popular over-ear headphones around, shows the demand is there. And the Beats 360 fulfill that niche brilliantly, with a secure fit, IPX4-rated water resistance, and swappable cushioning. They may not be the best over-ear headphones for other things (like high-resolution audio), but it’s hard to knock them when they get their main thing (customizable over-ear workout headphones) right.
From Gym to Street
Beats 360 Key Specifications

The Beats 360 are, first and foremost, fun headphones. That may not sound like much, but it’s a rarity in the sea of same-y over-ear headphones I’ve reviewed. The 360 have a slim, smooth design that’s appealing, with a soft-touch finish and an adjustable headband with smooth, telescoping metal (similar to AirPods Max or Sonos Ace Ultra).
The main draw of the 360s is the swappable headband and ear cups. With a slight downward pull, the headband comes off, and the ear cups do the same with a satisfying twist. In the box, you get a cushion set (headband and two ear cups) color-matched to the headphones, but mixing and matching colors is a big part of the 360's appeal (and its marketing).
This video is about My MovieVideo: Harry Rabinowitz
Making them easy to remove also makes them easier to clean and replace—a headache with most other headphones—and I consider that crucial for anything I’m going to exercise with.
The cushions come in two fabric options: Performance Knit, a mesh-like fabric that’s decently breathable and durable, and UltraPlush, a much softer, faux-leather style material akin to what you’d find on other premium over-ear cans from Bose, Sony, and Sonos.
The Performance Knit ear cups are better for working out—they feel more breathable, especially when I start to sweat. For everyday listening, though, the UltraPlush is much softer and more comfortable over time.
Video: Harry Rabinowitz
To be clear, the Beats 360 didn’t make me suddenly love working out with over-ear headphones. I still think wireless workout earbuds, like Beats’ own Powerbeats Pro 2, are the way to go, but the 360s are absolutely better than other over-ear options. The clamping force is strong enough that the headphones stay secure for most (but not all) exercises, without feeling so strong that they’re uncomfortable. Bicycle kicks and sprints still caused them to shift around a bit, unsurprisingly.
On the scale, the 360 are a middleweight. They are heavier than Sony and Bose over-ear headphones, but lighter than the AirPods Max. It's a good balance. Could they be a little lighter? Sure. Do they feel super heavy? Not really.
I appreciate the physical button controls, especially when working out. I do wish the buttons were a little more distinct and easy to recognize by feel alone. Things like a small tactile dot on the volume up button or a slight divot between the volume up and down would go a long way to helping me distinguish the all-smooth buttons.
I found myself swapping to the UltraPlush cushions whenever I wasn’t working out, and I started calling this “normal mode” and the Performance Knit setup “sport mode." In everyday use, the slightly strong clamping force of the 360s switches from a pro to a con—they get uncomfortable to wear after a few hours of office work.
Noise-canceling and transparency are highlights here. While not as strong as flagship headphones from Sony or Bose, the Beats 360 are close enough, and the ANC plus natural sound isolation did a good job shushing coworkers, cafés, the office cafeteria, and crowded New York City subway cars. With ANC enabled, you get 32 hours of battery life, which is very strong.
Connectivity is also simple and easy. Like other recent Beats headphones, the 360s pair instantly with Apple devices, and they support Apple device swapping, Apple Find My, and Siri. On Android, you get fast pairing, Google’s Find Hub, voice assistant with a button press, a few other Google/Android audio switching features, and the stand-alone Beats app. There's no wired connectivity, which is fine, since a cord is the last thing you want to deal with while exercising.
It’s only when I listen to my favorite playlist in the comfort of my office that the 360s' biggest weakness reared its ugly head: sound quality. Simply put: They sound OK, but not for headphones that cost $350. Unfortunately, they do not sound nearly as good as the $300 Sony WH-1000XM4C, $350 Sonos Ace, or $370 Bose QuietComfort Headphones (2nd Gen).
The first time I listened to music with the Beats 360 (after testing the Bose QC for weeks), I literally yelled, “Where are the mids?!” Listening on the Beats 360 feels like someone scooped out the midrange—guitars and vocals in certain genres seem weak or lost. On cheaper headphones, this wouldn’t be something I would harp on much, but for a $350 flagship headphone, it’s a miss, especially when the 360s get so much else right. Simply put, I won’t be reaching for the Beats 360 when I want to get lost in my favorite album or soundtrack.
Reliable Workout Buddy
I can see the Beats 360 doing very well for the gym. At $350, they're pricey but significantly less expensive than Apple AirPods Max, making them a good alternative for Apple users. To be fair, the Bose QuietComfort Ultra (2nd Gen) and Sony WH-1000XM6 are also cheaper than AirPods Max and provide better sound quality than the 360s, but lack the fitness chops. The removable ear cups and headband are downright fun, and mixing and matching colors is a breath of fresh air in headphone land.
These are not the best-sounding over-ear headphones out there. They aren’t best in class at any one metric, actually. But the 360 are an intentional trade-off—OK everyday performance for superior workout performance. If that compromise is where the Beats 360 want to hang their hat, they’ve got next to no over-ear headphones putting up a good fight in the workout space.
Personally, I almost always wear wireless earbuds or open earbuds when I work out. I still find them vastly more comfortable and more convenient for the job. But that’s just me. And if the Beats 360 finally get people to stop wearing AirPods Max to run in, I’m rooting for them.

U.S. and China to Cut Tariffs on $60 Billion of Goods
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

The U.S. and China have agreed to cut tariffs on $60 billion worth of goods, from U.S. coal to Chinese toys.
The late Sunday announcement falls under the “30-for-30” framework, covering roughly $30 billion of U.S. exports to China and $30 billion of Chinese exports to the U.S. The U.S.-China Board of Trade, established during President Donald Trump’s visit to Beijing in May, recommended more favorable tariff treatment for “non-sensitive” products.
The proposed cuts would bring relief to a wide range of goods, including live horses, camels, and fishing tackle. The White House has not yet specified the size of tariff reductions or when the cuts will be implemented, although the Chinese Commerce Ministry said tariffs on around 90% of the products on each list would return to “most favored nation” levels, referring to ordinary baseline tariff rates that vary based on product.
TIME has reached out to the White House and Chinese Commerce Ministry for comment.
“The Trump Administration will continue to pursue fair, balanced, and reciprocal trade with China by ensuring compliance with commitments on agricultural and energy purchases, pursuing balanced trade in non-sensitive goods, and securing market access for American farmers, manufacturers, businesses, and workers,” U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said in a statement on Sunday.
The Chinese Commerce Ministry said on Monday that the agreement would “further stabilize” U.S.-China trade relations and “create favorable conditions” for Chinese exports to the U.S.
The agreement marks the latest effort to ease economic tensions between the two global superpowers after an escalating trade war last year brought tariffs to prohibitively high levels. It comes days after Chinese President Xi Jinping and Trump met in Washington, D.C., and agreed to extend a trade truce until Jan. 10. The two countries have repeatedly extended their trade truce since May 2025, when they agreed to lower additional duties to 30% on Chinese goods and 10% on U.S. goods. After the Supreme Court struck down Trump’s emergency tariffs in February, the Trump Administration imposed a separate 12.5% levy on many Chinese products, on top of earlier Section 301 tariffs targeting Chinese trade practices and Section 232 sectoral tariffs.
Trump has sought to use tariffs to shrink the U.S. trade deficit with China and bring manufacturing back to the U.S. Greer told CNBC on Friday that the deficit on goods trade with China has fallen by 40% since Trump took office. The deficit is on track to hit $140 billion this year, he said, compared to $295 billion in 2024, according to Census Bureau data.
But the tariff war has also strained both economies and pushed Chinese exporters to seek other markets. American business owners previously told TIME that abrupt tariff changes had driven up costs and forced them to consider shifting production out of China, which could be prohibitively expensive.
Read More: Surveys Show More Americans Warming to China
“This is less the demolition of a tariff wall than the opening of a safety valve: enough to let off steam, not enough to change the structure of the conflict,” says Henry Gao, professor of law at Singapore Management University. “It may give both sides breathing room, but it is better designed to pause a trade war than to end one—and may simply prepare the ground for the next round of fighting.”
Deborah Elms, Head of Trade Policy at the Singapore-based Hinrich Foundation, tells TIME that the cuts “are a mostly symbolic way of indicating that tariffs can be cut without tackling the major challenges.”
But, she adds, it’s still a positive: “At a minimum, it provides a mechanism for future conversations about trade and tariffs which might be more serious.”
What products are covered?
The agreement recommends lower tariffs on 77 categories of Chinese products. These include bed linen, garden umbrellas, car seats, fish hooks, billiard balls, curtains, electric shavers, inflatable balls, and jute wall hangings. It also includes holiday decorations, which could bring relief to U.S. businesses if implemented before the end-of-year holiday season.
The agreement also recommends lowering tariffs on 1,619 categories of U.S. products. These include a range of food items, like butter, offal, corn, wheat, frozen meat, seafood, and foie gras. It also recommends reduced tariffs on cosmetics, wood products, scientific devices like MRI systems, rabbit hair, and coal. Several types of live animals are also included: donkeys, mules, horses, whales, dolphins, and dugongs.
Washington’s focus on “everyday Chinese consumer goods,” Gao says, demonstrates “an effort to lower household costs and offer voters tangible price relief ahead of the midterm elections” in November. For Beijing, the American goods on its list, including agriculture, energy, timber, and medical equipment, “address domestic needs while also benefiting politically influential U.S. constituencies,” he says.
China’s “extremely long list” covers a huge amount of goods that are not exported to China in significant amounts,” Elms adds.
Zhu Tian, vice president, co-dean, and professor of economics at China Europe International Business School in Shanghai, tells TIME the choice of products reflects a “cautious” approach, suggesting the agreement is more “a confidence-building measure” between the two sides.
The White House also said on Friday that China agreed to import at least 10 million metric tons of coal per year from the U.S. in 2027 and 2028. China previously agreed in November to resume purchases of U.S. sorghum and increase purchases of U.S. soybeans.
During Trump’s first term, China pledged to increase its purchases of U.S. agricultural products, including soybeans, but fell short of certain commitments.
What is the “30-for-30” framework?
Under the so-called “30-for-30” framework, the U.S. and China respectively recommended $30 billion worth of non-sensitive trade, based on 2024 trade values, that “could benefit from more favorable tariff treatment in the future,” Greer said on Sunday.
The list would improve market access for roughly 30% of U.S. exports to China, Greer said.
The Board of Trade “gives the détente an institutional framework,” Gao tells TIME. But he notes that it has avoided “the core disputes over technology, subsidies, industrial policy, and national security.”
Many of the concessions, which are likely to be implemented through domestic measures rather than binding treaty commitments, could be easily reversed, he cautions. And with the truce set to expire in January, Gao says “this looks less like durable peace than a half-time break in a boxing match between two heavyweights: both sides get a breather, but the bell has not rung for the final round.”
Sensitive goods, which are excluded from the framework, include semiconductors, batteries, and electric vehicles. “Both governments are liberalizing where it is politically useful, while preserving pressure where it is strategically necessary,” Gao says.
Still, the “30-for-30” framework could become a “useful template for quick, transactional trade bargains” between the U.S. and other countries, Gao says. Such a framework would allow countries to “match concessions by dollar value, shield strategic sectors, and deliver politically visible wins without the burden of negotiating a comprehensive trade agreement.”
What does this mean for businesses and consumers?
The amount of goods covers roughly 21% of U.S. exports to China and 7% of Chinese exports to the U.S. based on 2024 trade values, which put U.S. exports to China at $143.5 billion and Chinese exports to the U.S. at $438.9 billion. The tariff cuts “offer meaningful relief to particular exporters, importers, and consumers,” Gao says, although he cautions that it remains a proposal and is not yet implemented.
Lingering uncertainty, including over whether the trade truce will extend beyond Jan. 10, could still make it harder for businesses to plan, particularly those that began exploring alternative suppliers during last year’s tariff war.
“Equal trade values do not necessarily produce equal economic gains, and easily reversible tariff cuts offer businesses little certainty for long-term investment or supply-chain planning,” says Gao.
Notably, U.S. whole soybeans are not on China’s list and still face an additional 10% tariff. The crop has been a key bargaining point in trade talks after Beijing reduced purchases of the product, taking a toll on American farmers.
“Clearly, if you are an American importer that has not yet received your Christmas ornament orders, these cuts are going to be helpful,” Elms says, referring to the inclusion of wooden Christmas ornaments and artificial flowers on the U.S. list of Chinese products. “But in the main, the tariff cuts on offer are not going to relieve economic pressures on consumers in either market.”
