Borrowers again 'hit over the head' to bring inflation down
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
09:00:46 UTC
18:00:46 KST

analysis
Australia's rising interest rates are not just down to government spending
Why is Australia stuck in an inflation problem that has sent interest rates to 15-year highs?
If you listen only to the opposition, some economic commentators, and sections of the press, it's entirely down to government financial mismanagement at the federal and state levels.
If, instead, you choose to listen to the person most responsible for your mortgage rate, it's a bit of everything all at once.
"The bottom line is that there are a number of pressures all bearing down on inflation at the moment," RBA governor Michele Bullock told reporters following the meeting where the bank's board raised its benchmark rate to 4.6 per cent.
The most serious energy supply shock in 50 years has collided with the biggest technology investment boom on record, pushing up the cost of imported fuel and tech equipment, at the same time as Australia was at the tail end of a housing boom and consumer spending spree.
Speaking specifically about the energy shock, Ms Bullock (and the rest of the board in its post-meeting statement) emphasised the role the lingering, and worsening, conflict has played in stoking inflation.
"The longer it goes, the more likely it is that businesses will just try to pass through the cost increases,"
"Now, will they be able to? If they're in industries, for example, where there's excess demand, they might be able to pass it on."
This is not the pandemic version of excess demand, where ultra-low rates and mammoth stimulus payments to households and businesses sent the economy hurtling down a supply-constrained, pothole-strewn back road at 100 kilometres an hour.
This is the economic equivalent of not noticing the speed limit has changed and doing 60 in a roadwork zone.
In other words, the current "excess demand" isn't feeling very excess for most households, even though they're the ones (if they have a mortgage) being asked to pay the penalty.
In the more wonky language of the post-meeting statement, the RBA board explained:
"Growth in aggregate demand needs to remain subdued for a period to reduce capacity pressures and bring inflation back to target."
In plain English, we need you, mortgage borrowers, to enjoy a lower standard of living so that the economy has capacity to build lots of data centres and pay for more expensive fuel imports while inflation still comes down.
As independent economist Chris Richardson told The Business last night:
"Inflation is just too much money chasing too little stuff.
"But no Reserve Bank, no government can wave a magic wand and make Australia produce more stuff overnight.
"So the question becomes, who gets less money to spend? Who gets hit over the head? We have a system that uses interest rates to to basically hit borrowers over the head."
Loading...
So is the government off the hook?
Not entirely. While it has been keen to talk up the effect of the Middle East crisis, Michele Bullock said that was not the sole driver of Australia's inflation woes.
"This isn't all about the Middle East conflict," she told reporters.
"It is making things much worse, but we did start from a position of excess demand anyway, and that's why we started raising interest rates even before the conflict started."
Loading...
Her response is still well short of the critique launched by Opposition Leader Angus Taylor.
"The current interest rates are a result of Labor's actions, let's be clear,"
"And we know that this is a government that is spending too much."
A criticism that drew a sharp rebuke from Treasurer Jim Chalmers.
"I delivered the first surplus, in fact the first two surpluses, for a decade and a half," he fired back at reporters questioning his fiscal credentials.
"Average real spending growth has been less than half our predecessors and less than it was before COVID."
When you look at international comparisons, it's hard to argue that Australia has the second-highest central bank interest rate among advanced economies because of extreme fiscal indiscipline.
As this OECD chart shows, when it comes to deficit spending, which is what matters for the net amount of demand the government is injecting into the economy, Australia is broadly around the middle of the pack, and a long way behind the budget train wreck that is the US.
If the government's deficit is part of the problem, Angus Taylor's solution of "axing Labor's toxic taxes" in the absence of concrete plans to slash government services or payments to make up for the lost revenue, and then some, is hardly a fiscally responsible alternative.
As Richardson noted in an AFR column earlier this year, despite the argy-bargy between Australia's politicians over modest tax rises here and spending restraint there, Canberra is fiddling while the nation's finances are in a slow burn.
"If inflation is too much money chasing too little stuff and governments give us extra money — and they did a lot of that, state and federal in recent years — they become part of the problem and make the Reserve Bank's life harder," Richardson observed.
Loading
Is there another way to lower inflation?
Yes, but the ball is firmly in the government's court.
When asked by The Australian's Matthew Cranston whether adjusting the super guarantee to take some money out of people's pay but leave it in their future retirement nest egg might be a more "nuanced" way to tackle inflation, Bullock declined to comment, saying, "That's not at all within our gift."
Preliminary research undertaken by the progressive Centre for Policy Development think tank suggests that temporarily increasing the super guarantee by 0.5 per cent might take about $2 billion per quarter out of the economy, similar to the effect of a 0.25 percentage point rate hike.
If you want government spending restraint, another option is to index administered prices to the midpoint of the RBA's target band, rather than the consumer price index.
The CPD's economists, led by Warwick Smith, found administered prices accounted for 7.2 per cent of the 26.8 per cent cumulative inflation between 2020-2026.
"This bakes cost-push shocks (such as oil spikes) into statutory prices a year later, feeding a price spiral, inspiring extra wage claims and extending the duration of inflation episodes," they argued.
Limiting those regulated price increases would be incredibly painful for the public and corporate operators in those industries as they would be unable to offset their input cost increases, but it would be an effective way to help short-circuit inflation.
The reality is, there is no painless way to lower inflation, especially when it's largely imported and overseas corporates and governments are the main profiteers
"We get to pick our poison, but we can't avoid the fact that it is poison to bring inflation down," Richardson said.
The difference is that we could force more people to take the poison rather than dosing up one particular section of the population so much it almost kills them.

Gaza’s child amputees find hope and support at Al-Bait Village
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
08:57:59 UTC
17:57:59 KST

Breadcrumb
From limb loss to rehabilitation: Inside Al-Bait Village, where Gaza's child amputees are learning to live again
Upon arriving at Al-Bait, the first village in Deir al Balah in central Gaza, providing education, healthcare and rehabilitation to orphaned children and children who have lost limbs, I expected to see children whose lives had been shattered by the devastation caused by Israel's ongoing genocidal war.
Instead, what stood out was the effort being made to give the children back something they had lost even before their limbs: the feeling of simply being children.
That sense of normality showed up in the ordinary things around the village: children sitting together for meals, drawings covering the walls, and teachers welcoming them as they arrived for the day, making the place feel less like a centre for children affected by the war and more like a new home.
This feeling of home is reflected in the name Al-Bait, which translates to 'the house' in English, and the idea for such a place came from an experience Abu Majed, the founder, had several months before the village opened.
In July 2025, while Gaza was experiencing one of the most difficult stages of the war and famine, Abu Majed left his home looking for food for his starving family.
Markets were empty and, after losing hope of finding anything, he headed towards an aid distribution point, hoping to find something among those returning from there.
On that journey, Abu Majed saw scenes that would later lead him to create Al-Bait Village.
While the sounds of bombing filled the area, he saw a mother trying to protect her child amid the fear and chaos and heard her saying, "I lost your father. Who do I have left if you leave me too?"
On his way back, he also saw two children who had lost limbs waiting for one of their relatives to return from an aid distribution point.
The scenes stayed with him after he returned home, and he began thinking about what he could do for children whose lives had changed in a single moment.
The project began to take shape in November 2025, with the village welcoming its first children at the beginning of 2026.
With limited funding and resources to begin with, a group of volunteers worked to transform a rented building into a suitable space for children, initially aiming to support around 130 children.
As more children began coming to the village, that number grew to around 240 children aged four to 14.
A new sense of routine
The daily routine at Al-Bait is designed around giving the children a sense of structure.
Every morning, a village bus picks them up and brings them to the centre, where teachers welcome them at the door before their day begins with education and skill-building activities.
Their time there isn't limited to books and lessons; some days are spent making wooden models, while others involve dabke, singing, and activities related to technology and artificial intelligence.
That routine also includes medical and psychological support, as the village provides healthcare and regular medical check-ups alongside rehabilitation for children who have lost limbs.
Every week, a psychologist meets with the children individually, as workers say not all the effects of the war show up in their bodies.
Some of what they carry shows up as fear, silence, or difficulty returning to daily life after experiences that have changed everything.
The children's physical and emotional needs can also affect how they adjust to the village itself.
Workers say some children arrived suffering from malnutrition and psychological trauma, while during their first days others did not want to study or stay at the village.
After months of displacement and fear, returning to any form of normal life could feel unfamiliar, but over time the place became part of their lives.
For some children, leaving the village has also been difficult because of the routine and community they found there.
One child who had returned to northern Gaza cried upon learning he would no longer be able to return to Al-Bait Village, so the team later arranged monthly transportation for him to continue attending.
For children who have lost limbs, however, the support they receive at the village is only one part of the much longer process of adjusting to life after their injuries.
Life without a limb
The loss of limbs among children has become one of the most devastating consequences of the war in Gaza, with thousands reported to have lost one or more limbs since Israel began its attacks on the Gaza Strip.
For them, the injury does not end at the moment of amputation, as the lack of suitable prosthetic limbs and rehabilitation programmes can affect their movement, independence and ability to return to the lives they had before.
The experiences of people who have lost limbs came into renewed focus in September 2026 after the controversy surrounding Adidas' campaign featuring an amputee Israeli veteran.
The campaign prompted criticism and calls for a boycott, while activists drew attention to people who have lost limbs in Gaza, and Adidas later apologised for the campaign.
But behind the debate around the advert are the stories of children facing a different reality: losing a limb, waiting for a prosthetic and going through a long process of rehabilitation to regain some independence.
For the children at Al-Bait Village, those difficulties show up in the details of their everyday lives, with each child experiencing how their injury has changed what they can do.
Mahmoud, a 10-year-old boy, was inside his home while his mother was preparing food when they were hit. He says his sister was killed before she could eat, while his own leg was amputated up to his hip.
"I was standing inside the home while mama was preparing food. Suddenly, we were hit. Even my sister was killed before she could eat. I was injured, and my leg was amputated up to my hip," he tells The New Arab.
Before his injury, Mahmoud loved playing, especially football, and imagined himself growing up like his older brother, going to the gym and practising sports.
Now, he says the hardest thing is going outside and moving around like other children, which has also changed ordinary parts of his life, such as buying shoes.
"The hardest thing for me is going outside and moving like the other children," he says. "I buy boots, but I only wear one of them."
For Mahmoud, the solution he wants is a prosthetic limb, which he sees as a way of regaining some of the movement he has lost.
"I want to have a prosthetic limb," he adds.
Abdul Rahman, 12, has already received one. Before his injury, much of his life revolved around playing outside and riding his bicycle, and he was sitting outside his home when he got off his bike to help a neighbour charge a battery.
Moments later, the bombing happened, leaving him injured and without his leg.
The injury affected more than just Abdul Rahman's ability to move; he says he became embarrassed about going outside and spent most of his time on his phone.
Later, receiving a prosthetic limb helped him regain some independence and made it easier to move around.
"I was embarrassed to go outside and move around. I spent all my time on my phone," he says. "Since I got the prosthetic limb, I have been able to move better."
Abdul Rahman adds that he dreams of having an advanced electronic prosthetic limb, but his priorities shift as he talks about the other children at Al-Bait Village who are still waiting for prosthetics.
Rather than focusing on what he wants for himself, he says he wants the other children to have the same opportunity to move more independently.
"I don't want an electronic prosthetic limb anymore. I just want all my friends here to have prosthetic limbs too," he explains.
The long road to independence
Mohammed Musleh, a child from northern Gaza who was displaced to Deir al Balah, is also still adjusting to the changes caused by his injury.
His father had gone to an aid distribution point in the Al Nabulsi area during the famine, and after his father was delayed, Mohammed and his brother went looking for him before they were hit by shelling.
Before the injury, Mohammed says he was able to run, carry water jerrycans and do whatever he wanted, but he now needs help with many parts of his daily life even though he has received a prosthetic limb.
"I used to run, do whatever I wanted, and carry water jerrycans," he says. "Now I feel trapped."
Mohammed says the prosthetic limb has helped him, but only partly restored the independence he had before his injury.
"The prosthetic limb helped me by about 50%," he continues.
His experience reflects a wider problem facing the children at Al-Bait Village, because receiving a prosthetic limb is not necessarily the end of the process.
Children still need rehabilitation and time to learn how to use their prosthetics, while access to suitable limbs and the equipment needed to support their recovery remains a major challenge.
Al-Bait Village continues to support children who already have prosthetics and help others whenever resources become available, but the need remains much greater than what the village can provide on its own.
For children still waiting, losing a limb can affect ordinary parts of life, from moving around outside and playing with friends to doing things as simple as putting on a pair of shoes.
That is why the work at Al-Bait goes beyond rehabilitation. The village is also trying to provide children with a place to learn, eat together, participate in activities, and spend time with others who have experienced similar things, while supporting them through the emotional and physical effects of the ongoing genocide.
Months after Abu Majed first saw children who had lost their limbs while searching for food for his own family, he now stands among hundreds of children inside the village that grew out of that experience.
The shortage of prosthetic limbs and medical equipment continues to limit the children's ability to fully rebuild their lives, but Al-Bait Village is trying to give them somewhere to continue with their education, receive support and experience parts of childhood that the war has taken away from them.
Hassan Herzallah is a Gaza-based translator, writer and storyteller. He is in his third year studying English translation at the Islamic University of Gaza and continues his education online after the university was bombed. He contributes to Mondoweiss, Palestine Chronicle, The Massachusetts Review and other international outlets, documenting life under siege and displacement

Gokhan Ergocun

Germany's general public debt rose 1% quarter-on-quarter in the second quarter of 2026, driven by higher borrowing in special federal funds.
 
The country's general public budget owed the non-public sector €2.75 trillion ($3.12 trillion) at the end of the second quarter of 2026.
 
Preliminary data from the Federal Statistical Office (Destatis) showed that public debt increased by 1%, or €26.3 billion, compared to the first quarter of the year.
The general public budget includes the federal government, states, municipalities and social security, along with all extra budgets, while the non-public sector comprises credit institutions and private companies.
Federal debt grew by 1.1%, or €20.5 billion, from the previous quarter to reach €1.9 trillion.
 
Two special funds drove this increase, just as they did in the previous quarter.
The Infrastructure and Climate Neutrality fund increased its debt by 39.1%, or €13.8 billion, to €48.9 billion.
The Bundeswehr special fund expanded its debt by 8.8%, or €4.2 billion, to €51.6 billion.
State governments held €646.2 billion in debt at the end of the second quarter, marking a 0.5%, or €2.9 billion, increase from the previous quarter.

US, China cooperate on global AI governance despite intensifying competition
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
08:56:16 UTC
17:56:16 KST

Yunus Turk and Emir Yildirim
29 September 2026•Update: 29 September 2026
The intensifying competition between the US and China in artificial intelligence (AI) continues alongside efforts to cooperate on governance rules, monitor AI-powered cyberattacks, and prevent frontier models from being controlled by non-state actors.
Two distinct approaches to global AI governance are emerging from the US and China, while a third approach is coming from the UN, according to a recent report by the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS).
The number of partner countries in the US-led Silica Initiative, focusing on AI and semiconductor supply chains, reached 24 in June, while, on the other side, some 29 countries joined the rival Chinese-led World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization (WAICO) as founding members, the report published on Sept. 21 showed.
Pax Silica was made up of participants primarily from high-income economies and the US’ security partners in Europe, the Indo-Pacific, the Middle East, and Latin America. WAICO members are, in contrast, from low- and middle-income countries, with Kazakhstan being the only country participating in both initiatives.
The key AI agenda items between the US and China mostly focus on cooperation in tracking AI-powered cyberattacks, China’s access to advanced American models, Washington’s restrictions on open-source Chinese models, and preventing state-of-the-art frontier AI models from falling into the hands of non-state actors.
During Chinese President Xi Jinping’s visit to Washington last week, talks between Xi and his American counterpart, Donald Trump, focused on developing AI in a human-centered and controllable way, as well as potential risks.
The CSIS report stated that the dialogue between the two parties could focus on developing common definitions to serve as a foundation for future discussion, such as determining which systems can be classified as frontier models.
One of the key elements of technological competition between the two countries is access to high-performance chips used in developing models.
US export controls on advanced technologies make it difficult for Chinese AI labs to access such chips and other computing resources, while China is moving toward developing its own semiconductor and AI capabilities.
The report highlighted that there is still no established mechanism for the parties to verify model security compliance, which stands in the way of potential AI security regulations.
 
US-China issues ‘no longer limited to trade deficits or tariffs’
 
Arzu Al, a political economy professor at Marmara University, told Anadolu that the meeting between Xi and Trump in Washington should be regarded as a strategic balancing act to manage the costs of competition, noting that the core issue between the two nations is no longer limited to trade deficits or tariffs.
“AI, advanced semiconductors, data infrastructure, energy capacity, and critical minerals became integral parts of economic power, national security, and foreign policy capabilities,” she said.
“Xi emphasized that AI must remain under human control and that its risks and benefits should be addressed together, while Trump supported the continued dialogue and cooperation in the area – this by no means constitutes the end of their technological competition, but in fact, it shows that the competition is intensifying in some areas while other areas remain open to controlled cooperation,” she added.
Al stated that the structure we’re seeing today should not be explained through the lens of classic Cold War bloc formation between the countries, but through a “controlled techno bloc formation.”
While the US and China have yet to fully sever their economic ties, the two countries also do not want strategic interdependencies to limit their potential.
“What is decisive in the technopolitical order is not so much the interdependence but rather the extent to which the interdependence is asymmetrical and whether it can be weaponized to pressure one side,” she said.
Al noted that Taiwan coming up during the meeting showed that structural disagreements between the US and China on security matters persist.
“Maintaining serious competition in security and technology while cooperating on AI at the same time is not a contradiction – it is precisely the nature of the current relationship between the two countries,” she said.
“This is also precisely where the real significance of this meeting lies, as the competition between Washington and Beijing is not mutually exclusive, and both competition and cooperation will exist simultaneously in this new era – the struggle to grow technological capacity and access critical inputs will continue to be one of the fundamental axes of US-China relations,” she added.

A “very strong and robust” deployment of security forces was reportedly expected outside schools as high school students in the Ile-de-France region continued mobilizing after protests over the past week.
Students have been protesting overcrowded classes and schedules as well as teacher shortages.
 
Public sector strike expected

Ugandan kingdom enthrones ex-TV anchor after succession fight

Ugandan kingdom enthrones ex-TV anchor after succession fight
FORT PORTAL, Uganda, Sept 29 - A former television news anchor was crowned king of Uganda's Tooro Kingdom on Tuesday, becoming the 13th monarch of the Batooro people in a ritual-laden coronation that ended a succession dispute.
Edward Rukidi Kijanangoma succeeded King Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV, whose death last month from cancer at age 34 triggered a feud, with his mother saying a previously undisclosed son was entitled to the throne.
Uganda is a constitutional republic governed by an elected president, but four pre-colonial kingdoms remain as influential symbols of identity and heritage despite not having any political power.
A 21-member committee from the royal Babiito clan selected Kijanangoma, 56, who is Oyo Nyimba's cousin.
A source with knowledge of the succession dispute told Reuters that Uganda's central government pushed through that decision over the mother's objections.
Kijanangoma took the new royal name Edward Rukidi Nyabongo I in a traditional ceremony that included the slaughter of a bull and sprinkling of a hen's blood in Tooro's capital Fort Portal.
Nyabongo I walked to Karuziika Palace between midnight and 3 a.m. before taking part in a mock battle for the crown.
At Karuziika, young men dressed in tunics, orange shawls and skins held sticks and spears, some prostrating before the king.
Traditional dancers and drummers, some wearing calabashes, entertained guests who included President Yoweri Museveni.
Earlier, Charles Kayondo Kamurasi, the Omusuuga or head of the Babiito clan who had been wielding power since Oyo Nyimba's death, handed over authority to the new king in a church service at St. John's cathedral.
"We have a big task to protect our culture, our traditions and customs and good conduct among our people," Nyabongo I said in his maiden speech, pledging to rally his subjects to protect the environment.
TODDLER KING
Oyo Nyimba died in the US on August 27 while receiving treatment for angiosarcoma, an aggressive cancer.
He drew global attention in 1995 when enthroned at age 3 after the death of his father, with images of the toddler king in royal robes and a crown prompting widespread fascination.
Former colleagues of Nyabongo I at the state broadcaster UBC where he worked as a news anchor and editor, describe him as humble and down to earth.
"Everyone in Fort Portal is happy because of this new king. We are preparing. Women are ironing their masuka. Men are ironing their kanzus," said Tooro resident Elizabeth Kengonze in the run-up, referring to traditional clothes.
"People are practicing how they will sing Amakondere (praise music). We are very happy and grateful because Tooro, as a culture, is being promoted and the young ones are now knowing and learning how the Tooro culture was."
The coronation took place despite objections from Oyo Nyimba's mother, Best Kemigisa, and sister, Princess Ruth Komuntale. They say the late king left behind a young son and a will naming him as heir.
Oyo Nyimba was not married and was not publicly known to have children. The kingdom's prime minister first mentioned a child in a statement announcing his death.
Kamurasi said the clan knew of no child and had followed Tooro's customs in choosing a successor.
"The child they are claiming to be there is not known," he told media last week. REUTERS

President Donald Trump said he has offered Iran nothing to end the war, rejecting reports that he was willing to ease sanctions and release frozen funds for concrete steps on its nuclear program.
"This is untrue. I offered them NOTHING," Trump wrote on Truth Social Monday.
Axios and CNN both reported, citing unidentified U.S. officials, that Trump was willing to give Iran sanctions relief and free Iranian funds as part of a final deal on the condition that Iran showed "concrete progress" on the nuclear issue.
Trump has cited preventing Tehran from acquiring a nuclear bomb as a key goal of the war, along with ending its ability to attack its neighbors and creating conditions for Iranians to topple their leadership.
Iran does not have nuclear weapons and denies it wants to develop them, but argues it has the right to a domestic nuclear energy capacity.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, in an interview with the CBS show "Face the Nation," said Tehran was ready for talks on its nuclear program and other issues, but would not accept "bullying or coercion."
"Iran is not seeking war, but will defend itself against pressure, threats and attacks," Pezeshkian said, adding that it had already agreed that "we're not supposed to develop nuclear weapons."
U.S. and Iranian officials spoke separately with mediators Monday as part of a renewed effort to end the seven-month war, according to officials of both countries.
Iran insisted Sunday that only diplomacy can solve its conflict with the United States and Israel.
"Our conditions are clear, and any move toward reopening the Strait of Hormuz is contingent on these conditions being met," Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi posted on social media. "Only a negotiated solution can get them out of this deadlock."
Araghchi told reporters at the U.N. Friday the proposed deal would trigger a seven-day countdown to reopening the strait and a pause in regional fighting.
Trump on Saturday rejected the plan and argued that desperation was driving the Iranians' push for an agreement on the key waterway.
"They want to make a deal to open the Hormuz Strait immediately because they're losing so badly," Trump told reporters at the White House.
Araghchi said mediators facilitating Tehran's talks with Washington had not officially relayed a U.S. rejection.
"We are waiting for the mediators to convey the definitive views to us and we will make a decision based on them," Araghchi posted.
The war, which Trump launched alongside Israel in February as "Operation Epic Fury," has killed thousands of people, severely disrupted global energy supplies, pushing up oil prices and fueling global inflation.
Iran and its allies have responded by extending the conflict throughout the region. Iran has struck U.S. allies in the Gulf with drones and missiles, while its Houthi allies in Yemen have hit Saudi interests.
Saudi Arabia, the largest of the Gulf states, has been drawn deeper into the war this month as Houthi rebeles have advanced in Yemen, routing forces of the Saudi-backed government and threatening Saudi oil exports through the Red Sea.
Oil prices rose for a second successive session on Tuesday as lingering concern over Middle East supply outweighed signs of recovering crude exports from the region.
Brent crude futures had risen $1.49, or 1.4%, to $106.77 a barrel by 0326 GMT while U.S. West Texas Intermediate crude was at $93.94, up $1.34, or 1.5%. Both benchmarks closed the previous session at nearly $1 a barrel higher.

African leaders to gather in Egypt for ambitious business summit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
08:44:32 UTC
17:44:32 KST

Breadcrumb
African leaders to gather in Cairo for ambitious business summit as Egypt eyes expansion
African leaders will meet in Egypt on Friday for a business summit that Cairo hopes will bolster its clout across the continent.
The inaugural three-day Alamein Africa Forum is part of Egypt's push to reassert itself in a continent where China and Gulf states, particularly the United Arab Emirates, have emerged as major players.
After long focusing on the Middle East and the Mediterranean, Egypt is keen to rebuild its influence within Africa.
It has also sought to rally backing in its long-running dispute with Ethiopia over the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD), which it sees as a threat to its vital share of Nile waters.
Friday's forum is expected to bring together more than 20 heads of state and government representatives in the Mediterranean city of Alamein, alongside business leaders, bankers and development institutions.
"This is an African platform," Egypt's deputy foreign minister for African affairs Mohamed Abu Bakr Saleh told AFP. "A country in East Africa should be able to sign an agreement with a country in West, North or southern Africa through this platform."
Saleh said the forum would become a biennial event under an African Union mandate, focusing on infrastructure, trade, agriculture, healthcare, mining, technology and renewable energy.
Officials estimate Egyptian investments across Africa at around $14 billion. Among Egypt's flagship ventures is Tanzania's $3 billion Julius Nyerere Hydropower Project, built by a consortium led by Egyptian companies.
'Vast resources'
Yet trade within Africa remains limited, totalling just $192 billion in 2023 and only accounting for around 15 percent of the continent's total trade, compared with more than 55 percent in Asia and over 70 percent in Europe.
Africa also attracted about $70 billion in foreign direct investment in 2025, a fraction of the roughly $1.6 trillion invested globally, according to the UN.
"Africa possesses vast resources, but they are still not being exploited to the level we would like to see," Saleh said.
The gathering also takes place against the backdrop of an unresolved dispute between Egypt and Ethiopia over the $5 billion GERD, Africa's largest hydroelectric project.
Ethiopia says the dam, inaugurated last year, is vital for economic growth, while Egypt says it could threaten Nile water supplies without a binding operating agreement.
More than a decade of negotiations have failed to yield a settlement.
"Our position on Egypt's water security has not changed and will not change," Saleh said. "It is an existential issue for Egypt."

Israel has committed 5,147 violations of the Gaza ceasefire agreement in effect since Oct. 10, 2025, killing 1,421 Palestinians, the Government Media Office said Tuesday, warning of an imminent humanitarian catastrophe and as winter approaches.
“Humanitarian and relief conditions in the Gaza Strip had become dangerous and catastrophic, exposing hundreds of thousands of displaced Palestinians to deadly consequences,” the office said in a statement.
It dismissed Israeli claims that ample supplies had been allowed into Gaza as “misleading.”
“Israel permitted only 35% of the agreed number of trucks carrying humanitarian and relief aid and reconstruction materials to enter the enclave,” the office said. “Only 72,826 trucks were allowed to enter out of 210,600 humanitarian and relief trucks and trucks carrying reconstruction materials that were supposed to enter under the agreement.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan Ambassador to Paraguay Lee Yueh-jung (李岳融) said bilateral cooperation has benefited education, health care, trade, and economic development, La Nacion reported Tuesday.
In an op-ed published by La Nacion, Lee said the partnership will mark its 70th anniversary next year. He said cooperation has covered agriculture, aquaculture, support for small businesses, and microloans for women entrepreneurs.
Taiwan has also helped finance social housing and major infrastructure projects, including the Tres Bocas tunnel, Lee said. He highlighted education and health care as particularly important areas of cooperation.
The government has offered scholarships to Paraguayan students since 1991, with more than 900 pursuing undergraduate or graduate degrees in Taiwan. It also provides professional training in fields including medicine, nursing, engineering, cybersecurity, hairdressing, and culinary arts.
The two countries jointly established the Taiwan-Paraguay Polytechnic University to train engineers. The university has more than 300 graduates and plans to launch a master’s program and move to its permanent campus next year.
In health care, Taiwan has worked with Paraguay to introduce a digital information system at public health facilities. More than 1,300 facilities use the system, which has recorded over 61 million patient visits.
The system provides digital medical records and helps manage medicines, supplies, and staff. Lee said it also gives authorities real-time data to support health care decisions.
Trade between the two countries has also grown. Taiwan is the largest buyer of Paraguayan pork, a major buyer of its beef, and recently opened its market to Paraguayan poultry.
Lee said diversifying export markets has become increasingly important as trade tensions and economic pressure disrupt global supply chains. He encouraged Paraguayan businesses to build closer ties with Taiwanese companies and universities and explore opportunities for investment and cooperation.
Lee was also scheduled to attend the first Paraguay-Taiwan international forum at the Catholic University of Asuncion on Tuesday. The event was set to focus on Taiwan’s role in democracy, its geopolitical challenges, and its significance to Paraguay and Latin America.

Taiwan reports 12.3% drop in road deaths
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
08:39:16 UTC
17:39:16 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan recorded 1,569 road deaths from January through July, down 12.3% from the same period in the government’s 2023 baseline year, the Ministry of Transportation and Communications said Tuesday in a press release.
The ministry said all major road safety indicators had improved from the baseline, although elderly road deaths remained a concern. Wu Tung-ling (吳東凌), director-general of the Department of Railways, Highways, and Road Safety, said motorcycle fatalities fell by 206, or 18.1%, while pedestrian deaths declined by 18, or 9%, and deaths involving drunk driving fell by 82, or 54.3%, per CNA.
Compared with the same period last year, however, deaths among people aged 65 and older increased by 33, or about 5%, to 697. Wu said the increase was concentrated in Taoyuan, Taichung, and Hualien County.
Motorcycle crashes accounted for about half of the elderly deaths in those three localities, with many occurring when riders turned left at intersections. Pedestrian incidents accounted for about 20%, with many occurring while people were crossing roads.
The ministry designated 2023 as its baseline year because that marked the beginning of a four-year road safety improvement plan. Compared with the 2023 baseline, elderly road deaths fell by 22, or 3.1%.
Wu warned that data from previous years showed elderly road deaths tended to increase during the fourth quarter. He attributed the trend to larger temperature differences between day and night, shorter daylight hours in autumn and winter, and age-related declines in physical function.
Wu urged older people to take extra care when traveling early in the morning or at night and to wear brightly colored clothing or reflective accessories to make themselves more visible.
The ministry expanded its definition of drug-impaired driving incidents in July. Previously, the statistics counted only cases in which the party considered primarily responsible was impaired. They now also include cases in which another party was impaired and committed a traffic violation.
From January through June, 23 deaths were recorded in incidents involving drug-impaired driving, followed by seven in July alone. Officials said the revised definition was intended to present a more complete picture of such incidents and help police assess enforcement measures.

Russia plans record $200 billion military budget for 2027
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
08:39:08 UTC
17:39:08 KST

- Russia plans record defense spending of 17.1 trillion rubles in 2027, about 27% above its earlier plan, government documents seen by Reuters show.
- Moscow now expects a 2026 federal budget deficit of 3.2% of GDP, double its earlier forecast.
Russia plans to spend a record 17.1 trillion rubles ($201 billion) on its military in 2027, while its budget deficit this year is now expected to reach double the government’s earlier forecast, according to government documents seen by Reuters.
The defense figure is about 27% higher than the 13.5 trillion rubles Moscow had previously penciled in for 2027 and the largest since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Reuters reported Sept. 28. The documents show total defense spending of about 50 trillion rubles ($592 billion) over the next three years. The government is expected to send the draft budget to parliament by Oct. 1.
For 2026, the government had planned to spend 12.1 trillion rubles on defense, but the actual figure is classified and will not be published. Economist Janis Kluge of the German Institute for International and Security Affairs noted on X that the Finance Ministry had originally intended to cut defense spending slightly this year.
The government now expects the 2026 federal deficit to reach 3.2% of gross domestic product, up from its earlier estimate of 1.6%. Total spending this year is set to rise 13.2% to 48.6 trillion rubles, or 20.9% of GDP, while the forecast for oil and gas revenue, long the backbone of Russia’s budget, was cut to 7.6 trillion rubles from 8.9 trillion.
Kluge said the federal figure does not tell the whole story, because it leaves out Russia’s regional budgets and possibly its social security funds. He estimated the consolidated deficit across all levels of government will be close to 4% of GDP. Regional budgets were slightly in surplus on average as of Aug. 1, he said, but a sharp drop of about 0.7% of GDP is expected at the end of the year, pushing them into deficit.
Moscow plans to cover the gap by borrowing more and dipping into savings. Net borrowing this year will rise 26% to 5 trillion rubles, and the government will take 459 billion rubles, about 11% of the liquid assets in its National Wealth Fund, to reduce the deficit. State debt is projected to climb to 21.7% of GDP in 2027 from 19.9% this year, above the 20% level Russian authorities have described as safe.
The government has also announced tax increases for 2027, including a new windfall tax on metals and mining companies expected to raise about 200 billion rubles a year.
Defense is set to take about 35% of Russia’s total federal spending in 2027, according to figures cited by The Moscow Times and the Kyiv Post. Combined with national security spending, which covers the Interior Ministry, the National Guard and the security services, the total reaches 21.4 trillion rubles, or 43.9% of the budget.

In addition to its existing major customer, three other semiconductor companies are certifying Chung Hwa Chemical’s production lines for advanced processes.
Electronic-grade chemicals accounted for more than 40% of the company’s revenue in the second quarter. Shrinking semiconductor process nodes and rising demand for high-purity cleaning chemicals are driving rapid growth in the electronic-grade sulfuric acid market. Taiwan’s consumption is estimated to rise from 30 million kilograms per month last year to 60 million kilograms by 2027.
Beyond semiconductor chemicals, the company is expanding into higher-value specialty chemical applications, including materials for high-frequency electronics and other industrial uses. Chinese drugmaker Hengrui Pharma said Tuesday it has agreed to license global rights to an experimental weight-loss drug to Denmark’s Novo Nordisk in a deal potentially worth up to $2.6 billion.
The drug, HRS-1596, is a Phase I-ready GLP-1/GIP dual receptor agonist designed for once-weekly oral dosing, Hengrui said in a statement.
Under the agreement, Novo will receive exclusive rights to develop, manufacture and commercialize the drug globally, excluding mainland China, Hong Kong, Macao and Taiwan.
Hengrui will receive $300 million upfront and could receive additional development, regulatory and commercial milestone payments, bringing the potential deal value to $2.6 billion. It is also eligible for royalties on net sales.
HRS-1596 is designed to reduce weight and improve blood sugar control through mechanisms including appetite suppression, stimulation of insulin secretion and improved insulin sensitivity.
Hengrui said the drug has potential applications in obesity, type 2 diabetes and other metabolic diseases.
Chinese authorities have approved Hengrui to begin Phase I clinical trials of HRS-1596 for weight management and type 2 diabetes.
Novo, maker of obesity drug Wegovy and diabetes treatment Ozempic, has been expanding its pipeline of oral treatments for obesity and other cardiometabolic diseases. Its Wegovy pill was approved by the US Food and Drug Administration for weight management in 2025.
The Hengrui deal remains subject to US antitrust clearance and other customary conditions and is expected to close in the fourth quarter of 2026.

Electric bikes overtake ‘ordinary’ bikes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
08:37:51 UTC
17:37:51 KST

More electric bikes are now being sold than ordinary bikes, and 45 per cent of households in Flanders already own an electric bike according to figures from Fietsberaad, the advisory body on cycling policy. In terms of the total number of journeys, the electric bike is already more important than public transport. Moreover, users are getting younger and younger.
Fietsberaad, the knowledge and advisory body for cycling policy in Flanders, has highlighted the importance of the electric bike in a new report. It analysed figures and graphs from various travel behaviour surveys that have been carried out annually in Flanders since 2015. Its annual FietsDNA survey also provided insights.
The rise of the electric bike is undeniable and is particularly clear when we look at the ‘modal split’ – that is, the distribution of journeys across the various modes of transport used: car, bicycle, public transport or on foot.
Whereas in 2015 Flemings made less than one per cent of journeys by electric bike, last year this figure had already risen to over 7 per cent. The total number of cycle journeys, both electric and non-electric, has risen from 12 to 20 per cent over that period.
‘That increase can be attributed entirely to electric bikes,’ says Wout Baert of Fietsberaad, ‘as the number of journeys made by conventional bicycle remained virtually unchanged during that period.’
It becomes even clearer when we factor in the figures for journeys by public transport. Journeys by train, tram, bus and underground account for less than 5 per cent in the latest survey, whilst we already make 7 per cent of our journeys by electric bike. In Flanders the electric bike is outperforming public transport as a whole.
Increasingly a trend among young adults
Ten years ago, it was mainly people aged 55 and over who rode electric bikes, but in the most recent surveys we see the average age of e-bike riders falling.
In the 35 to 44 age group, the majority of cycle journeys are made by electric bike (54.7 per cent). This age group already covers 70 per cent of all the kilometres they cycle by electric bike.
In the younger group, aged 28 to 35, we are already seeing 21 per cent of journeys made by electric bike. More than half of the kilometres cycled (52 per cent) in this group are already covered on an electric bike.
Commuting
If we look solely at commuting, the latest report from 2025 shows that 22 per cent of journeys to and from work are already made by bicycle. Of that 22 per cent, just over 12 per cent are made on electric bikes and nearly 10 per cent on conventional bikes. Electric bikes have therefore become more important for commuting than conventional bikes.
“The many options for leasing a bicycle through work contribute to this, and people can choose from a range of electric lease bikes: speed pedelecs, cargo bikes, as well as fat bikes with thick tyres. It is worth noting here that the range – or the number of kilometres a person can travel – increases significantly with an electric bicycle.”

Israel's Democrats petition High Court to give party leader Yair Golan Shin Bet security

Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
08:36:07 UTC
17:36:07 KST

The High Court of Justice gave the government and Shin Bet (Israel Security Agency) until Thursday to respond to a petition seeking state protection for Democrats chairman Yair Golan, but declined on Tuesday to order immediate protection at this stage.
Justice Ofer Grosskopf said the authorities were expected to continually consider the need to protect Golan in accordance with the latest assessment of the threats against him.
The brief order did not decide whether Golan is entitled to Shin Bet protection. It required the state to submit a preliminary response by Thursday, ahead of any further court consideration of the petition.
The Democrats party and Golan petitioned the court on Tuesday to compel Shin Bet chief David Zini and the government to provide him with state protection amid what they described as dozens of explicit threats to kill him or harm his family.
The petitioners had asked the court to order immediate protection even before receiving the state’s response, keep it in place until the case was decided, and hold an urgent hearing. They also sought a preliminary state response within 72 hours.
The petition said Golan remained without protection from any state body despite the threats and the heightened tensions surrounding the October 27 election.
The party had warned that it would seek legal action after three written requests went unanswered. Two were addressed to the chairman of the Central Elections Committee and copied to security and legal officials. The third was sent directly to Zini on September 22, with a response requested by September 27, according to the petition.
Public advisory committee recommended Shin Bet security for Eisenkot
The Democrats said Israel Police had raised Golan’s threat level to four on a six-point scale, which the party described as high and identical to the rating assigned to Yashar chairman Gadi Eisenkot, another opposition party leader.
A public advisory committee recommended in late August that Eisenkot receive Shin Bet protection until the election but made no such recommendation concerning Golan. The Democrats accused the committee at the time of acting on political considerations.
Zini approved Shin Bet protection for Eisenkot on Sunday. Eisenkot’s team nevertheless confirmed to The Jerusalem Post on Tuesday that a security detail had not yet been assigned to him. The Shin Bet later confirmed that it had no intention of providing a security team for Eisenkot.
The Shin Bet said later on Tuesday that Zini had approved a series of measures to provide security to party leaders, which included intelligence units providing an intelligence oversight and support framework for the party leaders, authorization for security teams hired by party leaders to carry weapons, coordination between the Shin Bet and said security teams, and conducting periodic situation assessments to evaluate the threat level for each party leader.
Shin Bet chief Zini recently authorized to decide security for party leaders
Earlier this month, the Ministerial Committee for Shin Bet Affairs authorized Zini to determine the security arrangements required for party leaders who do not hold public office and are not otherwise entitled to state protection. The authorization remains in effect until the next Knesset is sworn in.
The petition includes screenshots of posts calling for Golan to be shot or hanged and threatening members of his family. It also says his name appeared in a death-threat letter attached to a brick thrown at Channel 12’s news studios on July 27, and that he was the only party leader named in the letter.
Under the Shin Bet Law, the agency is responsible for protecting people designated by the government. The petition argues that protecting Golan falls at the core of the agency’s responsibility to safeguard Israel’s democratic institutions.
“A candidate who cannot appear in public without risking his life is restricted in conducting his election campaign compared with candidates who are not subject to a similar threat,” the petition states. “Harming a candidate because of his political positions during an election period is an attack on the electoral process itself.”
“We will not sit idly by while the next political murder is being planned,” the Democrats said. “We demand that the High Court intervene immediately, before it is too late.”

Attorney-General pushes for Israel's Supreme Court to ban leader of Arab party Balad from election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
08:35:56 UTC
17:35:56 KST

Attorney-General Gali Baharav-Miara has asked the Supreme Court to approve the disqualification of Balad chairman Sami Abu Shehadeh from the October 27 election, according to a position filed on Tuesday.
In the filing, submitted ahead of Thursday’s hearings on candidate and party disqualifications, the attorney-general and chief prosecutor Amit Aisman argued that Abu Shehadeh meets the legal threshold for disqualification because he supported an armed struggle by a terrorist organization against the State of Israel.
The Supreme Court is reviewing the Central Elections Committee’s September 23 decision to disqualify Abu Shehadeh, as required before the disqualification of an individual candidate can become final.
Disqualification of Abu Shehadeh on the grounds of Basic Law
At the heart of the case is Section 7A of Basic Law: The Knesset. It establishes three grounds for disqualifying a candidate or electoral list: negating Israel’s existence as a Jewish and democratic state; incitement to racism; and supporting an armed struggle by an enemy state or terrorist organization against Israel.
The Elections Committee disqualified Abu Shehadeh on the first and third grounds. Baharav-Miara, however, asked the court to approve his disqualification only on the armed-struggle ground and to overturn the committee’s decision concerning Israel’s existence as a Jewish and democratic state.
The attorney-general’s position centered on an Arabic-language article Abu Shehadeh published on two news sites on October 8, 2023, while the Hamas-led attack was still underway.
“The article Abu Shehadeh published on October 8, 2023 - one day after the murderous terrorist attack began, and while it was still underway - expresses a position of support for the armed struggle of the Hamas terrorist organization against the State of Israel,” a statement on behalf of Baharav-Miara and Aisman said.
According to the filing, the article described the attack as a historic military, political and strategic event and argued that, if the small and besieged Gaza Strip could achieve intelligence concealment and operational surprise, others could do so.
The attorney-general argued that the article’s content, context and timing made it an exceptionally grave piece of evidence that could independently satisfy the normally stringent threshold for disqualification.
The filing also cited a social-media post showing three men whom the disqualification application identified as terrorists, accompanied by words of respect and appreciation.
Abu Shehadeh, in a response filed with the court, asked the justices to reject the disqualification. He argued that a single article containing no explicit call for violence could not meet the Supreme Court’s requirement for clear and convincing evidence of repeated conduct demonstrating that support for armed struggle was a dominant part of a candidate’s political activity.
He acknowledged that the article’s timing and its failure to condemn the October 7 massacre were problematic. He said he regretted publishing it and would not write or publish it in the same form today.
However, Abu Shehadeh maintained that the article was an attempt to analyze events as he understood them when it was written, rather than an expression of support for Hamas’s attack. He argued that its only practical proposal was a diplomatic initiative involving the Palestinian Authority and neighboring Arab states, intended to end the war and halt bloodshed on both sides.
His response said the Elections Committee had disregarded his repeated public condemnations of attacks on Israeli civilians and crimes committed by Hamas, as well as his parliamentary and civic record. It said no evidence had been presented of any concrete act by Abu Shehadeh supporting armed struggle or of involvement in unlawful activity.
The response also accused the committee and the attorney-general of applying different standards to Arab candidates and right-wing electoral lists. It argued that far larger bodies of evidence presented in attempts to disqualify Otzma Yehudit and Religious Zionism-Zehut had been found insufficient, while a single article was treated as sufficient in Abu Shehadeh’s case.
Approving the ban under those circumstances, the response said, would create “two separate tracks based on nationality” for exercising the right to vote and stand for election.
Adalah - The Legal Center for Arab Minority Rights in Israel, which represents Abu Shehadeh, similarly accused the attorney-general of “blatant discrimination between Jewish and Arab political candidates.”
“By her logic, those who called for genocide in Gaza and incited hate crimes and pogroms in the West Bank are free to run in the elections, while an Arab candidate is barred over a single article, which did not include any call for violence,” the organization said.
A-G says explanations 'unconvincing'
The attorney-general’s filing rejected Abu Shehadeh’s explanations as partial and unconvincing. It said they did not adequately address the article’s timing, its failure to condemn the attack or its discussion of the operational lessons others could draw from it.
Baharav-Miara’s new position goes further than her submission before the Elections Committee hearing. At that stage, representatives of her office said the article appeared to provide a basis for the armed-struggle allegation and that the committee should consider the request seriously after hearing Abu Shehadeh’s response, but stopped short of expressly recommending his disqualification.
During the committee hearing, a representative of the attorney-general said there was a basis for the request. After considering Abu Shehadeh’s affidavit and oral explanations, the attorney-general is now explicitly asking the Supreme Court to approve the disqualification on that ground.
The original application was filed by Otzma Yehudit and its chairman, National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir. Abu Shehadeh is running in third place on the Joint List.
Ben-Gvir welcomed the attorney-general’s position, saying, “Even the attorney-general and the state attorney cannot deny the evidence we presented against Sami Abu Shehadeh.” He criticized the attorney-general’s office for not gathering the material itself and credited attorney David Bavli, No. 11 on Otzma Yehudit’s electoral list, with compiling it.
Committee representatives voted 30-4 to disqualify Abu Shehadeh on the Jewish-and-democratic-state ground. Committee chairman Supreme Court Justice Noam Sohlberg also voted on the armed-struggle ground, bringing the tally on that ground to 31-4.
The court will review Abu Shehadeh’s disqualification on Thursday before the same nine-justice panel that will subsequently hear challenges concerning the disqualifications of MK Ofer Cassif and the Joint List.

Raytheon to build record numbers of AMRAAM missiles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
08:31:04 UTC
17:31:04 KST

- The U.S. Air Force awarded Raytheon a multi-year AMRAAM contract worth up to $20.7 billion, running through June 2033.
- The deal includes foreign military sales to 16 countries and follows a February agreement to build at least 1,900 AMRAAMs a year.
The U.S. Air Force has awarded Raytheon a multi-year contract worth up to $20.7 billion to build AMRAAM air-to-air missiles, a deal the company says will push production of the weapon to record levels.
The award, announced Sept. 25 by the U.S. Department of War, covers complete missiles, spare guidance sections and related work, and runs through June 30, 2033. Raytheon will build the missiles in Tucson, Arizona. The contract does not say how many missiles it will buy.
The AMRAAM, short for Advanced Medium-Range Air-to-Air Missile and also known as the AIM-120, is a radar-guided missile fighter jets use to shoot down enemy aircraft beyond visual range. Now in its fifth generation, it is carried on 14 aircraft and ground platforms and fielded by 44 countries, and has recorded more than 7,000 successful live firings in tests and combat, Raytheon said. It is also the main interceptor for NASAMS, the ground-based air defense system Norway and Raytheon developed together, which Ukraine uses against Russian cruise missiles and drones.
Raytheon described the deal as a five-year multi-year contract with two option years, awarded under the Department of War’s “Arsenal of Freedom” push to expand munitions production. Multi-year contracts let the Pentagon buy several years’ worth of weapons at once, which gives manufacturers the confidence to invest in factories and suppliers and usually lowers the price per missile.
The award follows a framework agreement Raytheon and the Department of War signed on Feb. 4, 2026, under which the company committed to producing at least 1,900 AMRAAMs a year. That agreement was one of five covering Tomahawk cruise missiles, AMRAAM and three Standard Missile interceptor variants. RTX, Raytheon’s parent company, said it nearly doubled AMRAAM output in 2025 compared with 2024 and is working with small and mid-sized suppliers across the country, as well as exploring co-production with international partners, to raise it further.
Much of the demand comes from abroad. The contract includes foreign military sales to 16 countries: Australia, Belgium, Canada, the Czech Republic, Denmark, Finland, Germany, Italy, Japan, Kuwait, the Netherlands, Norway, Poland, Sweden, Taiwan and the United Kingdom.
The contract is a sole-source award, meaning Raytheon did not compete for it, and part of it is an undefinitized contract action. That lets work begin before the government and the company agree on final prices and terms, up to a set ceiling, in this case $20.7 billion.
Only a small share of the money has been committed so far. The Department of War obligated $85,715 in fiscal 2026 U.S. Air Force weapons procurement funds and about $154.3 million in foreign military sales funds at the time of award. The rest will be released as the contract is finalized and future budgets are approved.
The Air Force Life Cycle Management Center at Robins Air Force Base, Georgia, manages the contract.

UNGA 81: Five key takeaways from general debate
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
08:30:40 UTC
17:30:40 KST

UNGA 81: Five key takeaways from general debate
UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres warns the future will be shaped by four tests: AI, climate change, war and inequality.
The 81st United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) concluded on Monday with artificial intelligence (AI), the Israel-Palestine conflict and the US-Israel war on Iran dominating world leaders’ addresses during the general debate.
UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres, in his final address before his term ends, warned that the future of the world would be shaped by four tests: AI, climate change, wars and inequality.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Turkiye calls for UN Security Council veto to end: Could it happen?
- list 2 of 3Jerusalem Daily: violence continues as the world watches the UNGA
- list 3 of 3German, Russian foreign ministers hold rare talks amid rising tensions
“Across all four tests, the decisive issue is power. Power over force, money, energy, technology, rules and the future. That is why the UN Charter – and the work of the United Nations – matter more than ever,” Guterres said.
Speeches ranged from calls to reform the UN to appeals for upholding international law, as the global body has been undermined by the unilateral foreign policy pushed by United States President Donald Trump.
Here are the biggest takeaways from this year’s summit:
Palestine
The situation in Palestine was a key issue among members amid Israel’s ongoing genocidal war on Gaza despite the so-called “ceasefire” and escalating settler pogroms in the occupied West Bank.
France, Canada, Iraq, the United Kingdom and others called for Palestinian sovereignty during their speeches.
“What credibility do we have if we continue to remain inactive in the face of Gaza,” French President Emmanuel Macron said in his address.
“Some boast of a supposed peace, but this peace hasn’t reopened humanitarian routes for a single second,” he said, adding: “Must we stand by and watch this spectacle that shames us all?”
Macron, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, his Canadian counterpart Mark Carney and Saudi Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan Al Saud chaired a meeting at the UNGA on Palestinian statehood, which is being actively undermined by Israel. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s government has accelerated construction of illegal settlements and provided impunity to settlers in the occupied territory.
At the same time, the US-led Board of Peace unveiled a 66-project reconstruction blueprint with proposed funding of $2.4bn for the Gaza Strip on the sidelines of the UNGA.
However, the board’s plan excludes the UN agency for Palestinian refugees (UNRWA), saying it has no role in the future of Gaza. The decision was described by Palestinian political analyst and playwright Ahmed Najar to Al Jazeera as aligned with Israeli efforts to “marginalise and ultimately dismantle the agency, removing it not only from Gaza’s present but from its future”.
Dozens of delegates left the hall in protest as Netanyahu delivered his speech, in which he declared that Israeli forces would continue fighting against Hamas and Iran.
Trump defends military action on Venezuela, Iran
In his address, Trump emphasised that while others spoke of peace, he “made peace”.
Trump defended his actions in abducting the then-Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro in January and said, since his military operation, hundreds of political prisoners had been freed in the South American country and that Caracas had signed the largest oil deal in history last month, covering “65 billion barrels of oil, which will benefit both Venezuela and the United States enormously and help drive down the cost of energy all over the world”.
“It was perhaps the biggest deal ever made. To the victor belong the spoils – you’ve all heard that,” Trump boasted.
Trump reiterated that he would never allow Tehran to have nuclear weapons and that the 12-day war in July 2025 had “obliterated their nuclear programme beneath mountains of rubble” as the ongoing US-Israel war on Iran had sunk “159 ships of their navy” to the bottom of the sea.
“I have a big decision to make – will a deal be made with Iran that lets them rebuild and create a far greater country than it ever was before … or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again,” he said, adding: “I believe we make a deal right after the elections.”
Popular Iranian officials
During sideline talks and one-on-one meetings, Iranian officials were in demand.
In his speech to delegates, President Masoud Pezeshkian emphasised that Iran had only “defended ourselves” amid attacks on his country and killings of Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, scientists and children.
“We are not terrorists, our innocent people have been the targets of cowardly attacks and aggressions imposed upon our country,” he said.
Pezeshkian added Iran would not accept that peaceful nuclear technology is held exclusively in the hands of a few countries.
“We will not bow our head and give up the right that is inherently ours,” he said.
Meanwhile, on the sidelines of the summit, Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi met his counterparts from India, Qatar, Turkiye, Pakistan, Ukraine and other countries.
He also met US Special Envoy Steve Witkoff and Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner in a four-hour meeting mediated by Qatar.
AI dominance
World leaders used their time at the podium to call for a global approach to using AI as interest in the technology grows, but fears that it could escalate if unchecked are also growing.
In his address, Finnish President Alexander Stubb said AI was the “most consequential technology in the history of mankind”.
“It will impact science, the economy, politics, security, and the very essence of our humanity. Humans can and should be in the driver’s seat. We have a choice: we can compete, cooperate or slow down. For me, cooperation is the best way forward,” he said.
While discussions are moving away from a good-versus-bad dichotomy, officials disagreed on approaches.
While Guterres and the European Union called for safety standards and international rules, Trump said AI innovation should not be constrained by international regulation, adding that the US should control its AI sector.
Xi skips the UNGA
Chinese President Xi Jinping skipped the UNGA despite being in the US for a summit with Trump. He sent Vice President Han Zheng to attend.
Xi rarely attends the UNGA. He had sent Premier Li Qiang in his place last year. In 2024, Foreign Minister Wang Yi attended the annual gathering.
Without mentioning Iran in his address, Han reiterated Beijing’s position that “sovereignty and security of countries in the Middle East, including the Gulf, should be respected”.
“China calls for advancing the governance of the West Bank and the post-conflict reconstruction of Gaza in accordance with the principle of the Palestinians governing Palestine. It also calls for bringing the Palestinian question back onto the right track of the two-state solution at an early date,” he said.
Han also called for a “people-centred approach and develop AI for the positive and for good, narrow the digital divide, and promote development that is universally beneficial”.

UK police release on bail five men held over airbase incident, 'surprising' the US
British police said Monday five men arrested near an airbase used by the United States were released on bail, as Washington asserted a "foreign actor" was involved in the suspected bomb plot.
US President Donald Trump, speaking in Washington, said he was "surprised that they released them", adding that "I wouldn't have done that".
For his part, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Monday that a suspected bomb plot near a UK airbase used by the United States was the work of a "foreign actor."
"It's one that clearly involves the hands of a foreign actor," Rubio told Sean Hannity on broadcaster Fox News in an interview Monday, adding that he would not go into further detail.
The release of the five—all London-based Britons in their mid-20s—came as British Prime Minister Andy Burnham announced an emergency meeting of top officials to ensure they have "the full picture".
Earlier, Iran had denied involvement in any plot to target the Royal Air Force (RAF) Fairford base in Gloucestershire, southwest England, following the security scare there early Sunday.
Here's what we know so far:
Counter-terror probe
UK counter-terror police are leading the investigation after authorities received reports Sunday of three "suspicious" white vans near the airbase, which has been used by the United States to bomb Iran.
Police said in their latest update Monday that the five men held, who all live in inner London boroughs, were being released on bail.
"This does not mean the investigation is over," Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor, the head of Counter Terrorism Policing, said, adding the five would be subject to "stringent" bail conditions.
He said officers were "considering this from every possible angle, including that this may be activity committed by proxies, or individuals either knowingly or unknowingly, working on behalf of a foreign state".
The men were arrested on suspicion of explosives offences and "preparation of a terrorist act" under UK anti-terrorism laws, according to police.
They had been travelling in the three suspect vehicles, which have since been subject to "extensive examination, with the support of military assets and forensic experts".
Bomb-disposal team
Authorities have not confirmed details of the threat but bomb-disposal experts were seen working at the scene.
The Daily Mail and Press Association both reported late Monday they understood from sources that tests on materials in the back of the vans established they were "not viable explosives".
A farmer living in the village of Whelford near the airbase said she rang the police after seeing the vans blocking a road and a group of masked men.
The anonymous woman told media on Monday that she believed the police had "dropped the ball" on the threat.
But UK Defence Minister Wes Streeting said the farmer only had a "partial picture".
Iran denies involvement
Trump said on Sunday that Britain and United States had had the suspects "under investigation" for a while and alleged "they were looking to do big damage to our fort".
After hearing news of their bail, Trump said Monday the case "might be" linked to Iran but declined to elaborate.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the incident "clearly involves the hands of a foreign actor", without giving further details.
Iran's embassy in London said on X that it "categorically rejects and strongly condemns" the "unfounded and malicious speculations" that Tehran was involved.
US bombers
Britain gave the United States permission in March to use Fairford for "specific defensive operations into Iran" to destroy Iranian missiles at source.
US bombers and other planes have since been seen taking off and landing from the base—the only one on Britain's mainland used for this purpose.
Residents in the rural Cotswolds area surrounding Fairford said the site, which hosts a range of US military equipment and personnel, had seen increased activity and security in recent months.
Authorities evacuated around 85 households from the village early on Sunday, and they were allowed to return home the next day.
Tehran has previously warned London against allowing its bases to be used by the United States in operations against Iran.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has accused London of "putting British lives in danger" by allowing the bases to be used "for aggression against Iran".

OpenAI apologises to Australia over unauthorised government website access
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
08:28:42 UTC
17:28:42 KST

OpenAI apologised to Australia on Tuesday after revealing that its artificial intelligence models accessed government websites without authorisation during internal training and evaluation.
“In June, during internal training and evaluation our models accessed Australian government websites in ways they were not authorised to,” the company said.
“We also should have handled our response better. We are sorry and working to do better in the future.”
The company said it identified the activity in mid-August while reviewing earlier training and evaluation work following a separate incident involving AI research platform Hugging Face.
The apology came five days after Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese disclosed the Medicare portal incident in New York on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly.
Albanese said on September 24 that an OpenAI agent had gained unauthorised access to Services Australia’s Medicare Statistics Reporting Service.
The agent accessed public and non-public files, prompting a forensic investigation with assistance from the Australian Signals Directorate.
Australian officials said the portal contains aggregate Medicare statistics and is separate from systems handling individual Medicare claims and personal information.
OpenAI said its review identified activity involving four Australian government organisations: Services Australia, the NSW Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research, the Victorian Department of Health and the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare.
At Services Australia, an experimental internal model had been assigned a research task concerning government spending per person on medicines for skin conditions in Victorian communities.
Australian task force to be established
OpenAI said the model struggled to obtain the information and then took unauthorised actions that allowed it to access material beyond what was publicly available.
The company said the model examined technical information and source code and accessed internal files, credentials and aggregate statistics.
However, OpenAI said its review found no evidence that individual patient or client records were accessed.
“We did not intend for this activity to occur, and the access to the service and follow-on activity should not have happened,” it said.
OpenAI said its models also accessed systems operated by the other three agencies but did not access individual crime records, medical records or identifiable survey responses.
The company said it has strengthened safeguards, including additional network restrictions and monitoring.
It also pledged technical support for affected agencies and assistance in strengthening Australia’s cyber defences.
OpenAI said it will establish an Australian task force with independent experts to develop recommendations on AI-related cybersecurity and improve coordination between AI developers and governments.
Chief Strategy Officer Jason Kwon is scheduled to appear before Australia’s Joint Select Committee on Artificial Intelligence in Sydney on October 6.
