City of Brussels imposes restrictions on souvenir shops and hospitality around the Grote Markt
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
07:26:51 UTC
16:26:51 KST

The City of Brussels intends to tighten the rules for businesses around the capital’s historic market square, the Grote Markt, in order to create greater diversity in the range of shops on offer. For example, the number of souvenir shops will be limited to a maximum of 20. Restrictions will also be imposed on the number of cafés and restaurants: in most streets, no more than one in three businesses will be permitted to be a hospitality venue.
City of Brussels imposes restrictions on souvenir shops and hospitality around the Grote Markt
Socks featuring Manneken Pis. Caps with the Atomium. Magnets, key rings, postcards… You don’t have to look far around the Grote Markt to buy a souvenir of Brussels. There are around 40 souvenir shops. Too many, according to the Brussels city cabinet.
The city cabinet is currently working on the approval of the ‘Grote Markt and Surroundings’ Special Zoning Plan, which, amongst other things, will restrict the number of souvenir shops daily La Dernière Heure reports. The office of Anaïs Maes, alderwoman for Urban Development, has confirmed the plans to Brussels media outlet BRUZZ.
One of the proposed measures is to limit the number of souvenir shops to around 20. At present, there are twice that number – around 40. The reduction will be achieved by a phase-out policy: existing licensed souvenir shops may remain open, but if they close, something else must take their place.
Rejecting an application
In the streets around the Grote Markt, the City of Brussels also wishes to limit the number of pubs and restaurants: in future, no more than one-third of commercial premises may be hospitality establishments. An exception may be made for streets consisting exclusively of hospitality outlets. Existing cafés and restaurants will not have to close. However, the City may refuse to issue a new licence if there are already too many hospitality businesses in that street or area.
Furthermore, the City wishes to ensure that the residential function is preserved in the area around the Grote Markt: a maximum of 20 per cent of the available floor space may be used for tourist accommodation, such as hotels or other tourist lodgings.
The City also wishes to work towards a more climate-resilient Grote Markt and its surroundings. One of the climate objectives is to significantly reduce the amount of concrete, tarmac and other hard surfaces: from 94 per cent of the surface area to 75 per cent.
Night shops
The debate about a more diverse range of shops around the Grote Markt is nothing new. As early as 2013, restrictions were placed on night shops, but the ‘homogeneous range’ of souvenir shops and snack bars remained a problem. Among those who spoke out on this issue in the past was Sofie Rombouts, who closed her stationery shop, Mofelito Paperito, in the heart of the city centre in 2024.
The City has long recognised the problems but did not want to rush into anything, explains Alderwoman Maes. “It is important to have a clear vision for the future of our historic centre,” she explains. “In this way, we protect our heritage and ensure the liveability and attractiveness of this area.”
Behind the scenes, the plans had already been in the pipeline for several years. “A consultancy firm was appointed as early as 2021,” says a spokesperson for Maes’s office. It then took nearly five years before the plans could be put out for public consultation, as approval had to be obtained at various levels. “This involves a legislative framework, so various intermediate steps must be approved by the regional authorities.”
The Special Zoning Plan is not yet final: it will be subject to public consultation. Anyone who wishes to do so may comment on the plans during this phase. From early November, the City will also organise meetings with the local residents affected.

Gaza doctors face tough decisions as patients face long waits for diagnoses
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
07:26:37 UTC
16:26:37 KST

Gaza doctors face tough decisions as patients face long waits for diagnoses
Medical staff struggle to treat patients with shortages in testing equipment.
Deir el-Balah, Gaza – At Al-Aqsa Martyrs Hospital here in central Gaza, Bassem Hassan, director of the laboratory department, deals with medical tests whose results will determine the futures of his patients.
Hassan’s team gives doctors the information they need to diagnose a range of illnesses, from kidney disease to diabetes, and without this crucial information, they will not know how to proceed with their cases.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Israel’s ambassador to the US says son injured in West Bank car-ramming
- list 2 of 4‘My hands are empty’: Displaced Palestinians struggle to survive
- list 3 of 4‘No role for UNRWA in Gaza’: Does the Board of Peace toe Israeli lines?
- list 4 of 4Mapping Israel’s 300 checkpoints: Where they are and how they work
But Israel’s genocidal war and siege on Gaza has resulted in widespread damage to medical infrastructure and shortages of key materials needed to make diagnoses.
There has been a suspension of all blood gas testing, which is particularly important for cardiac and intensive-care patients, and shortages of blood-collection tubes, which are essential for clinical chemistry tests.
Automated clinical chemistry analysers, which laboratories rely on for more than 60 percent of their tests, have also stopped operating. Some sterilisation equipment and refrigerators used to store blood and plasma have also ceased working.
“Given these limited resources, tests are prioritised according to the severity of each case with priority given to kidney, cancer and heart patients as well as those in intensive care,” Hassan told Al Jazeera.
Doctors know that laboratory test results are needed to determine the correct medication dosages given to patients, monitor their responses to treatment and make urgent medical decisions.
Without this information, doctors are left without a key part of the jigsaw puzzle that could determine the death or survival of a patient.
As the third anniversary of the war on Gaza approaches, more than three-quarters of medical imaging equipment in the enclave is out of service. Shortages of laboratory testing materials are at 87 percent, and there is a 74 percent deficit in essential consumables required for laboratory and diagnostic testing.
Gaza’s ministry of health has warned that with these dire shortages and repeated breakdowns of medical equipment, blood banks and laboratories risk shutting down.
This would most affect patients suffering from critical conditions, such as electrolyte imbalances, high potassium levels, impaired kidney function and heart disease.
Marwan Al-Azaiza, head of the cardiology department at Al-Aqsa Martyrs Hospital, told Al Jazeera that due to these shortages at public hospitals, doctors sometimes have to use private laboratories if the patients can afford this added expense.
“In other cases, doctors rely on clinical examinations, electrocardiograms and the indicators available to them, even though this does not constitute a complete substitute for the tests needed to confirm or rule out certain diagnoses,” he said.
Medical teams are looking to coordinate with charities, health organisations and relief institutions to provide broader care for the people of Gaza.
Meanwhile, only five of the 18 CT scanners in Gaza remain operational, and the remaining ones are running beyond their capacity.
There are also no magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) services in Gaza after the destruction of nine machines in Israeli attacks.
Mohammed Abu Salmiya, director of al-Shifa Hospital in Gaza City, told Al Jazeera that medical teams are now forced to restrict laboratory tests, X-rays and CT scans to the most urgent cases.
“This reality forces doctors to make difficult choices between patients, deciding who needs the test immediately and whose test can be postponed,” he told Al Jazeera.
“Although this approach is necessary under the current shortages, it means that many other patients remain on waiting lists with diagnostic tests delayed even when they are needed to diagnose their conditions or monitor their treatment.”
Yousef al-Athamneh, 57, from Deir el-Balah suffers from kidney failure and requires dialysis three times a week. He worries about the shortages of bicarbonate, bloodlines, dialysis machines, intravenous fluids and other materials that are needed for his dialysis sessions.
“What frightens me most is the possibility that one day dialysis supplies will run out or that a machine will break down while replacement parts are unavailable, leaving me unable to access the treatment that keeps me alive,” he told Al Jazeera. “All we ask is for the most basic necessities of medical care to be available, so that we can go to our dialysis sessions with the reassurance that we will return home to our families.”
Khalil Al-Daqran, spokesperson for Al-Aqsa Martyrs Hospital, said cancer patients are facing shortages of chemotherapy drugs and other medicines. The destruction of the Turkish-Palestinian Friendship Hospital, the only hospital in Gaza that had specialised in cancer treatment, has also added to the strain on medical teams.
Israel’s tightened siege on Gaza means it is almost impossible for cancer patients to seek treatment abroad, Al-Daqran added.
Overall, 350,000 patients with chronic diseases, including diabetes and high blood pressure, face medication shortages, which pose a threat to the continuity of their treatment and their lives, he added.
“Cancer patients, people living with chronic illnesses and those suffering from heart and kidney disease require regular treatment that cannot be postponed while doctors are being forced to work with extremely limited resources,” Al-Daqran said.
“What we need now is guaranteed access to medicines, medical supplies and equipment, so that shortages do not become an additional cause of deaths that could have been prevented.”

Lack of empathy over terror concerns, trade 'bump': Jaishankar explains what weighs on India-US ties
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
07:26:06 UTC
16:26:06 KST

Jaishankar said the two sides had reached “more or less an understanding” on the trade agreement.
NEW DELHI: External affairs minister S Jaishankar has flagged a lack of “understanding or empathy” in the United States towards India's concerns over cross-border terrorism, saying the issue has affected bilateral ties.Speaking at the Asia Society in New York after the conclusion of the UN General Assembly’s High-Level Week, Jaishankar said terrorism remains a key concern for India, given its experience of cross-border attacks over several decades.“Terrorism emanating from its neighbour is one of India’s primary concerns, and if this is not fully appreciated by New Delhi's partners, it impacts bilateral ties,” Jaishankar said, in an apparent reference to India-US relations amid closer engagement between Washington and Islamabad.“What for us in India is particularly important is the issue of terrorism... There are very few countries which have been subjected to the kind of terrorism that we have from a neighbor as part of a deliberate, conscious policy over many decades. It is something which matters so deeply to us. There isn't enough understanding or appreciation or empathy of that. I think that creates a problem too,” he said.
India-US ties: Trade talks remain a key issueJaishankar also discussed the challenges facing India-US relations, including negotiations on a trade agreement.
He said the talks were complex because of the fundamental differences between the two economies, including India’s large base of small producers, farmers and factories.“Much of the world has had a more difficult relationship with the US... In our case, one was the trade negotiation. If you look at the stakes involved, the complexity of it involved, bear in mind, India is a society of small producers, small agriculture producers, small factories. Apart from the per capita gap between India and the US, the nature of production and the nature of society are very different. A trade negotiation required a certain amount of patience and detailing to see it through,” he said.
Jaishankar said the two sides had reached “more or less an understanding” on the trade agreement, but changes in the US tariff framework had created a new challenge.“We have reached a situation where there is more or less an understanding on the trade agreement. But as my trade minister has said on more than one occasion, the issue is now what has changed on the American side. On the American side, reciprocal tariffs were struck down. So there's now a new basis for tariff imposition, which is 301. And the 301 process is still in the works... that did create bumps last year for the relationship. If that agreement is closed out, that would be one point which would contribute to a better relationship,” he added.He also highlighted the growing influence of public opinion on diplomacy, particularly in democratic countries, saying social media had added a new dimension to international relations.“Today the economics of mobility and the politics of mobility are at odds with each other.... That certainly, in public perception, is an issue... our diplomacy today is not just conducted by states, leaders, ministers, or even by diplomats. In a social media era, there is a very big public opinion factor, which, particularly in democratic societies, makes itself felt. I think that's a reality we have to take into account... We would certainly hope for and expect the relationship to move on an upward trajectory. But I have to be real about the issues that we confront. And to the extent we are able to move ahead on some of these issues, I think we'll have a better relationship. Let's apply the lens of...”Jaishankar says India-China ties improvingOn India-China relations, Jaishankar said ties were better than they were in 2025 and had improved further compared with 2024, pointing to the easing of the border standoff.“If you asked me, compared to where you were in 2025, is the relationship better today? I would say yes. Compared to 2024, even more so... After what happened in 2020 and the long standoff that we had on the border, the relationship had really been impacted... once the border standoff was resolved, it was natural that this would start to improve,” he said.Jaishankar said India had consistently conveyed to Beijing that a prolonged standoff between the two countries would not benefit either side.“We have long been telling the Chinese, personally at my level, that a standoff between us, a dip in our relationship, doesn't help either of us. Third parties will take advantage of that... It took a little while for the Chinese side to agree with that, for whatever reason. But I don't think that long standoff served our interests. It certainly didn't serve theirs... what we've had is that, as the border comes back more towards normalcy, the relationship comes back more towards normalcy... If it happens, it helps both of us,” he said.He said the two countries had arrived at a basic principle that the state of the border determines the broader state of the relationship.“We came down to a very fundamental principle, which is that the state of the border determines the state of the relationship. You can't have tension...on the border and say the relationship should be normal. So what we've had is, as the border comes back more towards normalcy, the relationship comes back more towards normalcy, and if the relationship comes back more towards normalcy, it helps both of us,” Jaishankar said.Ukraine, Iran conflicts pose risks to Global SouthJaishankar also highlighted the economic impact of the Ukraine and Iran-Gulf conflicts on developing economies, particularly through energy and food security.“If you look at these two conflicts, the Ukraine and the Iran-Gulf conflict, they've actually had a devastating impact on Global South economies. We are particularly concerned about the energy situation, because the market is very tight. On top of that, if people play politics with it, it adds to the market complications. It will drive up prices at a time when people should be stabilizing prices. A part of it is the security of oil supplies, and another is the politics of oil supplies. They are feeding into each other. They're creating a double crisis or an aggravated crisis,” he said.“When it comes to food, we are looking at a situation today where some of the major grain exporters will not be able to send out their shipments... We are looking at significant fertilizer shortages... On top of it, we are looking at Super El Niño. There is going to be a major food crisis, probably in the coming months...” he added.'World moving towards greater multipolarity'Jaishankar said the world was moving “quite visibly” towards greater multipolarity and outlined what he described as a broader approach India could pursue in such an environment.He said countries that were seen as stable, consistent and reliable could become important partners as the global order becomes more competitive.“One, you build a reputation for yourself as stable, consistent, reliable, so that others view you in a very dynamic, volatile world as a steadying factor... Partners tend to gravitate towards you. You're the good person in the neighborhood. The second would be that the more you diversify and you find common interests, common ground, I think the more of a balancing structure can be created. What we have to do is to take self-interest and temper it with a certain long-term, I would say, predictability and stability, which is also part of intelligent self-interest, and try to create something along those lines...”He said countries, particularly major trading economies, would seek stability rather than prolonged volatility saying, “...not everybody wants the Hobbesian scenario that you painted; it is very volatile. It's actually very risky in real life. People will not expose their trade accounts to that kind of volatility. For the big trading countries, their economies are exposed to that. Everybody will want to find some accounts of stability.
.. I think the world will go for that kind of mix... The world is more competitive. It's tough. A new dynamic will come.""A new culture will come. New negotiations and new bargains will be struck. When the smoke clears at some point in time, you will see the different points joined by lines of different lengths. There will be a new geometry that will come about. I would still count on the self-interest of countries, their sensibilities and their desire ultimately to stabilize their own lives as a driving force. I think that is the direction we are heading. And we can see that in some of our relationships," he added.

Interview: Xi-Trump summit raises expectations for greater global stability: scholar
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
15:21:48 CST
16:21:48 KST

SINGAPORE, Sept. 29 (Xinhua) -- The recent summit between Chinese President Xi Jinping and U.S. President Donald Trump has added new substance to the constructive China-U.S. relationship of strategic stability, raising expectations for greater stability around the world, a public policy scholar has said.
By agreeing to build "a constructive relationship of strategic stability based on respect, fairness and reciprocity," the two presidents have provided a paradigm for countries to resolve differences fairly, said Gu Qingyang, an associate professor at the Lee Kuan Yew School of Public Policy at the National University of Singapore, in an interview with Xinhua.
The new vision shows that China and the United States are willing to resolve differences on the basis of respecting each other's development paths and core interests, while allowing reasonable room for each other's development and taking into account the common interests of both countries and the wider world, he said.
It also reflects a commitment to treating each other as equal partners, pursuing mutual benefit and balancing rights and obligations, Gu said.
"It offers new ideas for a complex international environment and gives a troubled world a reassuring anchor of stability," Gu said, noting that countries, regardless of size or strength, should resolve differences and manage disputes through consultation on an equal footing rather than through zero-sum competition.
Gu said Xi's remarks that building a constructive China-U.S. relationship of strategic stability is neither an expedient measure nor something that can be achieved overnight reflects a key feature of China's approach to relations with the United States: a long-term perspective.
It requires action of all sectors, across all fields and at all levels in the two countries while looking to lasting engagement across generations, he said, citing Xi's invitation for 100,000 young Americans to visit China for exchanges and study programs over the next five years.
This is, in effect, about engaging younger generations and building lasting ties between the people of the two countries, Gu said.
"China and the United States, as two major countries, need to engage across all fronts to understand each other's concerns and interests, and build a relationship in which their interests are mutually reinforcing," he said.
ASEAN countries welcome candid dialogue between China and the United States and hope it will help make the regional and global environment more stable and predictable, he said.
Gu said ASEAN countries see the next decade as critical for development, while at the same time, they have felt the impact of global uncertainty, including disruptions to industrial and supply chains in recent years caused by unilateral tariffs and practices of decoupling and supply chain severance.
Looking ahead, Gu said the interests of China and the United States, as well as those of the wider world, require the two countries to avoid confrontation.
A constructive China-U.S. relationship of strategic stability will help create a relatively stable environment for China, the United States and the wider world over the medium and long term, he said. ■

Australian central bank raises interest rates to 15-year high
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
15:21:19 CST
16:21:19 KST

SYDNEY, Sept. 29 (Xinhua) -- Australia's central bank on Tuesday raised interest rates to a 15-year high, citing inflation driven by AI and the conflict in the Middle East.
The Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) said its Monetary Policy Board voted unanimously to lift the cash rate target from 4.35 percent to 4.60 percent, the highest figure since November 2011.
It marks the fourth rate rise delivered by the RBA so far in 2026 after three previous increases of 0.25 percentage points in February, March and May.
Economists and Australia's major banks had unanimously predicted the decision to raise the cash rate target on Tuesday.
The Monetary Policy Board said in its decision statement that the conflict in the Middle East has broadened, causing global energy prices to rise much higher than assumed when the board decided to keep interest rates on hold in August.
"The Middle East conflict remains unresolved, and there are scenarios where inflation is higher and activity lower than forecast. Global oil supply disruptions are maintaining upward pressure on global and domestic energy prices and inflation," it said.
Additionally, it said that AI-related demand is driving rapid growth in global prices for technology-related goods.
Speaking earlier on Tuesday, Treasurer Jim Chalmers said that the conflict in the Middle East has been "absolutely disastrous" from a cost-of-living and economic perspective.
"We're seeing inflation going up around the world; we're seeing interest rates going up around the world. And unfortunately, Australia's not immune from the same pressures," he told Australian Broadcasting Corporation (ABC) radio.
After the decision was handed down, Chalmers told reporters that the conflict is not the only factor in Australia's inflation challenge, but it is a very big factor and has made high inflation linger for longer.
The latest data from the Australian Bureau of Statistics showed that annual inflation fell from 3.8 percent in June to 3.5 percent in July.
The trimmed mean, the measure of underlying inflation preferred by the RBA, remained steady at 3.6 percent. The central bank targets annual inflation of 2-3 percent.
The statistics bureau will release inflation data for August on Wednesday, and the Monetary Policy Board will next meet at the start of November.
The board said in its decision statement on Tuesday that it will continue to do what it considers necessary to bring inflation sustainably back to target, including further increasing the cash rate target.
RBA Governor and Monetary Policy Board Chair Michele Bullock said at a media conference following Tuesday's meeting that the full effects from the rate rises in the first half of 2026 have not yet flowed through the economy.
"We raised interest rates three times earlier in the year. A lot of that effect is still to flow through. This is one more. What we are predicting here is that this will be restrictive enough," she said.
David Bassanese, chief economist at Sydney-based fund manager Betashares, told the ABC that he expects the central bank to lift rates by another 0.25 percentage points in November, warning that the Australian economy is set for a period of stagflationary conditions. ■

Israel, which says Hamas has been rearming and launching attacks in violation of an October ceasefire, has stepped up strikes on the group in recent weeks.

Hamas has denied trying to carry out attacks or rebuild its arsenal, and accuses Israel of undermining the Gaza deal.

At least 1,400 Palestinians have been killed in Gaza since the ceasefire took effect, according to the territory’s health officials, while the Israeli military says four Israeli soldiers have been killed.

Undoubtedly, China’s message demonstrates that the U.S. cannot use coercion to force all nations to serve its own interests or facilitate the plunder of other countries; thus, China’s stance is of great significance. Evidence indicates that China rejects U.S. unilateralist demands, as it is an independent nation that makes decisions based on its own principles and interests.

US forces set to complete withdrawal from Iraq after 2 decades
Departure from Iraq bases seen as a boost to Iran and its allies, even as Washington wages war against Tehran
US forces are set to pull out from their last bases in Iraq by Wednesday, a departure celebrated as a victory by Iran and its allies who now have deep influence in the country where 4,500 Americans died during more than two decades of war.
Iraqi security experts say the withdrawal – agreed in 2024 under President Joe Biden and carried out by Donald Trump’s administration even as it wages war against Iran – could give Tehran and its powerful allies free rein, while also allowing other US enemies to stage a comeback, including Islamic State.
“Iran stands to benefit strategically from the coalition’s departure because it removes a military presence that for years acted as a counterweight to Tehran’s influence in Iraq,” said Jasim al-Bahadli, an Iraqi security analyst specialising in studying armed Shiite groups aligned with Iran.
He predicted that the pro-Iranian militia groups would not only portray the departure as a victory for their movement, but also “seek to translate that momentum into greater influence over security and political decision-making”.

Live fire on this scale is rare, Royal Navy commander says
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
08:00:19 BST
16:00:19 KST

Most of what the Royal Navy and its allies practise is not live firing, which is what set apart the exercise that ended with the sinking of the decommissioned American frigate USS Klakring off the Outer Hebrides, according to Commander Peter Meigh, speaking from range control on South Uist.
Meigh described Atlantic Thunder as a bilateral exercise between Britain and the United States “designed to demonstrate and train our lethality against surface platforms in the North Atlantic theatre.” What distinguishes it, in his account, is that the weapons are real. “This activity is really different because it’s a live fire exercise. The vast majority of our training is not live fire due to the cost and complexity both of battle space and safety,” he said. “It’s that demonstration of really high end war fighting that hopefully we will never need to use, but invariably you need to be able to use it if the time comes, and making sure that our weapon systems work as we expect. We know how to use them, and we can employ them effectively.”
The range he operates from covers an area larger than England and Wales together. “Atlantic Thunder takes place off the north west coast of the United Kingdom in an area known as the Ministry of Defence Hebrides range, and it’s an area of around 75,000 square miles of air and sea space off the Outer Hebrides,” he said. “We are sat here in range control on South Uist, but the action is taking place 60 to 100 miles west of us in the North Atlantic, which is a challenging environment for air and maritime units to operate.”
Those conditions are the reason for holding it there rather than something to be put up with. “The seas are rough, the winds are strong. There’s no shelter. Clearly, that’s useful for a safety consideration, but it makes employing force difficult, and that’s partly why we do it, because this is potentially a battle space that we will need to fight in in the future, and we need to understand how we achieve that quickly and deliver force where necessary,” the commander said.
Reaching the moment of firing takes years of work before anyone puts to sea. “The planning timeline for Atlantic Thunder is over two years,” Meigh said, adding that he had held a meeting that day about Atlantic Thunder 28 and that it was not the first. “There is a huge amount of detail that needs to go in when you are delivering a live fire exercise as complicated as this, utilising a large number of weapon systems. There’s the logistics planning of how you get the people and equipment in the right place at the right time across thousands of miles, coming from the continental US for some elements of it, from Naples, from Rota, from Lakenheath, from Portsmouth.”
Safety and environmental work runs alongside all of that, and he described the planning as covering the safety of participants, the safety of maritime and air users in the vicinity who are not taking part, the environmental consequences of putting weapons into the water and the sky, and the sinking of a decommissioned warship “which has to be stripped of all sensitive materials so that it doesn’t pollute the environment.” Beyond that sits what he called safety trace planning, understanding where things can and cannot be in order to achieve the mission safely.
The data taken away afterwards is the reason for the whole undertaking. “It’s all about planning, executing, and debriefing,” Meigh said. “It’s about how you plan together, how you execute together, but then how you debrief, how you can gather high quality data, both from the weapon system, but also ground truth data, which this range up here we are very well set up for. So gathering a second point of view, not just what your weapon system says, but ground truth data that is calibrated so that you can analyse what you think happened and what actually happened in a large amount of detail, so that you can learn from it to make sure that systems are behaving as you believe they were. You can understand what command decisions were made, and then you can adjust as appropriate in the future.”
On the alliance the whole exercise rests on, the commander was unambiguous. “It positively reinforces the long-standing relationship that the UK and the US have across our armed services. It’s one of the closest partners I’ve worked with in my 20-plus years of being in the navy,” he said. “Our language helps, but equally, that closeness of how we can share information at the highest levels is really important. That’s something that’s unique about Atlantic Thunder, because we’re able to speak at a very classified level, and share that information.”
Atlantic Thunder is the largest exercise Meigh has run in his career, and he was previously on the staff running Joint Warrior, the multinational exercise led by Britain, and the Formidable Shield series of integrated air and missile defence exercises, which brings twelve nations together with the United States as the largest partner, both of which use the same waters off the north west of Scotland.
The weapons employed covered a wide range across different environments, surface to surface and air to surface, from both British and American units. Sixth Fleet has confirmed that the Naval Strike Missile was fired from HMS Portland and Sea Venom from a Wildcat helicopter, while USS Paul Ignatius fired an anti-surface variant of the Standard Missile 6 and the submarine USS Massachusetts finished the frigate with a Mark 48 Advanced Capability Torpedo, as we reported.
Meigh came back to the partnership when summing up what the exercise had shown. “Atlantic Thunder is a brilliant example of how the UK and US work together really well in delivering warfighting efficiencies and working together as partners. Be that on the range, be that in the mission planning, or out at sea.”

Japanese firms pull back from China amid geopolitical tensions, supply chain shifts
The research found 1,221 new Japanese entrants in China since the last survey in 2024, but that was still less than during Covid-19
As of June, 10,118 Japanese enterprises were identified as having a presence in China, the lowest number since 2010, according to a survey and analysis released on Monday by the corporate credit research and business intelligence firm Teikoku Databank.
The research also turned up 1,221 new Japanese entrants in China since the last survey in 2024, less than the total during the depressed Covid-19 pandemic years between 2020 and 2022. It identified 4,137 companies that had withdrawn from China or could not be accounted for since the last survey.
The Tokyo-based firm drew its findings from a database of about 1.51 million companies, a credit investigation report file containing some 2 million companies and publicly available information.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
06:58:45 UTC
15:58:45 KST

Central Tokyo recorded its 34th consecutive day of rain Tuesday, the longest streak since records began, according to Japan’s weather agency.
Rain has fallen in the Japanese capital every day since August 27, with approaching typhoons, a stationary autumn rain front and a low-pressure trough contributing to the prolonged wet weather, Kyodo News reported, citing the agency.
The previous record was 33 consecutive days of precipitation, registered between June 27 and July 29 2019.
The heaviest rainfall during the current streak came on September 21, when central Tokyo received 156 millimetres of rain.
Total rainfall in central Tokyo reached 629 millimetres through Monday, roughly three times the average precipitation for the entire month of September, according to Kyodo.
Rain also swept across large parts of eastern and western Japan on Tuesday.
Echizen in central Japan’s Fukui prefecture recorded more than 30 millimetres of rainfall within an hour early on Tuesday morning.
The prolonged spell is not expected to end immediately.
Rain is forecast to continue mainly across eastern Japan until around Thursday, partly due to the lingering autumn rain front, the report said.
Japan’s autumn rain front typically brings extended periods of unsettled weather as seasonal air masses interact over the country.

Turkish authorities detained the chairman of the country’s top football referees body and six other football officials on Sept. 29 in an investigation centered on allegations of official document forgery and workplace harassment.
Ferhat Gündoğdu, head of the Turkish Football Federation’s (TFF) Central Referee Board (MHK), was taken into custody during simultaneous early-morning raids conducted across four provinces.
The operation, dubbed the “Referees File” by the Istanbul Chief Public Prosecutor’s Office, was launched following a formal complaint and utilized financial audits from the Financial Crimes Investigation Board (MASAK), telecommunications records, witness testimony and expert reports. Authorities allege the suspects improperly influenced referee classifications, promotional exams and match appointments through fraudulent documentation and systematic intimidation.
Alongside Gündoğdu, those detained include TFF Active Referees Association President Ferdi Karadoruk, former MHK Vice President Ahmet Şahin, former board member Yunus Yıldırım and several regional and association administrators across Istanbul, Ankara, Elazığ and Manisa.
Reacting to the sweeping detentions, Justice Minister Akın Gürlek emphasized the government’s unwavering stance on legal accountability and integrity in sports.
“Football is our citizens’ shared passion and an important value of ours,” Gürlek said.
“Ensuring fair competition on the field and impartial, transparent refereeing processes is the foundation of public trust in football. Our state is determined to investigate, within the framework of the law, any allegations of irregularities that undermine this trust.”
Gürlek noted that the administration is fully attuned to public concerns surrounding officiating and fairness.
“We are well aware of our sports fans’ sensitivities regarding refereeing processes and their expectations for justice. No one’s position, title, or duty constitutes a reason for privilege before the law,” he stated. “We will resolutely continue our fight for clean football in order to shed light on allegations that undermine trust in Turkish football.”

Nvidia unveils security platform to stop AI agents from going rogue
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
06:56:42 UTC
15:56:42 KST

A logo of Nvidia is displayed at at the Computex Taipei exhibition in Taipei, Taiwan. (AP File Photo)
Nvidia has unveiled a new security platform designed to stop artificial intelligence agents from going rogue, saying it sets “boundaries” that could have stopped previous breaches.
The announcement of the company’s Open Agent Safety Platform follows a series of revelations from top AI companies about their models escaping and breaking into other organizations.
The disclosures sparked furious debate about the safety of advanced artificial intelligence systems, including self-improving models that some fear could race out of human control.
Nvidia executives said in a media briefing on Sept. 28 the new, open-source system could have prevented a recent incident involving a swarm of OpenAI agents that autonomously hacked into AI company Hugging Face.
“From what we know, this new security platform could have stopped the breach if it was being used in frontier labs for model evaluation early on,” said the company’s vice president of enterprise AI, Justin Boitano, referring to companies at the forefront of AI.
Nvidia makes high-end chips that have emerged as the leading building blocks for AI.
Nvidia’s security software, called OpenShell, lets developers “formally verify an agent has enough authority to do its job and no more,” Boitano said.
Because it’s open source, it can be “extended” to run on rival computing platforms including those from Arm and Intel.
The platform also includes a separate security layer called Sentry that runs onboard chips to continuously monitor AI agent activity and can “intervene instantly” if the agent starts trying to move beyond its target, the company said.
Nvidia said more than 100 organizations are using the platform at its launch, including Microsoft, Perplexity, Accenture and JPMorgan Chase.

Kanpur plane crash: No distress call, flight-monitoring gaps emerge in AAIB probe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
06:56:08 UTC
15:56:08 KST

A four-seater, dual-engine Tecnam aircraft crashed in a fatal crash on the outskirts of the Natthapurwa village near the Ganga Barrage in Kanpur.
NEW DELHI: The Aircraft Accident Investigation Bureau (AAIB) has found that Garg Aviation did not fully follow required flight-monitoring procedures before its training aircraft crashed near Kanpur on August 27, killing an instructor and a trainee pilot.The seven-page preliminary report also recommends that the Directorate General of Civil Aviation issue clearer guidelines on how Flying Training Organisations should monitor flight data.The Tecnam P2006T twin-engine aircraft crashed near the Ganga Barrage less than 20 minutes after taking off from Kanpur's civil aerodrome. The 39-year-old instructor and 28-year-old trainee were killed.
No records of flight-data checks
AAIB said Garg Aviation told investigators that it carried out random checks of data from the aircraft's Garmin system. However, the operator could not provide records of those checks and did not have a Standard Operating Procedure explaining how the monitoring was conducted or what limits would trigger further action."When queried on flight data monitoring, the FTO stated that random monitoring of Garmin data was being carried out; however, no records of such monitoring were maintained, and there was no SOP defining how the monitoring was conducted or what exceedance limits were considered for it," AAIB said.
The Garmin data card acts as a type of flight-data recorder for small aircraft. AAIB said interim safety recommendations were necessary and called for stricter compliance with flight-data monitoring requirements."Further, DGCA may issue specific guidelines detailing the procedure to be followed for flight data monitoring, which shall be made part of the TPM," the probe agency said. TPM refers to the Training and Procedure Manual.
Aircraft stopped responding after final radio call
The aircraft, registered as VT-NBV, took off at around 11.11 am on August 27. About 14 minutes later, it made a radio call saying operations were normal and that it would contact the controller again after 10 minutes.That call never came."No further call was received from VT-NBV thereafter. The RT controller attempted to contact VT-NBV but received no response," AAIB said.The aircraft had no distress call before the crash. Garg Aviation was informed at around 12.10 pm that the plane had force-landed in the Ganga Barrage area, after which the company's team went to the site.AAIB said local residents had reported the crash through the 112 emergency helpline. Police and ambulance teams reached the site and took both occupants to a hospital in Kanpur, where they were declared dead.
Engines and flight data being examined
Investigators have recovered the Garmin data card from the wreckage and downloaded its information for analysis. Both engines have also been recovered and quarantined for detailed examination.
"Both engines have been retrieved and quarantined for further detailed examination. The investigation team is coordinating with the OEM for further examination," it said. OEM refers to Original Equipment Manufacturer.The investigation also involves Italy's ANSV and the US National Transportation Safety Board, which have each appointed an accredited representative. Tecnam has also provided a technical adviser.AAIB has sought documents relating to the aircraft and its operating crew from the DGCA as the investigation continues.The crash occurred at Kanpur's civil aerodrome, an uncontrolled aerodrome managed and maintained by the Airports Authority of India. An uncontrolled aerodrome does not have an operating control tower.

15:55:06 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) – The Ocean Affairs Council announced on Thursday that the Industrial Technology Research Institute has turned foam fishing floats into plastic pellets suitable for manufacturing, according to a press release.
The Ministry of the Environment's 2024 statistics show that fishing waste accounts for up to 70% of coastal waste, with foam floats responsible for 31.5% of the trash. Distant-water fishing uses floats that are later thrown away, burned, or buried.
The council said it used a two-pronged approach. It subsidized ITRI to convert foam into reusable thermoplastics and incentivized fisheries to use less foam and turn in disposed gear.
The council said its departments coordinated the effort by connecting authorities with fishing enterprises and recycling facilities. It noted that wharves now have collection sites, with disposables labelled and tracked.
The council said the institute is currently doing test manufacturing. It said that aside from recycling and reusing, it is encouraging consumers to use daily necessities made from reclaimed plastics.

He thanked nutritionists, cooks, quality-control staff, drivers, and others involved in preparing and delivering school meals. Their work includes sourcing ingredients, preparing food, controlling temperatures, and ensuring meals reach schools safely.
Lai said nearly 99% of ingredients used in school lunches are domestically produced and traceable. He credited government support and suppliers’ sourcing efforts with bringing more locally grown rice, vegetables, fruit, meat, and seafood into school meals.
The president also praised meal providers for handling food supply disruptions. During pork supply restrictions imposed amid African swine fever controls last October, providers quickly switched to chicken, eggs, and soy products.
Lai said the industry also responded when cooking oil supplies became tight this summer. Meal providers coordinated supplies to keep school lunch services running.

Congress attacks EC over SIR row, says will fight ‘to save’ voters’ rights (Image source: X)
NEW DELHI: Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge on Tuesday accused the Election Commission of compromising the integrity of the electoral process through the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of voter rolls and changes to voter-enrolment rules. He also stated that the party would step up its campaign against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar and the government.Addressing the Congress Working Committee (CWC) meeting, Kharge said the party faced a “historic responsibility” to protect democracy and the Constitution, drawing a parallel between the Congress’ fight for voting rights during British rule and its current campaign over voter rolls.He alleged that names were being removed from electoral rolls “at the behest of the BJP and the Modi government” and accused the CEC of becoming a “puppet” of the government.
On the contrary the Election Commission has maintained that its decisions have full legal sanction and that differing views among commissioners are part of institutional deliberations.Kharge also targeted changes to Form 6, which is used for enrolling new voters.
He alleged that the rules had been changed in a way that could disenfranchise young voters. He also contrasted Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government with the decision of the Rajiv Gandhi government in 1988 to lower the voting age from 21 to 18.“They didn't provide jobs, and now they don't even want to give the right to vote,” Kharge said, alleging that the government feared questions from the youth.Also read: ‘All SIR rollout decisions unanimous’: EC says agendas for all meetings to be circulated in advance
Kharge congratulated Rahul Gandhi for raising questions over voter rolls in Mahadevpuram, Aland and constituencies in Haryana and Maharashtra.He referred to allegations involving duplicate voters, doubtful addresses, multiple voters registered at the same address and entries linked to Form 6, saying the Election Commission should have acted on the issues.“If the Election Commission had shown even a little seriousness in that direction, they would not be in the dock today, and their credibility would have been preserved,” he said.Kharge also praised Congress workers who organised protests at the block, district and state levels following Rahul's campaign.The Congress has been pressing for Kumar's resignation amid a controversy over reported differences within the Election Commission over the SIR exercise. The poll panel has said that operational queries raised by Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi were part of normal institutional deliberations and that its orders followed established procedures.Kharge also questioned the decision-making process behind SIR, asking whether it was wrong to seek clarity on who approved the exercise and why the two election commissioners were allegedly kept out of the internal portal.
Congress lists five demands
Kharge laid out five demands that he said the Congress would pursue:
Full data on major changes to voter lists should be made public.
Voters whose names have been removed should receive complete information and a full opportunity to appeal.
Political parties should receive voter lists and essential related data in a simple format and in a timely manner.
Serious discrepancies should be independently investigated within a fixed timeframe.
Election-related data and decisions should be transparent so that no political party can claim information is being withheld.
“The most important thing is that India's voters must have the confidence that their vote is secure,” Kharge said.
He said the Congress did not view the issue merely as a contest over winning or losing elections, arguing that governments may change but democracy and the Constitution were permanent.
Kharge targets PM Modi, Shah and Election Commission
Kharge also accused the BJP and RSS of systematically weakening independent institutions and said the Congress wanted the Election Commission to be strong enough to command the trust of both the ruling party and opposition.He alleged that two election commissioners had themselves described the CEC's actions as arbitrary and unfair and said those responsible should be removed.
Kharge also demanded Prime Minister Narendra Modi's resignation “on moral grounds”, alleging that the CEC had acted under his pressure.
The Congress president compared the current controversy with demonetisation, calling the alleged removal of voters from electoral rolls “vote demonetisation”.“In demonetisation, the poor stood in line. In vote demonetisation, the poor has been thrown out of the line altogether,” he said, arguing that voting was the biggest political tool available to poor, Dalit and marginalised citizens.The CWC meeting comes ahead of a meeting of opposition INDIA bloc parties on Wednesday, where a joint strategy on the SIR controversy and the demand for Kumar's removal is expected to be discussed. The opposition is also considering another removal notice against the CEC in Parliament.

Trump denies offering Iran sanctions relief, Tehran says ready for talks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
06:47:43 UTC
15:47:43 KST

Qatari mediators press peace deal between US and Iran
WASHINGTON/CAIRO, Sept 29 - Qatar said on Tuesday it hopes that shuttle diplomacy between Iran and the US can lead to a breakthrough despite US President Donald Trump's denial of media reports that he was willing to ease sanctions and release frozen funds in exchange for Iranian concessions on its nuclear program.
"We are exchanging messages between the parties, and we're working towards establishing a common ground in order to get into a deal that would save all of us from the repercussions of the conflict," Qatari Foreign Ministry spokesperson Majed al-Ansari told reporters.
The US and Iran have failed to find an off-ramp from their war, now in its eighth month. Negotiations appeared to intensify during last week's UN General Assembly meeting in New York, but have so far not yielded any agreement to reopen the Strait of Hormuz.
Doha once again has emerged as would-be peacemaker after previously playing a supporting role in producing the June memorandum of understanding that led to a brief ceasefire. US and Iranian officials spoke separately with Qatari mediators on Monday. It was unclear if another exchange took place on Tuesday.
Trump repeated his position that Iran must not obtain a nuclear weapon and that the war would be over soon.
The conflict has degraded Iran's conventional forces and damaged its already ailing economy, but Tehran has fought back with missile and drone strikes on US allies in the Gulf and by restricting oil tanker traffic in the strategic Strait of Hormuz, which has pushed up world energy prices.
"I don't know if they are going to give up yet but they'll give up," Trump told reporters on Tuesday.
"They are doing very poorly," he added.
On Monday night, Trump took to social media to deny reports by Axios and CNN, citing unidentified US officials, that Trump was willing to give Iran sanctions relief and release frozen Iranian funds as part of a final deal on the condition that Iran showed "concrete progress" on the nuclear issue.
"This is untrue. I offered them NOTHING," Trump wrote on Truth Social.
Trump has cited preventing Tehran from acquiring a nuclear bomb as a central goal of the war, along with ending its ability to attack its neighbors and creating conditions for Iranians to topple their leadership.
Iran does not have nuclear weapons and denies it wants to develop them, but argues it has the right to a nuclear program for civilian purposes.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, in an interview with the CBS show "Face the Nation" that aired on Sunday, said Tehran was ready for talks on its nuclear program and other issues, but would not accept "bullying or coercion."
IRANIAN PEACE PROPOSAL
At the United Nations General Assembly last week, Iran floated a peace proposal that would trigger a seven-day countdown to reopening the strait and a pause in fighting.
Trump on Saturday rejected the plan although Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi said on Sunday that Washington had not officially relayed a US rejection through mediators.
The war has killed thousands of people and severely disrupted global energy supplies, fueling inflation.
Saudi Arabia, the largest of the Gulf states, was drawn deeper into the war this month as Iranian-aligned Houthi fighters advanced in Yemen, routing forces of the Saudi-backed government and threatening Saudi oil exports through the Red Sea.
Oil prices settled 2.5% lower on Tuesday as investors focused on signs of recovering crude exports from the Middle East, but prices were still on track for monthly gains on lingering concern about supply disruptions.
The US government on Tuesday offered to loan energy companies up to 40 million barrels of oil from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve, the last US batch of crude from a global deal to unleash reserves in the wake of the Iran war.
The United States also stepped up its economic pressure on Iran, sanctioning 10 individuals and entities, including some based in China, Hong Kong and Pakistan, saying they helped Iran procure weapons and components. REUTERS

What's worrying the RBA now? The risks it couldn't ignore
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
06:45:05 UTC
15:45:05 KST

Key Points
- The RBA has raised interest rates to address "three big risks".
- An economist says there are already indications of another rate raise at the board's next meeting in November.
The head of the Reserve Bank hopes the fourth rate rise of the year announced on Tuesday will turn the tide on the past six months of elevated inflation.
The RBA announced interest rates would rise to 4.6 per cent from 4.35 per cent and didn’t rule out a potential fifth rate rise this year in November to try to tame inflation.
"The hope here is that this will be restrictive enough," Michele Bullock told reporters on Tuesday afternoon. "Now, will it be enough? I don't know."
The rate rise follows six months of underlying inflation of around 3.5 per cent, above the board's target range of 2-3 per cent.
The RBA's mandate is to reduce inflation into this band, while protecting as many jobs as it can.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
'Three big risks'
In justifying the call to increase rates, Bullock said the effect of the first three rate rises this year are still flowing through.
However, "three big risks" have also started to materialise over this time.
"One was the Middle East conflict going on for longer and fuel prices rising again," she said, citing previous guidance which had predicted that oil and energy prices would have stabilised by now.
The second challenge, according to Bullock, is the "AI boom", which was adding to demand both in Australia and overseas, although she said the risk had not fully materialised.
This boom has partly driven up prices for technology-related goods.
Finally she said domestic capacity pressures were higher than anticipated, referring to an economic situation where too much money is chasing too few goods.
"It's difficult to estimate output gaps and how tight the labour market is," she acknowledged, explaining that inflation numbers and unit labour costs come into play.
The Australian Bureau of Statistics is due to release the latest inflation figures on Wednesday morning.
Will there be another rate rise this year?
Several key economic indicators will be released before the RBA meets again in November, giving policymakers more data to assess the inflation outlook.
However, major bank ANZ is already predicting interest rates will then rise to 4.85 per cent.
Betashares chief economist David Bassanese said there are already indications the board could hike rates again.
"For starters, the Board's decision was unanimous. The Board also explicitly warned that it may raise rates again if needed," he said in a statement.
"Ominously, the Bank noted that local firms are facing higher costs and are either raising prices or "looking to do so". This suggests that inflation could rise even further in the months ahead."
Bullock declined to predict what the board would decide at its next meeting in November, saying the RBA will do what it has to do to reduce inflation.
"But if we can avoid massive job losses and a massive increase in the unemployment rate, that is a really important thing to be able to try and do."

Farshid Moussavi Receives the 2026 Soane Medal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
06:30:00 UTC
15:30:00 KST

Farshid Moussavi has been awarded the 2026 Soane Medal for her contributions to architectural practice, history, and theory. The Iranian-born architect and educator, who founded Farshid Moussavi Architecture (FMA) in 2011, will receive the medal at the Royal Academy in London on November 24, 2026, where she will also deliver a public lecture. The annual award, established by Sir John Soane's Museum in 2017, recognizes individuals whose work has contributed to a broader understanding of architecture and its role in society.
Moussavi's practice spans architecture, education, and writing, with projects ranging from cultural and residential buildings to retail interiors. Recent works by FMA include the Museum of Contemporary Art in Cleveland, La Folie Divine apartments in Montpellier, Îlot 19 housing in La Défense-Nanterre, Paris, and the Harrods Toy Department in London. The Museum of Contemporary Art in Cleveland and La Folie Divine reflect the practice's engagement with cultural and residential programs, while Îlot 19 forms part of the mixed-use development of the La Défense-Nanterre district. The practice's largest project to date, the Ismaili Center Houston in Texas, was completed in November 2025 following an international competition.
Born in Shiraz, Iran, in 1965, Moussavi studied at Harvard University Graduate School of Design, University College London, and the University of Dundee. Alongside her professional practice, she has maintained a longstanding involvement in architectural education, teaching at institutions including the Architectural Association, the Berlage Institute, Harvard University, UCLA, Princeton University, and Columbia University. She currently serves as Professor in Practice of Architecture at the Harvard University Graduate School of Design and previously headed the Institute of Architecture at the Academy of Fine Arts in Vienna.
Moussavi has also developed a body of architectural writing addressing the relationship between design, culture, and contemporary practice. She is the author of four books, including Architecture and Micropolitics in 2022. Her research has also addressed social housing and adaptive reuse, while her work on French architect Renée Gailhoustet contributed to renewed attention around Gailhoustet's approach to collective housing.
The 2026 Soane Medal was selected by a jury of architects, critics, and curators chaired by architect Amin Taha. Moussavi joins previous recipients including Madelon Vriesendorp, Hanif Kara, Anne Lacaton and Jean-Philippe Vassal, Peter Barber, Marina Tabassum, Denise Scott Brown, Kenneth Frampton, and Rafael Moneo. Vriesendorp received the 2025 medal and was the first UK-based female artist to receive the award since its establishment.
The 2026 Soane Medal comes amid a series of recent recognitions highlighting contributions to architecture across different contexts. Polish-American architect Daniel Libeskind received the 2026 Praemium Imperiale for Architecture, while Japanese architect Kengo Kuma was selected for the 2027 Andrée Putman Lifetime Achievement Award, recognizing his influence on architecture and the built environment. The 2026 OBEL Award, meanwhile, was given to the Balearic Social Housing Model for its approach to public housing administration and the housing shortage in Spain.

Australia raises interest rates to 15-year high
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
06:29:01 UTC
15:29:01 KST

Australia raises interest rates to 15-year high
Reserve Bank of Australia lifts benchmark rate to 4.6 percent amid stubborn inflation.
Australia’s central bank has raised interest rates to a 15-year high, spelling higher mortgage payments for millions of Australian households.
The Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) on Tuesday lifted the benchmark rate by 0.25 percent to 4.6 percent, its highest since 2011.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Rubio, Saudi Arabia’s foreign minister hold talks on Yemen, Hormuz Strait
- list 2 of 4Pope Leo says AI risk concerns not ‘fake news’
- list 3 of 4More than 80 reported abducted in Nigeria as police find human remains
- list 4 of 4Public transport drivers strike in Manila over soaring fuel prices
The RBA said inflation remained elevated and that previously flagged “upside risks” had materialised, including higher energy prices due to the United States-Israel war on Iran and an AI-driven surge in tech costs.
“There continue to be heightened uncertainties about the outlook for domestic economic activity and inflation,” the bank’s monetary board said in a statement.
“The Middle East conflict remains unresolved, and there are scenarios where inflation is higher and activity lower than forecast,” it said.
“Global oil supply disruptions are maintaining upward pressure on global and domestic energy prices and inflation. A period of prolonged uncertainty may also cause growth to be lower overseas and in Australia.”
Australia’s annual rate of inflation stood at 3.5 percent in July, well above the central bank’s 2–3 percent target.
Central banks typically raise their benchmark interest rate when policymakers believe prices are rising too fast.
Higher interest rates raise the cost of borrowing, including mortgages, cooling consumer demand and bringing down inflation.
The latest hike is set to heap further strain on Australian households already grappling with three previous increases this year.
In a research report earlier this month, Roy Morgan said nearly one-third of Australian mortgage holders, or nearly 1.8 million people, were at risk of “mortgage stress” – where households spend 25-45 percent of after-tax income on payments – as of July.
Australia’s Treasurer Jim Chalmers, who is not responsible for setting interest rates, acknowledged that the hike would mean greater hardship for many Australians.
“We know a lot of Australians are under pressure and this will make things harder,” Chalmers said in a post on X.
“Inflation and interest rates are going up around the world but we know that doesn’t take the sting out of today’s decision.”
Chalmers said the government would take responsibility for “our part of the fight against inflation”.
“That means continuing to manage the budget responsibly, rolling out tax cuts and cost of living help, and addressing the longer term challenges in our economy in an uncertain global environment,” he said.

SEOUL, Sept. 29 (Xinhua) -- The number of farming households in South Korea rose in double figures over the past five years in 2025 due to an expanded census scope, statistical ministry data showed Tuesday.
The country recorded 1,276,000 agriculture, fishing and forestry households as of Dec. 1, 2025, up 19.7 percent compared to five years ago, according to the Ministry of Data and Statistics.
The total population within the sectors expanded 8.0 percent to 2,575,000 in the five-year period.
The growth was attributed to the expansion of the census register, which captured households that went undetected in previous surveys, rather than a structural rebound.
The proportion of the elderly population aged 65 or older in the sectors made up 51.0 percent of the total in 2025, up 9.0 percentage points from five years earlier.
It stood far ahead of the country's overall elderly population ratio of 20.7 percent in 2025.
Two-member households remained the dominant type at 53.8 percent, while single-person households climbed 7.2 percentage points to 27.2 percent over the past five years. ■

UN Charter "enemy state clauses" should stay: Chinese envoy
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
14:27:12 CST
15:27:12 KST

UNITED NATIONS, Sept. 28 (Xinhua) -- A Chinese envoy on Monday told the General Assembly that the "enemy state clauses" in the UN Charter shall not be altered or deleted given Japan's re-militarization.
In exercising the right of reply at the General Debate of the UN General Assembly, Sun Lei, China's deputy permanent representative to the United Nations, noted that Japan, in its statement delivered at the debate on Sept. 22, called for deletion of the "enemy state clauses," citing its "exclusively defense-oriented policy."
China firmly opposes Japan's request, he said, adding that Japan joined the United Nations after recognizing its militarist crimes and accepting the UN Charter in its entirety.
The post-war system of Japan is contingent on deep self-reflection on its history of aggression and a clear break from militarism. However, more than 80 years later, the administration of Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, instead of self-reflection, has spared no effort to glorify and whitewash Japan's war crimes, and has attempted to cover up its ongoing expansion of military capacities by fabricating narratives about threats from neighboring countries, said Sun.
In recent years, Japan has drastically increased military spending, relaxed restrictions on the export of lethal weapons, advanced the deployment of intermediate and long-range missiles, strengthened offensive military capacities, stockpiled large amounts of sensitive nuclear materials, pushed for amending its pacifist constitution, attempted to break free from the three non-nuclear principles, and even clamored for becoming a "war-capable nation," he noted.
"All these facts are proof that Japan's re-militarization has become a real threat to regional and global peace and stability," he said.
Upholding the post-war international order, defending the outcomes of the victory of World War II (WWII), and maintaining regional peace and stability are the shared responsibility of the international community, said the envoy.
"The enemy state clauses in the UN Charter are a vital institutional arrangement aimed at preventing fascism and militarism from threatening international peace and security ever again. They provide important institutional safeguards for defending the post-war international order and remain extremely relevant today," he said.
China urges Japan to draw profound lessons from history and immediately stop its dangerous acts of re-militarization. China also calls on the international community to distinguish right from wrong, remain vigilant, jointly uphold the outcomes of the victory of WWII, and safeguard world peace and stability, he added. ■

Laos eases pig movement to stabilize pork supply amid stronger swine fever controls
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
14:27:05 CST
15:27:05 KST

VIENTIANE, Sept. 29 (Xinhua) -- Lao authorities have strengthened surveillance and disease-control measures against African Swine Fever (ASF) while easing regulated pig movements to help maintain a stable pork supply to local markets.
Lao News Agency on Monday quoted Sengphet Chanthasen, head of the livestock and fisheries sector in Lao capital Vientiane, as saying that ASF outbreaks were detected on Sept. 4 in two villages in Sangthong and Naxaithong districts of Lao capital. He said the outbreaks have remained contained within the affected areas.
Under the guidelines, areas are divided into three zones: red zones, where active outbreaks require strict movement controls; yellow zones, which serve as surveillance buffer areas; and green zones, where pig movements are permitted under specified conditions.
Pigs from green zones must undergo technical inspections before transport. Pigs weighing more than 100 kilograms and destined for slaughterhouses must test negative for ASF before being moved. Authorities have also designated transport routes to approved slaughterhouses, which are required to conduct pre- and post-slaughter inspections and maintain strict hygiene standards.
Sengphet said the revised movement rules are intended to balance disease control with the need to maintain an adequate and stable pork supply for consumers.
The livestock and fisheries sector will continue inspecting livestock transport, preventing illegal pork from entering outbreak zones, and taking action against unauthorised roadside meat sales and unapproved slaughtering facilities. ■

Feature: Afghan returnees seek humanitarian aid as winter approaches
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
14:26:55 CST
15:26:55 KST

Children of Afghan returnees are seen at a makeshift camp on the outskirts of Mazar-i-Sharif, capital of northern Balkh province, Afghanistan, Sept. 16, 2026. According to the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR), around 6 million Afghans have returned to Afghanistan from neighboring countries over the past three years, with Pakistan and Iran accounting for the majority of returnees. The large-scale returns have placed additional pressure on communities and humanitarian agencies, as many returnees need shelter, employment, education, health care and other basic services.(Photo by Saifurahman Safi/Xinhua)
MAZAR-I-SHARIF, Afghanistan, Sept. 29 (Xinhua) -- As winter approaches, Ghous Mohammad, an Afghan returnee living with his 14-member family in a makeshift camp on the outskirts of Mazar-i-Sharif, THE capital of northern Balkh province, worries about how they will survive the cold season.
"Winter is approaching, but we have nothing -- no coal, no stove and no blankets to keep ourselves warm. We don't even have enough food," said the elderly Mohammad.
After spending nearly 30 years as a refugee in neighboring Pakistan, Mohammad returned to Afghanistan last year in hopes of rebuilding his life in his homeland. He said around 800 families now live in the makeshift camp, located in a desert area with limited access to water and other necessities.
"We have many problems, including poverty and unemployment. We don't have cash or enough food, flour or wheat. No one has helped us," said Mohammad, who lives in a four-room mud house with his wife, children and grandchildren.
The returnees spent about a year living under tents before some began building mud houses to protect themselves from the scorching summer heat and harsh winter cold, Mohammad said.
However, some families still live under tents because they cannot afford to build houses, while some young people have left the area again in search of work to support their families, he added.
"We face many problems, including a lack of clean water. We don't have a school, clinic or mosque, and there are no jobs or sources of income," said Mohammad, who returned to Afghanistan about a year ago.
A few medical workers visit the camp weekly to provide basic health services, he said.
Another returnee, Ghulam Mohammad, echoed the concerns, saying his family has almost no facilities to cope with the approaching winter.
"Winter is getting closer, but we have nothing to cope with the cold weather. We don't have blankets, coal or a stove," said Ghulam Mohammad, the breadwinner of a four-member family who currently lives in a tent.
"We need shelter. We need a school and a health clinic," he said.
Born in a refugee camp in Pakistan 25 years ago, Ghulam Mohammad returned to Afghanistan for the first time last year. Despite the economic difficulties, he said he was happy to be back in his homeland.
According to the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR), around 6 million Afghans have returned to Afghanistan from neighboring countries over the past three years, with Pakistan and Iran accounting for the majority of returnees.
The large-scale returns have placed additional pressure on communities and humanitarian agencies, as many returnees need shelter, employment, education, health care and other basic services.
Mawlawi Asadullah Wafa, head of the Refugees and Repatriation Directorate in Balkh province, said the government has planned to establish townships for returnees and has distributed land plots for them to build houses.
However, many returnees are unable to construct houses because of a lack of financial resources, Wafa said.
About 25,000 refugee families returned to Balkh province in 2025, while around 1,500 families have returned so far this year, he said, adding that land distribution for returnees is continuing.
"They (the returnees) need shelter, but they cannot build houses because of financial difficulties, while winter is approaching," Wafa said.
"We want national and international aid agencies, as well as donor countries, to help build shelters for returnees who have already received land plots for this purpose," he added. ■

Central Tokyo logs record 34 straight days of rain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
06:21:48 UTC
15:21:48 KST

Faisal Mahmud
29 September 2026•Update: 29 September 2026
Central Tokyo recorded its 34th consecutive day of rain Tuesday, the longest streak since records began, according to Japan’s weather agency.
Rain has fallen in the Japanese capital every day since Aug. 27, with approaching typhoons, a stationary autumn rain front and a low-pressure trough contributing to the prolonged wet weather, Kyodo News reported, citing the agency.
The previous record was 33 consecutive days of precipitation, registered between June 27 and July 29, 2019.
The heaviest rainfall during the current streak came on Sept. 21, when central Tokyo received 156 millimeters (6.1 inches) of rain.
Total rainfall in central Tokyo reached 629 millimeters (24.8 inches) through Monday, roughly three times the average precipitation for the entire month of September, according to Kyodo.
Rain also swept across large parts of eastern and western Japan on Tuesday.
Echizen in central Japan’s Fukui prefecture recorded more than 30 millimeters (1.2 inches) of rainfall within an hour early Tuesday morning.
The prolonged spell is not expected to end immediately.
Rain is forecast to continue mainly across eastern Japan until around Thursday, partly due to the lingering autumn rain front, the report said.
Japan’s autumn rain front typically brings extended periods of unsettled weather as seasonal air masses interact over the country.

Authorities weigh new oversight measures after fund market turmoil
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
06:20:40 UTC
15:20:40 KST

The turmoil in Türkiye’s fund market and a series of subsequent liquidation decisions have brought oversight mechanisms in capital markets to the forefront of discussions in Ankara, with potential new measures aimed at preventing similar problems from recurring now under consideration, daily Milliyet has reported.
Following the turmoil, the ruling Justice and Development Party (AKP) has been evaluating potential measures, including limits on the combined positions held in individual stocks by funds managed by the same portfolio management company, minimum liquidity thresholds linked to stress tests, and the establishment of an early warning system for real-time monitoring of risks.
AKP spokesperson Ömer Çelik said regulatory and supervisory bodies were carrying out their duties regarding the fund investigations. He added that the situation of investors affected by the process was being assessed by the relevant institutions and that a roadmap would be shared with the public once ongoing work is completed.
The Capital Markets Board (SPK), which had already launched a regulatory process before the crisis, has introduced a number of measures aimed at reducing risks, particularly in money market funds and equity hedge funds. These steps include restrictions on unsecured borrowing between related parties and regulations designed to prevent unusual price movements.
One of the proposals under consideration within the AKP is the introduction of limits on the aggregate exposure of funds managed by the same portfolio management company to a single stock. Rather than reviewing each fund’s position separately, regulators could calculate the combined holdings of all funds under the same manager and impose binding caps, particularly for stocks with low free-float levels.
Strengthening liquidity requirements is also on the agenda. According to the proposals being discussed, minimum liquidity thresholds could be set based on the results of existing stress tests, while funds falling below critical levels could face automatic restrictions on taking on additional risk.
As the judicial investigation into the fund crisis expands, AKP officials are also assessing its political implications alongside its economic and legal dimensions. After parliament reconvenes for the new legislative year on Oct. 1, the party may consider launching a parliamentary inquiry into all aspects of the crisis.
