Taiwan TSMC affiliate VIS mulls 2nd Singapore chip plant
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
04:26:55 UTC
13:26:55 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Vanguard International Semiconductor is accelerating its evaluation of a second fab in Singapore after receiving more customer requests than its first facility can handle, Nikkei Asia reported Monday.
TSMC is VIS’ largest shareholder, with a stake of about 19%, per CommonWealth Magazine. The two companies maintain a strategic partnership, with VIS licensing the chipmaker’s gallium nitride technology, which enables more efficient power use.
VIS’ fab, operated by VisionPower Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (VSMC), a joint venture between VIS and Dutch chipmaker NXP, was inaugurated Monday, per CNA. Test production began in June, just 18 months after construction started, and mass production is scheduled to begin in early 2027. The first batch of chips achieved a yield of at least 99%, VIS said.
The plant will produce power management and analog chips for automotive and industrial applications while also helping TSMC produce interposers used in advanced chip packaging for AI processors. VIS Chair Fang Leuh (方略) said demand for power-related and analog chips, particularly those used in data centers, continues to outstrip supply, per Nikkei Asia.
“We have received more requests from customers, so we are still evaluating and finalizing a second plant in terms of funding, demand, and technology nodes,” Fang said. “We will be very mindful of any future investment, given the significant capital required.”
The AI boom is also driving demand for chips beyond AI data centers, putting further pressure on supplies, according to Nikkei Asia. “Our existing capacity is stretched well beyond its limits,” Fang said, adding that VSMC has hired about 1,000 people and plans to increase its workforce to around 1,600 as production ramps up.
VIS specializes in power supply, power management, and analog chips rather than cutting-edge computing processors. VIS and NXP initially announced a NT$248.13 billion (US$7.8 billion) investment in the Singapore plant in 2024, later revising the figure to NT$213.18 billion after changes to equipment procurement plans.

Man who allegedly hid 3 spy cameras in Hong Kong gym changing rooms out on bail
Fung Kwok-wang, 34, granted HK$2,000 bail pending further probe into alleged voyeurism at 24/7 Fitness branch in Sha Tin but cannot leave city
A Hong Kong man who allegedly installed pinhole cameras in changing rooms at a branch of a popular gym chain has been released on bail pending further police investigation to identify potential victims.
Construction site foreman Fung Kwok-wang, 34, was not required to answer a count of voyeurism during his first appearance at Sha Tin Court on Tuesday, as prosecutors sought an eight-week adjournment for further police inquiries.
Acting Principal Magistrate Cheang Kei-hong granted the defendant HK$2,000 (US$255) bail on condition that he remain in Hong Kong, avoid contact with prosecution witnesses and stay away from the 24/7 Fitness branch on Lek Yuen Street in Sha Tin.
The case will be heard again on November 25.

Taiwan Tech Summit links Silicon Valley innovation with global talent
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
04:26:49 UTC
13:26:49 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — TaiwanNext Foundation held the 2026 Taiwan Tech Summit in Silicon Valley on Saturday, bringing together government officials and industry leaders to strengthen technology ties and attract global talent.
CNA reported that National Development Council Minister Yeh Chun-hsien (葉俊顯) said AI is rapidly reshaping industries worldwide. Taiwan’s strengths in chips and IT complement Silicon Valley’s ecosystem of tech companies, skilled workers, and startups, he said.
Yeh said innovation and talent will be crucial to Taiwan’s future competitiveness. Closer ties with Silicon Valley could create opportunities in research, investment, and business development, he added.
Industrial Technology Research Institute Chair Wu Tsung-tsong (吳政忠) said AI is increasingly being used in systems that can operate independently and interact with the physical world. Taiwan-US cooperation will be particularly important in robotics, autonomous systems, and unmanned vehicles, per UDN.
The institute is bringing together key technologies to develop a complete supply chain for unmanned systems, Wu said. It is also helping startups establish international partnerships and bring Taiwan-developed technology to overseas markets, per Rti.
As part of the summit, Taiwan Career Day brought together more than 30 companies and organizations seeking workers. Participants included Micron, MediaTek, TSMC, Delta Electronics, and Applied Materials, per CNA.
Talent Taiwan, a government-backed service for international professionals, provided guidance on the Employment Gold Card, taxes, visas, jobs, and starting a business. Its services are aimed at overseas tech workers, international students, and foreign specialists considering careers in Taiwan.
ITRI recruited experienced professionals in unmanned technology, AI, 6G, and silicon photonics. Engineers and other professionals from Google, Amazon, and Meta also offered one-on-one advice on resumes, career planning, and interviews.
TaiwanNext Foundation Chair Hsieh Kai-ting (謝凱婷) said the summit connects international professionals and startups with investors and major tech companies. She said these exchanges could strengthen technology and startup ties between Taiwan and Silicon Valley.

Chinese research vessel near Diaoyutai Islands could be helping prepare for Taiwan invasion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
04:26:27 UTC
13:26:27 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) – A Chinese research vessel was found to be conducting surveys in Japan’s exclusive economic zone near the Diaoyutai Islands, potentially collecting data that could be useful for a potential invasion of Taiwan, Kyodo News reported.
An analysis of automatic identification system data found that the Xiang Yang Hong 22 surveyed an area about 50 km west of the islands five times from March through July, covering a rectangular area about 66 km long and 11 km wide.
During one survey in July, the ship was found slowly sailing back and forth north-south at about 5 kph. Japan’s Coast Guard observed a tubular device extending from the vessel into the sea.
Sources from Japan’s Defense Ministry said information about the seafloor and other marine conditions would be helpful for military purposes, per Kyodo.
China has a fleet of more than 120 oceanographic research vessels, according to Taiwan’s Coast Guard Administration. Ryan D. Martinson, a China maritime strategy specialist at the US Naval War College, told AFP that civilian scientific organizations operating these ships share the data they collect with the Chinese military.
“That kind of data/knowledge is highly useful for Chinese naval forces, which will operate in these waters in the event of a conflict,” Martinson said. “It is especially important for anti-submarine warfare and submarine warfare.”
Kyodo reported that Japan has confirmed a spike in Chinese marine research activities within its EEZs around the Ryukyu Islands. As of last Friday, 13 such incidents had been recorded in the area, compared with six for all of 2025.
In August, another Chinese research vessel, Xiang Yang Hong 03, was observed operating over key undersea cables and deep-sea areas within Taiwan’s and Japan’s EEZs, per AFP. A Chinese coast guard cutter and a maritime militia fishing vessel escorted the ship.

Araghchi urges UN action against US aggression
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
04:23:02 UTC
13:23:02 KST

Iranian Foreign Minister Seyed Abbas Araghchi met with UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres in New York on the final day of his trip for the UN General Assembly's 81st session.
Araghchi briefed Guterres on the latest developments in West Asia following the military aggression by the United States and the Israeli regime against the country. He said that as a founding UN member, Iran expects the organization and its member states not to remain indifferent to flagrant violations of the UN Charter by a permanent Security Council member, and to explicitly condemn continued US interference and illegal threats.
Citing two rounds of illegal US and Israeli attacks on Iran within less than a year, occurring amid negotiations, along with an ongoing naval blockade and economic pressure, Araghchi stressed Iran's determination to defend its sovereignty and territorial integrity with full capability. He said Iran would continue to pursue accountability and justice for those responsible for war crimes by the US and the Zionist regime.
Araghchi said Iran has consistently favored diplomacy to safeguard its national interests and regional peace, but said the United States repeatedly abandoned diplomatic commitments over the past decade, contributing to regional instability. He also raised continued violence and mass killing by the Israeli regime in Palestinian territories, Lebanon, Syria and elsewhere in the region, urging the UN and Security Council to act to end Israeli impunity and stop the ongoing atrocities in Gaza and the West Bank.
Guterres, for his part, condemned violations of core principles of the UN Charter, particularly the use of force by major powers, and stressed the need for all countries to abide by international law and resolve disputes through diplomacy.
The meeting also addressed continued US violations of the UN Headquarters Agreement and obstruction of the normal functioning of Iran's mission. Araghchi conveyed Iran's formal protest over the host government's conduct and asked Guterres to take necessary measures to ensure US compliance with its obligations.

NY Times tech exec in domestic row with ex-wife shot dead by elderly in-laws

NY Times tech exec in domestic row with ex-wife shot dead by elderly in-laws
Soumya Karlamangla and Amy Qin
- Jonathan McKinsey, a New York Times tech executive, was shot dead by his elderly in-laws at a Dublin, California, parking lot on Sept 26 amid a turbulent family dispute.
- McKinsey, a transgender man, had a troubled marriage with his wife, Candice Jang, involving mutual restraining orders and child abuse allegations.
- His in-laws, Shouyong Zhang and Shili Chen, aged 76, were arrested for murder and related charges.
AI generated
SAN FRANCISCO – A Bay Area couple have been accused of shooting and killing their son-in-law at a suburban sports park on Sept 26, local police have said.
The man, Jonathan McKinsey, 40, was found dead with multiple gunshot wounds around 3pm in a car park at Dublin Sports Grounds, an athletic complex and playground in Dublin, California, about 56km east of downtown San Francisco, according to Dublin Police Services.
McKinsey was director of engineering for the games department of The New York Times, according to a company spokesman.
Before McKinsey began working at the Times in 2023, he worked for several tech companies, including Splunk, Coursera and Oracle, according to his LinkedIn profile.
The authorities did not describe a motive for the shooting, but McKinsey and his wife had a turbulent marriage and were living separately, records show.
Each filed requests for domestic violence restraining orders against the other in 2025. McKinsey also pleaded not guilty in 2025 to two charges of misdemeanour child abuse.
McKinsey was a transgender man and accused his wife, Candice Jang, and his in-laws of abusing him because of his identity, according to his filing for a restraining order in December 2025.
He said his mother-in-law called him and one of his sons a “pervert” and a “monster” after the boy tried on dresses, and he accused his father-in-law of punching him in the chest while he was recovering from double mastectomy surgery in 2010.
Assad Razawi, a resident of Dublin, said he was outside a grocery store near his car on Sept 26 at around 3pm when he heard what sounded like five or six gunshots coming from the sports park across the street.
When he looked over, he said he saw a man drop to the ground in the car park and another man and woman walking calmly away from the scene. The San Francisco Chronicle was first to report Razawi’s account.
Around the same time, a Dublin police sergeant was driving by the park when he saw a man lying on the ground and stopped to investigate, local police said.
Emergency personnel began arriving after receiving emergency calls from people in the park about the shooting.
Witnesses directed officers to two individuals standing nearby, whom police identified as Shouyong Zhang and Shili Chen, both 76.
They are a married couple who live in Dublin and are the parents of McKinsey’s wife, the police said.
Zhang and Chen were held on suspicion of murder, and detectives are continuing to investigate.
They also were held on suspicion of wilful discharge of a firearm with gross negligence, conspiracy and child endangerment likely to produce great bodily injury or death. It was not clear which children the last booking charge pertained to.
They are scheduled to be arraigned on Sept 30. It was unclear whether Zhang and Chen had legal representation.
Troubled marriage
Alameda County court records show that McKinsey’s wife, Jang, filed a request for a temporary restraining order citing domestic violence in October 2025.
She also sought a protective order against McKinsey for her three children and her mother.
A report from the Dublin Police Services noted that on Oct 17, an officer met with Jang, who said her husband struck their six-year-old “in the face with an open hand”.
When officers went to the residence to contact McKinsey, they discovered a two-year-old child in an upstairs bedroom who had been left without supervision.
The officers said McKinsey left the child alone for more than an hour while he went shopping.
McKinsey was later charged in Alameda County Superior Court with two misdemeanour counts of child abuse in connection with the separate incidents.
He pleaded not guilty to both charges and was released from jail on the condition that he complete 12 parenting classes. A pretrial hearing had been scheduled for October.
In December, McKinsey also filed for a temporary restraining order against his wife, citing domestic violence.
According to his request, his wife had been granted full custody of the children, and he feared for their safety.
That same month, he filed for divorce.
McKinsey said he was framed for the October incident in which the couple’s two-year-old son was found alone.
He said Jang was responsible for the children during the work week, and that she did not tell him before leaving that the child was sleeping in his crib upstairs. “She did this on purpose, to set me up,” he wrote.
In his filing, he accused his wife of regularly abusing their children and neglecting to properly bathe and feed them.
“When I protested about any of this, she threatened me with harm or said she would call the police and tell them I was hurting our children,” he said in the filing.
He said Jang once hit him on the head with a frying pan and forced him to ingest a cockroach.
He accused her, on another occasion, of striking him on the head with a mirror, which shattered as he tried to wrest it from her control and severed a tendon and nerve in his hand, requiring surgery and leaving him with a permanent loss of sensation in his thumb.

'Cuba's already fallen,' US Secretary of State says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
04:16:01 UTC
13:16:01 KST

Diyar Guldogan
29 September 2026•Update: 29 September 2026
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Monday that Cuba has already “fallen,” describing the island as a failed state with a dysfunctional economy and government.
In an interview with Fox News, Rubio argued that Cuba’s political and economic systems have failed to provide meaningful benefits to its population and said the country needs a period of transition toward greater political and economic freedom.
“Well, the truth is Cuba's already fallen,” he said. “It doesn't have a functional economy and it's governed by people who continue to preach about some revolution that has been dead for 20 years.”
Rubio said the Cuban government’s political model has failed to produce a functioning economy or government.
“The problem that Cuba has basically right now is it is a failed state in every sense of the word,” he said. “It's not a functional government and it's not a functional country. It just simply isn't.”
He also pointed to migration from Cuba as evidence of the country’s economic difficulties. He said that since 2021, nearly 20% of Cuba’s population has left the country, describing the migration as a consequence of a “complete failure.”
"We're hopeful that Cuba will choose a different path," Rubio said.
Rubio argued that economic reforms alone would not be sufficient to fundamentally change conditions on the island. He said political freedoms would need to accompany economic changes.
“In fact, you cannot have economic freedom in Cuba if you don't have political freedom first,” he said. “You have to have both happening at least at the same time. That will require a period of transition."

US senators urge Trump administration to extend Temporary Protected Status for Ukrainians
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
04:14:19 UTC
13:14:19 KST

Diyar Guldogan
29 September 2026•Update: 29 September 2026
A total of 31 US senators urged the Trump administration to extend and redesignate Temporary Protected Status (TPS) for Ukrainians living in the US as Russia’s war against Ukraine continues.
The bipartisan letter, led by Sen. Tammy Duckworth, asks Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin and Secretary of State Marco Rubio to issue an 18-month extension and redesignation of TPS for Ukraine before the current designation expires on Oct. 19.
The senators warned that allowing the protection to expire could force thousands of Ukrainians living in the US to return to a country still affected by active fighting, civilian casualties and widespread damage to critical infrastructure.
Ukraine was initially designated for TPS on April 19, 2022. The TPS was subsequently extended and redesignated through April 19, 2025 and extended again beginning April 20, 2025.
"Protecting the approximately 101,000 Ukrainian TPS holders currently living in the United States is a humanitarian imperative, but also a sound economic decision," they wrote.
According to the lawmakers, Ukrainian TPS holders contribute approximately $2.6 billion to the US economy each year and pay about $716 million in taxes annually.
“Current conditions in Ukraine clearly merit the continuation of TPS status,” the senators wrote, arguing that Ukrainian nationals cannot safely return while the war continues.

British warship hits frigate with live Naval Strike Missile
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
05:00:31 BST
13:00:31 KST

The Royal Navy used both of its newest anti-ship missiles during a joint US-UK live-fire exercise off the Hebrides that ended with the sinking of the decommissioned American frigate USS Klakring, firing the Naval Strike Missile from HMS Portland and Sea Venom from a Wildcat helicopter of 815 Naval Air Squadron operating from her flight deck.
The round Portland fired carried a warhead and was aimed at a real ship rather than a range target, which the service describes as the first Royal Navy firing of a Naval Strike Missile, although HMS Somerset launched one off Norway in September last year.
Lieutenant Commander Louise Kirkaldy, HMS Portland’s principal warfare officer, said: “The successful firing of Naval Strike Missile marks a significant milestone for the Royal Navy, demonstrating our ability to deliver credible, modern maritime strike capability. This achievement reflects the professionalism, dedication and teamwork of all those involved, whose hard work has ensured we remain ready to meet the challenges of today and tomorrow.”
Petty Officer James Kenyon, an above water warfare specialist aboard the frigate, fired it. “To be involved in such a high-profile exercise is the highlight of my career,” he said. “Being the first person to fire war-shot Naval Strike Missile and achieve a hit is a very proud moment, and one that will stay with me for the rest of my career. This was the culmination of over a year’s effort in planning and bringing the drills into service, and I am glad that I was able to contribute.”
Commander Dafydd Bryden, the ship’s commanding officer, said: “The opportunity to fire anti-ship missiles against a decommissioned warship is an important test of our warfighting capability. This engagement proved the effectiveness of these systems as well as the sailors and aircrew who operate them. We remain ready to fight and win at sea.”
Sea Venom was fired from the Wildcat during the same serial, and Captain Kelechi Ndukwe, commander of Task Force 65, confirmed to journalists that it was the missile’s first live firing since reaching initial operating capability, and that it hit the target. According to the Royal Navy, the helicopter completed the full kill chain by detecting, identifying and striking the target rather than simply releasing the weapon.
Lieutenant Commander Rhydian Edwards, test and evaluation commander at the Maritime Aviation Strike Operational Advantage Group, said: “This was a landmark moment for the Wildcat Force. For the first time we demonstrated the live firing of an operational Sea Venom missile against a representative maritime target. More importantly, we proved our ability to execute the full maritime strike kill chain under realistic operational conditions.
“This was about giving commanders confidence that Wildcat can find, fix and strike maritime targets using Sea Venom as part of a wider task group. The lessons learned from this activity will directly inform future tactics, training and operational capability development, ensuring Maritime Aviation Strike remains ready to fight and win when called upon.”
The Naval Strike Missile was brought into Royal Navy service under an interim arrangement to replace Harpoon, which left service in 2023, and has been fitted to Type 23 frigates and Type 45 destroyers using equipment transferred between hulls as ships enter and leave refit. Built by Kongsberg, the weapon is a sea-skimming missile with a low radar signature and a range well beyond that of the system it replaced, and it can strike land targets as well as ships. The service says it carries an advanced warhead, travels close to supersonic speeds and can reach targets more than 100 miles away while evading detection by skimming the sea, and that it will be complementary to the Future Cruise Anti-Ship Weapon, intended to become the fleet’s premier long-range anti-ship missile aboard the Type 26 and Type 31 frigates through the Mk41 vertical launch system.
Sea Venom, built by MBDA, is the Wildcat’s principal anti-ship weapon and replaced the Sea Skua carried by the Lynx. The Royal Navy describes it as designed to defeat corvette sized vessels or disable frigates, destroyers and other larger ships, with a Wildcat able to carry four at once, and says it can also be used overland against bunkers, buildings and vehicles. Readers will have seen the same missile turn up this week on a very different platform, fitted by STARK to an uncrewed surface vessel built near Plymouth.
The two British weapons were part of a wider engagement in which USS Paul Ignatius demonstrated the maximum damage and range capability of an anti-surface variant of the Standard Missile 6, and the submarine USS Massachusetts engaged the target with the Mark 48 Advanced Capability Torpedo, which delivered the final hit and sank the ship, as we reported.
Weapons were used in order of reach too we understand, with the longest range ordnance going first. Ndukwe said the American side started with the SM-6 before moving in to shorter range systems, a sequence designed to get the most out of the sensors fitted to the hull for battle damage assessment.
Atlantic Thunder 2026 was led by United States Sixth Fleet and drew in forces from five American task forces alongside the Royal Navy, the Royal Air Force and the United States Air Force. Lieutenant Commander Paul Atkins, the United Kingdom lead project officer for the exercise, said: “Atlantic Thunder 26 demonstrated the enduring strength of the UK-US alliance and the close partnership between the Royal Navy and the United States Navy. Operating together in a demanding environment, we showcased our ability to integrate seamlessly, share expertise and deliver a highly capable, interoperable maritime force. Through combined training and operations, we have strengthened our collective warfighting capability, reinforcing our ability to deter potential adversaries and deliver maritime combat power whenever and wherever it is required.”

How John Farnham pulled off one of music's greatest comebacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
04:00:00 UTC
13:00:00 KST

How John Farnham pulled off one of music's greatest comebacks with Whispering Jack
Forty years after its release, John Farnham's Whispering Jack remains one of the most remarkable stories in Australian music history.
The 1986 album spent 25 weeks at number one, produced enduring hits that remain part of our national conscience, and transformed John Farnham from a fading teen idol into one of the country's most beloved performers.
Its centrepiece, You're The Voice, is bigger than a pop song: the unofficial anthem still inspires singalongs at pubs, stadiums and festival fields decades later.
None of it was supposed to happen.
By the mid-80s, Farnham's career was drifting. Record labels weren't interested. His attempts at chart success weren't connecting.
A stint fronting world-conquering Aussie rockers Little River Band didn't kickstart the resurgence he hoped for.
So, Whispering Jack wasn't the work of a music industry machine backing a sure thing. It was the result of the work of a small team of people convinced they saw something the rest of the industry had missed.
One last chance
John Farnham's first taste of fame came early.
As Johnny Farnham, he dominated Australian charts in the late 1960s and early 1970s, scoring a massive hit with Sadie (The Cleaning Lady), the best selling Australian single of the '60s.
But, as tastes changed, Farnham's commercial fortunes faded. He moved into musical theatre and TV, proving he remained an endearing entertainer, but not necessarily a recording artist to watch.
A reinvention was needed. Johnny became John. And while he had flashes of success, like cracking back into the Top 10 with a version of The Beatles's Help in 1980, the momentum didn't stick.
His time with Little River Band proved valuable, particularly the exposure to large-scale touring in America, but didn't provide the breakthrough Farnham and his manager Glenn Wheatley, who died in 2022, were searching for.
By 1985, many in the industry believed Farnham's biggest successes were behind him. Wheatley never accepted that.
"We all knew what he had," Wheatley told News Corp in 2018. "He's one of the greatest singers of our time. We just had to find the right songs for him."
Finding songs wasn't too hard — there were plenty around. Finding someone willing to back the project was another story.
Neither record labels nor producers showed much interest. Eventually, Wheatley and Farnham decided to do it themselves.
"I had to find out whether I could get the money to make the album for a start," Farnham told the ABC's John Hall in 1987.
Wheatley's label became his record company and the gamble got bigger. The budget for the album was about $150,000.
Speaking to Jen Jewel Brown for the National Film and Sound Archive in 2014, Wheatley recalled: "I ended up having to do it on my label again. I had to mortgage my house to do it."
"I couldn't not do it; not to John," he recalled in Clark Forbes's 1989 book Whispering Jack.
"What the hell, I had nothing to lose either. I simply had to go for this."
Building Whispering Jack
The team eventually settled on live sound engineer Ross Fraser as producer. He wasn't a known name, and it wasn't a conventional move.
It turned out to be a masterstroke.
Together, Farnham, Fraser and Wheatley embarked on an exhaustive search for material.
"I must have listened to 2,000 songs, easy, from all over the world," Farnham told Hall.
"We sent telexes all over the world to all the publishers and record companies that we were looking for songs.
"We literally got two boxes, we put 'no' on one box and 'maybe' on the other box, and we just went through them all.
"I had to listen to the songs in their entirety because, being a budding songwriter myself, I understand how much work these people put into it. So, I had to at least give them that courtesy."
Even then, the work had barely begun.
The eventual album only contained 10 tracks, but every arrangement was meticulously worked over. A month of pre-production was followed by more than two months in the studio.
"We were in there for 18 hours a day, pumping away, and we really worked hard," Farnham told Hall.
You can still hear that commitment when you hit play on Whispering Jack 40 years on.
Its sound – synthesisers, drum machines and enormous production – is unmistakably rooted in the '80s. Yet somehow it doesn't feel trapped there.
The commitment in those performances — from Farnham and his band — and the strength of those songs prove this hard-won success was well deserved.
Finding You're The Voice
Whispering Jack was still missing something when a tape arrived from England.
"The last song we found was You're The Voice," Wheatley told the National Film and Sound Archive.
A publisher insisted Farnham would love it.
"When I first heard it, my heart almost stopped," Farnham told the Toronto Star in 1987. "I felt like I'd discovered lost treasure."
According to the story that has since become part of Australian music folklore, label manager Doris Tyler heard the song first and wasn't especially convinced. But Ross Fraser was.
Driving to Farnham's house one afternoon, the producer reportedly played the cassette over and over. The more he listened, the more certain he was that the song had to be on the record.
It made the cut, but when it was released, it wasn't an easy sell. Wheatley and the team were dogged in chasing airplay before commercial radio fully embraced it.
Once they did, there was no stopping it.
The pay-off
You're The Voice became a phenomenon and its success propelled Whispering Jack to number one, where it remained for 25 weeks.
Follow-up singles Pressure Down, A Touch of Paradise and Reasons kept momentum rolling. The album became much bigger than anyone had dared imagine.
That mortgage Wheatley took out to fund the album was repaid many times over. Whispering Jack went on to become the highest-selling album in Australia by an Australian artist.
It also reached number six in the UK and topped the charts in Sweden. You're The Voice charted across Europe, an unusual feat for an Australian artist at the time.
When Wheatley and Farnham heard the news that the album had reached number one, they were together in a car.
"I was saying, 'Do you realise John that we have a number one record?'" Wheatley recalled in Forbes's book Whispering Jack.
"I looked towards him at the traffic lights, and he had tears coming down his cheeks.
"He said, 'I can't believe this is happening'."
For Farnham, this wasn't just about commercial success, it was about vindication.
"I feel more credible now," he told the Toronto Star at the time.
"I'm really working hard.
"All my life things have come too easily to me. I put everything on the line this time. And now it feels as if I deserve it."

From Garden to Monument: Liberation Landscapes in African Cities
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
04:00:00 UTC
13:00:00 KST

Liberation does not always begin with a monument. It may begin in a garden, a yard, a clearing, a field; in the occupation of land and the possibility of gathering there. Across histories shaped by colonialism and dispossession, space has been more than the setting in which liberation takes place. It has been one of its practices: cultivated, occupied, hidden within, moved through and collectively remade.
Wolff Architects' research Liberation Gardens offers the garden as one way of reading these spatial practices, not simply as planted ground, but as a space through which survival, nourishment and emancipatory imagination can be sustained. The garden in this sense is not defined by landscape design so much as by relationships between people and land, cultivation and knowledge, occupation and autonomy. It can hold cultural production alongside subsistence, and forms of collective life that emerge under conditions of violence and dispossession. Liberation, understood spatially, becomes as much about the possibility of inhabiting differently as it is about arriving at a final condition of freedom.

This suitcase-sized spacecraft could hear the universe before stars existed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
03:45:39 UTC
12:45:39 KST

This suitcase-sized spacecraft could hear the universe before stars existed
- Date:
- September 28, 2026
- Source:
- University of Cambridge
- Summary:
- CosmoCube will use the far side of the Moon as a shield from Earth’s radio noise to search for a faint signal from the universe before the first stars existed. The suitcase-sized satellite could reveal how the cosmic dark ages ended and how dark matter helped build the first galaxies.
- Share:
A satellite no bigger than a small carry on suitcase could help scientists investigate one of the least understood periods in cosmic history: the roughly 150 million years of darkness before the universe's first stars began to shine.
Developed in the UK, the spacecraft is called CosmoCube. An international research team led by the University of Cambridge plans to send it around the Moon, where the lunar far side can block radio interference coming from Earth. In that unusually quiet environment, CosmoCube will listen for an extraordinarily faint signal left behind by the early universe.
Listening for a Signal From Before the First Stars
Scientists call this signal the 21 centimeter line. It comes from hydrogen atoms that existed during the period between the lingering afterglow of the Big Bang and Cosmic Dawn, when nuclear fusion switched on inside the first stars.
No one has directly observed this chapter of cosmic history.
The signal CosmoCube will seek originated more than 13.5 billion years ago, but detecting it from Earth is extremely difficult. Our planet's ionosphere prevents the relevant radio frequencies from reaching ground based observatories, while FM broadcasts, satellites and telecommunications produce additional interference that can overwhelm the faint cosmic signal.
The Moon offers a natural solution.
When CosmoCube passes behind the Moon, the lunar body will block radio noise from Earth for about 40 minutes during each two-hour orbit. Over the spacecraft's expected two-year mission, researchers hope to collect about 1000 hours of observations from one of the final largely unexplored eras in the universe.
Those measurements could help explain how the cosmos changed from a dark and relatively empty place into the rich universe of stars, galaxies and other structures seen today.
The project has received funding from the UK Space Agency, and researchers hope CosmoCube can launch within the next five years. Details of the mission have been published in Nature Astronomy.
Searching for Dark Matter's Early Influence
CosmoCube is designed to investigate more than the time before the first stars. Researchers also hope its observations will shed light on dark matter and its influence on the formation of the earliest cosmic structures.
Dark matter cannot be seen directly, but its gravitational effects are crucial for explaining how galaxies and other large structures hold together.
"This emission from hydrogen after the Big Bang, but before the first stars, will hopefully allow us to understand the role of dark matter in the early universe, how it worked to pull together hydrogen into the first stars and galaxies," said lead author Professor Eloy de Lera Acedo from Cambridge's Cavendish Laboratory.
To reach this ancient period, CosmoCube will observe radio frequencies between 10 and 50 MHz. These frequencies are largely inaccessible to telescopes operating from the ground, making the Moon an especially valuable location for the experiment.
"There's no other place where you can get the sort of shielding you need to detect such a faint signal, while at the same time looking at the whole of space," said de Lera Acedo, who is also affiliated with the Kavli Institute for Cosmology. "The far side of the Moon is really the only option: it solves multiple problems at once, opening a clear window to the very early universe."
Turning the Moon Into a Radio Shield
After reaching lunar orbit, CosmoCube will deploy a long, lightweight radio antenna. When the spacecraft moves behind the Moon, that antenna will search for the 21-centimeter hydrogen signal from the early universe while the lunar surface blocks interference from Earth.
Detecting such a weak signal requires extreme precision. CosmoCube will therefore continually monitor and adjust its own electronics using a 'Dicke switched' calibrator. The system will alternate between observing the sky and measuring several internal reference sources.
This process is intended to identify and remove tiny changes or electronic noise generated by the spacecraft itself, which could otherwise be mistaken for a signal from deep cosmic history.
Researchers will perform additional processing after the observations return to Earth. Advanced Bayesian statistical techniques will be used to separate the desired signal from foreground radio emissions, particularly those produced by our own galaxy.
Computer simulations and measurements gathered during the mission will also allow researchers to reconstruct how CosmoCube's antenna responds to different regions of the sky. Scientists can then correct for remaining distortions that might interfere with the results.
"Aside from the science, what makes our mission unique is its size: we're probing the earliest, deepest parts of the dark ages that others don't reach, but with a compact, relatively low-cost platform," said de Lera Acedo.
A Small Satellite With an Ambitious Mission
The radio silence available behind the Moon may become increasingly valuable. The US, India and other countries are also planning missions intended to take advantage of the unusually quiet radio environment on the lunar far side.
CosmoCube itself contains a highly integrated miniature radiometer that combines modern analog and digital technologies using so-called RF Systems on Chip technology (RFSoCs).
The CosmoCube spacecraft platform ('SSTL-21') is being developed in the UK by Surrey Space Technology Limited (SSTL), a company specializing in small satellite manufacturing.
Development of the instrument is already underway. Working laboratory prototypes have been built, environmental tests are being carried out, and researchers are collaborating with industry partners. UK academic partners include Portsmouth University and STFC RAL Space, while researchers from EU countries including Malta are also participating.
The CosmoCube team recently took part in the ESA mini Fast missions Call for Ideas, with the proposed mission targeting a cost below 50 million Euros.
"CosmoCube is aiming to do some ambitious science from a very small satellite in a challenging environment, and to do that requires some clever design techniques," said co-author Dr Will Grainger from STFC RAL Space. "We've worked with the project partners to develop representative models of the satellite and its payload. These have been tested in our facilities to ensure the thermal performance allows the payload to operate and perform the required sensitive measurements under the different temperature conditions it will experience whilst in orbit around the Moon. In the future, we hope to further develop the full payload in preparation for a full mission."
A New Window Into the Cosmic Dark Ages
If successful, CosmoCube could demonstrate that major discoveries about the earliest universe do not necessarily require enormous spacecraft.
Instead, a compact satellite positioned in one of the quietest radio environments available near Earth could provide scientists with access to an era that has so far remained beyond direct observation.
"This could be a real UK success story: the hardware, the software, the implementation and the technology is all being developed here, and it could help us answer one of the most profound questions in the universe," said de Lera Acedo.
The work was supported in part by the UK Space Agency, the Kavli Foundation, and the Science and Technology Facilities Council (STFC), part of UK Research and Innovation (UKRI). Eloy de Lera Acedo is a Fellow of Selwyn College, Cambridge.

OpenAI apologises for Medicare breach, shelves next gen ChatGPT
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
03:34:34 UTC
12:34:34 KST

OpenAI apologises for Medicare breach, shelves next gen ChatGPT
In short:
OpenAI says it wants to "rebuild trust with the Australian people" after an agent hacked into Medicare's Statistics Reporting Service.
The company said the breach was undertaken by an internal-only model that did not have the safeguards used in publicly available products.
OpenAI has also scrapped the release of GPT-6.1 Astra over safety concerns.
OpenAI has apologised for its AI agent breaching Medicare's Statistics Reporting Service, and has shelved its upcoming release of its next-generation ChatGPT model.
Last week, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said an OpenAI agent gained unauthorised access to the Medicare statistics portal administered by Services Australia.
In a blog post on OpenAI's website published on Tuesday morning, the company set out what they "will do to rebuild trust with the Australian people".
"In Australia, we are committing resources and expertise to support affected agencies," the post said.
The company also said they should have handled their response to the breach better.
"We are sorry and working to do better in the future,"
"This is a new kind of cyber incident which represents an emerging global challenge."
More details of the breach emerge
The ChatGPT maker said the breach happened during training on an "internal-only OpenAI model that was not intended for public release and without the full set of safeguards used in our publicly available products".
During this training, the agent discovered a way to gain non-public access to Services Australia Medicare's Statistics Reporting Service where it ran commands, retrieved internal files, credentials and statistics, as well as wrote files, the company said.
The company also confirmed an OpenAI model accessed the NSW Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research's public Crime Mapping Tool to research public crime statistics.
Agents also discovered an exposed access key to query the Victorian Agency for Health Information's reporting system.
"The extent to which this information should have been accessible is unclear, and depends on VAHI's access policies," the post said.
Lastly, the post outlined how agents retrieved statistics from the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare, where it downloaded material that "appears to have been publicly available".
"Separate attempts to bypass access controls were unsuccessful."
PM says OpenAI cooperating with government
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said "OpenAI have been very constructive and open in engaging" with the government taskforce investigating the hack.
"This is a challenge that the world is dealing with."
The prime minster said artificial intelligence can improve economic growth and productivity, but comes with risks.
"We've seen those risks exposed,"
"So we need to work this through, we see this as an opportunity, but we want to seize the benefit whilst mitigating the risks."
OpenAI said they would support Australian governments through credits from their $US1 billion ($1.42 billion) Daybreak for Frontline Defenders program — an initiative they describe as support for essential service providers to improve their frontline cyber defences.
The company also said it would establish a taskforce "with independent Australian expertise to develop practical policy recommendations".
OpenAI's chief strategy officer, Jason Kwon, will fly to Sydney to appear at the Joint Select Committee on Artificial Intelligence on October 6.
Next-gen ChatGPT model scrapped
OpenAI has scrapped the release of GPT-6.1 Astra, a next-generation AI model planned for an October debut, after internal testing found the system did not meet the company's safety and alignment standards.
GPT-6.1 Astra was expected to be integrated into ChatGPT and Codex and was designed to handle more complex tasks without human assistance.
OpenAI's head of safety systems, Saachi Jain, said GPT-6.1 Astra improved model laziness but "it didn't quite meet the bar in terms of staying within scope and authorisation, and how it communicates back to the user about the type of work it's done".
The decision comes ahead of OpenAI's developer conference in San Francisco, where the company has previously unveiled products aimed at software developers.

Taiwan adds five medals at Asian Games

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan added five medals on Monday at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games, including a silver in the men's 4x100-meter relay and four bronze medals in track and field, badminton, table tennis, and shooting.
The first medal of the day came from Lin Chung-wei (林仲威), who won bronze in the men's 400-meter hurdles in 48.74 seconds. The time was a personal best for Lin and placed him third behind Qatar's Bassem Hemeida and Japan's Taiju Goto, per UDN.
Lin entered the final after running 49.10 seconds in the heats, the second-fastest qualifying time. He remained among the leaders throughout the final and was level for second after clearing the final hurdle before crossing the line in third.
Lin's bronze gave Taiwan its second track and field medal of the games, following Fu Chao-hsuan's (傅兆玄) men's high jump gold on Sunday. A silver in the men's 4x100-meter relay brought Taiwan's track and field haul to three medals: one gold, one silver, and one bronze.
The relay team of Yang Chun-han (楊俊瀚), Lai Po-hsiang (賴柏翔), Chen Wen-pu (陳玟溥) and Huang Tso-chun (黃左軍) ran 38.32 seconds in the final to win silver and break Taiwan's national record, per CNA.
The time also marked the team's best performance of the season. The silver was Taiwan's first Asian Games men's 4x100-meter relay medal since the 2010 Guangzhou Games. The team had run 38.80 seconds in the qualifying round before improving significantly in the final.
Taiwan also collected three bronze medals in events outside track and field.
In badminton, mixed-doubles pair Ye Hong-wei (葉宏蔚) and Zhan You-zhen (詹又蓁) lost 21-13, 21-9 to China's Jiang Zhenbang and Wei Yaxin in the semifinals. Because the Asian Games badminton tournament does not hold a bronze-medal match, the semifinal loss secured Taiwan a bronze medal. The medal ended a 16-year wait for Taiwan in Asian Games mixed doubles, per CNA.
In table tennis, Lin Yun-ju (林昀儒) won bronze in men's singles after losing a seven-game semifinal to China's Lin Shidong. Lin reached the Asian Games men's singles semifinals for the first time and also won a bronze medal in the men's team event earlier in the Games.
Taiwan's fourth bronze of the day came in the women's 25-meter pistol team event. Cheng Yen-ching (鄭晏晴), Tien Chia-chen (田家榛), and Chen Yu-ru (陳俞如) combined for 1,734 points to finish third behind China and South Korea, per an NTNU press release.
Taiwan's medal tally in the Asian Games includes three gold, eight silver, and 23 bronze medals, for 34 medals overall. Taiwan was ranked 13th in the medal standings as of Monday night.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taipei Economic and Cultural Office in Chicago Director Dennis Lei (類延峰) called for stronger US support for Taiwan as China seeks to limit its international engagement, WVIK reported Sunday.

He also cited bipartisan backing in the US Congress, saying more than 60 senators and representatives had expressed solidarity with Taiwan. Taipei will continue working with Washington and other partners to preserve cross-strait stability, he said.
Lei said closer Taiwan-US relations also bring economic benefits. About 40% of Taiwan’s outbound investment went to the US last year, making it the country’s largest overseas investment destination, compared with about 80% going to China in 2010, he said.
He attributed the shift to business decisions and changes in global supply chains. Taiwanese exports such as AI servers, semiconductors, electronics, and auto parts can also support US manufacturing, he said.
AI is another key area for collaboration. Taiwan produces advanced chips, while its companies manufacture about 90% of the world’s servers, giving the two sides complementary strengths in the technology sector, Lei said.
Lei also highlighted agricultural trade. The US remains Taiwan’s largest source of agricultural imports, while Taiwan announced plans last year to purchase NT$318.4 billion (US$10 billion) in US farm products.
On security, Lei said China continues to hold military exercises, employ gray-zone tactics, spread disinformation, and interfere with Taiwan’s democracy. He said Taipei would work with like-minded partners to safeguard regional peace.
As Washington and Beijing compete in AI and other advanced technologies, Lei said Taiwan-US collaboration is becoming increasingly important. Taiwan hopes to contribute its semiconductor and manufacturing strengths to help the US maintain its technological edge, he said.

North Korea warned the UN on Monday of longtime rival Japan's “attempts at rearmament” while emphasizing that multipolarity in international affairs was an “irresistible trend of the times.”
Addressing the 81st session of the UN General Assembly in New York, North Korean Vice Foreign Minister Kim Son-gyong accused Japan of taking advantage of the current volatile international environment.
He said Japan has accelerated its attempts at rearmament with an "unprecedented" commitment, including the revision of its Peace Constitution, the abandonment of its "exclusively defense-oriented policy," the reformation of its military structure and an arms buildup.
"Such actions are casting war clouds over the entire region," Kim warned.
He said that “under the signboard of counterattack capability," Japan has moved ahead with the development and possession of long-range attack weapons that put neighboring countries within striking range.
Condemning recent joint military exercises by the US, Japan and South Korea, Kim accused the United States of conspiring "with its allies to systematically amend and update the anti-North Korea nuclear war scenarios through "provocative war rehearsals of all hues and military build-up."
"The US-Japan-South Korea military alliance, unmistakably aimed at the DPRK, is being evolved by the United States into a more offensive and aggressive military bloc with a nuclear element," he said, referring to the Democratic People's Republic of Korea, North Korea’s official name.
He reiterated that North Korea's nuclear status is "uncompromisingly" fixed and can never be reversed in any circumstances.
"I would like to reiterate the official position of the DPRK government: the status of the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea as a nuclear weapons state that has been uncompromisingly and permanently fixed both physically and legally with absolutely no turning back, can never be reversed in any circumstances or by any means, no matter how hard and loudly the hostile forces may deny in chorus with all sorts of rhetoric," he said.
Kim observed that multilateralism and multipolarization have emerged as an “irresistible aspiration and trend of the times based on justice and equity.“
"Gone are the days when an individual member state unilaterally imposed its will on the rest of the world and dominated the international political arena."
Kim also indirectly described the US-Israeli war on Iran as "state-sponsored terrorism.”
"The new year started with the most despicable, world startling act of state-sponsored terrorism, followed by worldwide outbreaks of other appalling incidents and events," he said.
Urging the UN to firmly secure its authority and future by promoting equality and cooperation among sovereign states, Kim said the world body should no longer be misused for the sinister political purposes of ''specific forces.''
He said the effects of a disaster-prone abnormal climate have given rise to a succession of extreme high temperatures, droughts, heavy rains and floods in many countries and regions, seriously threatening the survival of mankind.
This, coupled with the spread of communicable diseases and hikes in oil prices, worsened the socio-economic crisis, he added.

Scientists expected these Galápagos sea turtles to wander. They stayed put
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
03:12:23 UTC
12:12:23 KST

Scientists expected these Galápagos sea turtles to wander. They stayed put
Scientists found a surprising population of Galápagos sea turtles that seems to prefer staying close to home rather than roaming the open ocean.
- Date:
- September 28, 2026
- Source:
- Frontiers
- Summary:
- Yellow-morph green sea turtles in the Galápagos surprised scientists by staying remarkably close to home instead of making the long journeys typically associated with sea turtles. Satellite tracking showed that none left the marine reserve during the study, revealing just how important the islands’ coastal habitats may be to their survival.
- Share:
Sea turtles are known for extraordinary journeys across the ocean. They can navigate using cues from Earth's magnetic field, the sun, and ocean currents, traveling long distances to find food before eventually returning toward the places where they were born to reproduce.
That reputation made one population in the Galápagos especially surprising. Rather than roaming across vast stretches of ocean, these turtles appeared to spend much of their time close to home.
"Here we show that 'yellow-morph' green sea turtles - one of two genetically distinct forms - occupy individual foraging areas which span one or more islands in the Galápagos. We expected them to migrate to distant beaches in the western Pacific to reproduce, yet interestingly, none of our satellite-tagged turtles even left the Galápagos Marine Reserve over the three years of our study," said Dr. John W Rowe, a professor at Alma College in the United States and the corresponding author of a new study in Frontiers in Amphibian and Reptile Science.
Two Distinct Types of Green Sea Turtle
Green sea turtles stand apart from the other six living sea turtle species because adults are primarily vegetarian. Young turtles begin life eating both plants and animals, but as they mature, their diet shifts mainly to seagrasses and algae.
Scientists recognize two genetically distinct forms involved in this study. Yellow morph green sea turtles are generally found across tropical and subtropical parts of the western Pacific, while black morphs occur in the eastern Pacific west of the Americas and south of southern California.
The Galápagos is the only known place where both forms share the same waters. There, yellow and black morphs mingle and feed on the same types of marine vegetation.
They are not completely alike, however. Young yellow morphs tend to grow more quickly than young black morphs, suggesting that there may be physiological differences between them that scientists have not yet fully characterized.
Tracking Turtles Across the Galápagos
Rowe and his colleagues wanted to better understand where yellow morphs spend their time, how much territory they use, and whether they travel between islands within the 198,000 sq km Galápagos Marine Reserve.
In 2015, the team carefully captured nine adults in shallow water near four islands. The group included seven males and two females. Researchers gave the turtles nicknames and attached electronic transmitters that sent location signals to the low orbit Argos satellite network.
The turtles were followed for as long as 418 days. Tracking generally ended when a tag detached or stopped sending signals.
The results revealed a strong preference for shallow coastal habitat. Although the turtles occasionally traveled as far as 25km from shore, most remained much closer to the islands.
Five of the nine spent most of the study near a single island. Bernardo and Sara moved between Isabela and San Cristóbal, while Leandro traveled between Isabela and Española.
Ainoa was the most adventurous of the group. After being tagged near San Cristóbal, she later traveled to Santa Cruz and then to Isabela.
The researchers also noticed a seasonal pattern. Movement between islands occurred only during the cooler period from April through October.
On average, each turtle used a home range covering 1,498 sq km, although the size of that territory differed considerably from one animal to another.
Surprisingly Reluctant To Leave
Taken together, the tracking data suggest that yellow morph green sea turtles living around the Galápagos can be remarkably homebound.
The researchers cautioned that their observations capture only a limited period in the turtles' lives. Longer migrations could occur at other times and therefore may not have appeared during the study.
That possibility is especially important for females.
"Since female yellow-morph green sea turtles are not known to lay eggs on the beaches of the Galápagos, we believe that they will eventually leave the area to return to their natal beaches in the western Pacific. In contrast, some female black-morph green turtles do nest in the Galápagos: depending on the individual, those may be year-round residents in the archipelago, travel to other nearby oceanic islands, or even to feeding grounds off Central and South America," said coauthor Dr. Juan Pablo Muñoz Pérez, a professor at the Universidad San Francisco de Quito in Ecuador.
Protecting a Network of Turtle Habitat
The findings also carry implications for conservation. Because some turtles move among several islands, protecting only one favored feeding location may not be enough.
Researchers emphasized the importance of preserving the coastal waters and routes between islands that the turtles depend on as they move throughout the archipelago.
"Since individual turtles may rely on waters around multiple islands, the quality of habitat that is available for foraging should be maintained intact across all islands, and not allowed to degrade anywhere," said Rowe.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Frontiers. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Juan Pablo Muñoz-Pérez, Daniela Estefania Alarcón-Ruales, Lyndsey K. Tanabe, Catherine E. Hart, Maike Heidemeyer, Todd Steiner, Randall Arauz, Carlos A. Valle, John W. Rowe. Movements of yellow-morphotype green turtles (Chelonia mydas) in the Galápagos Marine Reserve. Frontiers in Amphibian and Reptile Science, 2026; 4 DOI: 10.3389/famrs.2026.1837921

Better the French You Know
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
03:10:35 UTC
12:10:35 KST

French is a global language with nearly 400 million speakers, the majority of whom live outside of France, and now there is renewed interest in the language as France and Canada have become even more attractive destinations, especially for visitors from the US looking for liberté, egalité, et fraternité.
Another phenomenon encouraging visitors to Francophone countries is the growth of “Generation F,” or Generation Francophone, the new generation of young creatives throughout the Francophone world who “bring the French language to life.”
Once you’ve made the decision to spend time in a French-speaking country, the big choice for most Americans is between France or Québec, the heart of the Francophonie in North America. This decision depends on many factors, ranging from short-term goals to long-term residency plans, so the best advice is to try them both.
French language and Francophone culture bring us together. Any regional differences are the result of our shared—yet unique—history and experience, instructive and enjoyable, rather than barriers to understanding and appreciation.
While French speakers may not need to be concerned about basic communicative language, there are differences in the French spoken around the world, just as there are with other international and global languages.
An initial difference may be in the level of formality used by European speakers of French as opposed to North Americans, with the tutoiement, or informal address, even more easily used among North American Francophones. Some learners may be surprised by the use of char for voiture or auto, or of bon matin instead of bonjour. Even the use of English terms differs between European French and French in the Americas. For example, a university in Québec may grant a maîtrise, while a European Francophone university may grant a master(s). An expression like laisser les bons temps rouler—“let the good times roll”—may not be readily understood beyond Louisiana or North America. In addition, a Francophone from Louisiana may not at first recognize the term poudrerie, used to describe dry, fine snow that may drift with the wind to make highways plowed after snow once again treacherous. Even the word francophone is used relatively less frequently in France than in many other places where French is one of two or more official or prevalent languages.
French is among the most widely used languages in many countries around the world, so communication among cultures and crossing borders—in French—are topics of interest not only to French-speaking Americans but also to Francophones around the world. Any discussion of French, as it is spoken globally, needs to include the Dictionnaire des Francophones, an online collaborative dictionary that includes contributions from around the world.
The French spoken in the US includes influences from around the world, as well as contemporary additions. French is the most widely spoken language after English in Northern New England (Maine, New Hampshire, and Vermont) and Louisiana.
In Québec, the Centre de la Francophonie des Amériques (CFA) works to encourage communication and collaboration among Francophones and Francophone communities in the Americas. In the US, the Franco-American Centre in New Hampshire (FAC), CODOFIL (the Conseil pour le Développment du Français en Louisiane), and the Nous Foundation in New Orleans are among organizations that encourage and support French language and culture in the US. In addition, Villa Albertine, the American Association of Teachers of French (AATF), and the Alliance Francaise and Federation des Alliances Françaises des USA work to promote French language and Francophone culture in the US.
Francoresponsabilité—using French whenever and as often as possible—comes to us from Québec and is being put into practice in Louisiana with the Oui Initiative. While the Francophone communities throughout the US and the rest of the Americas may not have the same history, there are many shared ideas and values. Communication among historically relatively isolated communities has been strengthened through modern media and ease of travel.
French has had a presence in what is now the US since the earliest years of the European presence. In Québec, French is the sole official language. French is also widely spoken throughout the US, most notably in New England and Louisiana. In New England, many Francophones are of French-Canadian descent, and they are now being joined by more recent arrivals from around the world. Louisiana has long been a crossroads of French and Francophone culture. In Louisiana, although many of the earliest Francophones were from Québec, the language includes many Caribbean and African influences, along with Acadian (Cajun) elements resulting primarily from Le Grand Dérangement, the expulsion of many Acadians from Canada. Contracts in French are legally accepted in Louisiana and the Code Napoléon still forms the basis of the legal system.
While some words and expressions may differ in French from region to region, this is not actually a barrier to communication but often a starting point for communication and story-telling across cultures, similar to British and American Englishes.
French offers abundant travel and educational opportunities, ranging from tourism and short-term language study to degree programs to immigration—Canadian citizenship is a possibility for many Americans with Franco-American ancestry, and residency permits for France are easier to obtain than most people realize.
Relatively few US students take advantage of the opportunities to study in France or Québec, but enrollments are on the rise…

Column: Beware of Japanese right-wing's attempt to revive militarism
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
11:07:04 CST
12:07:04 KST

by Zhou Yaxin
Ninety-five years ago, the Sept. 18th Incident shocked China and the world.
It marked the beginning of Japan's long-premeditated aggression against China. The Chinese people rose up in resistance and fought an arduous War of Resistance until securing victory 14 years later, at a staggering cost of 35 million military and civilian casualties.
While the historical wounds have yet to heal, present-day concerns are mounting by the day.
Ninety-five years on, the poisonous legacy of militarism has yet to be fully addressed. Japan's right-wing forces are still going to great lengths to downplay, if not glorify, the history of aggression.
August 15, the day of Japan's unconditional surrender, should be an occasion for it to deeply reflect and repent. This year, however, Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, in her capacity as head of the Liberal Democratic Party, made a cash offering to the notorious Yasukuni Shrine that honors 14 Class-A war criminals of World War II. According to Japanese media, she worshiped the shrine from afar, while multiple incumbent cabinet members and lawmakers visited the shrine in person. At the National Memorial Ceremony for the War Dead, Takaichi made no mention of "reflection" or "lessons," the customary language used by successive prime ministers, laying bare her stubborn refusal to reflect on history.
After the end of World War II, Japan never did any serious soul-searching about its war of aggression, nor did it fully purge the remnants of militarism. Many war criminals returned to politics and the Japan Self-Defense Forces (JSDF). These right-wing figures, inheriting the militarist ideology, have tampered with textbooks and historical records and carried out PR and whitewashing campaigns in an attempt to downplay and glorify the history of aggression and colonialism, and indoctrinate Japan's younger generation with right-wing historical narratives. They express "regret over defeat" and portray Japan as a "victim" instead of reflecting on and repenting for its war crimes. By doing so, they distort perceptions among the Japanese people and the international community, and seek public support for the right-wing government's re-militarization agenda.
The right-wing forces represented by Takaichi are also accelerating efforts to revise Japan's three key security documents and seek constitutional revision to expand military capabilities. They have lifted the ban on exports of lethal weapons and signaled an intent to revise Japan's Three Non-Nuclear Principles. They have deployed long-range missiles with "enemy base strike capabilities." Japan's defense budget has grown for 14 consecutive years, surging to over 9 trillion yen (about 57 billion U.S. dollars) in fiscal 2026, or 2 percent of the country's GDP. Instead of adhering to its "exclusively defense-oriented" policy, Japan has now ripped off the mask of a "peaceful" nation and is attempting to make itself a "war-capable" nation again.
A comparison between Japan today and Japan before World War II reveals striking similarities:
In 1882, Aritomo Yamagata coined the "line of advantage" theory, framing the Korean Peninsula and China as Japan's "lifeline" and laying the ideological groundwork for Japan's annexation of the Korean Peninsula and aggression against China. In November 2025, Takaichi associated a so-called "Taiwan contingency" with a "survival-threatening situation," thereby grossly interfering in China's internal affairs and fabricating an excuse for meddling in Taiwan-related affairs.
Before World War II, Japan invaded Asian countries and imposed colonial rule under the pretext of "Pan-Asianism" and "liberating Asia." Today, Japan justifies its military buildup and expansion in the name of pursuing "proactive pacifism" and upholding the "Indo-Pacific order."
Before World War II, Japan inculcated unwavering loyalty to the Emperor among its people through the Imperial Rescript on Education. Today, the National Defense Academy of Japan retains the "tradition" of making students walk dozens of kilometers overnight to the Yasukuni shrine to worship the war criminals enshrined there. Under the poisonous influence of militarism, a serving JSDF member went so far as to intrude into the Chinese Embassy in Japan with a knife.
Even more dangerously, whenever Japan's economy falls into a slump, it tends to pursue external expansion to divert attention. After the Meiji Restoration, Japan vigorously developed modern industry, but suffered from insufficient domestic capital, widespread bankruptcies among farmers, acute social tensions, severe fiscal pressure, and a narrow domestic market. To secure overseas sources of raw materials and markets for its goods, Japan launched the First Sino-Japanese War, from which it obtained massive reparations and access to the Chinese market. The Showa Financial Crisis of 1927 and the Great Depression of 1929 caused anxiety in Japan, eventually leading to the growth of militarist forces and the launch of external aggression.
Today, the yen has hit a 40-year low, Japan's national debt has risen to over 200 percent of its GDP, prices are soaring, and more than 1,000 companies are going bankrupt each month. The Takaichi government seeks to prop up Japan's economy by bolstering the defense industry and aggressively selling arms abroad, at the risk of reopening Pandora's box of militarism.
In disregard of the postwar international order, Japan is trying to break free from the constraints of the postwar system. It is accelerating re-militarization and posing a real threat to peace and stability in the Asia-Pacific.
History must never be forgotten. Otherwise, past mistakes will be repeated. On the 95th anniversary of the Sept. 18th Incident, we shall never forget the suffering endured by the people of China and other Asian countries that were invaded, nor the atrocities committed by Japanese militarists. All peace-loving nations and peoples should remain vigilant against the resurgence of militarism in Japan and guard against attempts by Japan's right-wing forces to create a new Sept. 18th Incident.
Editor's note: The author is an international affairs observer.
The views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the positions of Xinhua News Agency.

NASA, Boeing outline next steps for Starliner
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-29
11:06:50 CST
12:06:50 KST

LOS ANGELES, Sept. 28 (Xinhua) -- NASA said Monday it plans to conduct an uncrewed Starliner-1 mission to the International Space Station (ISS) as early as December this year or January 2027, with a crewed Starliner-2 mission targeted for 2028.
NASA also announced plans to exercise options for a fifth and sixth Starliner flight to and from the ISS, and said it will work with Boeing and United Launch Alliance to certify the Vulcan rocket for Starliner crew transportation after the final flight of the Atlas V rocket.
The uncrewed Starliner-1 will serve as an engineering evaluation mission to validate improvements made to the spacecraft, verify improved thermal environments, obtain performance data needed for system qualification and identify residual risks ahead of crewed missions, according to NASA.
The agency will use data from Starliner-1 to continue implementing corrective actions identified by its Program Investigation Team and complete the testing and certification required for crewed flight, NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said, adding that the current plan is to return astronauts to space on Starliner-2 by 2028.
Boeing's Starliner spacecraft launched in June 2024 on its first crewed flight test, carrying NASA astronauts Butch Wilmore and Suni Williams, and docked with the ISS. During the flight, some of the spacecraft's reaction control thrusters did not perform as expected, and helium leaks were detected.
NASA ultimately decided to return Starliner to Earth uncrewed, while the two astronauts later returned to Earth aboard a SpaceX Dragon spacecraft in March 2025.
In February, NASA released findings from its Program Investigation Team into the 2024 crewed flight test. The investigation identified 61 recommendations for NASA.
Based on the findings, Boeing has made thermal modifications to Starliner's service module, which NASA will evaluate on Starliner-1. NASA and Boeing also have jointly decided to implement an additional thruster valve design modification to support spacecraft certification and future crewed flights.
Following Starliner-1, NASA and Boeing will complete the service module thruster valve design modification. Boeing will also implement other improvements, including installing new crew module thrusters and batteries, as well as making minor modifications to the parachute system to improve performance and reliability, NASA said. ■

The result was based on a survey of 1,760 manufacturers and 1,403 non-manufacturers conducted between Sept. 10 and 17.
Manufacturers picked subdued domestic demand, expensive raw materials, and economic uncertainty as key barriers to doing business, while non-manufacturers selected faltering consumer demand, an uncertain economic situation, and higher labor costs.
The economic sentiment index (ESI), which reflects sentiment among both businesses and consumers, stood at 99.9 in September, up 0.5 points from a month earlier. ■
